<span id="cb105-8"><a href="#cb105-8" aria-hidden="true" tabindex="-1"></a>  app <span class="op">=</span> <span class="cf">await</span> <span class="fu">buildApp</span>({ databaseUrl<span class="op">:</span> container<span class="op">.</span><span class="fu">getConnectionUri</span>() })<span class="op">;</span></span>
<span id="cb105-9"><a href="#cb105-9" aria-hidden="true" tabindex="-1"></a>  <span class="cf">await</span> <span class="fu">runMigrations</span>(container<span class="op">.</span><span class="fu">getConnectionUri</span>())<span class="op">;</span></span>
<span id="cb105-10"><a href="#cb105-10" aria-hidden="true" tabindex="-1"></a>}<span class="op">,</span> <span class="dv">60_000</span>)<span class="op">;</span></span>
<span id="cb105-11"><a href="#cb105-11" aria-hidden="true" tabindex="-1"></a><span class="fu">afterAll</span>(() <span class="kw">=&gt;</span> container<span class="op">.</span><span class="fu">stop</span>())<span class="op">;</span></span>
<span id="cb105-12"><a href="#cb105-12" aria-hidden="true" tabindex="-1"></a><span class="fu">beforeEach</span>(() <span class="kw">=&gt;</span> <span class="fu">truncateAllTables</span>())<span class="op">;</span>                                 <span class="co">// isolation between tests</span></span>
<span id="cb105-13"><a href="#cb105-13" aria-hidden="true" tabindex="-1"></a></span>
<span id="cb105-14"><a href="#cb105-14" aria-hidden="true" tabindex="-1"></a><span class="fu">it</span>(<span class="st">&#39;user A cannot read user B’s order&#39;</span><span class="op">,</span> <span class="kw">async</span> () <span class="kw">=&gt;</span> {</span>
<span id="cb105-15"><a href="#cb105-15" aria-hidden="true" tabindex="-1"></a>  <span class="kw">const</span> order <span class="op">=</span> <span class="cf">await</span> <span class="fu">seedOrder</span>({ customerId<span class="op">:</span> <span class="st">&#39;user-b&#39;</span> })<span class="op">;</span></span>
<span id="cb105-16"><a href="#cb105-16" aria-hidden="true" tabindex="-1"></a>  <span class="cf">await</span> <span class="fu">request</span>(app)</span>
<span id="cb105-17"><a href="#cb105-17" aria-hidden="true" tabindex="-1"></a>    <span class="op">.</span><span class="fu">get</span>(<span class="vs">`/v1/orders/</span><span class="sc">${</span>order<span class="op">.</span><span class="at">id</span><span class="sc">}</span><span class="vs">`</span>)</span>
<span id="cb105-18"><a href="#cb105-18" aria-hidden="true" tabindex="-1"></a>    <span class="op">.</span><span class="fu">set</span>(<span class="st">&#39;Authorization&#39;</span><span class="op">,</span> <span class="vs">`Bearer </span><span class="sc">${</span><span class="fu">tokenFor</span>(<span class="st">&#39;user-a&#39;</span>)<span class="sc">}</span><span class="vs">`</span>)</span>
<span id="cb105-19"><a href="#cb105-19" aria-hidden="true" tabindex="-1"></a>    <span class="op">.</span><span class="fu">expect</span>(<span class="dv">404</span>)<span class="op">;</span></span>
<span id="cb105-20"><a href="#cb105-20" aria-hidden="true" tabindex="-1"></a>})<span class="op">;</span></span></code></pre></div>
<p>Why real databases rather than in-memory substitutes or mocked
drivers: query syntax, indexes, constraints, transactions and isolation
behave differently, and that’s where the bugs are. Testcontainers makes
it practical locally and in CI.</p>
<h3 id="keeping-a-suite-trustworthy">4.4 Keeping a suite
trustworthy</h3>
<ul>
<li><strong>Flaky tests</strong> are worse than missing ones: people
learn to ignore red builds. Quarantine, fix within days, or delete.
Usual causes: shared state between tests, real time and timezones (use
fake timers and fixed clocks), ordering assumptions, network calls to
real third parties, async work not awaited.</li>
<li><strong>Test data:</strong> builders/factories
(<code>aUser().withRole('admin').build()</code>) instead of large shared
fixtures.</li>
<li><strong>Coverage:</strong> a useful signal of untested code, a poor
target. 80% with meaningful assertions beats 100% that asserts nothing.
Check that critical paths (payments, auth, permissions) are covered
rather than chasing a number.</li>
<li><strong>Speed:</strong> run unit tests on every save, integration
tests in parallel in CI; keep the main pipeline under about 10 minutes
or people stop waiting for it.</li>
<li><strong>AI-generated tests:</strong> useful for breadth, but review
that they assert behaviour, not just call functions; generated tests
often mirror the implementation and pass even when it’s wrong.</li>
</ul>
<h3 id="git-merge-vs-rebase-branching-strategies">4.5 Git: merge vs
rebase, branching strategies</h3>
<table>
<colgroup>
<col style="width: 33%" />
<col style="width: 33%" />
<col style="width: 33%" />
</colgroup>
<thead>
<tr>
<th></th>
<th>Merge</th>
<th>Rebase</th>
</tr>
</thead>
<tbody>
<tr>
<td>History</td>
<td>Keeps true history with merge commits</td>
<td>Linear history, commits rewritten</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>Safety</td>
<td>Never rewrites shared history</td>
<td>Never rebase branches others have pulled</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>Typical use</td>
<td>Merging PRs into main (or squash-merge)</td>
<td>Updating your own feature branch on top of main; cleaning commits
before review (<code>rebase -i</code>)</td>
</tr>
</tbody>
</table>
<table>
<colgroup>
<col style="width: 33%" />
<col style="width: 33%" />
<col style="width: 33%" />
</colgroup>
<thead>
<tr>
<th>Strategy</th>
<th>How</th>
<th>Fits</th>
</tr>
</thead>
<tbody>
<tr>
<td><strong>Trunk-based</strong></td>
<td>Short-lived branches (hours to 2 days), merge to main daily, feature
flags hide unfinished work, main always deployable</td>
<td>Continuous delivery, strong CI, most modern product teams</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td><strong>GitHub Flow</strong></td>
<td>Branch per feature, PR, merge to main, deploy main</td>
<td>Simple web services</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td><strong>GitFlow</strong></td>
<td><code>develop</code>, <code>release/*</code>, <code>hotfix/*</code>
branches alongside <code>main</code></td>
<td>Versioned releases (mobile apps, on-prem software); heavy for
SaaS</td>
</tr>
</tbody>
</table>
<p><strong>My preference:</strong> trunk-based with small PRs (under
~400 lines changed), squash merge, conventional commits, feature flags.
Long-lived branches cause painful merges and late integration bugs.</p>
<p><strong>Commands worth knowing cold:</strong>
<code>git rebase -i main</code> (squash/fixup),
<code>git cherry-pick</code> (hotfix to a release branch),
<code>git bisect</code> (binary search for the commit that introduced a
bug), <code>git reflog</code> (recover “lost” commits),
<code>git revert</code> (undo on shared branches, instead of rewriting
history).</p>
<p><strong>Code review as a lead:</strong> review for correctness,
design, naming and tests first, style last (automate style with Prettier
and lint). Ask questions rather than issue orders, approve with minor
comments, and keep turnaround under a working day.</p>
<h3
id="ci-pipeline-github-actions-bitbucket-pipelines-is-equivalent">4.6 CI
pipeline (GitHub Actions; Bitbucket Pipelines is equivalent)</h3>
<div class="sourceCode" id="cb106"><pre
class="sourceCode yaml"><code class="sourceCode yaml"><span id="cb106-1"><a href="#cb106-1" aria-hidden="true" tabindex="-1"></a><span class="fu">name</span><span class="kw">:</span><span class="at"> ci</span></span>
<span id="cb106-2"><a href="#cb106-2" aria-hidden="true" tabindex="-1"></a><span class="fu">on</span><span class="kw">:</span></span>
<span id="cb106-3"><a href="#cb106-3" aria-hidden="true" tabindex="-1"></a><span class="at">  </span><span class="fu">pull_request</span><span class="kw">:</span></span>
<span id="cb106-4"><a href="#cb106-4" aria-hidden="true" tabindex="-1"></a><span class="at">  </span><span class="fu">push</span><span class="kw">:</span><span class="at"> </span><span class="kw">{</span><span class="at"> </span><span class="fu">branches</span><span class="kw">:</span><span class="at"> </span><span class="kw">[</span><span class="at">main</span><span class="kw">]</span><span class="at"> </span><span class="kw">}</span></span>
<span id="cb106-5"><a href="#cb106-5" aria-hidden="true" tabindex="-1"></a><span class="fu">jobs</span><span class="kw">:</span></span>
<span id="cb106-6"><a href="#cb106-6" aria-hidden="true" tabindex="-1"></a><span class="at">  </span><span class="fu">verify</span><span class="kw">:</span></span>
<span id="cb106-7"><a href="#cb106-7" aria-hidden="true" tabindex="-1"></a><span class="at">    </span><span class="fu">runs-on</span><span class="kw">:</span><span class="at"> ubuntu-latest</span></span>
<span id="cb106-8"><a href="#cb106-8" aria-hidden="true" tabindex="-1"></a><span class="at">    </span><span class="fu">steps</span><span class="kw">:</span></span>

<span id="cb106-15"><a href="#cb106-15" aria-hidden="true" tabindex="-1"></a><span class="at">      </span><span class="kw">-</span><span class="at"> </span><span class="fu">run</span><span class="kw">:</span><span class="at"> pnpm turbo run lint typecheck --affected</span><span class="co">       # only packages changed by this PR</span></span>
<span id="cb106-16"><a href="#cb106-16" aria-hidden="true" tabindex="-1"></a><span class="at">      </span><span class="kw">-</span><span class="at"> </span><span class="fu">run</span><span class="kw">:</span><span class="at"> pnpm turbo run test --affected</span></span>
<span id="cb106-17"><a href="#cb106-17" aria-hidden="true" tabindex="-1"></a><span class="at">      </span><span class="kw">-</span><span class="at"> </span><span class="fu">run</span><span class="kw">:</span><span class="at"> pnpm turbo run test:integration --affected</span><span class="co">     # Testcontainers needs Docker, available on ubuntu runners</span></span>
<span id="cb106-18"><a href="#cb106-18" aria-hidden="true" tabindex="-1"></a><span class="at">      </span><span class="kw">-</span><span class="at"> </span><span class="fu">run</span><span class="kw">:</span><span class="at"> git show origin/main:openapi.yaml &gt; base.yaml</span><span class="co">   # needs fetch-depth: 0 on checkout</span></span>
<span id="cb106-19"><a href="#cb106-19" aria-hidden="true" tabindex="-1"></a><span class="at">      </span><span class="kw">-</span><span class="at"> </span><span class="fu">run</span><span class="kw">:</span><span class="at"> docker run --rm -v &quot;$PWD:/specs&quot; tufin/oasdiff breaking /specs/base.yaml /specs/openapi.yaml --fail-on ERR</span></span>
<span id="cb106-20"><a href="#cb106-20" aria-hidden="true" tabindex="-1"></a><span class="at">      </span><span class="kw">-</span><span class="at"> </span><span class="fu">run</span><span class="kw">:</span><span class="at"> pnpm audit --audit-level=high</span></span></code></pre></div>
<p>Pipeline principles: fast feedback first (lint and types before slow
tests), only build what changed (Turborepo/Nx), lockfile installs,
branch protection requiring green CI and one approval, secrets from the
CI secret store, and build the Docker image once and promote the same
artifact through environments (Week 3).</p>
<h3 id="how-id-answer-hour-4-4">How I’d answer — Hour 4</h3>
<p><strong>Q1. What’s your testing strategy for a Node
microservice?</strong> “Unit tests with fakes for business rules;
integration tests for every endpoint against real Postgres or Mongo in
Testcontainers, covering validation, auth and permissions; contract
tests or OpenAPI validation for service boundaries; and a few end-to-end
tests for critical journeys. Coverage is a signal, not a target, and
flaky tests get fixed or removed quickly.”</p>
<p><strong>Q2. Merge or rebase?</strong> “Rebase my own branch onto main
to keep it current and clean up commits before review; never rebase
shared branches. PRs land on main with squash merge, so main reads as
one commit per change.”</p>
<p><strong>Q3. Trunk-based or GitFlow?</strong> “Trunk-based for a SaaS
product with good CI: short-lived branches, daily merges, feature flags
for unfinished work, main always deployable. GitFlow makes sense for
versioned releases like mobile apps or on-prem products where several
versions are supported at once.”</p>
<p><strong>Q4. How do you find which commit introduced a bug?</strong>
“<code>git bisect</code>: mark a known good and a known bad commit, and
Git binary-searches between them. With a test script,
<code>git bisect run</code> automates it.”</p>
<p><strong>Q5. How do you deal with flaky tests?</strong> “Treat them as
bugs. Quarantine so they don’t block everyone, fix within a few days,
and look for the usual causes: shared state, real clocks, unawaited
async work, order dependence, or calls to real external services.”</p>

<h1 id="week-2-study-notes-databases-db-design-react-angular">Week 2
Study Notes — Databases, DB design, React, Angular</h1>
<p>This week shifts from runtime to data and frontends: the areas where
design decisions are hardest to undo.</p>
<h1 id="day-6-mon-mongodb-deep-dive">Day 6 (Mon) — MongoDB deep
dive</h1>
<h2 id="hour-1-mongodb-data-modeling">Hour 1 — MongoDB data
modeling</h2>
<p>Most MongoDB performance problems are modeling problems in disguise:
relational schemas ported one table per collection, arrays that grow
without limit, or <code>$lookup</code>s on every request. The core rule:
<strong>model for how the data is read and written, not for how it looks
in an ER diagram.</strong> Interviewers test whether you can apply that
rule and defend embedding decisions.</p>
<h3 id="the-basics-that-shape-every-decision">1.1 The basics that shape
every decision</h3>
<ul>
<li>A <strong>document</strong> is a BSON object (JSON plus types like
<code>ObjectId</code>, <code>Date</code>, <code>Decimal128</code>,
binary). Maximum size: <strong>16 MB</strong>.</li>
<li>Writes to a <strong>single document are atomic</strong>, including
nested fields and arrays. Anything that must change together atomically
is a strong candidate to live in one document.</li>
<li>There are no joins at query time except <code>$lookup</code> in
aggregations, which is far more expensive than a SQL join on indexed
keys.</li>
<li>Schemas are flexible but not optional: the shape still exists in
your code. Enforce it with validation (1.5).</li>
</ul>
<h3 id="embed-vs-reference">1.2 Embed vs reference</h3>
<table>
<colgroup>
<col style="width: 50%" />
<col style="width: 50%" />
</colgroup>
<thead>
<tr>
<th>Embed when</th>
<th>Reference when</th>
</tr>
</thead>
<tbody>
<tr>
<td>Data is read together almost every time</td>
<td>Data is often read on its own</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>Relationship is one-to-few (a handful to low hundreds)</td>
<td>One-to-many with large or unbounded “many”</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>Child has no meaning without the parent</td>
<td>Child is shared by many parents (many-to-many)</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>Child is updated with the parent</td>
<td>Child changes often and independently</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>You need atomic updates across parent and child</td>
<td>Embedding would risk the 16 MB limit or huge documents</td>
</tr>
</tbody>
</table>
<p>Worked example, e-commerce:</p>
<div class="sourceCode" id="cb107"><pre
class="sourceCode js"><code class="sourceCode javascript"><span id="cb107-1"><a href="#cb107-1" aria-hidden="true" tabindex="-1"></a><span class="co">// orders: embed line items and a SNAPSHOT of what was bought</span></span>
<span id="cb107-2"><a href="#cb107-2" aria-hidden="true" tabindex="-1"></a>{</span>
<span id="cb107-3"><a href="#cb107-3" aria-hidden="true" tabindex="-1"></a>  <span class="dt">_id</span><span class="op">:</span> <span class="fu">ObjectId</span>(<span class="st">&#39;...&#39;</span>)<span class="op">,</span></span>
<span id="cb107-4"><a href="#cb107-4" aria-hidden="true" tabindex="-1"></a>  <span class="dt">customerId</span><span class="op">:</span> <span class="fu">ObjectId</span>(<span class="st">&#39;...&#39;</span>)<span class="op">,</span>           <span class="co">// reference: customers are their own entity</span></span>
<span id="cb107-5"><a href="#cb107-5" aria-hidden="true" tabindex="-1"></a>  <span class="dt">status</span><span class="op">:</span> <span class="st">&#39;paid&#39;</span><span class="op">,</span></span>
<span id="cb107-6"><a href="#cb107-6" aria-hidden="true" tabindex="-1"></a>  <span class="dt">items</span><span class="op">:</span> [                               <span class="co">// embed: bounded, read with the order, never shared</span></span>
<span id="cb107-7"><a href="#cb107-7" aria-hidden="true" tabindex="-1"></a>    { <span class="dt">productId</span><span class="op">:</span> <span class="fu">ObjectId</span>(<span class="st">&#39;...&#39;</span>)<span class="op">,</span> <span class="dt">name</span><span class="op">:</span> <span class="st">&#39;Running shoe&#39;</span><span class="op">,</span> <span class="dt">priceAtPurchase</span><span class="op">:</span> <span class="dv">499900</span><span class="op">,</span> <span class="dt">qty</span><span class="op">:</span> <span class="dv">1</span> }<span class="op">,</span></span>
<span id="cb107-8"><a href="#cb107-8" aria-hidden="true" tabindex="-1"></a>  ]<span class="op">,</span></span>
<span id="cb107-9"><a href="#cb107-9" aria-hidden="true" tabindex="-1"></a>  <span class="dt">shippingAddress</span><span class="op">:</span> { <span class="dt">line1</span><span class="op">:</span> <span class="st">&#39;...&#39;</span><span class="op">,</span> <span class="dt">city</span><span class="op">:</span> <span class="st">&#39;Pune&#39;</span><span class="op">,</span> <span class="dt">pin</span><span class="op">:</span> <span class="st">&#39;411001&#39;</span> }<span class="op">,</span> <span class="co">// embed: copy at order time</span></span>
<span id="cb107-10"><a href="#cb107-10" aria-hidden="true" tabindex="-1"></a>  <span class="dt">total</span><span class="op">:</span> { <span class="dt">amount</span><span class="op">:</span> <span class="dv">499900</span><span class="op">,</span> <span class="dt">currency</span><span class="op">:</span> <span class="st">&#39;INR&#39;</span> }<span class="op">,</span></span>
<span id="cb107-11"><a href="#cb107-11" aria-hidden="true" tabindex="-1"></a>  <span class="dt">createdAt</span><span class="op">:</span> <span class="fu">ISODate</span>(<span class="st">&#39;2026-11-20T10:00:00Z&#39;</span>)<span class="op">,</span></span>
<span id="cb107-12"><a href="#cb107-12" aria-hidden="true" tabindex="-1"></a>}</span>
<span id="cb107-13"><a href="#cb107-13" aria-hidden="true" tabindex="-1"></a></span>
<span id="cb107-14"><a href="#cb107-14" aria-hidden="true" tabindex="-1"></a><span class="co">// reviews: separate collection, referenced by productId (unbounded, read separately, paginated)</span></span>
<span id="cb107-15"><a href="#cb107-15" aria-hidden="true" tabindex="-1"></a>{ <span class="dt">_id</span><span class="op">:</span> <span class="fu">ObjectId</span>(<span class="st">&#39;...&#39;</span>)<span class="op">,</span> <span class="dt">productId</span><span class="op">:</span> <span class="fu">ObjectId</span>(<span class="st">&#39;...&#39;</span>)<span class="op">,</span> <span class="dt">userId</span><span class="op">:</span> <span class="fu">ObjectId</span>(<span class="st">&#39;...&#39;</span>)<span class="op">,</span> <span class="dt">rating</span><span class="op">:</span> <span class="dv">5</span><span class="op">,</span> <span class="dt">text</span><span class="op">:</span> <span class="st">&#39;...&#39;</span> }</span></code></pre></div>
<p>The order stores the product name and price <strong>as they were at
purchase</strong>. That’s not denormalisation for speed; it’s
correctness: an invoice must not change when the catalogue price
changes.</p>
<p><strong>The anti-pattern to name:</strong> unbounded arrays. Pushing
every review, log entry or follower into one document grows it toward 16
MB; well before that, every update rewrites a large document and index
entries on that array multiply. If an array can grow without a natural
limit, it belongs in its own collection.</p>
<h3 id="schema-design-patterns">1.3 Schema design patterns</h3>
<table>
<colgroup>
<col style="width: 33%" />
<col style="width: 33%" />
<col style="width: 33%" />
</colgroup>
<thead>
<tr>
<th>Pattern</th>
<th>Problem it solves</th>
<th>Example</th>
</tr>
</thead>
<tbody>
<tr>
<td><strong>Extended reference</strong></td>
<td>Avoid <code>$lookup</code> for a few fields read every time</td>
<td>Order stores <code>customer: { _id, name, email }</code> copied from
the customer</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td><strong>Subset</strong></td>
<td>Large related data, only a slice shown usually</td>
<td>Product embeds its 10 latest reviews; the rest live in
<code>reviews</code></td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td><strong>Computed</strong></td>
<td>Expensive aggregates recomputed on every read</td>
<td>Product stores <code>ratingAvg</code>, <code>ratingCount</code>,
updated on each new review</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td><strong>Bucket</strong></td>
<td>Huge numbers of small time-series records</td>
<td>One document per sensor per hour holding an array of readings (or
use native time-series collections)</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td><strong>Outlier</strong></td>
<td>A few items break the normal shape (a celebrity with 10M
followers)</td>
<td>Normal docs embed; outliers set <code>hasOverflow: true</code> and
spill into extra docs</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td><strong>Attribute</strong></td>
<td>Many optional, varied fields to search on</td>
<td><code>attrs: [{ k: 'color', v: 'red' }, { k: 'size', v: 'M' }]</code>
with one index on <code>attrs.k, attrs.v</code></td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td><strong>Polymorphic</strong></td>
<td>Different shapes in one collection</td>
<td><code>payments</code> with
<code>type: 'card' \| 'upi' \| 'wallet'</code> and type-specific
fields</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td><strong>Schema versioning</strong></td>
<td>Migrating shapes gradually</td>
<td><code>schemaVersion: 2</code>; code handles both, background job
upgrades old docs</td>
</tr>
</tbody>
</table>
<p>The trade-off with every duplication pattern (extended reference,
subset, computed): reads get cheaper, writes get more complicated and
data can drift. Ask: how stale can the copy be? Customer name on an old
order: never needs updating. Product rating average: update with
<code>$inc</code> in the same operation that inserts the review, or
eventually via an event.</p>
<h3 id="relationship-cheat-sheet">1.4 Relationship cheat sheet</h3>
<table>
<colgroup>
<col style="width: 50%" />
<col style="width: 50%" />
</colgroup>
<thead>
<tr>
<th>Relationship</th>
<th>Default modeling</th>
</tr>
</thead>
<tbody>
<tr>
<td>One-to-one</td>
<td>Embed (user + profile) unless the part is large and rarely read</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>One-to-few</td>
<td>Embed array (user + addresses)</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>One-to-many (hundreds to thousands)</td>
<td>Array of references in the parent, or parent reference in
children</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>One-to-squillions (unbounded)</td>
<td>Parent reference in each child (log entries have
<code>serviceId</code>)</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>Many-to-many</td>
<td>Arrays of references on one or both sides (students ↔︎ courses), or a
link collection when the link has its own data (enrolments with grade,
date)</td>
</tr>
</tbody>
</table>
<h3 id="validation-and-mongoose">1.5 Validation and Mongoose</h3>
<p>Server-side validation guards against any client, script or service
writing bad data:</p>
<div class="sourceCode" id="cb108"><pre
class="sourceCode js"><code class="sourceCode javascript"><span id="cb108-1"><a href="#cb108-1" aria-hidden="true" tabindex="-1"></a>db<span class="op">.</span><span class="fu">createCollection</span>(<span class="st">&#39;orders&#39;</span><span class="op">,</span> {</span>
<span id="cb108-2"><a href="#cb108-2" aria-hidden="true" tabindex="-1"></a>  <span class="dt">validator</span><span class="op">:</span> {</span>
<span id="cb108-3"><a href="#cb108-3" aria-hidden="true" tabindex="-1"></a>    <span class="dt">$jsonSchema</span><span class="op">:</span> {</span>
<span id="cb108-4"><a href="#cb108-4" aria-hidden="true" tabindex="-1"></a>      <span class="dt">bsonType</span><span class="op">:</span> <span class="st">&#39;object&#39;</span><span class="op">,</span></span>
<span id="cb108-5"><a href="#cb108-5" aria-hidden="true" tabindex="-1"></a>      <span class="dt">required</span><span class="op">:</span> [<span class="st">&#39;customerId&#39;</span><span class="op">,</span> <span class="st">&#39;status&#39;</span><span class="op">,</span> <span class="st">&#39;items&#39;</span><span class="op">,</span> <span class="st">&#39;total&#39;</span><span class="op">,</span> <span class="st">&#39;createdAt&#39;</span>]<span class="op">,</span></span>
<span id="cb108-6"><a href="#cb108-6" aria-hidden="true" tabindex="-1"></a>      <span class="dt">properties</span><span class="op">:</span> {</span>
<span id="cb108-7"><a href="#cb108-7" aria-hidden="true" tabindex="-1"></a>        <span class="dt">status</span><span class="op">:</span> { <span class="dt">enum</span><span class="op">:</span> [<span class="st">&#39;pending_payment&#39;</span><span class="op">,</span> <span class="st">&#39;paid&#39;</span><span class="op">,</span> <span class="st">&#39;shipped&#39;</span><span class="op">,</span> <span class="st">&#39;cancelled&#39;</span>] }<span class="op">,</span></span>
<span id="cb108-8"><a href="#cb108-8" aria-hidden="true" tabindex="-1"></a>        <span class="dt">items</span><span class="op">:</span> { <span class="dt">bsonType</span><span class="op">:</span> <span class="st">&#39;array&#39;</span><span class="op">,</span> <span class="dt">minItems</span><span class="op">:</span> <span class="dv">1</span><span class="op">,</span> <span class="dt">maxItems</span><span class="op">:</span> <span class="dv">200</span> }<span class="op">,</span></span>
<span id="cb108-9"><a href="#cb108-9" aria-hidden="true" tabindex="-1"></a>        <span class="dt">total</span><span class="op">:</span> { <span class="dt">bsonType</span><span class="op">:</span> <span class="st">&#39;object&#39;</span><span class="op">,</span> <span class="dt">required</span><span class="op">:</span> [<span class="st">&#39;amount&#39;</span><span class="op">,</span> <span class="st">&#39;currency&#39;</span>] }<span class="op">,</span></span>
<span id="cb108-10"><a href="#cb108-10" aria-hidden="true" tabindex="-1"></a>      }<span class="op">,</span></span>
<span id="cb108-11"><a href="#cb108-11" aria-hidden="true" tabindex="-1"></a>    }<span class="op">,</span></span>
<span id="cb108-12"><a href="#cb108-12" aria-hidden="true" tabindex="-1"></a>  }<span class="op">,</span></span>
<span id="cb108-13"><a href="#cb108-13" aria-hidden="true" tabindex="-1"></a>  <span class="dt">validationAction</span><span class="op">:</span> <span class="st">&#39;error&#39;</span><span class="op">,</span></span>
<span id="cb108-14"><a href="#cb108-14" aria-hidden="true" tabindex="-1"></a>})<span class="op">;</span></span></code></pre></div>
<p><strong>Mongoose vs the native driver:</strong> Mongoose gives
schemas, validation, middleware (hooks), population and a familiar model
API; the cost is overhead per document (hydrating model instances),
hidden queries (<code>populate</code> is an extra query per path, not a
join) and a layer between you and the database. My usage: Mongoose with
<code>.lean()</code> for read paths (returns plain objects, much faster)
and explicit projections; the native driver for bulk jobs and
performance-critical paths. Always keep shared Zod schemas at the API
boundary regardless.</p>
<p><strong>Money:</strong> store integer minor units
(<code>499900</code> paise) or <code>Decimal128</code>. Never JavaScript
floating-point numbers for currency.</p>
<h3 id="how-id-answer-hour-1-5">How I’d answer — Hour 1</h3>
<p><strong>Q1. Embed or reference? How do you decide?</strong> “By
access pattern. Embed when data is read together, the relationship is
bounded, the child has no life of its own, and I want atomic updates;
for example, line items in an order. Reference when the many side is
large or unbounded, data is shared or read independently, or embedding
risks growing documents; for example, reviews for a product. Often both:
reference plus a small embedded copy of the fields I read every
time.”</p>
<p><strong>Q2. Why store the product price inside the order instead of
referencing the product?</strong> “Because the order must reflect what
the customer actually paid. It’s a historical snapshot, not a cache. If
I referenced the product, a price change would rewrite history on
invoices.”</p>
<p><strong>Q3. What’s wrong with storing all comments of a post in an
array?</strong> “Unbounded growth. The document grows toward the 16 MB
limit, every update rewrites and re-indexes a large array, and reading
the post always drags all comments along. I’d keep comments in their own
collection, indexed by post and date, and optionally embed the latest
few with the subset pattern.”</p>
<p><strong>Q4. MongoDB is schemaless, so how do you control data
quality?</strong> “It’s schema-flexible, not schemaless. I validate at
the API with Zod, define Mongoose schemas or <code>$jsonSchema</code>
validators on the collections, and version document shapes so migrations
can run gradually.”</p>
<h3 id="practice-15">Practice</h3>
<ul class="task-list">
<li><label><input type="checkbox" />Model the capstone’s products,
reviews, carts and orders; for each relationship write one line
justifying embed vs reference</label></li>
<li><label><input type="checkbox" />Implement the computed pattern:
inserting a review updates <code>ratingAvg</code> and
<code>ratingCount</code> on the product</label></li>
<li><label><input type="checkbox" />Add a <code>$jsonSchema</code>
validator to <code>orders</code> and prove an invalid insert is
rejected</label></li>
</ul>
<h2 id="hour-2-indexes-and-query-performance">Hour 2 — Indexes and query
performance</h2>
<p>The single most common production MongoDB issue is a missing or wrong
index that’s invisible at 10,000 documents and fatal at 10 million.
Interviewers give you a query and ask for the index. Get fluent with the
ESR rule and reading <code>explain()</code>, and you’ll answer most of
these in under a minute.</p>
<h3 id="what-an-index-is">2.1 What an index is</h3>
<p><strong>What it is:</strong> a sorted B-tree of field values pointing
to documents. Without one, MongoDB scans every document (COLLSCAN). With
one, it walks a small part of the tree (IXSCAN) and fetches only
matching documents.</p>
<p>The cost side, which seniors always mention: every index slows writes
(each insert/update maintains it), uses RAM and disk, and the most-used
indexes plus hot documents (the <strong>working set</strong>) should fit
in memory. Ten indexes on a write-heavy collection is a smell.</p>
<h3 id="index-types">2.2 Index types</h3>
<table>
<colgroup>
<col style="width: 33%" />
<col style="width: 33%" />
<col style="width: 33%" />
</colgroup>
<thead>
<tr>
<th>Type</th>
<th>Example</th>
<th>Use</th>
</tr>
</thead>
<tbody>
<tr>
<td>Single field</td>
<td><code>{ email: 1 }</code></td>
<td>Lookups by one field; <code>unique: true</code> for natural
keys</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>Compound</td>
<td><code>{ customerId: 1, createdAt: -1 }</code></td>
<td>Filters + sort on several fields; field order matters</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>Multikey</td>
<td>Index on an array field <code>{ tags: 1 }</code></td>
<td>Automatic for arrays; a compound index can include at most one array
field</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>Text</td>
<td><code>{ name: 'text', description: 'text' }</code></td>
<td>Basic keyword search; one per collection. Atlas Search (Lucene) for
real search</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>Hashed</td>
<td><code>{ userId: 'hashed' }</code></td>
<td>Even distribution for sharding; equality only, no ranges</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>TTL</td>
<td><code>{ expiresAt: 1 }, { expireAfterSeconds: 0 }</code></td>
<td>Auto-delete sessions, OTPs, idempotency keys (a background task
removes them roughly every 60 s)</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>Partial</td>
<td><code>{ email: 1 }, { partialFilterExpression: { deletedAt: null } }</code></td>
<td>Index only relevant docs; unique email among active users only</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>Sparse</td>
<td><code>{ referralCode: 1 }, { sparse: true }</code></td>
<td>Skip docs missing the field (partial is the more flexible
replacement)</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>Wildcard</td>
<td><code>{ 'attrs.$**': 1 }</code></td>
<td>Unpredictable field names; useful but broad</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>Geospatial</td>
<td><code>{ location: '2dsphere' }</code></td>
<td>“Stores near me”</td>
</tr>
</tbody>
</table>
<h3 id="the-esr-rule-for-compound-indexes">2.3 The ESR rule for compound
indexes</h3>
<p>Order fields in a compound index as <strong>E</strong>quality, then
<strong>S</strong>ort, then <strong>R</strong>ange.</p>
<p>Query: a customer’s paid orders above ₹1,000, newest first.</p>
<div class="sourceCode" id="cb109"><pre
class="sourceCode js"><code class="sourceCode javascript"><span id="cb109-1"><a href="#cb109-1" aria-hidden="true" tabindex="-1"></a>db<span class="op">.</span><span class="at">orders</span><span class="op">.</span><span class="fu">find</span>({ <span class="dt">customerId</span><span class="op">:</span> id<span class="op">,</span> <span class="dt">status</span><span class="op">:</span> <span class="st">&#39;paid&#39;</span><span class="op">,</span> <span class="st">&#39;total.amount&#39;</span><span class="op">:</span> { <span class="dt">$gte</span><span class="op">:</span> <span class="dv">100000</span> } })</span>
<span id="cb109-2"><a href="#cb109-2" aria-hidden="true" tabindex="-1"></a>         <span class="op">.</span><span class="fu">sort</span>({ <span class="dt">createdAt</span><span class="op">:</span> <span class="op">-</span><span class="dv">1</span> })<span class="op">.</span><span class="fu">limit</span>(<span class="dv">20</span>)<span class="op">;</span></span>
<span id="cb109-3"><a href="#cb109-3" aria-hidden="true" tabindex="-1"></a></span>
<span id="cb109-4"><a href="#cb109-4" aria-hidden="true" tabindex="-1"></a><span class="co">// Index following ESR:</span></span>
<span id="cb109-5"><a href="#cb109-5" aria-hidden="true" tabindex="-1"></a>db<span class="op">.</span><span class="at">orders</span><span class="op">.</span><span class="fu">createIndex</span>({ <span class="dt">customerId</span><span class="op">:</span> <span class="dv">1</span><span class="op">,</span> <span class="dt">status</span><span class="op">:</span> <span class="dv">1</span><span class="op">,</span> <span class="dt">createdAt</span><span class="op">:</span> <span class="op">-</span><span class="dv">1</span><span class="op">,</span> <span class="st">&#39;total.amount&#39;</span><span class="op">:</span> <span class="dv">1</span> })<span class="op">;</span></span>
<span id="cb109-6"><a href="#cb109-6" aria-hidden="true" tabindex="-1"></a><span class="co">//                      E               E           S                R</span></span></code></pre></div>
<p>Why: equality fields narrow to one contiguous section of the index;
within it, entries are already in <code>createdAt</code> order, so no
in-memory sort is needed and <code>limit(20)</code> stops after 20
entries; the range condition is checked on index keys without breaking
the sort. Put the range before the sort
(<code>{ customerId, status, total.amount, createdAt }</code>) and
MongoDB must collect every matching document and sort them in memory,
which is a <code>SORT</code> stage in the plan and a common cause of
slow queries and memory errors.</p>
<p><strong>Prefix rule:</strong> an index on
<code>{ a: 1, b: 1, c: 1 }</code> also serves queries on <code>a</code>
and on <code>a, b</code>, but not on <code>b</code> alone or
<code>c</code> alone. So <code>{ customerId: 1, createdAt: -1 }</code>
makes a separate <code>{ customerId: 1 }</code> index redundant.</p>
<p><strong>Sort direction:</strong> for a single-field sort direction
doesn’t matter; for multi-field sorts, the index must match the
directions or their exact inverse (<code>{ a: 1, b: -1 }</code> supports
sorts <code>a:1,b:-1</code> and <code>a:-1,b:1</code>).</p>
<h3 id="reading-explain">2.4 Reading <code>explain()</code></h3>
<div class="sourceCode" id="cb110"><pre
class="sourceCode js"><code class="sourceCode javascript"><span id="cb110-1"><a href="#cb110-1" aria-hidden="true" tabindex="-1"></a>db<span class="op">.</span><span class="at">orders</span><span class="op">.</span><span class="fu">find</span>({ <span class="dt">customerId</span><span class="op">:</span> id<span class="op">,</span> <span class="dt">status</span><span class="op">:</span> <span class="st">&#39;paid&#39;</span> })<span class="op">.</span><span class="fu">sort</span>({ <span class="dt">createdAt</span><span class="op">:</span> <span class="op">-</span><span class="dv">1</span> })<span class="op">.</span><span class="fu">limit</span>(<span class="dv">20</span>)</span>
<span id="cb110-2"><a href="#cb110-2" aria-hidden="true" tabindex="-1"></a>  <span class="op">.</span><span class="fu">explain</span>(<span class="st">&#39;executionStats&#39;</span>)<span class="op">;</span></span></code></pre></div>
<p>What to look at:</p>
<table>
<colgroup>
<col style="width: 33%" />
<col style="width: 33%" />
<col style="width: 33%" />
</colgroup>
<thead>
<tr>
<th>Field</th>
<th>Healthy</th>
<th>Problem</th>
</tr>
</thead>
<tbody>
<tr>
<td><code>winningPlan.stage</code> tree</td>
<td><code>IXSCAN</code> → <code>FETCH</code> → <code>LIMIT</code></td>
<td><code>COLLSCAN</code>; a <code>SORT</code> stage (in-memory
sort)</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td><code>nReturned</code></td>
<td>20</td>
<td>—</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td><code>totalKeysExamined</code></td>
<td>Close to <code>nReturned</code></td>
<td>Many times larger: index not selective or wrong order</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td><code>totalDocsExamined</code></td>
<td>Close to <code>nReturned</code> (0 for covered queries)</td>
<td>Thousands of docs examined to return 20</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td><code>executionTimeMillis</code></td>
<td>Low single digits</td>
<td>Hundreds</td>
</tr>
</tbody>
</table>
<p>The ratio <strong>docs examined : docs returned</strong> is the
number I check first. Close to 1:1 is ideal.</p>
<p><strong>Covered query:</strong> when the index contains every field
in the filter and the projection (and <code>_id</code> is excluded),
MongoDB answers from the index alone: <code>totalDocsExamined: 0</code>.
Useful for hot, narrow queries like “does this email exist”.</p>
<h3 id="query-patterns-that-defeat-indexes">2.5 Query patterns that
defeat indexes</h3>
<ul>
<li><code>$regex: /shoe/i</code> (unanchored or case-insensitive) scans
the whole index or collection. Anchored <code>^shoe</code> with matching
case can use the index; for case-insensitive lookups, use a collation
index or store a lowercased copy; for real search use Atlas Search.</li>
<li><code>$ne</code>, <code>$nin</code> and <code>$not</code> are poorly
selective.</li>
<li><code>$or</code> needs an index for <strong>each</strong> branch,
otherwise it falls back to a scan.</li>
<li>Large <code>skip()</code> values: the server still walks every
skipped entry; use cursor pagination (Day 5).</li>
<li>Queries on a field that’s sometimes a string and sometimes a number:
types sort separately, results surprise you.</li>
<li>Sorting on a field not in the index: in-memory sort, limited to 100
MB per stage before it must spill to disk or fail.</li>
</ul>
<h3 id="finding-slow-queries-in-production">2.6 Finding slow queries in
production</h3>
<ul>
<li><strong>Slow query log / profiler:</strong> queries over
<code>slowms</code> (100 ms by default) are logged;
<code>db.setProfilingLevel(1, { slowms: 50 })</code> captures them in
<code>system.profile</code>.</li>
<li><strong><code>$indexStats</code></strong> shows how often each index
is used; unused indexes are pure write cost, drop them (after hiding
them first with <code>hideIndex</code> to check nothing breaks).</li>
<li><strong>Atlas Performance Advisor</strong> suggests indexes from
real slow queries; treat suggestions as hints and check ESR
yourself.</li>
<li>Build indexes on large production collections carefully: modern
versions build without blocking reads and writes for long, but builds
still consume I/O; do it off-peak and on a rolling basis across replica
set members for very large collections.</li>
</ul>
<h3 id="how-id-answer-hour-2-5">How I’d answer — Hour 2</h3>
<p><strong>Q1. Design an index for: a customer’s orders by status,
newest first, paginated.</strong>
“<code>{ customerId: 1, status: 1, createdAt: -1 }</code>. Equality
fields first, then the sort field, so the index returns documents
already ordered and the limit stops early. If I add a range filter, it
goes after the sort field. I’d confirm with explain that it’s IXSCAN
with no SORT stage and that docs examined is close to docs
returned.”</p>
<p><strong>Q2. What’s the ESR rule and why does it work?</strong>
“Equality, Sort, Range. Equality narrows to one contiguous block of
index entries, which is already sorted on the next field, so no
in-memory sort is needed. A range in the middle would split that block
into many sections, each sorted separately, forcing an in-memory
sort.”</p>
<p><strong>Q3. A query got slow as data grew. How do you
investigate?</strong> “Find it in the slow query log or profiler, run
explain with executionStats, and look for COLLSCAN, a SORT stage, or
docs examined far above docs returned. Then fix the index following ESR,
or the query: anchoring regexes, replacing skip with cursor pagination,
adding projections. Then confirm with explain and check
<code>$indexStats</code> to drop indexes nobody uses.”</p>
<p><strong>Q4. Why not just index every field?</strong> “Each index
slows every write, consumes RAM that should hold the working set, and
many single-field indexes don’t help compound queries anyway. I index
for the actual query patterns and remove unused ones.”</p>

<code>{ createdAt: -1, customerId: 1 }</code> and with the ESR index;
compare <code>explain</code> output</label></li>
<li><label><input type="checkbox" />Create a TTL index for idempotency
keys and a partial unique index on email for active users</label></li>
<li><label><input type="checkbox" />Write a covered query for “does this
email exist” and confirm <code>totalDocsExamined: 0</code></label></li>
</ul>
<h2 id="hour-3-the-aggregation-pipeline">Hour 3 — The aggregation
pipeline</h2>
<p>The aggregation pipeline is where MongoDB does reporting, analytics
and joins. In interviews you’ll be asked to write one on the spot (“top
5 products by revenue last month”) and then asked how it performs on 50
million orders. Practise writing them from memory; the syntax is
unforgiving under pressure.</p>
<h3 id="how-it-works">3.1 How it works</h3>
<p><strong>What it is:</strong> a sequence of stages; each takes a
stream of documents and passes a transformed stream to the next, like a
Unix pipe.</p>
<table>
<colgroup>
<col style="width: 33%" />
<col style="width: 33%" />
<col style="width: 33%" />
</colgroup>
<thead>
<tr>
<th>Stage</th>
<th>Does</th>
<th>SQL equivalent</th>
</tr>
</thead>
<tbody>
<tr>
<td><code>$match</code></td>
<td>Filter</td>
<td><code>WHERE</code></td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td><code>$project</code> / <code>$set</code> / <code>$unset</code></td>
<td>Reshape, compute, drop fields</td>
<td><code>SELECT</code> expressions</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td><code>$group</code></td>
<td>Group and accumulate (<code>$sum</code>, <code>$avg</code>,
<code>$min</code>, <code>$max</code>, <code>$push</code>,
<code>$addToSet</code>, <code>$first</code>)</td>
<td><code>GROUP BY</code></td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td><code>$sort</code> / <code>$limit</code> / <code>$skip</code></td>
<td>Order and page</td>
<td><code>ORDER BY</code> / <code>LIMIT</code> /
<code>OFFSET</code></td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td><code>$unwind</code></td>
<td>One document per array element</td>
<td>Joining to a child table</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td><code>$lookup</code></td>
<td>Left outer join to another collection</td>
<td><code>LEFT JOIN</code></td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td><code>$facet</code></td>
<td>Several sub-pipelines over the same input</td>
<td>Several queries at once</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td><code>$bucket</code> / <code>$bucketAuto</code></td>
<td>Group into ranges</td>
<td><code>CASE</code> + <code>GROUP BY</code></td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td><code>$setWindowFields</code></td>
<td>Running totals, moving averages, ranks</td>
<td>Window functions</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td><code>$merge</code> / <code>$out</code></td>
<td>Write results to a collection</td>
<td><code>INSERT INTO ... SELECT</code> / materialised view</td>
</tr>
</tbody>
</table>
<h3 id="real-reports">3.2 Real reports</h3>
<p><strong>Daily revenue for the last 30 days (IST):</strong></p>
<div class="sourceCode" id="cb111"><pre
class="sourceCode js"><code class="sourceCode javascript"><span id="cb111-1"><a href="#cb111-1" aria-hidden="true" tabindex="-1"></a>db<span class="op">.</span><span class="at">orders</span><span class="op">.</span><span class="fu">aggregate</span>([</span>
<span id="cb111-2"><a href="#cb111-2" aria-hidden="true" tabindex="-1"></a>  { <span class="dt">$match</span><span class="op">:</span> { <span class="dt">status</span><span class="op">:</span> <span class="st">&#39;paid&#39;</span><span class="op">,</span> <span class="dt">createdAt</span><span class="op">:</span> { <span class="dt">$gte</span><span class="op">:</span> thirtyDaysAgo } } }<span class="op">,</span>   <span class="co">// first: uses index</span></span>
<span id="cb111-3"><a href="#cb111-3" aria-hidden="true" tabindex="-1"></a>  { <span class="dt">$group</span><span class="op">:</span> {</span>
<span id="cb111-4"><a href="#cb111-4" aria-hidden="true" tabindex="-1"></a>      <span class="dt">_id</span><span class="op">:</span> { <span class="dt">$dateTrunc</span><span class="op">:</span> { <span class="dt">date</span><span class="op">:</span> <span class="st">&#39;$createdAt&#39;</span><span class="op">,</span> <span class="dt">unit</span><span class="op">:</span> <span class="st">&#39;day&#39;</span><span class="op">,</span> <span class="dt">timezone</span><span class="op">:</span> <span class="st">&#39;Asia/Kolkata&#39;</span> } }<span class="op">,</span></span>
<span id="cb111-5"><a href="#cb111-5" aria-hidden="true" tabindex="-1"></a>      <span class="dt">revenue</span><span class="op">:</span> { <span class="dt">$sum</span><span class="op">:</span> <span class="st">&#39;$total.amount&#39;</span> }<span class="op">,</span></span>
<span id="cb111-6"><a href="#cb111-6" aria-hidden="true" tabindex="-1"></a>      <span class="dt">orders</span><span class="op">:</span> { <span class="dt">$sum</span><span class="op">:</span> <span class="dv">1</span> }<span class="op">,</span></span>
<span id="cb111-7"><a href="#cb111-7" aria-hidden="true" tabindex="-1"></a>  } }<span class="op">,</span></span>
<span id="cb111-8"><a href="#cb111-8" aria-hidden="true" tabindex="-1"></a>  { <span class="dt">$sort</span><span class="op">:</span> { <span class="dt">_id</span><span class="op">:</span> <span class="dv">1</span> } }<span class="op">,</span></span>
<span id="cb111-9"><a href="#cb111-9" aria-hidden="true" tabindex="-1"></a>  { <span class="dt">$project</span><span class="op">:</span> { <span class="dt">_id</span><span class="op">:</span> <span class="dv">0</span><span class="op">,</span> <span class="dt">day</span><span class="op">:</span> <span class="st">&#39;$_id&#39;</span><span class="op">,</span> <span class="dt">revenue</span><span class="op">:</span> <span class="dv">1</span><span class="op">,</span> <span class="dt">orders</span><span class="op">:</span> <span class="dv">1</span><span class="op">,</span> <span class="dt">aov</span><span class="op">:</span> { <span class="dt">$round</span><span class="op">:</span> [{ <span class="dt">$divide</span><span class="op">:</span> [<span class="st">&#39;$revenue&#39;</span><span class="op">,</span> <span class="st">&#39;$orders&#39;</span>] }<span class="op">,</span> <span class="dv">0</span>] } } }<span class="op">,</span></span>
<span id="cb111-10"><a href="#cb111-10" aria-hidden="true" tabindex="-1"></a>])<span class="op">;</span></span></code></pre></div>
<p>The timezone detail matters: without it, days are UTC, and an order
at 2 a.m. IST counts toward the previous day in reports.</p>
<p><strong>Top 5 products by revenue last month, with
names:</strong></p>
<div class="sourceCode" id="cb112"><pre
class="sourceCode js"><code class="sourceCode javascript"><span id="cb112-1"><a href="#cb112-1" aria-hidden="true" tabindex="-1"></a>db<span class="op">.</span><span class="at">orders</span><span class="op">.</span><span class="fu">aggregate</span>([</span>
<span id="cb112-2"><a href="#cb112-2" aria-hidden="true" tabindex="-1"></a>  { <span class="dt">$match</span><span class="op">:</span> { <span class="dt">status</span><span class="op">:</span> <span class="st">&#39;paid&#39;</span><span class="op">,</span> <span class="dt">createdAt</span><span class="op">:</span> { <span class="dt">$gte</span><span class="op">:</span> monthStart<span class="op">,</span> <span class="dt">$lt</span><span class="op">:</span> monthEnd } } }<span class="op">,</span></span>

<span id="cb112-6"><a href="#cb112-6" aria-hidden="true" tabindex="-1"></a>      <span class="dt">revenue</span><span class="op">:</span> { <span class="dt">$sum</span><span class="op">:</span> { <span class="dt">$multiply</span><span class="op">:</span> [<span class="st">&#39;$items.priceAtPurchase&#39;</span><span class="op">,</span> <span class="st">&#39;$items.qty&#39;</span>] } }<span class="op">,</span></span>
<span id="cb112-7"><a href="#cb112-7" aria-hidden="true" tabindex="-1"></a>      <span class="dt">unitsSold</span><span class="op">:</span> { <span class="dt">$sum</span><span class="op">:</span> <span class="st">&#39;$items.qty&#39;</span> }<span class="op">,</span></span>
<span id="cb112-8"><a href="#cb112-8" aria-hidden="true" tabindex="-1"></a>  } }<span class="op">,</span></span>
<span id="cb112-9"><a href="#cb112-9" aria-hidden="true" tabindex="-1"></a>  { <span class="dt">$sort</span><span class="op">:</span> { <span class="dt">revenue</span><span class="op">:</span> <span class="op">-</span><span class="dv">1</span> } }<span class="op">,</span></span>
<span id="cb112-10"><a href="#cb112-10" aria-hidden="true" tabindex="-1"></a>  { <span class="dt">$limit</span><span class="op">:</span> <span class="dv">5</span> }<span class="op">,</span></span>
<span id="cb112-11"><a href="#cb112-11" aria-hidden="true" tabindex="-1"></a>  { <span class="dt">$lookup</span><span class="op">:</span> { <span class="dt">from</span><span class="op">:</span> <span class="st">&#39;products&#39;</span><span class="op">,</span> <span class="dt">localField</span><span class="op">:</span> <span class="st">&#39;_id&#39;</span><span class="op">,</span> <span class="dt">foreignField</span><span class="op">:</span> <span class="st">&#39;_id&#39;</span><span class="op">,</span> <span class="dt">as</span><span class="op">:</span> <span class="st">&#39;product&#39;</span><span class="op">,</span></span>
<span id="cb112-12"><a href="#cb112-12" aria-hidden="true" tabindex="-1"></a>               <span class="dt">pipeline</span><span class="op">:</span> [{ <span class="dt">$project</span><span class="op">:</span> { <span class="dt">name</span><span class="op">:</span> <span class="dv">1</span><span class="op">,</span> <span class="dt">category</span><span class="op">:</span> <span class="dv">1</span> } }] } }<span class="op">,</span>   <span class="co">// only 5 lookups, after limit</span></span>
<span id="cb112-13"><a href="#cb112-13" aria-hidden="true" tabindex="-1"></a>  { <span class="dt">$unwind</span><span class="op">:</span> <span class="st">&#39;$product&#39;</span> }<span class="op">,</span></span>
<span id="cb112-14"><a href="#cb112-14" aria-hidden="true" tabindex="-1"></a>])<span class="op">;</span></span></code></pre></div>
<p>Note the order: <code>$lookup</code> <strong>after</strong>
<code>$sort</code> and <code>$limit</code>, so it joins 5 documents
instead of every product sold.</p>
<p><strong>Paginated list plus total count in one round
trip:</strong></p>
<div class="sourceCode" id="cb113"><pre
class="sourceCode js"><code class="sourceCode javascript"><span id="cb113-1"><a href="#cb113-1" aria-hidden="true" tabindex="-1"></a>db<span class="op">.</span><span class="at">products</span><span class="op">.</span><span class="fu">aggregate</span>([</span>
<span id="cb113-2"><a href="#cb113-2" aria-hidden="true" tabindex="-1"></a>  { <span class="dt">$match</span><span class="op">:</span> { <span class="dt">category</span><span class="op">:</span> <span class="st">&#39;shoes&#39;</span><span class="op">,</span> <span class="dt">active</span><span class="op">:</span> <span class="kw">true</span> } }<span class="op">,</span></span>
<span id="cb113-3"><a href="#cb113-3" aria-hidden="true" tabindex="-1"></a>  { <span class="dt">$facet</span><span class="op">:</span> {</span>
<span id="cb113-4"><a href="#cb113-4" aria-hidden="true" tabindex="-1"></a>      <span class="dt">items</span><span class="op">:</span> [{ <span class="dt">$sort</span><span class="op">:</span> { <span class="dt">createdAt</span><span class="op">:</span> <span class="op">-</span><span class="dv">1</span> } }<span class="op">,</span> { <span class="dt">$skip</span><span class="op">:</span> <span class="dv">40</span> }<span class="op">,</span> { <span class="dt">$limit</span><span class="op">:</span> <span class="dv">20</span> }]<span class="op">,</span></span>
<span id="cb113-5"><a href="#cb113-5" aria-hidden="true" tabindex="-1"></a>      <span class="dt">total</span><span class="op">:</span> [{ <span class="dt">$count</span><span class="op">:</span> <span class="st">&#39;count&#39;</span> }]<span class="op">,</span></span>
<span id="cb113-6"><a href="#cb113-6" aria-hidden="true" tabindex="-1"></a>      <span class="dt">byBrand</span><span class="op">:</span> [{ <span class="dt">$group</span><span class="op">:</span> { <span class="dt">_id</span><span class="op">:</span> <span class="st">&#39;$brand&#39;</span><span class="op">,</span> <span class="dt">n</span><span class="op">:</span> { <span class="dt">$sum</span><span class="op">:</span> <span class="dv">1</span> } } }]<span class="op">,</span>   <span class="co">// filter counts for the UI</span></span>
<span id="cb113-7"><a href="#cb113-7" aria-hidden="true" tabindex="-1"></a>  } }<span class="op">,</span></span>
<span id="cb113-8"><a href="#cb113-8" aria-hidden="true" tabindex="-1"></a>])<span class="op">;</span></span></code></pre></div>
<p>Convenient, but each facet processes every matched document. On large
result sets, an exact total is expensive; consider an estimated count or
“has more” instead.</p>
<p><strong>7-day moving average with window functions:</strong></p>
<div class="sourceCode" id="cb114"><pre
class="sourceCode js"><code class="sourceCode javascript"><span id="cb114-1"><a href="#cb114-1" aria-hidden="true" tabindex="-1"></a>{ <span class="dt">$setWindowFields</span><span class="op">:</span> {</span>
<span id="cb114-2"><a href="#cb114-2" aria-hidden="true" tabindex="-1"></a>    <span class="dt">sortBy</span><span class="op">:</span> { <span class="dt">day</span><span class="op">:</span> <span class="dv">1</span> }<span class="op">,</span></span>
<span id="cb114-3"><a href="#cb114-3" aria-hidden="true" tabindex="-1"></a>    <span class="dt">output</span><span class="op">:</span> { <span class="dt">revenue7d</span><span class="op">:</span> { <span class="dt">$avg</span><span class="op">:</span> <span class="st">&#39;$revenue&#39;</span><span class="op">,</span> <span class="dt">window</span><span class="op">:</span> { <span class="dt">documents</span><span class="op">:</span> [<span class="op">-</span><span class="dv">6</span><span class="op">,</span> <span class="dv">0</span>] } } }<span class="op">,</span></span>
<span id="cb114-4"><a href="#cb114-4" aria-hidden="true" tabindex="-1"></a>} }</span></code></pre></div>
<h3 id="performance">3.3 Performance</h3>
<ul>
<li><strong><code>$match</code> and <code>$sort</code> early</strong>,
ideally first, so they can use indexes. Only stages at the start of the
pipeline use indexes; after <code>$group</code> or <code>$unwind</code>,
everything is in memory.</li>
<li><strong>Project only what you need</strong> before heavy stages to
shrink documents (the optimiser does some of this, but be explicit with
<code>$lookup</code> sub-pipelines).</li>
<li><strong><code>$lookup</code></strong> needs an index on
<code>foreignField</code>; without one, it scans the foreign collection
per input document. Avoid <code>$lookup</code> in hot request paths; if
you need it on every read, the model probably wants an extended
reference (Hour 1).</li>
<li><strong><code>$unwind</code> multiplies documents.</strong> On
orders with 10 items, 1 million orders become 10 million documents.
Filter first.</li>
<li><strong>Memory:</strong> each stage is limited to 100 MB of RAM;
beyond that it must spill to disk (<code>allowDiskUse</code>, on by
default in recent versions), which is slow. Seeing heavy spilling is a
sign the pipeline needs restructuring or pre-aggregation.</li>
<li><strong>Don’t run heavy analytics on the primary.</strong> Use
<code>readPreference: 'secondary'</code> or dedicated analytics nodes,
or pre-aggregate.</li>
<li><strong>Pre-aggregation:</strong> for dashboards, compute daily
rollups on a schedule (or incrementally) with <code>$merge</code> into a
<code>daily_sales</code> collection, and query that. Reading 30 rollup
documents beats aggregating 5 million orders on every page load.</li>
</ul>
<div class="sourceCode" id="cb115"><pre
class="sourceCode js"><code class="sourceCode javascript"><span id="cb115-1"><a href="#cb115-1" aria-hidden="true" tabindex="-1"></a><span class="co">// Nightly (or hourly) rollup into a materialised view</span></span>
<span id="cb115-2"><a href="#cb115-2" aria-hidden="true" tabindex="-1"></a>{ <span class="dt">$merge</span><span class="op">:</span> { <span class="dt">into</span><span class="op">:</span> <span class="st">&#39;daily_sales&#39;</span><span class="op">,</span> <span class="dt">on</span><span class="op">:</span> <span class="st">&#39;_id&#39;</span><span class="op">,</span> <span class="dt">whenMatched</span><span class="op">:</span> <span class="st">&#39;replace&#39;</span><span class="op">,</span> <span class="dt">whenNotMatched</span><span class="op">:</span> <span class="st">&#39;insert&#39;</span> } }</span></code></pre></div>
<h3 id="how-id-answer-hour-3-5">How I’d answer — Hour 3</h3>
<p><strong>Q1. Write a pipeline for the top 5 products by revenue last
month.</strong> Write the pipeline from 3.2, then add: “Match first on
status and date so it uses the <code>{ status, createdAt }</code> index,
unwind items, group by product, sort and limit, and only then look up
product names for those five.”</p>
<p><strong>Q2. The sales dashboard aggregation takes 12 seconds. What do
you do?</strong> “Check explain on the pipeline: is the first
<code>$match</code> using an index, is <code>$unwind</code> exploding
documents, is a <code>$lookup</code> scanning without an index? Fix
those first. If it’s still heavy because it aggregates millions of
orders each time, pre-aggregate into a daily rollup collection with
<code>$merge</code>, updated on a schedule or from change streams, and
run it against a secondary so it doesn’t compete with checkout
traffic.”</p>
<p><strong>Q3. How does <code>$lookup</code> compare to a SQL
join?</strong> “It’s a left outer join, but it’s per document and much
less optimised than a relational join planner. With an index on the
foreign field it’s fine for small result sets, like enriching the top 20
rows. Needing it on every hot read is a modeling smell; I’d embed the
few fields I need instead.”</p>
<p><strong>Q4. Why does stage order matter?</strong> “Only the leading
stages can use indexes, and every stage processes what the previous one
emits. Filtering and limiting early shrinks the work for everything
after it; joining or unwinding early multiplies it.”</p>

<ul class="task-list">

(IST), top 5 products, revenue per category per month, repeat-customer
rate</label></li>
<li><label><input type="checkbox" />Run the top-products pipeline with
<code>$lookup</code> before vs after <code>$limit</code>; compare
timings with explain</label></li>
<li><label><input type="checkbox" />Build a <code>daily_sales</code>

</ul>
<h2 id="hour-4-replication-consistency-transactions-sharding">Hour 4 —
Replication, consistency, transactions, sharding</h2>
<p>This is the system-design end of MongoDB. The classic question is
“pick a shard key for orders”, but the ones that separate seniors are
about consistency: why a user doesn’t see the order they just placed,
what happens to writes during a failover, and when a transaction is the
right tool.</p>
<h3 id="replica-sets">4.1 Replica sets</h3>
<p><strong>What it is:</strong> a group of <code>mongod</code> nodes
holding the same data. One <strong>primary</strong> takes all writes;
<strong>secondaries</strong> replicate them asynchronously by replaying
the primary’s <strong>oplog</strong> (an ordered log of operations).</p>
<ul>
<li>If the primary fails, the remaining voting members elect a new one,
typically within about 10–15 seconds. Drivers retry writes that failed
during the switch (retryable writes, on by default).</li>
<li>Use an <strong>odd number of voting members</strong> (3 or 5) so a
majority can always be formed; spread them across availability
zones.</li>
<li>Replicas are for high availability and read scaling of
stale-tolerant reads, not a backup. Deleting a collection replicates
instantly; you still need point-in-time backups.</li>
</ul>
<h3 id="write-concern-read-concern-read-preference">4.2 Write concern,
read concern, read preference</h3>
<table>
<colgroup>
<col style="width: 33%" />
<col style="width: 33%" />
<col style="width: 33%" />
</colgroup>
<thead>
<tr>
<th>Setting</th>
<th>Options</th>
<th>What it controls</th>
</tr>
</thead>
<tbody>
<tr>
<td>Write concern</td>
<td><code>w: 1</code>, <code>w: 'majority'</code> (default in modern
versions), <code>j: true</code></td>
<td>How many nodes must acknowledge a write before it’s reported
successful</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>Read concern</td>
<td><code>local</code>, <code>majority</code>, <code>snapshot</code>,
<code>linearizable</code></td>
<td>Whether you may read data that could still be rolled back</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>Read preference</td>
<td><code>primary</code> (default), <code>primaryPreferred</code>,
<code>secondary</code>, <code>secondaryPreferred</code>,
<code>nearest</code></td>
<td>Which node serves the read</td>
</tr>
</tbody>
</table>
<p><strong>Why <code>w: 'majority'</code> matters:</strong> with
<code>w: 1</code>, a write acknowledged only by the primary can be
<strong>rolled back</strong> if that primary fails before secondaries
copy it. For orders and payments: majority write concern, always.</p>
<p><strong>The read-your-own-writes trap:</strong> reading from
secondaries can return data that’s seconds behind (replication lag). A
user places an order, the next page reads from a secondary, and the
order is “missing”. Fixes: read from the primary for anything the user
just changed; or use <strong>causally consistent sessions</strong>,
which make a later read wait until the node has caught up to the
session’s last write. Send to secondaries only reads that tolerate
staleness: analytics, reports, recommendations.</p>
<h3 id="transactions">4.3 Transactions</h3>
<p><strong>What they are:</strong> multi-document ACID transactions
across collections (replica sets and sharded clusters).</p>
<div class="sourceCode" id="cb116"><pre
class="sourceCode js"><code class="sourceCode javascript"><span id="cb116-1"><a href="#cb116-1" aria-hidden="true" tabindex="-1"></a><span class="kw">const</span> session <span class="op">=</span> client<span class="op">.</span><span class="fu">startSession</span>()<span class="op">;</span></span>
<span id="cb116-2"><a href="#cb116-2" aria-hidden="true" tabindex="-1"></a><span class="cf">try</span> {</span>
<span id="cb116-3"><a href="#cb116-3" aria-hidden="true" tabindex="-1"></a>  <span class="cf">await</span> session<span class="op">.</span><span class="fu">withTransaction</span>(<span class="kw">async</span> () <span class="kw">=&gt;</span> {          <span class="co">// retries TransientTransactionError for you</span></span>
<span id="cb116-4"><a href="#cb116-4" aria-hidden="true" tabindex="-1"></a>    <span class="kw">const</span> res <span class="op">=</span> <span class="cf">await</span> inventory<span class="op">.</span><span class="fu">updateOne</span>(</span>
<span id="cb116-5"><a href="#cb116-5" aria-hidden="true" tabindex="-1"></a>      { sku<span class="op">,</span> <span class="dt">available</span><span class="op">:</span> { <span class="dt">$gte</span><span class="op">:</span> qty } }<span class="op">,</span></span>
<span id="cb116-6"><a href="#cb116-6" aria-hidden="true" tabindex="-1"></a>      { <span class="dt">$inc</span><span class="op">:</span> { <span class="dt">available</span><span class="op">:</span> <span class="op">-</span>qty<span class="op">,</span> <span class="dt">reserved</span><span class="op">:</span> qty } }<span class="op">,</span></span>
<span id="cb116-7"><a href="#cb116-7" aria-hidden="true" tabindex="-1"></a>      { session }<span class="op">,</span></span>
<span id="cb116-8"><a href="#cb116-8" aria-hidden="true" tabindex="-1"></a>    )<span class="op">;</span></span>
<span id="cb116-9"><a href="#cb116-9" aria-hidden="true" tabindex="-1"></a>    <span class="cf">if</span> (res<span class="op">.</span><span class="at">modifiedCount</span> <span class="op">===</span> <span class="dv">0</span>) <span class="cf">throw</span> <span class="kw">new</span> <span class="fu">OutOfStockError</span>(sku)<span class="op">;</span></span>
<span id="cb116-10"><a href="#cb116-10" aria-hidden="true" tabindex="-1"></a>    <span class="cf">await</span> orders<span class="op">.</span><span class="fu">insertOne</span>(order<span class="op">,</span> { session })<span class="op">;</span></span>
<span id="cb116-11"><a href="#cb116-11" aria-hidden="true" tabindex="-1"></a>  }<span class="op">,</span> { <span class="dt">readConcern</span><span class="op">:</span> { <span class="dt">level</span><span class="op">:</span> <span class="st">&#39;snapshot&#39;</span> }<span class="op">,</span> <span class="dt">writeConcern</span><span class="op">:</span> { <span class="dt">w</span><span class="op">:</span> <span class="st">&#39;majority&#39;</span> } })<span class="op">;</span></span>
<span id="cb116-12"><a href="#cb116-12" aria-hidden="true" tabindex="-1"></a>} <span class="cf">finally</span> {</span>
<span id="cb116-13"><a href="#cb116-13" aria-hidden="true" tabindex="-1"></a>  <span class="cf">await</span> session<span class="op">.</span><span class="fu">endSession</span>()<span class="op">;</span></span>
<span id="cb116-14"><a href="#cb116-14" aria-hidden="true" tabindex="-1"></a>}</span></code></pre></div>
<p>Costs and limits to mention: transactions hold locks and memory,
conflicting transactions abort and retry, there’s a default lifetime
limit of 60 seconds, and they’re slower than single-document writes,
especially across shards. <strong>My rule:</strong> model so most
invariants fit inside one document (atomic by default); use transactions
for genuine multi-document invariants like reserving stock and creating
an order; never hold one open across a network call to another service.
Across services, use sagas instead (Week 3).</p>
<p>Also note the pattern inside:
<code>updateOne({ sku, available: { $gte: qty } }, { $inc: ... })</code>
is an <strong>atomic conditional update</strong>. Even without a
transaction, it prevents overselling because the check and the decrement
happen in one operation.</p>
<h3 id="change-streams">4.4 Change streams</h3>
<p><strong>What they are:</strong> a real-time feed of inserts, updates
and deletes, built on the oplog (replica set required).</p>
<div class="sourceCode" id="cb117"><pre
class="sourceCode js"><code class="sourceCode javascript"><span id="cb117-1"><a href="#cb117-1" aria-hidden="true" tabindex="-1"></a><span class="kw">const</span> stream <span class="op">=</span> db<span class="op">.</span><span class="fu">collection</span>(<span class="st">&#39;orders&#39;</span>)<span class="op">.</span><span class="fu">watch</span>(</span>
<span id="cb117-2"><a href="#cb117-2" aria-hidden="true" tabindex="-1"></a>  [{ <span class="dt">$match</span><span class="op">:</span> { <span class="dt">operationType</span><span class="op">:</span> { <span class="dt">$in</span><span class="op">:</span> [<span class="st">&#39;insert&#39;</span><span class="op">,</span> <span class="st">&#39;update&#39;</span>] } } }]<span class="op">,</span></span>
<span id="cb117-3"><a href="#cb117-3" aria-hidden="true" tabindex="-1"></a>  { <span class="dt">fullDocument</span><span class="op">:</span> <span class="st">&#39;updateLookup&#39;</span><span class="op">,</span> <span class="dt">resumeAfter</span><span class="op">:</span> lastSavedToken }<span class="op">,</span></span>
<span id="cb117-4"><a href="#cb117-4" aria-hidden="true" tabindex="-1"></a>)<span class="op">;</span></span>
<span id="cb117-5"><a href="#cb117-5" aria-hidden="true" tabindex="-1"></a><span class="cf">for</span> <span class="cf">await</span> (<span class="kw">const</span> change <span class="kw">of</span> stream) {</span>
<span id="cb117-6"><a href="#cb117-6" aria-hidden="true" tabindex="-1"></a>  <span class="cf">await</span> <span class="fu">publishToKafka</span>(<span class="st">&#39;orders&#39;</span><span class="op">,</span> change<span class="op">.</span><span class="at">fullDocument</span>)<span class="op">;</span></span>
<span id="cb117-7"><a href="#cb117-7" aria-hidden="true" tabindex="-1"></a>  <span class="cf">await</span> <span class="fu">saveResumeToken</span>(change<span class="op">.</span><span class="at">_id</span>)<span class="op">;</span>    <span class="co">// resume after restarts without missing events</span></span>
<span id="cb117-8"><a href="#cb117-8" aria-hidden="true" tabindex="-1"></a>}</span></code></pre></div>
<p>Uses: syncing to a search index, cache invalidation, feeding
analytics, and implementing the <strong>transactional outbox</strong>
(Week 3) so database writes and published events never disagree.</p>
<h3 id="sharding">4.5 Sharding</h3>
<p><strong>What it is:</strong> horizontal partitioning of one
collection across several replica sets (shards). Clients connect to
<code>mongos</code> routers, which use metadata from config servers to
send each query to the right shard(s).</p>
<p><strong>When:</strong> only after vertical scaling, indexes,
archiving old data and read offloading are not enough, typically when
the working set no longer fits in one machine’s RAM or write throughput
exceeds one primary. Sharding adds real operational complexity.</p>
<p><strong>Choosing a shard key</strong> (the decision that’s hardest to
undo):</p>
<table>
<colgroup>
<col style="width: 50%" />
<col style="width: 50%" />
</colgroup>
<thead>
<tr>
<th>Property</th>
<th>Why</th>
</tr>
</thead>
<tbody>
<tr>
<td>High cardinality</td>
<td>Many distinct values, so data can split into many chunks</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>Low frequency</td>
<td>No single value holds a huge share of documents (no hot key)</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>Non-monotonic</td>
<td><code>createdAt</code> or ObjectId alone send every new insert to
the same shard (hotspot)</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>Matches the main queries</td>
<td>Queries that include the shard key go to one shard
(<strong>targeted</strong>); queries without it go to every shard
(<strong>scatter-gather</strong>)</td>
</tr>
</tbody>
</table>
<table>
<colgroup>
<col style="width: 33%" />
<col style="width: 33%" />
<col style="width: 33%" />
</colgroup>
<thead>
<tr>
<th>Strategy</th>
<th>Good</th>
<th>Bad</th>
</tr>
</thead>
<tbody>
<tr>
<td>Hashed <code>{ customerId: 'hashed' }</code></td>
<td>Even write distribution</td>
<td>Range queries on the key become scatter-gather</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>Ranged <code>{ customerId: 1, createdAt: 1 }</code></td>
<td>Targeted queries for one customer’s orders in date order</td>
<td>Risk of hot ranges if values are skewed</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>Zones</td>
<td>Pin ranges to specific shards</td>
<td>Used for data residency (e.g. Indian customers’ data stays in an
Indian region)</td>
</tr>
</tbody>
</table>
<p>For an orders collection: <code>{ customerId: 1, _id: 1 }</code> or
hashed <code>customerId</code>. Not <code>createdAt</code> (monotonic
hotspot), not <code>status</code> (5 values, terrible cardinality).
Admin queries across all customers will be scatter-gather; route those
to analytics nodes or a separate store. Modern MongoDB can refine or
reshard a key, but resharding a large collection is still heavy, so
choose carefully.</p>
<h3 id="how-id-answer-hour-4-5">How I’d answer — Hour 4</h3>
<p><strong>Q1. Pick a shard key for an e-commerce orders
collection.</strong> “I’d start from the main queries: customers viewing
their own orders, and order lookups by ID. So the shard key is
<code>customerId</code>, either hashed for even writes, or compound
<code>{ customerId: 1, _id: 1 }</code> so one customer’s orders are
targeted to one shard. I’d avoid <code>createdAt</code> because it’s
monotonic and creates a write hotspot, and <code>status</code> because
it has a handful of values. Cross-customer reporting would be
scatter-gather, so it goes to analytics nodes or pre-aggregated
collections.”</p>
<p><strong>Q2. A user places an order and doesn’t see it on the next
page. Why?</strong> “Most likely reads go to secondaries and hit
replication lag. Reads after a user’s own write should go to the
primary, or use causally consistent sessions. Secondaries are for reads
that tolerate staleness.”</p>
<p><strong>Q3. When do you use MongoDB transactions?</strong> “When an
invariant genuinely spans documents, like reserving stock and creating
the order. First I try to model it so one document holds the invariant,
since single-document writes are atomic and cheaper. Transactions stay
short, use majority write concern, and never span calls to other
services; across services I use sagas with an outbox.”</p>
<p><strong>Q4. How do you prevent overselling stock?</strong> “An atomic
conditional update:
<code>updateOne({ sku, available: { $gte: qty } }, { $inc: { available: -qty } })</code>.
If it modifies zero documents, there wasn’t enough stock. No race
window, because the check and decrement are one operation. For a flash
sale with extreme contention, I’d add a Redis-based reservation layer in
front.”</p>
<p><strong>Q5. What’s the difference between <code>w: 1</code> and
<code>w: majority</code>?</strong> “<code>w: 1</code> returns once the
primary has the write; if the primary dies before replicating, the write
can be rolled back even though the client was told it succeeded.
Majority waits until most voting members have it, so it survives
failover. Anything financial uses majority.”</p>
<h3 id="end-of-day-6-checklist">End of Day 6 checklist</h3>
<ul class="task-list">
<li><label><input type="checkbox" />Capstone product catalogue in
MongoDB: products, reviews (computed rating), carts; documented
embed/reference decisions</label></li>
<li><label><input type="checkbox" />ESR indexes for the main queries,
verified with <code>explain('executionStats')</code></label></li>
<li><label><input type="checkbox" />Five aggregation reports written
from memory, plus a <code>$merge</code> daily rollup</label></li>
<li><label><input type="checkbox" />Stock reservation with an atomic
conditional update and an order insert in one transaction</label></li>
<li><label><input type="checkbox" />Change stream publishing product
updates, with resume tokens persisted</label></li>
