rehearsed out loud in under 2 minutes</label></li>
</ul>
<h1 id="day-7-tue-postgresql-mysql">Day 7 (Tue) — PostgreSQL /
MySQL</h1>
<h2 id="hour-1-relational-modeling">Hour 1 — Relational modeling</h2>
<p>Coming from years of MongoDB, the shift is this: in a relational
database, the schema is your strongest line of defence. Constraints
enforce rules no matter which service, script or intern writes the data.
Interviewers check whether you use them, or treat Postgres as a document
store with joins.</p>
<h3 id="keys-and-constraints">1.1 Keys and constraints</h3>
<table>
<colgroup>
<col style="width: 33%" />
<col style="width: 33%" />
<col style="width: 33%" />
</colgroup>
<thead>
<tr>
<th>Constraint</th>
<th>Guarantees</th>
<th>Example</th>
</tr>
</thead>
<tbody>
<tr>
<td><code>PRIMARY KEY</code></td>
<td>Unique, not null, one per table</td>
<td><code>id BIGINT GENERATED ALWAYS AS IDENTITY</code> or
<code>UUID</code></td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td><code>FOREIGN KEY</code></td>
<td>The referenced row exists</td>
<td><code>order_id REFERENCES orders(id) ON DELETE CASCADE</code></td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td><code>UNIQUE</code></td>
<td>No duplicates (also creates an index)</td>
<td><code>UNIQUE (email)</code>,
<code>UNIQUE (order_id, product_id)</code></td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td><code>NOT NULL</code></td>
<td>Value always present</td>
<td>Default for anything that is not truly optional</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td><code>CHECK</code></td>
<td>Row-level rule</td>
<td><code>CHECK (quantity &gt; 0)</code>,
<code>CHECK (status IN ('pending','paid'))</code></td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td><code>EXCLUDE</code> (Postgres)</td>
<td>No overlapping ranges</td>
<td>No double-booked rooms for overlapping time ranges</td>
</tr>
</tbody>
</table>
<div class="sourceCode" id="cb118"><pre
class="sourceCode sql"><code class="sourceCode sql"><span id="cb118-1"><a href="#cb118-1" aria-hidden="true" tabindex="-1"></a><span class="kw">CREATE</span> <span class="kw">TABLE</span> orders (</span>
<span id="cb118-2"><a href="#cb118-2" aria-hidden="true" tabindex="-1"></a>  <span class="kw">id</span>            BIGINT <span class="kw">GENERATED</span> ALWAYS <span class="kw">AS</span> IDENTITY <span class="kw">PRIMARY</span> <span class="kw">KEY</span>,</span>
<span id="cb118-3"><a href="#cb118-3" aria-hidden="true" tabindex="-1"></a>  public_id     UUID <span class="kw">NOT</span> <span class="kw">NULL</span> <span class="kw">DEFAULT</span> gen_random_uuid() <span class="kw">UNIQUE</span>,  <span class="co">-- exposed in APIs</span></span>
<span id="cb118-4"><a href="#cb118-4" aria-hidden="true" tabindex="-1"></a>  customer_id   BIGINT <span class="kw">NOT</span> <span class="kw">NULL</span> <span class="kw">REFERENCES</span> customers(<span class="kw">id</span>),</span>
<span id="cb118-5"><a href="#cb118-5" aria-hidden="true" tabindex="-1"></a>  status        TEXT <span class="kw">NOT</span> <span class="kw">NULL</span> <span class="kw">CHECK</span> (status <span class="kw">IN</span> (<span class="st">&#39;pending_payment&#39;</span>,<span class="st">&#39;paid&#39;</span>,<span class="st">&#39;shipped&#39;</span>,<span class="st">&#39;cancelled&#39;</span>)),</span>
<span id="cb118-6"><a href="#cb118-6" aria-hidden="true" tabindex="-1"></a>  total_paise   BIGINT <span class="kw">NOT</span> <span class="kw">NULL</span> <span class="kw">CHECK</span> (total_paise <span class="op">&gt;=</span> <span class="dv">0</span>),</span>
<span id="cb118-7"><a href="#cb118-7" aria-hidden="true" tabindex="-1"></a>  currency      <span class="dt">CHAR</span>(<span class="dv">3</span>) <span class="kw">NOT</span> <span class="kw">NULL</span> <span class="kw">DEFAULT</span> <span class="st">&#39;INR&#39;</span>,</span>
<span id="cb118-8"><a href="#cb118-8" aria-hidden="true" tabindex="-1"></a>  created_at    TIMESTAMPTZ <span class="kw">NOT</span> <span class="kw">NULL</span> <span class="kw">DEFAULT</span> now(),</span>
<span id="cb118-9"><a href="#cb118-9" aria-hidden="true" tabindex="-1"></a>  updated_at    TIMESTAMPTZ <span class="kw">NOT</span> <span class="kw">NULL</span> <span class="kw">DEFAULT</span> now(),</span>
<span id="cb118-10"><a href="#cb118-10" aria-hidden="true" tabindex="-1"></a>  version       <span class="dt">INT</span> <span class="kw">NOT</span> <span class="kw">NULL</span> <span class="kw">DEFAULT</span> <span class="dv">1</span>                            <span class="co">-- optimistic locking (Day 5)</span></span>
<span id="cb118-11"><a href="#cb118-11" aria-hidden="true" tabindex="-1"></a>);</span>
<span id="cb118-12"><a href="#cb118-12" aria-hidden="true" tabindex="-1"></a></span>
<span id="cb118-13"><a href="#cb118-13" aria-hidden="true" tabindex="-1"></a><span class="kw">CREATE</span> <span class="kw">TABLE</span> order_items (</span>
<span id="cb118-14"><a href="#cb118-14" aria-hidden="true" tabindex="-1"></a>  order_id      BIGINT <span class="kw">NOT</span> <span class="kw">NULL</span> <span class="kw">REFERENCES</span> orders(<span class="kw">id</span>) <span class="kw">ON</span> <span class="kw">DELETE</span> <span class="kw">CASCADE</span>,</span>
<span id="cb118-15"><a href="#cb118-15" aria-hidden="true" tabindex="-1"></a>  product_id    BIGINT <span class="kw">NOT</span> <span class="kw">NULL</span> <span class="kw">REFERENCES</span> products(<span class="kw">id</span>),</span>
<span id="cb118-16"><a href="#cb118-16" aria-hidden="true" tabindex="-1"></a>  unit_price_paise BIGINT <span class="kw">NOT</span> <span class="kw">NULL</span> <span class="kw">CHECK</span> (unit_price_paise <span class="op">&gt;=</span> <span class="dv">0</span>),</span>
<span id="cb118-17"><a href="#cb118-17" aria-hidden="true" tabindex="-1"></a>  quantity      <span class="dt">INT</span> <span class="kw">NOT</span> <span class="kw">NULL</span> <span class="kw">CHECK</span> (quantity <span class="kw">BETWEEN</span> <span class="dv">1</span> <span class="kw">AND</span> <span class="dv">100</span>),</span>
<span id="cb118-18"><a href="#cb118-18" aria-hidden="true" tabindex="-1"></a>  <span class="kw">PRIMARY</span> <span class="kw">KEY</span> (order_id, product_id)</span>
<span id="cb118-19"><a href="#cb118-19" aria-hidden="true" tabindex="-1"></a>);</span>
<span id="cb118-20"><a href="#cb118-20" aria-hidden="true" tabindex="-1"></a><span class="kw">CREATE</span> <span class="kw">INDEX</span> <span class="kw">ON</span> orders (customer_id, created_at <span class="kw">DESC</span>);   <span class="co">-- FKs are NOT indexed automatically in Postgres</span></span></code></pre></div>
<p>Two details people miss: <strong>Postgres does not index foreign key
columns automatically</strong> (deleting a customer then scans
<code>orders</code>); and an internal <code>BIGINT</code> key plus an
external UUID gives compact joins and indexes while not exposing
sequential IDs.</p>
<p><strong>Primary key choice:</strong> <code>BIGINT</code> identity is
compact and fast; random UUID v4 scatters inserts across the index (page
splits, worse cache locality); time-ordered <strong>UUID v7 /
ULID</strong> gives global uniqueness with insert locality. Good default
for distributed systems: UUID v7, which PostgreSQL 18 (September 2025)
generates natively with <code>uuidv7()</code>.</p>
<h3 id="normalization">1.2 Normalization</h3>
<p><strong>What it is:</strong> organising tables so each fact is stored
once, which prevents update, insert and delete anomalies.</p>
<table>
<colgroup>
<col style="width: 33%" />
<col style="width: 33%" />
<col style="width: 33%" />
</colgroup>
<thead>
<tr>
<th>Normal form</th>
<th>Rule</th>
<th>Violation example</th>
</tr>
</thead>
<tbody>
<tr>
<td>1NF</td>
<td>Atomic values, no repeating groups</td>
<td><code>phone_numbers = '98..., 97...'</code> in one column</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>2NF</td>
<td>1NF + every non-key column depends on the <strong>whole</strong>
key</td>
<td>In <code>order_items(order_id, product_id, product_name)</code>,
<code>product_name</code> depends only on <code>product_id</code></td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>3NF</td>
<td>2NF + no column depends on another non-key column</td>
<td><code>orders(customer_id, customer_city)</code>: city depends on the
customer, not the order</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>BCNF</td>
<td>Every determinant is a candidate key</td>
<td>Rare edge cases of 3NF; mention it exists</td>
</tr>
</tbody>
</table>
<p>Memory aid: every non-key column depends on “the key, the whole key,
and nothing but the key”.</p>
<p><strong>When to denormalise deliberately:</strong> historical
snapshots (price at purchase, shipping address on the order, just like
in MongoDB), read-heavy aggregates (<code>products.rating_avg</code>
maintained by a trigger or app logic), and reporting tables or
materialised views. Normalise first; denormalise with a reason and a
plan for keeping copies correct.</p>
<h3 id="data-types-that-avoid-bugs">1.3 Data types that avoid bugs</h3>
<table>
<colgroup>
<col style="width: 33%" />
<col style="width: 33%" />
<col style="width: 33%" />
</colgroup>
<thead>
<tr>
<th>Data</th>
<th>Use</th>
<th>Avoid</th>
</tr>
</thead>
<tbody>
<tr>
<td>Money</td>
<td><code>BIGINT</code> minor units or <code>NUMERIC(12,2)</code></td>
<td><code>FLOAT</code>, <code>REAL</code>, <code>DOUBLE</code>, Postgres
<code>MONEY</code> (locale-dependent)</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>Timestamps</td>
<td><code>TIMESTAMPTZ</code> (stored as UTC)</td>
<td><code>TIMESTAMP</code> without time zone for events</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>Strings</td>
<td><code>TEXT</code> (Postgres) + <code>CHECK</code> for length;
<code>VARCHAR(n)</code> in MySQL</td>
<td>Arbitrary <code>VARCHAR(255)</code> everywhere</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>Status sets</td>
<td><code>TEXT</code> + <code>CHECK</code>, or a lookup table</td>
<td>Postgres <code>ENUM</code> if values change often (altering is
awkward)</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>Flexible attributes</td>
<td><code>JSONB</code> (Postgres) with a GIN index</td>
<td>Using JSONB for core relational data you join or constrain on</td>
</tr>
</tbody>
</table>
<p><strong>Postgres JSONB</strong> gives you document flexibility inside
a relational database: product attributes that vary by category can live
in <code>attributes JSONB</code>, indexed with GIN and queried with
<code>@&gt;</code>. That often removes the need for a separate MongoDB
for semi-structured data.</p>
<h3 id="soft-deletes-audit-columns-multi-tenancy">1.4 Soft deletes,
audit columns, multi-tenancy</h3>
<ul>
<li><strong>Soft delete</strong> (<code>deleted_at TIMESTAMPTZ</code>):
keeps history but every query must filter it, unique constraints need
partial indexes (<code>UNIQUE (email) WHERE deleted_at IS NULL</code>),
and data protection laws may require real deletion. Use it deliberately,
not by default.</li>
<li><strong>Audit:</strong> <code>created_at</code>,
<code>updated_at</code> (via trigger or ORM), <code>created_by</code>;
for full history, an audit table filled by triggers or an outbox
event.</li>
<li><strong>Multi-tenancy:</strong> a <code>tenant_id</code> column on
every table plus Postgres <strong>Row-Level Security</strong> policies,
so a missing <code>WHERE tenant_id = ...</code> can’t leak data across
tenants.</li>
</ul>
<h3 id="orms-and-migrations">1.5 ORMs and migrations</h3>
<table>
<colgroup>
<col style="width: 25%" />
<col style="width: 25%" />
<col style="width: 25%" />
<col style="width: 25%" />
</colgroup>
<thead>
<tr>
<th>Tool</th>
<th>Style</th>
<th>Good</th>
<th>Watch out</th>
</tr>
</thead>
<tbody>
<tr>
<td>Prisma</td>
<td>Schema file, generated typed client</td>
<td>Excellent types and DX, migrations included</td>
<td>Complex SQL needs raw queries; historically heavier runtime</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>TypeORM</td>
<td>Decorator entities (Nest-friendly)</td>
<td>Familiar Active Record / Data Mapper</td>
<td>Type safety gaps, lazy-loading surprises</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>Drizzle / Kysely</td>
<td>SQL-like typed query builders</td>
<td>Close to SQL, light, fully typed</td>
<td>You write more SQL-shaped code (a plus for many)</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>Knex / raw <code>pg</code></td>
<td>Query builder / plain SQL</td>
<td>Full control</td>
<td>Types are manual</td>
</tr>
</tbody>
</table>
<p><strong>Migrations:</strong> versioned, in the repo, run
automatically in the deploy pipeline, never edited after being applied.
For zero-downtime changes, use <strong>expand and contract</strong>: add
the new column (nullable), deploy code that writes both, backfill in
batches, switch reads, then drop the old column in a later release.
Never rename or drop a column in the same deploy that changes the code
using it. On large Postgres tables,
<code>CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY</code> avoids locking writes.</p>
<h3 id="how-id-answer-hour-1-6">How I’d answer — Hour 1</h3>
<p><strong>Q1. Explain normalization up to 3NF with an example.</strong>
“1NF: one value per column, no lists in a field. 2NF: with a composite
key like <code>(order_id, product_id)</code>, product name depends only
on product, so it moves to <code>products</code>. 3NF: no non-key column
depends on another non-key column; customer city depends on the
customer, not the order, so it belongs in <code>customers</code>. The
goal is storing each fact once so updates can’t leave contradictions. I
denormalise deliberately for historical snapshots and read-heavy
aggregates.”</p>
<p><strong>Q2. UUID or auto-increment for primary keys?</strong>
“Auto-increment BIGINT is compact and fast but leaks volume and isn’t
globally unique. Random UUIDs are globally unique but fragment the
index. My default is UUID v7 for distributed systems, or a BIGINT
internal key plus a public UUID when join performance matters.”</p>
<p><strong>Q3. How do you change a column on a large production table
without downtime?</strong> “Expand and contract. Add the new column,
write to both from the application, backfill in batches, switch reads,
and drop the old column in a later release. Indexes get created
concurrently. Each step is backward compatible, so a rollback at any
point is safe.”</p>
<p><strong>Q4. Postgres or MongoDB for a new product?</strong> “Default
to Postgres when the data is relational, needs strong constraints and
transactions, or reporting with joins: orders, payments, inventory.
MongoDB when documents are naturally self-contained, read as a whole and
vary in shape: catalogues, content, events. Postgres with JSONB covers a
lot of semi-structured needs, so I need a clear reason to run both.”</p>
<h3 id="practice-18">Practice</h3>
<ul class="task-list">
<li><label><input type="checkbox" />Design the capstone’s
orders/payments schema in Postgres with all constraints, FK indexes and
a public UUID</label></li>
<li><label><input type="checkbox" />Write a Prisma or Drizzle schema for
it and generate the first migration</label></li>
<li><label><input type="checkbox" />Practise an expand-and-contract
migration: rename <code>total_paise</code> to <code>amount_paise</code>
in four safe steps</label></li>
</ul>
<h2 id="hour-2-sql-for-interviews">Hour 2 — SQL for interviews</h2>
<p>Many Node developers have written SQL through an ORM for years and
lose fluency with raw queries. Interviews almost always include a few: a
join, a group-by with a condition, and something needing a window
function (“top 3 products per category”, “second highest salary”). Write
each one by hand until it’s automatic.</p>
<p>Sample schema used below: <code>customers(id, name, city)</code>,
<code>orders(id, customer_id, status, total_paise, created_at)</code>,
<code>order_items(order_id, product_id, quantity, unit_price_paise)</code>,
<code>products(id, name, category)</code>,
<code>employees(id, name, dept_id, salary, manager_id)</code>.</p>
<h3 id="joins">2.1 Joins</h3>
<table>
<colgroup>
<col style="width: 50%" />
<col style="width: 50%" />
</colgroup>
<thead>
<tr>
<th>Join</th>
<th>Returns</th>
</tr>
</thead>
<tbody>
<tr>
<td><code>INNER JOIN</code></td>
<td>Rows with a match on both sides</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td><code>LEFT JOIN</code></td>
<td>Every left row; right side <code>NULL</code> when no match</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td><code>RIGHT JOIN</code></td>
<td>Mirror of LEFT (rarely used; rewrite as LEFT)</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td><code>FULL OUTER JOIN</code></td>
<td>Everything from both, <code>NULL</code>s where unmatched (not in
MySQL; emulate with <code>UNION</code>)</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td><code>CROSS JOIN</code></td>
<td>Every combination</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>Self join</td>
<td>Table joined to itself (employees and their managers)</td>
</tr>
</tbody>
</table>
<div class="sourceCode" id="cb119"><pre
class="sourceCode sql"><code class="sourceCode sql"><span id="cb119-1"><a href="#cb119-1" aria-hidden="true" tabindex="-1"></a><span class="co">-- Customers who never ordered (anti-join)</span></span>
<span id="cb119-2"><a href="#cb119-2" aria-hidden="true" tabindex="-1"></a><span class="kw">SELECT</span> c.<span class="kw">id</span>, c.name</span>
<span id="cb119-3"><a href="#cb119-3" aria-hidden="true" tabindex="-1"></a><span class="kw">FROM</span> customers c</span>
<span id="cb119-4"><a href="#cb119-4" aria-hidden="true" tabindex="-1"></a><span class="kw">LEFT</span> <span class="kw">JOIN</span> orders o <span class="kw">ON</span> o.customer_id <span class="op">=</span> c.<span class="kw">id</span></span>
<span id="cb119-5"><a href="#cb119-5" aria-hidden="true" tabindex="-1"></a><span class="kw">WHERE</span> o.<span class="kw">id</span> <span class="kw">IS</span> <span class="kw">NULL</span>;</span>
<span id="cb119-6"><a href="#cb119-6" aria-hidden="true" tabindex="-1"></a><span class="co">-- equivalent and often clearer:  WHERE NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM orders o WHERE o.customer_id = c.id)</span></span>
<span id="cb119-7"><a href="#cb119-7" aria-hidden="true" tabindex="-1"></a></span>
<span id="cb119-8"><a href="#cb119-8" aria-hidden="true" tabindex="-1"></a><span class="co">-- Employees with their manager&#39;s name (self join)</span></span>
<span id="cb119-9"><a href="#cb119-9" aria-hidden="true" tabindex="-1"></a><span class="kw">SELECT</span> e.name <span class="kw">AS</span> employee, m.name <span class="kw">AS</span> manager</span>
<span id="cb119-10"><a href="#cb119-10" aria-hidden="true" tabindex="-1"></a><span class="kw">FROM</span> employees e</span>
<span id="cb119-11"><a href="#cb119-11" aria-hidden="true" tabindex="-1"></a><span class="kw">LEFT</span> <span class="kw">JOIN</span> employees m <span class="kw">ON</span> m.<span class="kw">id</span> <span class="op">=</span> e.manager_id;</span></code></pre></div>
<p><strong>The classic trap:</strong> filtering the right side of a LEFT
JOIN in <code>WHERE</code> turns it into an INNER JOIN. Put that filter
in the <code>ON</code> clause instead:</p>
<div class="sourceCode" id="cb120"><pre
class="sourceCode sql"><code class="sourceCode sql"><span id="cb120-1"><a href="#cb120-1" aria-hidden="true" tabindex="-1"></a><span class="co">-- All customers with their paid orders count (customers with none show 0)</span></span>
<span id="cb120-2"><a href="#cb120-2" aria-hidden="true" tabindex="-1"></a><span class="kw">SELECT</span> c.name, <span class="fu">COUNT</span>(o.<span class="kw">id</span>) <span class="kw">AS</span> paid_orders</span>
<span id="cb120-3"><a href="#cb120-3" aria-hidden="true" tabindex="-1"></a><span class="kw">FROM</span> customers c</span>
<span id="cb120-4"><a href="#cb120-4" aria-hidden="true" tabindex="-1"></a><span class="kw">LEFT</span> <span class="kw">JOIN</span> orders o <span class="kw">ON</span> o.customer_id <span class="op">=</span> c.<span class="kw">id</span> <span class="kw">AND</span> o.status <span class="op">=</span> <span class="st">&#39;paid&#39;</span>   <span class="co">-- in ON, not WHERE</span></span>
<span id="cb120-5"><a href="#cb120-5" aria-hidden="true" tabindex="-1"></a><span class="kw">GROUP</span> <span class="kw">BY</span> c.<span class="kw">id</span>, c.name;</span></code></pre></div>
<p><strong><code>NOT IN</code> with NULLs:</strong>
<code>WHERE id NOT IN (SELECT customer_id FROM orders)</code> returns
nothing if any <code>customer_id</code> is NULL. Prefer
<code>NOT EXISTS</code>.</p>
<h3 id="aggregation">2.2 Aggregation</h3>
<p>Logical order of execution (why aliases from SELECT can’t be used in
WHERE):
<code>FROM / JOIN → WHERE → GROUP BY → HAVING → SELECT → DISTINCT → ORDER BY → LIMIT</code>.</p>
<div class="sourceCode" id="cb121"><pre
class="sourceCode sql"><code class="sourceCode sql"><span id="cb121-1"><a href="#cb121-1" aria-hidden="true" tabindex="-1"></a><span class="co">-- Customers who spent more than ₹50,000 in 2026, highest first</span></span>
<span id="cb121-2"><a href="#cb121-2" aria-hidden="true" tabindex="-1"></a><span class="kw">SELECT</span> customer_id, <span class="fu">SUM</span>(total_paise) <span class="op">/</span> <span class="fl">100.0</span> <span class="kw">AS</span> spent_inr, <span class="fu">COUNT</span>(<span class="op">*</span>) <span class="kw">AS</span> orders</span>
<span id="cb121-3"><a href="#cb121-3" aria-hidden="true" tabindex="-1"></a><span class="kw">FROM</span> orders</span>
<span id="cb121-4"><a href="#cb121-4" aria-hidden="true" tabindex="-1"></a><span class="kw">WHERE</span> status <span class="op">=</span> <span class="st">&#39;paid&#39;</span> <span class="kw">AND</span> created_at <span class="op">&gt;=</span> <span class="st">&#39;2026-01-01&#39;</span> <span class="kw">AND</span> created_at <span class="op">&lt;</span> <span class="st">&#39;2027-01-01&#39;</span></span>
<span id="cb121-5"><a href="#cb121-5" aria-hidden="true" tabindex="-1"></a><span class="kw">GROUP</span> <span class="kw">BY</span> customer_id</span>
<span id="cb121-6"><a href="#cb121-6" aria-hidden="true" tabindex="-1"></a><span class="kw">HAVING</span> <span class="fu">SUM</span>(total_paise) <span class="op">&gt;</span> <span class="dv">5000000</span></span>
<span id="cb121-7"><a href="#cb121-7" aria-hidden="true" tabindex="-1"></a><span class="kw">ORDER</span> <span class="kw">BY</span> spent_inr <span class="kw">DESC</span>;</span></code></pre></div>
<p><code>WHERE</code> filters rows before grouping; <code>HAVING</code>
filters groups after. Use half-open date ranges
(<code>&gt;= start AND &lt; end</code>) rather than <code>BETWEEN</code>
or wrapping the column in a function, so the index on
<code>created_at</code> is used and the last day isn’t cut off.</p>
<h3 id="ctes-and-subqueries">2.3 CTEs and subqueries</h3>
<div class="sourceCode" id="cb122"><pre
class="sourceCode sql"><code class="sourceCode sql"><span id="cb122-1"><a href="#cb122-1" aria-hidden="true" tabindex="-1"></a><span class="kw">WITH</span> monthly <span class="kw">AS</span> (</span>
<span id="cb122-2"><a href="#cb122-2" aria-hidden="true" tabindex="-1"></a>  <span class="kw">SELECT</span> date_trunc(<span class="st">&#39;month&#39;</span>, created_at) <span class="kw">AS</span> <span class="dt">month</span>, <span class="fu">SUM</span>(total_paise) <span class="kw">AS</span> revenue</span>
<span id="cb122-3"><a href="#cb122-3" aria-hidden="true" tabindex="-1"></a>  <span class="kw">FROM</span> orders <span class="kw">WHERE</span> status <span class="op">=</span> <span class="st">&#39;paid&#39;</span></span>
<span id="cb122-4"><a href="#cb122-4" aria-hidden="true" tabindex="-1"></a>  <span class="kw">GROUP</span> <span class="kw">BY</span> <span class="dv">1</span></span>
<span id="cb122-5"><a href="#cb122-5" aria-hidden="true" tabindex="-1"></a>)</span>
<span id="cb122-6"><a href="#cb122-6" aria-hidden="true" tabindex="-1"></a><span class="kw">SELECT</span> <span class="dt">month</span>, revenue,</span>
<span id="cb122-7"><a href="#cb122-7" aria-hidden="true" tabindex="-1"></a>       revenue <span class="op">-</span> <span class="fu">LAG</span>(revenue) <span class="kw">OVER</span> (<span class="kw">ORDER</span> <span class="kw">BY</span> <span class="dt">month</span>) <span class="kw">AS</span> change_vs_prev_month</span>
<span id="cb122-8"><a href="#cb122-8" aria-hidden="true" tabindex="-1"></a><span class="kw">FROM</span> monthly</span>
<span id="cb122-9"><a href="#cb122-9" aria-hidden="true" tabindex="-1"></a><span class="kw">ORDER</span> <span class="kw">BY</span> <span class="dt">month</span>;</span></code></pre></div>
<p>CTEs make complex queries readable. In modern Postgres (12+) they are
inlined by the planner unless they’re used more than once or marked
<code>MATERIALIZED</code>. <strong>Recursive CTEs</strong> walk
hierarchies:</p>
<div class="sourceCode" id="cb123"><pre
class="sourceCode sql"><code class="sourceCode sql"><span id="cb123-1"><a href="#cb123-1" aria-hidden="true" tabindex="-1"></a><span class="co">-- Everyone reporting (directly or indirectly) to employee 1</span></span>
<span id="cb123-2"><a href="#cb123-2" aria-hidden="true" tabindex="-1"></a><span class="kw">WITH</span> RECURSIVE reports <span class="kw">AS</span> (</span>
<span id="cb123-3"><a href="#cb123-3" aria-hidden="true" tabindex="-1"></a>  <span class="kw">SELECT</span> <span class="kw">id</span>, name, manager_id, <span class="dv">1</span> <span class="kw">AS</span> <span class="fu">depth</span> <span class="kw">FROM</span> employees <span class="kw">WHERE</span> manager_id <span class="op">=</span> <span class="dv">1</span></span>
<span id="cb123-4"><a href="#cb123-4" aria-hidden="true" tabindex="-1"></a>  <span class="kw">UNION</span> <span class="kw">ALL</span></span>
<span id="cb123-5"><a href="#cb123-5" aria-hidden="true" tabindex="-1"></a>  <span class="kw">SELECT</span> e.<span class="kw">id</span>, e.name, e.manager_id, r.<span class="fu">depth</span> <span class="op">+</span> <span class="dv">1</span></span>
<span id="cb123-6"><a href="#cb123-6" aria-hidden="true" tabindex="-1"></a>  <span class="kw">FROM</span> employees e <span class="kw">JOIN</span> reports r <span class="kw">ON</span> e.manager_id <span class="op">=</span> r.<span class="kw">id</span></span>
<span id="cb123-7"><a href="#cb123-7" aria-hidden="true" tabindex="-1"></a>)</span>
<span id="cb123-8"><a href="#cb123-8" aria-hidden="true" tabindex="-1"></a><span class="kw">SELECT</span> <span class="op">*</span> <span class="kw">FROM</span> reports;</span></code></pre></div>
<p>Use cases: org charts, category trees, threaded comments, bill of
materials.</p>
<h3 id="window-functions">2.4 Window functions</h3>
<p><strong>What they are:</strong> calculations across related rows
<strong>without collapsing them</strong> into one row the way
<code>GROUP BY</code> does. Syntax:
<code>fn() OVER (PARTITION BY ... ORDER BY ... [frame])</code>.</p>
<table>
<thead>
<tr>
<th>Function</th>
<th>Use</th>
</tr>
</thead>
<tbody>
<tr>
<td><code>ROW_NUMBER()</code></td>
<td>Unique sequence: 1, 2, 3, 4</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td><code>RANK()</code></td>
<td>Ties share a rank, gaps after: 1, 2, 2, 4</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td><code>DENSE_RANK()</code></td>
<td>Ties share a rank, no gaps: 1, 2, 2, 3</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td><code>LAG()</code> / <code>LEAD()</code></td>
<td>Previous / next row’s value</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td><code>SUM() / AVG() OVER (...)</code></td>
<td>Running totals, moving averages</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td><code>NTILE(n)</code></td>
<td>Split into n buckets (quartiles)</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td><code>FIRST_VALUE</code> / <code>LAST_VALUE</code></td>
<td>First or last in the window</td>
</tr>
</tbody>
</table>
<div class="sourceCode" id="cb124"><pre
class="sourceCode sql"><code class="sourceCode sql"><span id="cb124-1"><a href="#cb124-1" aria-hidden="true" tabindex="-1"></a><span class="co">-- Top 3 products by revenue in each category</span></span>
<span id="cb124-2"><a href="#cb124-2" aria-hidden="true" tabindex="-1"></a><span class="kw">WITH</span> product_revenue <span class="kw">AS</span> (</span>
<span id="cb124-3"><a href="#cb124-3" aria-hidden="true" tabindex="-1"></a>  <span class="kw">SELECT</span> p.<span class="kw">category</span>, p.name, <span class="fu">SUM</span>(oi.quantity <span class="op">*</span> oi.unit_price_paise) <span class="kw">AS</span> revenue</span>
<span id="cb124-4"><a href="#cb124-4" aria-hidden="true" tabindex="-1"></a>  <span class="kw">FROM</span> order_items oi <span class="kw">JOIN</span> products p <span class="kw">ON</span> p.<span class="kw">id</span> <span class="op">=</span> oi.product_id</span>
<span id="cb124-5"><a href="#cb124-5" aria-hidden="true" tabindex="-1"></a>  <span class="kw">GROUP</span> <span class="kw">BY</span> p.<span class="kw">category</span>, p.name</span>
<span id="cb124-6"><a href="#cb124-6" aria-hidden="true" tabindex="-1"></a>),</span>
<span id="cb124-7"><a href="#cb124-7" aria-hidden="true" tabindex="-1"></a>ranked <span class="kw">AS</span> (</span>
<span id="cb124-8"><a href="#cb124-8" aria-hidden="true" tabindex="-1"></a>  <span class="kw">SELECT</span> <span class="op">*</span>, <span class="fu">DENSE_RANK</span>() <span class="kw">OVER</span> (<span class="kw">PARTITION</span> <span class="kw">BY</span> <span class="kw">category</span> <span class="kw">ORDER</span> <span class="kw">BY</span> revenue <span class="kw">DESC</span>) <span class="kw">AS</span> rnk</span>
<span id="cb124-9"><a href="#cb124-9" aria-hidden="true" tabindex="-1"></a>  <span class="kw">FROM</span> product_revenue</span>
<span id="cb124-10"><a href="#cb124-10" aria-hidden="true" tabindex="-1"></a>)</span>
<span id="cb124-11"><a href="#cb124-11" aria-hidden="true" tabindex="-1"></a><span class="kw">SELECT</span> <span class="kw">category</span>, name, revenue <span class="kw">FROM</span> ranked <span class="kw">WHERE</span> rnk <span class="op">&lt;=</span> <span class="dv">3</span>;</span>
<span id="cb124-12"><a href="#cb124-12" aria-hidden="true" tabindex="-1"></a></span>
<span id="cb124-13"><a href="#cb124-13" aria-hidden="true" tabindex="-1"></a><span class="co">-- Running total of revenue per day</span></span>
<span id="cb124-14"><a href="#cb124-14" aria-hidden="true" tabindex="-1"></a><span class="kw">SELECT</span> <span class="dt">day</span>, revenue, <span class="fu">SUM</span>(revenue) <span class="kw">OVER</span> (<span class="kw">ORDER</span> <span class="kw">BY</span> <span class="dt">day</span>) <span class="kw">AS</span> cumulative</span>
<span id="cb124-15"><a href="#cb124-15" aria-hidden="true" tabindex="-1"></a><span class="kw">FROM</span> daily_revenue;</span>
<span id="cb124-16"><a href="#cb124-16" aria-hidden="true" tabindex="-1"></a></span>
<span id="cb124-17"><a href="#cb124-17" aria-hidden="true" tabindex="-1"></a><span class="co">-- Each customer&#39;s latest order (top-1 per group)</span></span>
<span id="cb124-18"><a href="#cb124-18" aria-hidden="true" tabindex="-1"></a><span class="kw">SELECT</span> <span class="op">*</span> <span class="kw">FROM</span> (</span>
<span id="cb124-19"><a href="#cb124-19" aria-hidden="true" tabindex="-1"></a>  <span class="kw">SELECT</span> o.<span class="op">*</span>, <span class="fu">ROW_NUMBER</span>() <span class="kw">OVER</span> (<span class="kw">PARTITION</span> <span class="kw">BY</span> customer_id <span class="kw">ORDER</span> <span class="kw">BY</span> created_at <span class="kw">DESC</span>) <span class="kw">AS</span> rn</span>
<span id="cb124-20"><a href="#cb124-20" aria-hidden="true" tabindex="-1"></a>  <span class="kw">FROM</span> orders o</span>
<span id="cb124-21"><a href="#cb124-21" aria-hidden="true" tabindex="-1"></a>) t <span class="kw">WHERE</span> rn <span class="op">=</span> <span class="dv">1</span>;</span>
<span id="cb124-22"><a href="#cb124-22" aria-hidden="true" tabindex="-1"></a><span class="co">-- Postgres shortcut: SELECT DISTINCT ON (customer_id) * FROM orders ORDER BY customer_id, created_at DESC;</span></span></code></pre></div>
<p>Window functions run after <code>WHERE</code> and
<code>GROUP BY</code>, so you can’t filter on them directly; wrap in a
subquery or CTE as above.</p>
<h3 id="classic-questions">2.5 Classic questions</h3>
<div class="sourceCode" id="cb125"><pre
class="sourceCode sql"><code class="sourceCode sql"><span id="cb125-1"><a href="#cb125-1" aria-hidden="true" tabindex="-1"></a><span class="co">-- Second highest salary (handles ties and returns NULL if none)</span></span>
<span id="cb125-2"><a href="#cb125-2" aria-hidden="true" tabindex="-1"></a><span class="kw">SELECT</span> <span class="fu">MAX</span>(salary) <span class="kw">FROM</span> employees <span class="kw">WHERE</span> salary <span class="op">&lt;</span> (<span class="kw">SELECT</span> <span class="fu">MAX</span>(salary) <span class="kw">FROM</span> employees);</span>
<span id="cb125-3"><a href="#cb125-3" aria-hidden="true" tabindex="-1"></a><span class="co">-- Nth highest (N = 3), general form</span></span>
<span id="cb125-4"><a href="#cb125-4" aria-hidden="true" tabindex="-1"></a><span class="kw">SELECT</span> <span class="kw">DISTINCT</span> salary <span class="kw">FROM</span> (</span>
<span id="cb125-5"><a href="#cb125-5" aria-hidden="true" tabindex="-1"></a>  <span class="kw">SELECT</span> salary, <span class="fu">DENSE_RANK</span>() <span class="kw">OVER</span> (<span class="kw">ORDER</span> <span class="kw">BY</span> salary <span class="kw">DESC</span>) <span class="kw">AS</span> r <span class="kw">FROM</span> employees</span>
<span id="cb125-6"><a href="#cb125-6" aria-hidden="true" tabindex="-1"></a>) t <span class="kw">WHERE</span> r <span class="op">=</span> <span class="dv">3</span>;</span>
<span id="cb125-7"><a href="#cb125-7" aria-hidden="true" tabindex="-1"></a></span>
<span id="cb125-8"><a href="#cb125-8" aria-hidden="true" tabindex="-1"></a><span class="co">-- Highest-paid employee per department</span></span>
<span id="cb125-9"><a href="#cb125-9" aria-hidden="true" tabindex="-1"></a><span class="kw">SELECT</span> dept_id, name, salary <span class="kw">FROM</span> (</span>
<span id="cb125-10"><a href="#cb125-10" aria-hidden="true" tabindex="-1"></a>  <span class="kw">SELECT</span> <span class="op">*</span>, <span class="fu">RANK</span>() <span class="kw">OVER</span> (<span class="kw">PARTITION</span> <span class="kw">BY</span> dept_id <span class="kw">ORDER</span> <span class="kw">BY</span> salary <span class="kw">DESC</span>) <span class="kw">AS</span> r <span class="kw">FROM</span> employees</span>
<span id="cb125-11"><a href="#cb125-11" aria-hidden="true" tabindex="-1"></a>) t <span class="kw">WHERE</span> r <span class="op">=</span> <span class="dv">1</span>;</span>
<span id="cb125-12"><a href="#cb125-12" aria-hidden="true" tabindex="-1"></a></span>
<span id="cb125-13"><a href="#cb125-13" aria-hidden="true" tabindex="-1"></a><span class="co">-- Employees earning more than their manager</span></span>
<span id="cb125-14"><a href="#cb125-14" aria-hidden="true" tabindex="-1"></a><span class="kw">SELECT</span> e.name <span class="kw">FROM</span> employees e <span class="kw">JOIN</span> employees m <span class="kw">ON</span> m.<span class="kw">id</span> <span class="op">=</span> e.manager_id <span class="kw">WHERE</span> e.salary <span class="op">&gt;</span> m.salary;</span>
<span id="cb125-15"><a href="#cb125-15" aria-hidden="true" tabindex="-1"></a></span>
<span id="cb125-16"><a href="#cb125-16" aria-hidden="true" tabindex="-1"></a><span class="co">-- Find duplicate emails</span></span>
<span id="cb125-17"><a href="#cb125-17" aria-hidden="true" tabindex="-1"></a><span class="kw">SELECT</span> email, <span class="fu">COUNT</span>(<span class="op">*</span>) <span class="kw">FROM</span> customers <span class="kw">GROUP</span> <span class="kw">BY</span> email <span class="kw">HAVING</span> <span class="fu">COUNT</span>(<span class="op">*</span>) <span class="op">&gt;</span> <span class="dv">1</span>;</span>
<span id="cb125-18"><a href="#cb125-18" aria-hidden="true" tabindex="-1"></a></span>
<span id="cb125-19"><a href="#cb125-19" aria-hidden="true" tabindex="-1"></a><span class="co">-- Delete duplicates, keeping the lowest id (Postgres)</span></span>
<span id="cb125-20"><a href="#cb125-20" aria-hidden="true" tabindex="-1"></a><span class="kw">DELETE</span> <span class="kw">FROM</span> customers c <span class="kw">USING</span> customers d</span>
<span id="cb125-21"><a href="#cb125-21" aria-hidden="true" tabindex="-1"></a><span class="kw">WHERE</span> c.email <span class="op">=</span> d.email <span class="kw">AND</span> c.<span class="kw">id</span> <span class="op">&gt;</span> d.<span class="kw">id</span>;</span>
<span id="cb125-22"><a href="#cb125-22" aria-hidden="true" tabindex="-1"></a></span>
<span id="cb125-23"><a href="#cb125-23" aria-hidden="true" tabindex="-1"></a><span class="co">-- Month-over-month growth %</span></span>
<span id="cb125-24"><a href="#cb125-24" aria-hidden="true" tabindex="-1"></a><span class="kw">SELECT</span> <span class="dt">month</span>, revenue,</span>
<span id="cb125-25"><a href="#cb125-25" aria-hidden="true" tabindex="-1"></a>       <span class="fu">ROUND</span>(<span class="fl">100.0</span> <span class="op">*</span> (revenue <span class="op">-</span> <span class="fu">LAG</span>(revenue) <span class="kw">OVER</span> (<span class="kw">ORDER</span> <span class="kw">BY</span> <span class="dt">month</span>)) <span class="op">/</span> <span class="fu">NULLIF</span>(<span class="fu">LAG</span>(revenue) <span class="kw">OVER</span> (<span class="kw">ORDER</span> <span class="kw">BY</span> <span class="dt">month</span>), <span class="dv">0</span>), <span class="dv">1</span>) <span class="kw">AS</span> growth_pct</span>
<span id="cb125-26"><a href="#cb125-26" aria-hidden="true" tabindex="-1"></a><span class="kw">FROM</span> monthly_revenue;</span>
<span id="cb125-27"><a href="#cb125-27" aria-hidden="true" tabindex="-1"></a></span>
<span id="cb125-28"><a href="#cb125-28" aria-hidden="true" tabindex="-1"></a><span class="co">-- Customers who ordered in 3 consecutive months (gaps-and-islands, a senior favourite)</span></span>
<span id="cb125-29"><a href="#cb125-29" aria-hidden="true" tabindex="-1"></a><span class="kw">WITH</span> m <span class="kw">AS</span> (</span>
<span id="cb125-30"><a href="#cb125-30" aria-hidden="true" tabindex="-1"></a>  <span class="kw">SELECT</span> <span class="kw">DISTINCT</span> customer_id, date_trunc(<span class="st">&#39;month&#39;</span>, created_at):<span class="ch">:date</span> <span class="kw">AS</span> <span class="dt">month</span> <span class="kw">FROM</span> orders</span>
<span id="cb125-31"><a href="#cb125-31" aria-hidden="true" tabindex="-1"></a>), g <span class="kw">AS</span> (</span>
<span id="cb125-32"><a href="#cb125-32" aria-hidden="true" tabindex="-1"></a>  <span class="kw">SELECT</span> customer_id, <span class="dt">month</span>,</span>
<span id="cb125-33"><a href="#cb125-33" aria-hidden="true" tabindex="-1"></a>         <span class="dt">month</span> <span class="op">-</span> (<span class="fu">ROW_NUMBER</span>() <span class="kw">OVER</span> (<span class="kw">PARTITION</span> <span class="kw">BY</span> customer_id <span class="kw">ORDER</span> <span class="kw">BY</span> <span class="dt">month</span>) <span class="op">*</span> <span class="dt">INTERVAL</span> <span class="st">&#39;1 month&#39;</span>) <span class="kw">AS</span> grp</span>
<span id="cb125-34"><a href="#cb125-34" aria-hidden="true" tabindex="-1"></a>  <span class="kw">FROM</span> m</span>
<span id="cb125-35"><a href="#cb125-35" aria-hidden="true" tabindex="-1"></a>)</span>
<span id="cb125-36"><a href="#cb125-36" aria-hidden="true" tabindex="-1"></a><span class="kw">SELECT</span> customer_id <span class="kw">FROM</span> g <span class="kw">GROUP</span> <span class="kw">BY</span> customer_id, grp <span class="kw">HAVING</span> <span class="fu">COUNT</span>(<span class="op">*</span>) <span class="op">&gt;=</span> <span class="dv">3</span>;</span></code></pre></div>
<p>The gaps-and-islands trick: subtracting a running row number from a
sequence gives the same value for consecutive runs, so grouping by it
finds streaks.</p>
<h3 id="how-id-answer-hour-2-6">How I’d answer — Hour 2</h3>
<p><strong>Q1. Difference between WHERE and HAVING?</strong> “WHERE
filters rows before grouping and can use indexes; HAVING filters groups
after aggregation, so it’s where conditions on SUM or COUNT go.”</p>
<p><strong>Q2. RANK vs DENSE_RANK vs ROW_NUMBER?</strong> “ROW_NUMBER is
always unique. RANK gives ties the same number and skips the next ones;
DENSE_RANK gives ties the same number without gaps. For ‘top N per group
including ties’ I use DENSE_RANK; for ‘exactly one per group’
ROW_NUMBER.”</p>
<p><strong>Q3. Why did my LEFT JOIN behave like an INNER JOIN?</strong>
“Probably a condition on the right table in WHERE. Unmatched rows have
NULLs there, the condition fails, and they’re dropped. Move the
condition into the ON clause.”</p>
<p><strong>Q4. Why prefer NOT EXISTS to NOT IN?</strong> “NOT IN returns
no rows if the subquery contains a NULL, because comparisons with NULL
are unknown. NOT EXISTS has no such trap and usually plans as an
anti-join.”</p>

<h2 id="hour-3-indexes-and-explain-analyze">Hour 3 — Indexes and EXPLAIN
ANALYZE</h2>
<p>Yesterday’s MongoDB index thinking carries over almost entirely; the
vocabulary changes. What’s new is reading Postgres query plans, which
interviewers love to show you (“why is this slow?”), and a few index
types MongoDB doesn’t have.</p>
<h3 id="index-types-postgres-with-mysql-notes">3.1 Index types
(Postgres, with MySQL notes)</h3>
<table>
<colgroup>
<col style="width: 33%" />
<col style="width: 33%" />
<col style="width: 33%" />
</colgroup>
<thead>
<tr>
<th>Type</th>
<th>Use</th>
<th>Example</th>
</tr>
</thead>
<tbody>
<tr>
<td>B-tree (default)</td>
<td>Equality, ranges, sorting, prefix <code>LIKE 'abc%'</code></td>
<td><code>CREATE INDEX ON orders (customer_id, created_at DESC);</code></td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>Composite</td>
<td>Several columns; <strong>leftmost prefix</strong> rule, same as
Mongo’s prefix rule</td>
<td><code>(customer_id, status, created_at)</code></td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>Covering (<code>INCLUDE</code>)</td>
<td>Extra columns stored in the index for index-only scans</td>
<td><code>CREATE INDEX ON orders (customer_id) INCLUDE (status, total_paise);</code></td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>Partial</td>
<td>Index a subset of rows</td>
<td><code>CREATE INDEX ON orders (created_at) WHERE status = 'pending_payment';</code></td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>Expression</td>
<td>Index a computed value</td>
<td><code>CREATE INDEX ON customers (lower(email));</code> then query
<code>WHERE lower(email) = ...</code></td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>GIN</td>
<td>JSONB, arrays, full-text search</td>
<td><code>CREATE INDEX ON products USING gin (attributes);</code> for
<code>attributes @&gt; '{"color":"red"}'</code></td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>GiST</td>
<td>Ranges, geometry, nearest-neighbour</td>
<td>PostGIS, exclusion constraints</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>BRIN</td>
<td>Huge, naturally ordered tables (time series)</td>
<td><code>CREATE INDEX ON events USING brin (created_at);</code> tiny
and cheap</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>Hash</td>
<td>Equality only</td>
<td>Rarely better than B-tree</td>
</tr>
</tbody>
</table>
<p><strong>Column order</strong> follows the same logic as ESR: equality
columns first, then the sort or range column. A query filtering on
<code>status</code> alone generally can’t use an index that starts with
<code>customer_id</code>. (PostgreSQL 18 added B-tree skip scan, which
can sometimes use such an index when the leading column has few distinct
values; don’t design around it.)</p>
<p><strong>MySQL/InnoDB difference worth knowing:</strong> the table
<strong>is</strong> the primary key B-tree (clustered index), and
secondary indexes store the primary key as their pointer. So a large or
random PK (like UUID v4) bloats every secondary index and fragments
inserts; that’s why MySQL schemas favour compact, increasing PKs.
Postgres stores rows in a separate heap, and all indexes point to row
locations.</p>
<h3 id="reading-explain-analyze">3.2 Reading EXPLAIN ANALYZE</h3>
<div class="sourceCode" id="cb126"><pre
class="sourceCode sql"><code class="sourceCode sql"><span id="cb126-1"><a href="#cb126-1" aria-hidden="true" tabindex="-1"></a><span class="kw">EXPLAIN</span> (<span class="kw">ANALYZE</span>, BUFFERS)</span>
<span id="cb126-2"><a href="#cb126-2" aria-hidden="true" tabindex="-1"></a><span class="kw">SELECT</span> <span class="kw">id</span>, status, total_paise <span class="kw">FROM</span> orders</span>
<span id="cb126-3"><a href="#cb126-3" aria-hidden="true" tabindex="-1"></a><span class="kw">WHERE</span> customer_id <span class="op">=</span> <span class="dv">42</span> <span class="kw">AND</span> created_at <span class="op">&gt;=</span> now() <span class="op">-</span> <span class="dt">interval</span> <span class="st">&#39;90 days&#39;</span></span>
<span id="cb126-4"><a href="#cb126-4" aria-hidden="true" tabindex="-1"></a><span class="kw">ORDER</span> <span class="kw">BY</span> created_at <span class="kw">DESC</span> <span class="kw">LIMIT</span> <span class="dv">20</span>;</span></code></pre></div>
<pre class="text"><code>Limit  (cost=0.43..18.92 rows=20 width=24) (actual time=0.031..0.064 rows=20 loops=1)
  -&gt;  Index Scan using orders_customer_id_created_at_idx on orders
        (cost=0.43..512.11 rows=553 width=24) (actual time=0.030..0.060 rows=20 loops=1)
        Index Cond: ((customer_id = 42) AND (created_at &gt;= (now() - &#39;90 days&#39;::interval)))
        Buffers: shared hit=24
Planning Time: 0.15 ms
Execution Time: 0.09 ms</code></pre>
<p>How to read it:</p>
<ul>
<li>Read <strong>inside out</strong>: the most indented node runs first
and feeds its parent.</li>
<li><code>cost=start..total</code> is the planner’s
<strong>estimate</strong> in arbitrary units; <code>actual time</code>
is real milliseconds per loop.</li>
<li>Compare estimated <code>rows</code> with actual <code>rows</code>. A
big mismatch (estimated 1, actual 200,000) means stale or insufficient
statistics, and the planner probably picked a bad plan. Run
<code>ANALYZE</code>, or raise the statistics target for skewed
columns.</li>
<li><code>loops</code>: multiply actual time by loops to get total cost
of a node inside a nested loop.</li>
<li><code>Buffers: shared hit</code> (from cache) vs <code>read</code>
(from disk).</li>
</ul>
<table>
<colgroup>
<col style="width: 33%" />
<col style="width: 33%" />
<col style="width: 33%" />
</colgroup>
<thead>
<tr>
<th>Node</th>
<th>Means</th>
<th>Good or bad</th>
</tr>
</thead>
<tbody>
<tr>
<td>Seq Scan</td>
<td>Read the whole table</td>
<td>Fine for small tables or when most rows match; bad for selective
queries on big tables</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>Index Scan</td>
<td>Walk index, fetch each row from the heap</td>
<td>Good for selective queries</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>Index Only Scan</td>
<td>Answer from the index alone</td>
<td>Best; needs covering index and a recently vacuumed table</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>Bitmap Index/Heap Scan</td>
<td>Collect matching row locations, then read pages in order</td>
<td>Good for medium selectivity or combining indexes</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>Nested Loop</td>
<td>For each outer row, look up inner rows</td>
<td>Great when outer side is small and inner is indexed</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>Hash Join</td>
<td>Build a hash table of one side</td>
<td>Good for large, unsorted joins</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>Merge Join</td>
<td>Merge two sorted inputs</td>
<td>Good when both sides are already sorted</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>Sort (with <code>external merge Disk</code>)</td>
<td>Sorting spilled to disk</td>
<td>Bad: add an index matching ORDER BY, or raise
<code>work_mem</code></td>
</tr>
</tbody>
</table>
<h3 id="why-the-planner-ignores-your-index">3.3 Why the planner ignores
your index</h3>
<ul>
<li>The query wraps the column in a function or cast:
<code>WHERE date(created_at) = '2026-11-20'</code> or
<code>WHERE lower(email) = ...</code> without an expression index.
Rewrite as a range or add an expression index.</li>
<li>Leading wildcard: <code>LIKE '%shoe%'</code> (use
<code>pg_trgm</code> GIN index or full-text search).</li>
<li>Type mismatch between the column and the parameter.</li>
<li>Low selectivity: if 40% of rows match, a sequential scan really is
cheaper.</li>
<li><code>OR</code> across different columns (sometimes a bitmap OR
works; sometimes rewrite as <code>UNION ALL</code>).</li>
<li>Stale statistics after a large data load.</li>
<li>Composite index doesn’t start with the filtered column.</li>
</ul>
<h3 id="finding-slow-queries-in-production-1">3.4 Finding slow queries
in production</h3>
<ul>
<li><strong><code>pg_stat_statements</code></strong>: aggregated stats
for every normalised query: total time, calls, mean time, rows. Sort by
<strong>total time</strong> to find what costs the most overall, which
is often a fast query called millions of times rather than one slow
report.</li>
<li><code>log_min_duration_statement = 250ms</code> logs slow
statements; <code>auto_explain</code> logs their plans.</li>
<li><code>pg_stat_user_indexes</code> shows index usage; unused indexes
are pure write cost.</li>
<li><code>pg_stat_activity</code> shows what’s running right now,
including long transactions and lock waits.</li>
<li>In MySQL: the slow query log, <code>EXPLAIN ANALYZE</code>
(8.0.18+), and <code>performance_schema</code>.</li>
</ul>
<p><strong>The ORM-specific problem:</strong> N+1 queries.
<code>orders.forEach(o =&gt; o.getCustomer())</code> runs one query per
order. Fix with eager loading (<code>include</code> in Prisma,
<code>relations</code> in TypeORM) or a single join, and watch the query
count per request in development logs.</p>
<h3 id="how-id-answer-hour-3-6">How I’d answer — Hour 3</h3>
<p><strong>Q1. Here’s a slow query and its plan. What do you look
at?</strong> “Read the plan inside out and find the node where most
actual time goes. Then check: is it a Seq Scan on a big table with a
selective filter (missing or unusable index)? Are estimated and actual
rows wildly different (stale stats)? Is there a Sort spilling to disk
(index for ORDER BY, or work_mem)? Is a Nested Loop running many
thousands of loops? Then fix the biggest one and re-run EXPLAIN ANALYZE
to confirm.”</p>
<p><strong>Q2. Why isn’t Postgres using my index on
<code>created_at</code>?</strong> “Common reasons: the query wraps the
column in a function like <code>date(created_at)</code>, so I’d rewrite
it as a half-open range; the filter isn’t selective enough, so a seq
scan is actually cheaper; statistics are stale after a bulk load; or the
composite index doesn’t start with that column.”</p>
<p><strong>Q3. What’s an index-only scan?</strong> “When every column
the query needs is in the index, Postgres can skip reading the table. I
make that possible with <code>INCLUDE</code> columns on a covering
index. It also needs the visibility map to be current, which vacuum
maintains, so it works best on tables that aren’t updated
constantly.”</p>
<p><strong>Q4. How do you find the most expensive queries in
production?</strong> “<code>pg_stat_statements</code>, sorted by total
execution time, not mean time. The biggest cost is often a quick query
called millions of times, which points at N+1 patterns or missing
caching, not just slow reports.”</p>
<h3 id="practice-20">Practice</h3>
<ul class="task-list">
<li><label><input type="checkbox" />Seed 5 million orders; run the
customer-orders query with no index, a single-column index and the
composite index; save the three plans</label></li>
<li><label><input type="checkbox" />Turn a
<code>WHERE date(created_at) = ...</code> query into a range and show
the plan change</label></li>
<li><label><input type="checkbox" />Enable
<code>pg_stat_statements</code> locally; generate an N+1 with the ORM
and find it there</label></li>
</ul>
<h2 id="hour-4-transactions-isolation-locking">Hour 4 — Transactions,
isolation, locking</h2>
<p>This is the hour fintech experience pays off. Concurrency bugs (two
requests both reading a balance of ₹500 and both spending it) don’t show
up in tests and are expensive in production. Interviewers ask about
isolation levels, but what they really want is: can you spot a race
condition and pick the right fix?</p>
<h3 id="acid">4.1 ACID</h3>
<ul>
<li><strong>Atomicity:</strong> all statements in a transaction commit,
or none do.</li>
<li><strong>Consistency:</strong> constraints hold before and
after.</li>
<li><strong>Isolation:</strong> concurrent transactions don’t see each
other’s partial work (to a degree set by the isolation level).</li>
<li><strong>Durability:</strong> once committed, it survives a crash
(write-ahead log).</li>
</ul>
<div class="sourceCode" id="cb128"><pre
class="sourceCode ts"><code class="sourceCode typescript"><span id="cb128-1"><a href="#cb128-1" aria-hidden="true" tabindex="-1"></a><span class="co">// node-postgres: every statement in a transaction MUST use the same client</span></span>
<span id="cb128-2"><a href="#cb128-2" aria-hidden="true" tabindex="-1"></a><span class="kw">const</span> client <span class="op">=</span> <span class="cf">await</span> pool<span class="op">.</span><span class="fu">connect</span>()<span class="op">;</span></span>
<span id="cb128-3"><a href="#cb128-3" aria-hidden="true" tabindex="-1"></a><span class="cf">try</span> {</span>
<span id="cb128-4"><a href="#cb128-4" aria-hidden="true" tabindex="-1"></a>  <span class="cf">await</span> client<span class="op">.</span><span class="fu">query</span>(<span class="st">&#39;BEGIN&#39;</span>)<span class="op">;</span></span>
<span id="cb128-5"><a href="#cb128-5" aria-hidden="true" tabindex="-1"></a>  <span class="cf">await</span> client<span class="op">.</span><span class="fu">query</span>(<span class="st">&#39;UPDATE accounts SET balance = balance - $1 WHERE id = $2&#39;</span><span class="op">,</span> [amt<span class="op">,</span> <span class="im">from</span>])<span class="op">;</span></span>
<span id="cb128-6"><a href="#cb128-6" aria-hidden="true" tabindex="-1"></a>  <span class="cf">await</span> client<span class="op">.</span><span class="fu">query</span>(<span class="st">&#39;UPDATE accounts SET balance = balance + $1 WHERE id = $2&#39;</span><span class="op">,</span> [amt<span class="op">,</span> to])<span class="op">;</span></span>
<span id="cb128-7"><a href="#cb128-7" aria-hidden="true" tabindex="-1"></a>  <span class="cf">await</span> client<span class="op">.</span><span class="fu">query</span>(<span class="st">&#39;INSERT INTO ledger (from_id, to_id, amount) VALUES ($1, $2, $3)&#39;</span><span class="op">,</span> [<span class="im">from</span><span class="op">,</span> to<span class="op">,</span> amt])<span class="op">;</span></span>
<span id="cb128-8"><a href="#cb128-8" aria-hidden="true" tabindex="-1"></a>  <span class="cf">await</span> client<span class="op">.</span><span class="fu">query</span>(<span class="st">&#39;COMMIT&#39;</span>)<span class="op">;</span></span>
<span id="cb128-9"><a href="#cb128-9" aria-hidden="true" tabindex="-1"></a>} <span class="cf">catch</span> (e) {</span>
<span id="cb128-10"><a href="#cb128-10" aria-hidden="true" tabindex="-1"></a>  <span class="cf">await</span> client<span class="op">.</span><span class="fu">query</span>(<span class="st">&#39;ROLLBACK&#39;</span>)<span class="op">;</span></span>
<span id="cb128-11"><a href="#cb128-11" aria-hidden="true" tabindex="-1"></a>  <span class="cf">throw</span> e<span class="op">;</span></span>
<span id="cb128-12"><a href="#cb128-12" aria-hidden="true" tabindex="-1"></a>} <span class="cf">finally</span> {</span>
<span id="cb128-13"><a href="#cb128-13" aria-hidden="true" tabindex="-1"></a>  client<span class="op">.</span><span class="fu">release</span>()<span class="op">;</span></span>
<span id="cb128-14"><a href="#cb128-14" aria-hidden="true" tabindex="-1"></a>}</span>
<span id="cb128-15"><a href="#cb128-15" aria-hidden="true" tabindex="-1"></a><span class="co">// Prisma: await prisma.$transaction(async (tx) =&gt; { ... })</span></span></code></pre></div>
<p>A classic Node bug: calling <code>pool.query('BEGIN')</code> and then
<code>pool.query(...)</code> for the next statements. Each call may get
a different connection, so the “transaction” isn’t one.</p>
<h3 id="anomalies-and-isolation-levels">4.2 Anomalies and isolation
levels</h3>
<table>
<colgroup>
<col style="width: 50%" />
<col style="width: 50%" />
</colgroup>
<thead>
<tr>
<th>Anomaly</th>
<th>What happens</th>
</tr>
</thead>
<tbody>
<tr>
<td>Dirty read</td>
<td>Reading another transaction’s uncommitted changes</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>Non-repeatable read</td>
<td>Same row read twice in one transaction returns different values</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>Phantom read</td>
<td>Same query run twice returns a different set of rows</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>Lost update</td>
<td>Two transactions read-modify-write the same row; one overwrites the
other</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>Write skew</td>
<td>Two transactions read overlapping data, each writes different rows,
together they break a rule</td>
</tr>
</tbody>
</table>
<table>
<colgroup>
<col style="width: 33%" />
<col style="width: 33%" />
<col style="width: 33%" />
</colgroup>
<thead>
<tr>
<th>Level</th>
<th>Prevents (by the SQL standard)</th>
<th>Defaults</th>
</tr>
</thead>
<tbody>
<tr>
<td>Read Uncommitted</td>
<td>Nothing</td>
<td>Postgres treats it as Read Committed</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>Read Committed</td>
<td>Dirty reads</td>
<td><strong>Postgres default</strong></td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>Repeatable Read</td>
<td>+ non-repeatable reads</td>
<td><strong>MySQL InnoDB default</strong>; in Postgres it’s snapshot
isolation and also prevents phantoms</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>Serializable</td>
<td>Everything, including write skew</td>
<td>Postgres uses SSI: transactions may fail with a serialization error
and must be retried</td>
</tr>
</tbody>
</table>
<p><strong>Write skew, the example worth knowing:</strong> a hospital
rule says at least one doctor must be on call. Two doctors each check
“is someone else on call?” (yes, the other), and both go off call in
parallel transactions. Each transaction alone was valid; together they
broke the rule. Only Serializable (or an explicit lock on the rows being
checked) prevents it.</p>
<h3 id="fixing-lost-updates-three-tools">4.3 Fixing lost updates: three
tools</h3>
<p>The buggy read-modify-write:</p>
<div class="sourceCode" id="cb129"><pre
class="sourceCode ts"><code class="sourceCode typescript"><span id="cb129-1"><a href="#cb129-1" aria-hidden="true" tabindex="-1"></a><span class="kw">const</span> { rows } <span class="op">=</span> <span class="cf">await</span> db<span class="op">.</span><span class="fu">query</span>(<span class="st">&#39;SELECT stock FROM products WHERE id = $1&#39;</span><span class="op">,</span> [id])<span class="op">;</span></span>
<span id="cb129-2"><a href="#cb129-2" aria-hidden="true" tabindex="-1"></a><span class="cf">if</span> (rows[<span class="dv">0</span>]<span class="op">.</span><span class="at">stock</span> <span class="op">&lt;</span> qty) <span class="cf">throw</span> <span class="kw">new</span> <span class="fu">OutOfStockError</span>()<span class="op">;</span></span>
<span id="cb129-3"><a href="#cb129-3" aria-hidden="true" tabindex="-1"></a><span class="cf">await</span> db<span class="op">.</span><span class="fu">query</span>(<span class="st">&#39;UPDATE products SET stock = $1 WHERE id = $2&#39;</span><span class="op">,</span> [rows[<span class="dv">0</span>]<span class="op">.</span><span class="at">stock</span> <span class="op">-</span> qty<span class="op">,</span> id])<span class="op">;</span> <span class="co">// race!</span></span></code></pre></div>
<table>
<colgroup>
<col style="width: 33%" />
<col style="width: 33%" />
<col style="width: 33%" />
</colgroup>
<thead>
<tr>
<th>Fix</th>
<th>How</th>
<th>Best when</th>
</tr>
</thead>
<tbody>
<tr>
<td><strong>Atomic update</strong></td>
<td><code>UPDATE products SET stock = stock - $1 WHERE id = $2 AND stock &gt;= $1</code>
and check rows affected</td>
<td>The rule fits in one statement; fastest, no lock held across round
trips</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td><strong>Pessimistic lock</strong></td>
<td><code>SELECT ... FOR UPDATE</code> inside a transaction, then
update</td>
<td>Complex logic between read and write; contention is expected</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td><strong>Optimistic lock</strong></td>
<td><code>UPDATE ... SET ..., version = version + 1 WHERE id = $1 AND version = $2</code>;
0 rows = conflict, retry or report</td>
<td>Conflicts are rare; user-facing edits (Day 5 ETags)</td>
</tr>
</tbody>
</table>
<p><strong>My order of preference:</strong> atomic statement first,
optimistic locking for user edits, pessimistic locking when the logic
can’t be expressed atomically.</p>
<h3 id="locks-worth-knowing">4.4 Locks worth knowing</h3>
<ul>
<li><code>SELECT ... FOR UPDATE</code>: lock rows until commit; other
writers (and other <code>FOR UPDATE</code> readers) wait.</li>
<li><code>NOWAIT</code>: fail immediately instead of waiting.</li>
<li><code>SKIP LOCKED</code>: skip rows someone else has locked. This
turns a table into a reliable <strong>job queue</strong> for multiple
workers:</li>
</ul>
<div class="sourceCode" id="cb130"><pre
class="sourceCode sql"><code class="sourceCode sql"><span id="cb130-1"><a href="#cb130-1" aria-hidden="true" tabindex="-1"></a><span class="kw">WITH</span> <span class="kw">next</span> <span class="kw">AS</span> (</span>
<span id="cb130-2"><a href="#cb130-2" aria-hidden="true" tabindex="-1"></a>  <span class="kw">SELECT</span> <span class="kw">id</span> <span class="kw">FROM</span> jobs</span>
<span id="cb130-3"><a href="#cb130-3" aria-hidden="true" tabindex="-1"></a>  <span class="kw">WHERE</span> status <span class="op">=</span> <span class="st">&#39;queued&#39;</span> <span class="kw">AND</span> run_at <span class="op">&lt;=</span> now()</span>
<span id="cb130-4"><a href="#cb130-4" aria-hidden="true" tabindex="-1"></a>  <span class="kw">ORDER</span> <span class="kw">BY</span> run_at</span>
<span id="cb130-5"><a href="#cb130-5" aria-hidden="true" tabindex="-1"></a>  <span class="kw">LIMIT</span> <span class="dv">10</span></span>
<span id="cb130-6"><a href="#cb130-6" aria-hidden="true" tabindex="-1"></a>  <span class="cf">FOR</span> <span class="kw">UPDATE</span> <span class="kw">SKIP</span> <span class="kw">LOCKED</span></span>
<span id="cb130-7"><a href="#cb130-7" aria-hidden="true" tabindex="-1"></a>)</span>
<span id="cb130-8"><a href="#cb130-8" aria-hidden="true" tabindex="-1"></a><span class="kw">UPDATE</span> jobs <span class="kw">SET</span> status <span class="op">=</span> <span class="st">&#39;running&#39;</span>, started_at <span class="op">=</span> now()</span>
<span id="cb130-9"><a href="#cb130-9" aria-hidden="true" tabindex="-1"></a><span class="kw">FROM</span> <span class="kw">next</span> <span class="kw">WHERE</span> jobs.<span class="kw">id</span> <span class="op">=</span> <span class="kw">next</span>.<span class="kw">id</span></span>
<span id="cb130-10"><a href="#cb130-10" aria-hidden="true" tabindex="-1"></a><span class="kw">RETURNING</span> jobs.<span class="op">*</span>;</span></code></pre></div>
<ul>
<li><strong>Advisory locks</strong>
(<code>pg_try_advisory_lock(key)</code>): application-defined locks,
handy for “only one instance runs this cron job”.</li>
<li><strong>Deadlocks:</strong> two transactions each hold a lock the
other needs. Postgres detects them and aborts one. Prevent them by
locking rows in a consistent order (e.g. always lower account ID first
in transfers), keeping transactions short, and retrying the aborted
one.</li>
</ul>
<h3 id="mvcc-and-vacuum-postgres">4.5 MVCC and vacuum (Postgres)</h3>
<p><strong>What MVCC is:</strong> multi-version concurrency control.
Updates write a new row version instead of overwriting; each transaction
sees the versions that were committed as of its snapshot. Readers don’t
block writers and writers don’t block readers.</p>
<p>The cost: old row versions (dead tuples) pile up and must be cleaned
by <strong>VACUUM</strong> (autovacuum runs it automatically). Things to
say in an interview:</p>
<ul>
<li><strong>Long-running transactions</strong> (an idle transaction left
open by a bug, a multi-hour report) prevent cleanup everywhere, causing
table and index <strong>bloat</strong> and slower queries. Monitor
<code>pg_stat_activity</code> for <code>idle in transaction</code> and
set <code>idle_in_transaction_session_timeout</code>.</li>
<li>Very update-heavy tables need autovacuum tuned more
aggressively.</li>
<li>MySQL InnoDB also uses MVCC, with undo logs instead of in-table
versions; long transactions there grow the undo history instead.</li>
</ul>
<h3 id="connections-replication-postgres-vs-mysql">4.6 Connections,
replication, Postgres vs MySQL</h3>
<p><strong>Connections:</strong> Postgres starts a process per
connection, so thousands of connections hurt. With many Node pods, put
<strong>PgBouncer</strong> in front (transaction pooling mode), keep
per-pod pools small, and remember transaction mode can’t keep session
state (session-level prepared statements, <code>SET</code>, advisory
locks held across transactions) unless the driver and PgBouncer version
support it.</p>
<p><strong>Replication:</strong> streaming replicas for high
availability and read scaling, with the same read-your-own-writes caveat
as MongoDB (replication lag). Logical replication or CDC (Debezium) to
feed other systems.</p>
<table>
<colgroup>
<col style="width: 33%" />
<col style="width: 33%" />
<col style="width: 33%" />
</colgroup>
<thead>
<tr>
<th></th>
<th>PostgreSQL</th>
<th>MySQL (InnoDB)</th>
</tr>
</thead>
<tbody>
<tr>
<td>Default isolation</td>
<td>Read Committed</td>
<td>Repeatable Read</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>Storage</td>
<td>Heap + separate indexes</td>
<td>Clustered by primary key</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>Strengths</td>
<td>Rich SQL, JSONB, CTEs, window functions, extensions (PostGIS,
pgvector, pg_trgm), partial/expression indexes, strong standards
compliance</td>
<td>Simple operations, very mature replication, widespread hosting, good
for straightforward high-read OLTP</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>Watch out</td>
<td>Vacuum and bloat, connection limits</td>
<td>Weaker constraint and DDL history (improved in 8.0), fewer advanced
features</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>Typical pick</td>
<td>Default for new systems with complex data</td>
<td>Existing ecosystems, teams with deep MySQL operations
experience</td>
</tr>
</tbody>
</table>
<h3 id="how-id-answer-hour-4-6">How I’d answer — Hour 4</h3>
<p><strong>Q1. Explain isolation levels and their anomalies.</strong>
“Read Committed prevents dirty reads, Repeatable Read prevents
non-repeatable reads, Serializable prevents everything including write
skew. Postgres defaults to Read Committed and MySQL to Repeatable Read.
In practice I don’t rely on raising the isolation level everywhere; I
identify the specific race and fix it with an atomic statement, a row
lock or optimistic locking. I use Serializable for the few flows where
write skew is possible, with retries on serialization failures.”</p>
<p><strong>Q2. Two requests withdraw from the same wallet at once. How
do you prevent overdraft?</strong> “A single atomic statement:
<code>UPDATE wallets SET balance = balance - $1 WHERE id = $2 AND balance &gt;= $1</code>,
and treat zero rows affected as insufficient funds, inside a transaction
that also writes the ledger entry. If the logic is more complex,
<code>SELECT ... FOR UPDATE</code> on the wallet row first. Plus an
idempotency key on the API so a retried request can’t withdraw
twice.”</p>
<p><strong>Q3. What causes deadlocks and how do you avoid them?</strong>
“Two transactions locking the same rows in opposite orders, like
transfers A→B and B→A at the same time. I lock in a consistent order,
such as by account ID, keep transactions short with no network calls
inside, and retry when the database aborts one.”</p>
<p><strong>Q4. How would you build a job queue on Postgres?</strong> “A
jobs table, and workers claim batches with
<code>SELECT ... FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED</code>, so they never pick the
same job and never block each other. Add <code>run_at</code> for delays,
attempts and backoff for retries, and a visibility timeout for jobs
whose worker died. For high volume I’d move to a broker, but for
moderate loads this avoids new infrastructure.”</p>
<p><strong>Q5. What is MVCC and what’s its operational cost?</strong>
“Each update creates a new row version and every transaction reads from
its own snapshot, so readers and writers don’t block each other. The
cost is dead row versions that vacuum must clean. Long open transactions
stop that cleanup and cause bloat, so I monitor for idle-in-transaction
sessions and set timeouts.”</p>
