<h1 id="day-8-wed-db-design-scaling-redis">Day 8 (Wed) — DB design,
scaling, Redis</h1>
<h2 id="hour-1-designing-a-database-end-to-end">Hour 1 — Designing a
database end to end</h2>
<p>“Design the database for X” is a standard round for senior roles.
Candidates often jump straight to tables. The interviewer is watching
for process: requirements first, access patterns before schema, and
explicit trade-offs. Days 6 and 7 gave you the tools; today is about
running the whole exercise in 35 minutes.</p>
<h3 id="a-repeatable-process">1.1 A repeatable process</h3>
<ol type="1">
<li><strong>Clarify requirements (3–5 min).</strong> Core entities and
actions; scale (users, writes per second, data growth per year);
consistency needs (money? inventory?); read/write ratio; latency
targets; retention and compliance (PII, data residency).</li>
<li><strong>List access patterns.</strong> Write them as sentences with
frequency: “customer views their last 20 orders (very frequent)”, “admin
searches orders by date range and status (rare)”. This list drives every
later decision.</li>
<li><strong>Identify entities and relationships.</strong> Sketch the ER
model: entities, cardinalities, which data is shared vs owned.</li>
<li><strong>Choose storage per data type</strong> (1.2): not everything
belongs in one database.</li>
<li><strong>Design the schema</strong> for the top access patterns; mark
what’s embedded, denormalised or snapshotted and why.</li>
<li><strong>Indexes</strong> for each frequent pattern; constraints for
each invariant.</li>
<li><strong>Concurrency and integrity:</strong> where can races happen?
Which fix (atomic update, lock, version)?</li>
<li><strong>Scale and lifecycle:</strong> growth, partitioning or
sharding key, archiving, caching, backups.</li>
<li><strong>Summarise trade-offs</strong> you made and what you’d
revisit at 10× scale.</li>
</ol>
<h3 id="sql-vs-nosql-a-decision-framework">1.2 SQL vs NoSQL: a decision
framework</h3>
<table>
<colgroup>
<col style="width: 25%" />
<col style="width: 25%" />
<col style="width: 25%" />
<col style="width: 25%" />
</colgroup>
<thead>
<tr>
<th>Question</th>
<th>Points to relational (Postgres/MySQL)</th>
<th>Points to document (MongoDB)</th>
<th>Other stores</th>
</tr>
</thead>
<tbody>
<tr>
<td>Are relationships rich and queried in many directions?</td>
<td>Yes</td>
<td>No, mostly read as aggregates</td>
<td>Graph DB (Neo4j) if traversal is the core</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>Are there strict invariants across entities (money, stock)?</td>
<td>Yes, constraints and transactions</td>
<td>Possible, but you work harder</td>
<td>—</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>Is the shape highly variable per record?</td>
<td>JSONB can handle some</td>
<td>Yes</td>
<td>—</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>Is reporting with ad hoc joins needed?</td>
<td>Yes</td>
<td>Harder</td>
<td>Warehouse (BigQuery, Snowflake, ClickHouse)</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>Extreme write throughput, simple key access, multi-region?</td>
<td>Harder</td>
<td>Possible with sharding</td>
<td>Cassandra, DynamoDB</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>Time series, metrics, events</td>
<td>Possible (Timescale)</td>
<td>Time-series collections</td>
<td>InfluxDB, ClickHouse</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>Full-text search, facets, relevance</td>
<td>Basic (<code>tsvector</code>, pg_trgm)</td>
<td>Atlas Search</td>
<td>Elasticsearch / OpenSearch</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>Caching, counters, sessions, leaderboards</td>
<td>—</td>
<td>—</td>
<td>Redis</td>
</tr>
</tbody>
</table>
<p><strong>Polyglot persistence:</strong> use the right store for each
workload, e.g. Postgres for orders and payments, MongoDB for the
catalogue, Redis for carts and sessions, Elasticsearch for search, a
warehouse for analytics. The cost is operational: every store needs
backups, monitoring, expertise, and a way to keep copies in sync (events
or CDC). <strong>My rule:</strong> one primary database by default; add
a store only when a concrete workload clearly needs it.</p>
<h3 id="worked-example-e-commerce-order-platform">1.3 Worked example:
e-commerce order platform</h3>
<p><strong>Requirements (stated assumptions):</strong> 2 million
customers, 50,000 products, 20,000 orders/day with 10× peaks on sale
days, payments must never double-charge, stock must never oversell,
customers see order history instantly, admins run reports.</p>
<p><strong>Access patterns:</strong></p>
<table>
<colgroup>
<col style="width: 33%" />
<col style="width: 33%" />
<col style="width: 33%" />
</colgroup>
<thead>
<tr>
<th>Pattern</th>
<th>Frequency</th>
<th>Store and design</th>
</tr>
</thead>
<tbody>
<tr>
<td>Browse and search products by category, filters</td>
<td>Very high</td>
<td>Catalogue in MongoDB (variable attributes) + search index;
cached</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>View product page</td>
<td>Very high</td>
<td>MongoDB doc with computed rating; Redis/CDN cache</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>Add to cart, view cart</td>
<td>High</td>
<td>Redis hash per cart with TTL; persisted on checkout</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>Place order (reserve stock, create order, start payment)</td>
<td>Medium, spiky</td>
<td>Postgres transaction: atomic stock decrement + order insert;
idempotency key</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>Payment webhook updates order</td>
<td>Medium</td>
<td>Postgres; idempotent by provider event ID</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>Customer views order history</td>
<td>High</td>
<td>Postgres index <code>(customer_id, created_at DESC)</code>, cursor
pagination</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>Admin reports (sales per day/category)</td>
<td>Low, heavy</td>
<td>Read replica or warehouse; daily rollups</td>
</tr>
</tbody>
</table>
<p><strong>Core relational schema (orders side):</strong></p>
<pre class="text"><code>customers(id PK, public_id UNIQUE, email UNIQUE, name, created_at)
addresses(id PK, customer_id FK, line1, city, pin, is_default)
inventory(product_id PK, available CHECK &gt;= 0, reserved CHECK &gt;= 0, version)
orders(id PK, public_id UNIQUE, customer_id FK, status CHECK, total_paise, currency,
       shipping_address JSONB  -- snapshot at order time
       idempotency_key UNIQUE (customer_id, idempotency_key), created_at, updated_at)
order_items(order_id FK, product_id, product_name, unit_price_paise, quantity, PK(order_id, product_id))
payments(id PK, order_id FK, provider, provider_payment_id UNIQUE, status, amount_paise, created_at)
order_events(id PK, order_id FK, type, payload JSONB, created_at)   -- audit trail / outbox</code></pre>
<p>Decisions to say out loud: product name and price are
<strong>snapshotted</strong> into <code>order_items</code>;
<code>provider_payment_id UNIQUE</code> makes webhook processing
idempotent; stock lives in Postgres because it’s an invariant tied to
orders, while descriptive product data lives in MongoDB;
<code>order_events</code> doubles as an audit log and a transactional
outbox (Week 3).</p>
<h3 id="data-lifecycle">1.4 Data lifecycle</h3>
<p>Always mention these briefly; they show production experience:</p>
<ul>
<li><strong>Growth:</strong> 20,000 orders/day ≈ 7.3 million/year; with
items and events, plan partitioning by month for <code>orders</code>
after a few years, or archive older than 2 years to cold storage.</li>
<li><strong>Backups:</strong> point-in-time recovery, tested restores
(an untested backup isn’t a backup).</li>
<li><strong>PII and compliance:</strong> encrypt sensitive columns or
the whole volume, limit access, support deletion requests (India’s DPDP
Act, GDPR for EU users), mask data in non-production environments.</li>
<li><strong>Retention:</strong> keep financial records for the legally
required period; delete logs and sessions by TTL.</li>
</ul>
<h3 id="how-id-answer-hour-1-7">How I’d answer — Hour 1</h3>
<p><strong>Q1. Design the database for an e-commerce platform.</strong>
Walk the process: requirements and scale, access patterns table, choice
of stores, core schema, indexes, concurrency (atomic stock decrement,
idempotency keys, unique provider payment ID), then lifecycle. Finish
with: “At 10×, I’d partition orders by month, move reporting to a
warehouse fed by CDC, and consider sharding by customer.”</p>
<p><strong>Q2. When would you use more than one database?</strong> “When
a workload has needs the primary store can’t serve well: full-text
search with relevance goes to Elasticsearch, ephemeral high-throughput
data like carts and sessions to Redis, analytics to a warehouse. Each
added store costs operations and consistency work, so I add one only
with a clear reason and sync it via events or CDC rather than dual
writes.”</p>
<p><strong>Q3. Why not write to both Postgres and Elasticsearch in the
same request?</strong> “Dual writes aren’t atomic. If the second write
fails, the two stores disagree with no record of it. I write to the
source of truth and propagate changes through an outbox or CDC, which
retries until the search index catches up.”</p>
<h3 id="practice-21">Practice</h3>
<ul class="task-list">
<li><label><input type="checkbox" />Write the access-patterns table for
the capstone (at least 10 patterns) and map each to a store, schema and
index</label></li>
<li><label><input type="checkbox" />Draw the full capstone ERD (Postgres
side) and commit it to the repo as a Mermaid diagram</label></li>
<li><label><input type="checkbox" />Time yourself: design a ride-hailing
app’s database in 35 minutes, talking out loud</label></li>
</ul>
<h2 id="hour-2-scaling-the-data-layer">Hour 2 — Scaling the data
layer</h2>
<p>The database is almost always the hardest part of a system to scale,
because it holds state. A senior answer is a ladder: you climb only as
far as the load requires, cheapest and least disruptive steps first.
Jumping straight to “shard it” is a red flag for interviewers.</p>
<h3 id="the-scaling-ladder">2.1 The scaling ladder</h3>
<table>
<colgroup>
<col style="width: 33%" />
<col style="width: 33%" />
<col style="width: 33%" />
</colgroup>
<thead>
<tr>
<th>Step</th>
<th>What</th>
<th>Cost / risk</th>
</tr>
</thead>
<tbody>
<tr>
<td>1. Optimise</td>
<td>Indexes, query fixes, N+1 removal, connection pooling</td>
<td>Cheap; often 10–100× gains</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>2. Scale up</td>
<td>Bigger instance (CPU, RAM for the working set, faster disks)</td>
<td>Cheap until it isn’t; has a ceiling</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>3. Cache</td>
<td>Redis / CDN for hot reads (Hour 3)</td>
<td>Moderate; invalidation and staleness</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>4. Read replicas</td>
<td>Send stale-tolerant reads to replicas</td>
<td>Moderate; replication lag, read-your-writes issues</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>5. Move workloads out</td>
<td>Analytics to a warehouse, search to Elasticsearch, queues to a
broker</td>
<td>Moderate; sync via CDC/events</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>6. Partition</td>
<td>Split big tables inside one database (by time, by tenant)</td>
<td>Moderate; query patterns must include the key</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>7. Split by domain</td>
<td>Separate databases per service (orders DB, catalogue DB)</td>
<td>High; no cross-domain joins or transactions</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>8. Shard</td>
<td>Split one dataset across many database servers</td>
<td>Highest; resharding, cross-shard queries, operations</td>
</tr>
</tbody>
</table>
<h3 id="read-replicas">2.2 Read replicas</h3>
<p>Good for read-heavy systems where some reads tolerate a little
staleness. Route explicitly in code (a <code>readPool</code> and a
<code>writePool</code>), and keep on the primary: anything read right
after the user writes it, anything used to make a write decision
(balance checks), and admin screens where staleness confuses people.
Monitor replication lag and stop routing to a replica that falls too far
behind.</p>
<h3 id="partitioning-inside-one-database">2.3 Partitioning (inside one
database)</h3>
<p><strong>What it is:</strong> one logical table split into physical
pieces by a key, while queries still target the parent table.</p>
<div class="sourceCode" id="cb132"><pre
class="sourceCode sql"><code class="sourceCode sql"><span id="cb132-1"><a href="#cb132-1" aria-hidden="true" tabindex="-1"></a><span class="kw">CREATE</span> <span class="kw">TABLE</span> <span class="kw">events</span> (</span>
<span id="cb132-2"><a href="#cb132-2" aria-hidden="true" tabindex="-1"></a>  <span class="kw">id</span> BIGINT <span class="kw">GENERATED</span> ALWAYS <span class="kw">AS</span> IDENTITY,</span>
<span id="cb132-3"><a href="#cb132-3" aria-hidden="true" tabindex="-1"></a>  tenant_id BIGINT <span class="kw">NOT</span> <span class="kw">NULL</span>,</span>
<span id="cb132-4"><a href="#cb132-4" aria-hidden="true" tabindex="-1"></a>  <span class="kw">type</span> TEXT <span class="kw">NOT</span> <span class="kw">NULL</span>,</span>
<span id="cb132-5"><a href="#cb132-5" aria-hidden="true" tabindex="-1"></a>  payload JSONB,</span>
<span id="cb132-6"><a href="#cb132-6" aria-hidden="true" tabindex="-1"></a>  created_at TIMESTAMPTZ <span class="kw">NOT</span> <span class="kw">NULL</span>,</span>
<span id="cb132-7"><a href="#cb132-7" aria-hidden="true" tabindex="-1"></a>  <span class="kw">PRIMARY</span> <span class="kw">KEY</span> (<span class="kw">id</span>, created_at)              <span class="co">-- partition key must be part of the PK</span></span>
<span id="cb132-8"><a href="#cb132-8" aria-hidden="true" tabindex="-1"></a>) <span class="kw">PARTITION</span> <span class="kw">BY</span> <span class="kw">RANGE</span> (created_at);</span>
<span id="cb132-9"><a href="#cb132-9" aria-hidden="true" tabindex="-1"></a></span>
<span id="cb132-10"><a href="#cb132-10" aria-hidden="true" tabindex="-1"></a><span class="kw">CREATE</span> <span class="kw">TABLE</span> events_2026_11 <span class="kw">PARTITION</span> <span class="kw">OF</span> <span class="kw">events</span></span>
<span id="cb132-11"><a href="#cb132-11" aria-hidden="true" tabindex="-1"></a>  <span class="cf">FOR</span> <span class="kw">VALUES</span> <span class="kw">FROM</span> (<span class="st">&#39;2026-11-01&#39;</span>) <span class="kw">TO</span> (<span class="st">&#39;2026-12-01&#39;</span>);</span></code></pre></div>
<p>Benefits: queries with a date filter scan only relevant partitions
(<strong>partition pruning</strong>); dropping a whole month is instant
(<code>DROP TABLE events_2024_01</code>) instead of a huge
<code>DELETE</code> that bloats the table; indexes stay smaller. Types:
<strong>range</strong> (time, the most common), <strong>list</strong>
(region, tenant tier), <strong>hash</strong> (even spread). Tools like
<code>pg_partman</code> create future partitions automatically. Queries
that don’t include the partition key scan every partition, so choose the
key from the access patterns.</p>
<h3 id="sharding-across-servers">2.4 Sharding (across servers)</h3>
<p><strong>What it is:</strong> each server (shard) holds a subset of
rows; the application or a router sends each query to the right
shard.</p>
<table>
<colgroup>
<col style="width: 25%" />
<col style="width: 25%" />
<col style="width: 25%" />
<col style="width: 25%" />
</colgroup>
<thead>
<tr>
<th>Strategy</th>
<th>How</th>
<th>Good</th>
<th>Bad</th>
</tr>
</thead>
<tbody>
<tr>
<td>Range</td>
<td><code>customer_id 1–1M</code> → shard 1</td>
<td>Range queries stay on one shard</td>
<td>Hotspots if new data clusters (newest IDs all on one shard)</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>Hash</td>
<td><code>hash(customer_id) % N</code></td>
<td>Even spread</td>
<td>Changing N moves almost everything (fixed by consistent
hashing)</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>Directory / lookup</td>
<td>A table maps key → shard</td>
<td>Flexible moves, per-tenant placement</td>
<td>Lookup service is a dependency and must be fast</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>Geo / tenant</td>
<td>EU customers → EU shard</td>
<td>Data residency, latency</td>
<td>Uneven sizes</td>
</tr>
</tbody>
</table>
<p><strong>Problems sharding brings:</strong> cross-shard joins and
transactions disappear (design so most operations stay within one shard
key); global unique constraints get hard (use UUIDs or ID generators
like Snowflake IDs); aggregates need scatter-gather; rebalancing as data
grows; hot keys (one celebrity customer or tenant) can overload a single
shard.</p>
<p><strong>Before building it yourself,</strong> consider managed
options that shard for you: MongoDB sharding, Citus (distributed
Postgres), Vitess (MySQL, used by large platforms), or distributed SQL
like CockroachDB, YugabyteDB, Spanner. Mentioning these shows you know
hand-rolled sharding is a last resort.</p>
<h3 id="consistent-hashing">2.5 Consistent hashing</h3>
<p><strong>Problem:</strong> with <code>hash(key) % N</code>, adding one
server changes N, and almost every key maps to a different server, so
caches empty and data must move.</p>
<p><strong>What it is:</strong> place servers and keys on the same hash
ring (0 to 2^32). Each key belongs to the first server clockwise from
it. Adding or removing a server only moves the keys between it and its
neighbour, roughly 1/N of the keys.</p>
<p><strong>Virtual nodes:</strong> each physical server appears at many
points on the ring (100–200 vnodes), which evens out the load and lets a
larger server take more vnodes.</p>
<p>Used by: Cassandra and DynamoDB partitioning, Redis Cluster (with
fixed 16,384 hash slots, a related idea), load balancers with sticky
routing, distributed caches.</p>
<h3 id="cqrs-read-models">2.6 CQRS read models</h3>
<p><strong>What it is:</strong> Command Query Responsibility
Segregation: writes go to a model optimised for correctness (normalised
Postgres), and events update separate read models optimised for specific
queries (a denormalised MongoDB document, an Elasticsearch index, a
Redis leaderboard).</p>
<p>Example: the order service writes normalised orders; an event updates
a <code>customer_order_summary</code> document with recent orders and
totals, which the “My account” page reads in one fetch.</p>
<p>Trade-offs: read models are <strong>eventually consistent</strong>
(milliseconds to seconds behind) and you now maintain projection code
and replays. Use it where read and write needs genuinely diverge, not
for every CRUD screen.</p>
<h3 id="how-id-answer-hour-2-7">How I’d answer — Hour 2</h3>
<p><strong>Q1. Our Postgres database is at 90% CPU. What do you
do?</strong> “Climb the ladder. First <code>pg_stat_statements</code> to
find the top queries by total time and fix indexes and N+1s; that’s
usually the biggest win. Check connection counts and add PgBouncer. Then
cache hot reads in Redis, move stale-tolerant reads and reports to a
replica, and offload analytics. Scale the instance up if needed.
Partitioning or sharding only if the data size or write rate truly
exceeds one server.”</p>
<p><strong>Q2. Partitioning vs sharding?</strong> “Partitioning splits a
table into pieces inside one database server: easier pruning, faster
deletes of old data, smaller indexes, no change to the application.
Sharding spreads data across many servers to scale writes and storage
beyond one machine, at the cost of cross-shard joins, transactions and
much more operational work.”</p>
<p><strong>Q3. Explain consistent hashing.</strong> “Servers and keys
are hashed onto the same ring and each key goes to the next server
clockwise. Adding a server only takes over keys from its neighbour,
about 1/N of them, instead of reshuffling everything like modulo
hashing. Virtual nodes spread each server around the ring to balance
load.”</p>
<p><strong>Q4. How would you pick a shard key for a multi-tenant
SaaS?</strong> “Usually <code>tenant_id</code>, because almost every
query is scoped to one tenant, so it stays on one shard with its joins
and transactions. Large tenants can get dedicated shards via a directory
mapping, and very small ones are packed together. Cross-tenant analytics
goes to a warehouse.”</p>
<h3 id="practice-22">Practice</h3>
<ul class="task-list">
<li><label><input type="checkbox" />Partition the capstone’s
<code>order_events</code> table by month with <code>pg_partman</code>;
verify partition pruning with EXPLAIN</label></li>
<li><label><input type="checkbox" />Implement a read/write pool split in
the order repository; route order history to the replica, but “just
placed” reads to the primary</label></li>
<li><label><input type="checkbox" />Implement a small consistent-hash
ring with virtual nodes in TypeScript; measure how many keys move when
adding a node</label></li>
</ul>
<h2 id="hour-3-redis-deep-dive">Hour 3 — Redis deep dive</h2>
<p>Most Node developers use Redis as <code>get</code>/<code>set</code>
with a TTL. Senior interviews go further: which data structure fits a
leaderboard, why a cache made an outage worse, whether a Redis lock is
safe for payments, and what happens when Redis restarts. Redis appears
in almost every system design answer, so know it properly.</p>
<h3 id="what-it-is-1">3.1 What it is</h3>
<p><strong>What it is:</strong> an in-memory data structure server.
Commands execute on a single main thread (network I/O can use extra
threads in recent versions), so each command is atomic and extremely
fast, but one slow command blocks everyone.</p>
<p>Licensing context worth knowing: Redis moved to a source-available
licence in March 2024, which triggered the Linux Foundation fork
<strong>Valkey</strong> (AWS offers ElastiCache for Valkey at a lower
price than ElastiCache for Redis). With Redis 8 (May 2025) Redis became
open source again under AGPLv3 and folded the former Redis Stack
features (JSON, search, time series, probabilistic types, and new vector
sets) into core. Both are command-compatible for everything in this
hour.</p>
<h3 id="data-structures-and-what-to-use-them-for">3.2 Data structures
and what to use them for</h3>
<table>
<colgroup>
<col style="width: 33%" />
<col style="width: 33%" />
<col style="width: 33%" />
</colgroup>
<thead>
<tr>
<th>Structure</th>
<th>Commands</th>
<th>Use case</th>
</tr>
</thead>
<tbody>
<tr>
<td>String</td>
<td><code>SET k v EX 300 NX</code>, <code>GET</code>, <code>INCR</code>,
<code>INCRBY</code></td>
<td>Cache entries, counters, rate-limit counters, idempotency keys,
locks</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>Hash</td>
<td><code>HSET cart:42 sku123 2</code>, <code>HGETALL</code>,
<code>HINCRBY</code></td>
<td>Objects with fields: carts, user sessions, product summaries</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>List</td>
<td><code>LPUSH</code>, <code>RPOP</code>, <code>LRANGE</code>,
<code>BLPOP</code></td>
<td>Simple queues, recent-activity lists (with <code>LTRIM</code>)</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>Set</td>
<td><code>SADD</code>, <code>SISMEMBER</code>, <code>SINTER</code></td>
<td>Unique visitors per day, tags, “users who liked”</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>Sorted set</td>
<td><code>ZADD board 1500 user:7</code>,
<code>ZREVRANGE board 0 9 WITHSCORES</code>, <code>ZRANK</code></td>
<td>Leaderboards, priority queues, rate-limit sliding windows,
“trending”</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>Stream</td>
<td><code>XADD</code>, <code>XREADGROUP</code>, <code>XACK</code></td>
<td>Durable event log with consumer groups (lightweight Kafka-like)</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>Pub/Sub</td>
<td><code>PUBLISH</code>, <code>SUBSCRIBE</code></td>
<td>Fire-and-forget broadcasts: cache invalidation, WebSocket fan-out
across pods</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>HyperLogLog</td>
<td><code>PFADD</code>, <code>PFCOUNT</code></td>
<td>Approximate unique counts in ~12 KB (unique visitors)</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>Bitmap</td>
<td><code>SETBIT</code>, <code>BITCOUNT</code></td>
<td>Daily active flags per user ID, feature flags</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>Geo</td>
<td><code>GEOADD</code>, <code>GEOSEARCH</code></td>
<td>Nearby stores or drivers</td>
</tr>
</tbody>
</table>
<p><strong>Pub/Sub vs Streams:</strong> Pub/Sub delivers only to
subscribers connected right now; if a pod is restarting, it misses
messages. Streams persist messages, support consumer groups,
acknowledgements and replay. Use Pub/Sub for best-effort notifications,
Streams (or a real broker) for work that must not be lost.</p>
<h3 id="caching-patterns">3.3 Caching patterns</h3>
<table>
<colgroup>
<col style="width: 25%" />
<col style="width: 25%" />
<col style="width: 25%" />
<col style="width: 25%" />
</colgroup>
<thead>
<tr>
<th>Pattern</th>
<th>How</th>
<th>Good</th>
<th>Risk</th>
</tr>
</thead>
<tbody>
<tr>
<td><strong>Cache-aside</strong> (lazy)</td>
<td>App reads cache; on miss reads DB and fills cache; on write updates
DB and deletes key</td>
<td>Simple, only caches what’s used, cache failure isn’t fatal</td>
<td>First request after expiry is slow; stampede on hot keys</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>Read-through</td>
<td>Cache library loads from DB on miss</td>
<td>Cleaner app code</td>
<td>Same staleness issues</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>Write-through</td>
<td>Write to cache and DB together</td>
<td>Cache always fresh for written keys</td>
<td>Slower writes; caches data nobody reads</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>Write-behind</td>
<td>Write to cache, flush to DB asynchronously</td>
<td>Very fast writes</td>
<td>Data loss if cache dies before flushing; rarely right for business
data</td>
</tr>
</tbody>
</table>
<p><strong>My default:</strong> cache-aside with TTL plus explicit
invalidation on writes (delete, don’t update the key, to avoid races
where an older value overwrites a newer one). Plus the stampede
protections from Day 4: TTL jitter and single-flight rebuilds.</p>
<p><strong>The outage pattern to mention:</strong> the cache hides how
much load the database really gets. When Redis restarts or a big key set
expires at once, the full load hits a database sized for 10% of traffic,
and it falls over (the <strong>thundering herd</strong> / cold cache
problem). Defences: jittered TTLs, request coalescing, warming critical
keys, rate-limiting cache rebuilds, and capacity-planning the DB for a
cold-cache scenario.</p>
<h3 id="memory-eviction-persistence">3.4 Memory, eviction,
persistence</h3>
<ul>
<li>Set <code>maxmemory</code> and a <strong>policy</strong>.
<code>noeviction</code> (the default) returns errors when full; for a
pure cache, use <code>allkeys-lru</code> or <code>allkeys-lfu</code>;
<code>volatile-*</code> policies evict only keys with a TTL, useful when
Redis mixes cache data with data that must stay.</li>
<li><strong>Persistence:</strong> RDB (periodic snapshots: compact, fast
restarts, loses data since the last snapshot) and AOF (append-only log
of writes, <code>fsync</code> every second by default: lose about a
second at most). Pure cache: persistence can be off. Sessions, carts,
rate limits: AOF on.</li>
<li>Avoid <strong>big keys</strong> (a hash with millions of fields, a
50 MB string): they block the thread when read or deleted (use
<code>UNLINK</code> instead of <code>DEL</code> for async
deletion).</li>
<li>Never run <code>KEYS *</code> in production; it scans everything and
blocks. Use <code>SCAN</code> with a cursor.</li>
<li><strong>Hot keys</strong> (one key getting most traffic) can
saturate a single node even in a cluster; mitigate with local in-process
caching or key replication.</li>
</ul>
<h3 id="high-availability-and-scaling">3.5 High availability and
scaling</h3>
<table>
<colgroup>
<col style="width: 50%" />
<col style="width: 50%" />
</colgroup>
<thead>
<tr>
<th>Setup</th>
<th>What it gives</th>
</tr>
</thead>
<tbody>
<tr>
<td>Primary + replicas</td>
<td>Read scaling, copies of data; replication is asynchronous, so a
failover can lose the last writes</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>Sentinel</td>
<td>Monitors and promotes a replica on primary failure; clients ask
Sentinel for the current primary</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>Redis Cluster</td>
<td>Shards data across nodes by <strong>16,384 hash slots</strong>; each
primary has replicas; clients are redirected to the right node</td>
</tr>
</tbody>
</table>
<p>In a cluster, multi-key commands and Lua scripts must touch keys in
the same slot. Force related keys together with <strong>hash
tags</strong>: <code>cart:{user42}</code> and
<code>cart-meta:{user42}</code> hash only the part in braces.</p>
<h3 id="distributed-locks-use-with-care">3.6 Distributed locks: use with
care</h3>
<div class="sourceCode" id="cb133"><pre
class="sourceCode ts"><code class="sourceCode typescript"><span id="cb133-1"><a href="#cb133-1" aria-hidden="true" tabindex="-1"></a><span class="kw">const</span> token <span class="op">=</span> crypto<span class="op">.</span><span class="fu">randomUUID</span>()<span class="op">;</span></span>
<span id="cb133-2"><a href="#cb133-2" aria-hidden="true" tabindex="-1"></a><span class="kw">const</span> ok <span class="op">=</span> <span class="cf">await</span> redis<span class="op">.</span><span class="fu">set</span>(<span class="vs">`lock:report:</span><span class="sc">${</span>id<span class="sc">}</span><span class="vs">`</span><span class="op">,</span> token<span class="op">,</span> <span class="st">&#39;PX&#39;</span><span class="op">,</span> <span class="dv">30_000</span><span class="op">,</span> <span class="st">&#39;NX&#39;</span>)<span class="op">;</span>   <span class="co">// acquire with expiry</span></span>
<span id="cb133-3"><a href="#cb133-3" aria-hidden="true" tabindex="-1"></a><span class="cf">if</span> (<span class="op">!</span>ok) <span class="cf">return</span><span class="op">;</span>                                                                 <span class="co">// someone else holds it</span></span>
<span id="cb133-4"><a href="#cb133-4" aria-hidden="true" tabindex="-1"></a><span class="cf">try</span> {</span>
<span id="cb133-5"><a href="#cb133-5" aria-hidden="true" tabindex="-1"></a>  <span class="cf">await</span> <span class="fu">generateReport</span>(id)<span class="op">;</span></span>
<span id="cb133-6"><a href="#cb133-6" aria-hidden="true" tabindex="-1"></a>} <span class="cf">finally</span> {</span>
<span id="cb133-7"><a href="#cb133-7" aria-hidden="true" tabindex="-1"></a>  <span class="co">// release only if we still own it: compare-and-delete must be atomic, hence Lua</span></span>
<span id="cb133-8"><a href="#cb133-8" aria-hidden="true" tabindex="-1"></a>  <span class="cf">await</span> redis<span class="op">.</span><span class="fu">eval</span>(</span>
<span id="cb133-9"><a href="#cb133-9" aria-hidden="true" tabindex="-1"></a>    <span class="st">&quot;if redis.call(&#39;get&#39;, KEYS[1]) == ARGV[1] then return redis.call(&#39;del&#39;, KEYS[1]) else return 0 end&quot;</span><span class="op">,</span></span>
<span id="cb133-10"><a href="#cb133-10" aria-hidden="true" tabindex="-1"></a>    <span class="dv">1</span><span class="op">,</span> <span class="vs">`lock:report:</span><span class="sc">${</span>id<span class="sc">}</span><span class="vs">`</span><span class="op">,</span> token<span class="op">,</span></span>
<span id="cb133-11"><a href="#cb133-11" aria-hidden="true" tabindex="-1"></a>  )<span class="op">;</span></span>
<span id="cb133-12"><a href="#cb133-12" aria-hidden="true" tabindex="-1"></a>}</span></code></pre></div>
<p>The senior caveat: a Redis lock is <strong>best-effort</strong>. If
the holder pauses (GC, network) longer than the expiry, the lock
expires, another process takes it, and both now think they hold it. Even
the multi-node Redlock algorithm has well-known criticism on this point.
So: fine for <strong>efficiency</strong> (avoid two workers doing the
same report), not sufficient for <strong>correctness</strong> (money,
stock). For correctness, rely on the database: unique constraints,
conditional updates, <code>SELECT FOR UPDATE</code>, or fencing tokens
checked by the resource being protected.</p>
<h3 id="other-everyday-uses">3.7 Other everyday uses</h3>
<ul>
<li><strong>Rate limiting:</strong> atomic Lua script implementing a
token bucket or sliding window (Day 4), keyed by user or API key.</li>
<li><strong>Sessions:</strong> hash per session with TTL refreshed on
activity.</li>
<li><strong>Idempotency keys:</strong>
<code>SET idem:{key} 'in_progress' NX EX 86400</code>, then store the
response.</li>
<li><strong>Leaderboards:</strong> sorted sets, <code>ZINCRBY</code> on
each score change, <code>ZREVRANGE</code> for the top 10,
<code>ZREVRANK</code> for a user’s position. O(log N) updates even with
millions of players.</li>
<li><strong>Queues:</strong> BullMQ (built on Redis) for background jobs
in Node: retries, delays, priorities, rate limits, a dashboard. A very
common, solid choice before needing RabbitMQ or Kafka.</li>
</ul>
<h3 id="how-id-answer-hour-3-7">How I’d answer — Hour 3</h3>
<p><strong>Q1. How would you build a real-time leaderboard for a million
users?</strong> “A Redis sorted set: <code>ZINCRBY</code> when a score
changes, <code>ZREVRANGE 0 9 WITHSCORES</code> for the top 10,
<code>ZREVRANK</code> for a user’s rank, all O(log N). Persist scores in
the main database as the source of truth, and rebuild the set from it if
Redis is lost. For per-period boards, one key per week with a TTL.”</p>
<p><strong>Q2. Which caching strategy do you use and how do you keep it
consistent?</strong> “Cache-aside with TTLs: read from cache, fall back
to the DB and populate. On writes, update the DB then delete the key
rather than updating it, to avoid races. TTL jitter and single-flight
protect against stampedes. For data where staleness is unacceptable,
like balances, I don’t cache at all.”</p>
<p><strong>Q3. Is a Redis lock safe for preventing double
payments?</strong> “Not on its own. A lock can expire while its holder
is paused, so two processes can both believe they hold it. I use it to
avoid duplicate work, but correctness comes from the database: an
idempotency key with a unique constraint and conditional updates, so
even if two workers run, only one charge is recorded.”</p>
<p><strong>Q4. Redis went down and the whole platform followed. Why, and
what would you change?</strong> “The database was sized for cached
traffic, and every request fell through to it at once. I’d make the app
degrade gracefully when Redis is unavailable (short timeouts, circuit
breaker, serve without cache with rate limiting), run Redis with
replicas and automatic failover, use jittered TTLs, and load-test the
cold-cache scenario so the database can survive it.”</p>

with a 7-day TTL</label></li>
<li><label><input type="checkbox" />Build a product-views leaderboard
with a sorted set and a unique-visitors count with
HyperLogLog</label></li>
<li><label><input type="checkbox" />Add a BullMQ queue for order
confirmation emails with retries and backoff</label></li>

test showing what happens when the TTL is shorter than the
work</label></li>
</ul>
<h2 id="hour-4-cap-consistency-models-two-design-exercises">Hour 4 —
CAP, consistency models, two design exercises</h2>
<p>CAP comes up in nearly every system design round, and it’s usually
misquoted. Learn the precise version in 15 minutes, then spend the rest
of the hour on two full database designs out loud. Those designs are the
real practice.</p>
<h3 id="cap-stated-correctly">4.1 CAP, stated correctly</h3>
<p><strong>What it says:</strong> in a distributed system, when a
<strong>network partition</strong> happens (nodes can’t talk to each
other), you must choose between:</p>
<ul>
<li><strong>Consistency (C):</strong> every read sees the latest write
(or gets an error), or</li>
<li><strong>Availability (A):</strong> every request gets a non-error
response, possibly with stale data.</li>
</ul>
<p>Partitions aren’t optional in real networks, so “CA systems” don’t
exist in a distributed setting. The real choice is <strong>CP or AP
during a partition</strong>:</p>
<ul>
<li><strong>CP:</strong> refuse or delay some requests to stay correct.
Example: a bank balance, seat inventory, a leader-based database
refusing writes on the minority side.</li>
<li><strong>AP:</strong> keep answering, reconcile later. Example:
shopping cart, likes count, social feed, DNS.</li>
</ul>
<p><strong>PACELC</strong> adds the part that matters day to day:
<strong>if Partition, choose A or C; Else (normal operation), choose
Latency or Consistency.</strong> Synchronous replication to another
region gives consistency but adds latency to every write; asynchronous
replication is fast but can lose or lag data. DynamoDB and Cassandra
lean PA/EL (tunable); Spanner and CockroachDB lean PC/EC.</p>
<p>The senior point: the choice is <strong>per feature, not per
system</strong>. In one e-commerce platform, payments and stock are CP,
while recommendations, reviews and view counts are AP.</p>
<h3 id="consistency-models">4.2 Consistency models</h3>
<table>
<colgroup>
<col style="width: 33%" />
<col style="width: 33%" />
<col style="width: 33%" />
</colgroup>
<thead>
<tr>
<th>Model</th>
<th>Guarantee</th>
<th>Example</th>
</tr>
</thead>
<tbody>
<tr>
<td>Strong / linearizable</td>
<td>Reads always see the latest committed write</td>
<td>Primary database reads, Spanner</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>Sequential</td>
<td>Everyone sees operations in the same order</td>
<td>Some coordination systems</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>Causal</td>
<td>Related operations seen in order (a reply after its comment)</td>
<td>MongoDB causal sessions</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>Read-your-writes</td>
<td>A user always sees their own updates</td>
<td>Read from primary after writes (Day 6)</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>Monotonic reads</td>
<td>You never see data go backwards in time</td>
<td>Stick a user to one replica</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>Eventual</td>
<td>Replicas converge if writes stop</td>
<td>DNS, caches, CQRS read models, likes counts</td>
</tr>
</tbody>
</table>
<p><strong>Quorums</strong> (Dynamo-style systems): with N replicas,
write to W and read from R. If <strong>R + W &gt; N</strong>, every read
overlaps at least one replica with the latest write. N=3, W=2, R=2 is
the common balanced choice; W=1 favours write latency, R=1 favours read
latency.</p>
<h3 id="design-exercise-1-movie-ticket-booking-bookmyshow">4.3 Design
exercise 1: movie ticket booking (BookMyShow)</h3>
<p><strong>Key requirement:</strong> no seat is ever sold twice, even
with thousands of people trying to book the same show when sales open.
That makes seat booking <strong>CP</strong>; browsing movies and
showtimes is <strong>AP</strong> and heavily cached.</p>
<p><strong>Schema (Postgres):</strong></p>
<pre class="text"><code>cities(id, name)
theatres(id, city_id, name, address)
screens(id, theatre_id, name)
seats(id, screen_id, row_label, number, category)             -- physical layout
movies(id, title, language, duration_min, certificate)
shows(id, screen_id, movie_id, starts_at, base_price_paise)   -- index (movie_id, starts_at), (screen_id, starts_at)
show_seats(show_id, seat_id, status, held_by, held_until, booking_id, price_paise,
           PRIMARY KEY (show_id, seat_id))                     -- one row per seat per show
bookings(id, user_id, show_id, status, total_paise, idempotency_key UNIQUE, created_at)
payments(id, booking_id, provider_payment_id UNIQUE, status, amount_paise)</code></pre>
<p><strong>Holding seats atomically</strong> (user picks 3 seats; hold
for 10 minutes while paying):</p>
<div class="sourceCode" id="cb135"><pre
class="sourceCode sql"><code class="sourceCode sql"><span id="cb135-1"><a href="#cb135-1" aria-hidden="true" tabindex="-1"></a><span class="kw">UPDATE</span> show_seats</span>
<span id="cb135-2"><a href="#cb135-2" aria-hidden="true" tabindex="-1"></a><span class="kw">SET</span> status <span class="op">=</span> <span class="st">&#39;held&#39;</span>, held_by <span class="op">=</span> $user, held_until <span class="op">=</span> now() <span class="op">+</span> <span class="dt">interval</span> <span class="st">&#39;10 minutes&#39;</span></span>
<span id="cb135-3"><a href="#cb135-3" aria-hidden="true" tabindex="-1"></a><span class="kw">WHERE</span> show_id <span class="op">=</span> $show <span class="kw">AND</span> seat_id <span class="op">=</span> <span class="kw">ANY</span>($seats)</span>
<span id="cb135-4"><a href="#cb135-4" aria-hidden="true" tabindex="-1"></a>  <span class="kw">AND</span> (status <span class="op">=</span> <span class="st">&#39;available&#39;</span> <span class="kw">OR</span> (status <span class="op">=</span> <span class="st">&#39;held&#39;</span> <span class="kw">AND</span> held_until <span class="op">&lt;</span> now()));</span>
<span id="cb135-5"><a href="#cb135-5" aria-hidden="true" tabindex="-1"></a><span class="co">-- In a transaction: if rows updated != number of seats requested, ROLLBACK and tell the user</span></span>
<span id="cb135-6"><a href="#cb135-6" aria-hidden="true" tabindex="-1"></a><span class="co">-- some seats were just taken. No two users can hold the same seat.</span></span></code></pre></div>
<p><strong>Confirming after payment:</strong>
<code>UPDATE show_seats SET status = 'booked', booking_id = $b WHERE show_id = $show AND seat_id = ANY($seats) AND held_by = $user AND held_until &gt; now()</code>.
If the hold expired before the payment webhook arrived, refund
automatically. Expired holds become available lazily (the condition
above) without needing a cleanup job to be on time.</p>
<p><strong>Scale and peaks:</strong> cache city → movies → shows
listings (minutes of staleness are fine); cache the seat map for a few
seconds and always re-check at hold time; for huge launches, put a
<strong>virtual waiting room</strong> (queue) in front so only a
controlled number of users reach seat selection; partition
<code>show_seats</code> by show date and archive past shows. The
trade-off to say: the seat map may show a seat as free that was just
taken; the hold step is the authority.</p>
<h3 id="design-exercise-2-social-feed-instagram-style">4.4 Design
exercise 2: social feed (Instagram-style)</h3>
<p><strong>Key requirements:</strong> very read-heavy (feeds opened far
more often than posts are created), eventual consistency is acceptable
(a post may appear a few seconds late), media is large.</p>
<p><strong>Storage choices:</strong></p>
<table>
<colgroup>
<col style="width: 33%" />
<col style="width: 33%" />
<col style="width: 33%" />
</colgroup>
<thead>
<tr>
<th>Data</th>
<th>Store</th>
<th>Why</th>
</tr>
</thead>
<tbody>
<tr>
<td>Users, profiles</td>
<td>Postgres</td>
<td>Relational, moderate size</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>Follows</td>
<td>Postgres table <code>(follower_id, followee_id)</code> with indexes
both ways, or a graph store at huge scale</td>
<td>“Who do I follow” and “who follows me”</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>Posts metadata</td>
<td>Wide-column (Cassandra/DynamoDB) partitioned by
<code>user_id</code>, sorted by time; or sharded Postgres</td>
<td>Huge write volume, always read by author and time</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>Media</td>
<td>Object storage (S3) + CDN</td>
<td>Large files, served close to users</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>Feeds</td>
<td>Redis sorted set per user (post IDs scored by time), capped at a few
hundred</td>
<td>Feed reads in O(log N)</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>Likes / counters</td>
<td>Redis <code>INCR</code>, flushed to the database asynchronously; or
sharded counters</td>
<td>Very high write contention on popular posts</td>
</tr>
</tbody>
</table>
<p><strong>Feed generation: the classic trade-off:</strong></p>
<ul>
<li><strong>Fan-out on write (push):</strong> when a user posts, a
worker adds the post ID to every follower’s feed. Reads are instant.
Breaks for celebrities: one post by an account with 50 million followers
means 50 million writes.</li>
<li><strong>Fan-out on read (pull):</strong> at read time, fetch recent
posts from everyone the user follows and merge. No write amplification,
but slow reads for users following thousands.</li>
<li><strong>Hybrid (what large platforms do):</strong> push for normal
accounts; for accounts above a follower threshold, don’t fan out, and
merge their recent posts in at read time. Ranking (ML) then reorders the
candidate list.</li>
</ul>
<p>Other points: post creation publishes an event; fan-out runs
asynchronously on a queue; inactive users’ feeds aren’t precomputed
(build on next login); everything around likes and counts is AP and
eventually consistent.</p>
<h3 id="how-id-answer-hour-4-7">How I’d answer — Hour 4</h3>
<p><strong>Q1. Explain CAP. Is MongoDB CP or AP?</strong> “During a
network partition you choose between consistency and availability.
Partitions are unavoidable, so it’s CP versus AP. MongoDB with majority
write concern and primary reads behaves CP: the minority side can’t
accept writes. Reading from secondaries makes reads more available but
possibly stale. In practice the choice is per feature: payments CP,
feeds AP. PACELC adds that even without partitions you trade latency
against consistency.”</p>
<p><strong>Q2. How do you prevent two people booking the same
seat?</strong> “One row per seat per show, and a conditional update that
moves seats from available, or expired hold, to held for this user,
checking that the number of rows updated equals the number requested,
all in one transaction. Payment confirmation is another conditional
update checking the hold is still ours. The database is the single
source of truth; caches only display.”</p>
<p><strong>Q3. Fan-out on write or read for a news feed?</strong>
“Hybrid. Fan-out on write for most users so feed reads are a single
Redis lookup, but skip fan-out for celebrity accounts and merge their
recent posts at read time, avoiding millions of writes per post. Fan-out
runs asynchronously from a queue, and the feed is eventually consistent,
which users accept.”</p>

<h1 id="day-9-thu-react-interview-revision-machine-coding">Day 9 (Thu) —
React, interview revision + machine coding</h1>
<h2 id="hour-1-how-react-renders">Hour 1 — How React renders</h2>
<p>Four years of React means you’ve fixed plenty of “why does this
re-render?” bugs. The interview version asks you to explain the
mechanism precisely and to know when memoization helps and when it’s
noise. Most React performance questions reduce to this hour.</p>
<h3 id="render-vs-commit">1.1 Render vs commit</h3>
<p><strong>What happens on an update:</strong></p>
<ol type="1">
<li><strong>Trigger:</strong> state changes (<code>setState</code>,
<code>useReducer</code> dispatch), a parent re-renders, or a consumed
context value changes.</li>
<li><strong>Render phase:</strong> React calls your component functions
to get a new element tree (plain objects describing UI). This must be
pure: no side effects, no DOM access. It can be paused, restarted or
discarded in concurrent rendering.</li>
<li><strong>Reconciliation:</strong> React diffs the new tree against
the previous one to find what changed.</li>
<li><strong>Commit phase:</strong> React applies the minimal DOM
changes, then runs <code>useLayoutEffect</code> (synchronously, before
paint), the browser paints, then <code>useEffect</code> runs.</li>
</ol>
<p>“Re-render” means step 2 ran. It does not mean the DOM changed. Many
re-renders are cheap; they matter only when the component or its subtree
is expensive or renders very often.</p>
<p><strong>“Virtual DOM”:</strong> the element tree React keeps in
memory and diffs. The point isn’t that it’s faster than the DOM in
general; it’s that it lets you write UI as a function of state and lets
React batch and minimise real DOM work.</p>
<h3 id="reconciliation-rules">1.2 Reconciliation rules</h3>
<p>A full tree diff is O(n³) in theory; React gets O(n) with two
assumptions:</p>
<ul>
<li><strong>Different element types produce different trees.</strong> If
<code>&lt;div&gt;</code> becomes <code>&lt;section&gt;</code>, or
<code>&lt;UserCard&gt;</code> becomes <code>&lt;AdminCard&gt;</code>,
React unmounts the old subtree (state lost) and mounts a new one.</li>
<li><strong>Keys identify children across renders</strong> in a
list.</li>
</ul>
<p><strong>Keys in practice:</strong></p>
<div class="sourceCode" id="cb136"><pre
class="sourceCode jsx"><code class="sourceCode javascriptreact"><span id="cb136-1"><a href="#cb136-1" aria-hidden="true" tabindex="-1"></a><span class="co">// Bug: index as key in a list that can be reordered, filtered or prepended</span></span>
<span id="cb136-2"><a href="#cb136-2" aria-hidden="true" tabindex="-1"></a>{todos<span class="op">.</span><span class="fu">map</span>((t<span class="op">,</span> i) <span class="kw">=&gt; </span><span class="fu">&lt;TodoRow</span> <span class="ot">key</span><span class="op">=</span><span class="va">{</span>i<span class="va">}</span> <span class="ot">todo</span><span class="op">=</span><span class="va">{</span>t<span class="va">}</span> <span class="fu">/&gt;</span>)}</span>
<span id="cb136-3"><a href="#cb136-3" aria-hidden="true" tabindex="-1"></a><span class="co">// Inserting at the top shifts every index: React reuses the wrong component instances,</span></span>
<span id="cb136-4"><a href="#cb136-4" aria-hidden="true" tabindex="-1"></a><span class="co">// so input text, checkbox state or focus appears on the wrong row.</span></span>
<span id="cb136-5"><a href="#cb136-5" aria-hidden="true" tabindex="-1"></a></span>
<span id="cb136-6"><a href="#cb136-6" aria-hidden="true" tabindex="-1"></a><span class="co">// Correct: a stable, unique ID from the data</span></span>
<span id="cb136-7"><a href="#cb136-7" aria-hidden="true" tabindex="-1"></a>{todos<span class="op">.</span><span class="fu">map</span>((t) <span class="kw">=&gt; </span><span class="fu">&lt;TodoRow</span> <span class="ot">key</span><span class="op">=</span><span class="va">{</span>t<span class="op">.</span><span class="at">id</span><span class="va">}</span> <span class="ot">todo</span><span class="op">=</span><span class="va">{</span>t<span class="va">}</span> <span class="fu">/&gt;</span>)}</span></code></pre></div>
<p>Index keys are acceptable only for static lists that never reorder
and hold no state. Generating keys with <code>Math.random()</code> or
<code>crypto.randomUUID()</code> during render is worse: every render
remounts every row.</p>
<p><strong>Keys as a reset tool:</strong> changing a component’s
<code>key</code> deliberately remounts it with fresh state.
<code>&lt;ProfileForm key={userId} /&gt;</code> resets the form when
switching users, without effects that copy props into state.</p>
<p><strong>Position matters too:</strong> a component’s state is tied to
its position in the tree. Rendering the same component conditionally in
two different JSX positions creates two separate instances.</p>
<h3 id="why-a-component-re-renders">1.3 Why a component re-renders</h3>
<table>
<colgroup>
<col style="width: 50%" />
<col style="width: 50%" />
</colgroup>
<thead>
<tr>
<th>Cause</th>
<th>Notes</th>
</tr>
</thead>
<tbody>
<tr>
<td>Its own state changed</td>
<td>Setting the same value (by <code>Object.is</code>) bails out</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>Its parent re-rendered</td>
<td><strong>The default</strong>: all children re-render regardless of
props, unless memoized</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>A context it consumes changed</td>
<td>Every consumer re-renders when the provider value changes
identity</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>A custom hook’s internal state changed</td>
<td>Hooks are part of the component</td>
</tr>
</tbody>
</table>
<p>The second row surprises people: props don’t need to change. A parent
re-render re-renders the whole subtree by default.</p>
<p><strong>Fixing unnecessary re-renders, cheapest first:</strong></p>
<ol type="1">
<li><strong>Move state down</strong> to the component that uses it, so
fewer things re-render.</li>
<li><strong>Lift content up / pass children:</strong> a component that
changes often can accept <code>children</code> created by its parent;
those children elements keep their identity and don’t re-render.</li>
</ol>
<div class="sourceCode" id="cb137"><pre
class="sourceCode jsx"><code class="sourceCode javascriptreact"><span id="cb137-1"><a href="#cb137-1" aria-hidden="true" tabindex="-1"></a><span class="co">// Before: every mouse move re-renders the expensive tree</span></span>

<span id="cb137-10"><a href="#cb137-10" aria-hidden="true" tabindex="-1"></a>  <span class="cf">return </span><span class="kw">&lt;div</span> <span class="ot">onMouseMove</span><span class="op">=</span><span class="va">{</span>(e) <span class="kw">=&gt;</span> <span class="fu">setPos</span>({ <span class="dt">x</span><span class="op">:</span> e<span class="op">.</span><span class="at">clientX</span><span class="op">,</span> <span class="dt">y</span><span class="op">:</span> e<span class="op">.</span><span class="at">clientY</span> })<span class="va">}</span><span class="kw">&gt;</span><span class="fu">&lt;Cursor</span> <span class="ot">pos</span><span class="op">=</span><span class="va">{</span>pos<span class="va">}</span> <span class="fu">/&gt;</span><span class="va">{</span>children<span class="va">}</span><span class="kw">&lt;/div&gt;</span><span class="op">;</span></span>
<span id="cb137-11"><a href="#cb137-11" aria-hidden="true" tabindex="-1"></a>}</span>
<span id="cb137-12"><a href="#cb137-12" aria-hidden="true" tabindex="-1"></a><span class="kw">function</span> <span class="fu">Page</span>() { <span class="cf">return </span><span class="fu">&lt;MouseTracker&gt;&lt;ExpensiveTree</span> <span class="fu">/&gt;&lt;/MouseTracker&gt;</span><span class="op">;</span> }</span></code></pre></div>
<ol start="3" type="1">
<li><strong>Split contexts</strong> (state vs dispatch, or by concern)
and memoize the provider value, so consumers re-render only for what
they use. Or use a store with selectors (Zustand, Redux) for frequently
changing global state.</li>
<li><strong>Memoize</strong> (1.4) when the above isn’t enough.</li>
</ol>
<h3 id="memo-usememo-usecallback">1.4 memo, useMemo, useCallback</h3>
<table>
<colgroup>
<col style="width: 33%" />
<col style="width: 33%" />
<col style="width: 33%" />
</colgroup>
<thead>
<tr>
<th>Tool</th>
<th>Does</th>
<th>Use when</th>
</tr>
</thead>
<tbody>
<tr>
<td><code>React.memo(Component)</code></td>
<td>Skips re-render if props are shallow-equal</td>
<td>Component is expensive or renders often with the same props</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td><code>useMemo(fn, deps)</code></td>
<td>Caches a computed value</td>
<td>Expensive computation, or to keep an object/array prop referentially
stable for a memoized child or an effect dependency</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td><code>useCallback(fn, deps)</code></td>
<td>Caches a function identity</td>
<td>Passing callbacks to memoized children or using them in effect
deps</td>
</tr>
</tbody>
</table>
<div class="sourceCode" id="cb138"><pre
class="sourceCode jsx"><code class="sourceCode javascriptreact"><span id="cb138-1"><a href="#cb138-1" aria-hidden="true" tabindex="-1"></a><span class="kw">const</span> Row <span class="op">=</span> <span class="fu">memo</span>(<span class="kw">function</span> <span class="fu">Row</span>({ item<span class="op">,</span> onSelect }) { <span class="co">/* expensive */</span> })<span class="op">;</span></span>

<p><strong>When memoization is wasted:</strong> wrapping cheap
components; <code>useCallback</code> for a function passed to a
non-memoized child (the child re-renders anyway); passing a new inline
object (<code>style={{...}}</code>) to a memoized child, which defeats
<code>memo</code>; <code>useMemo</code> for trivial calculations.
Memoization has its own cost: comparing deps and holding memory.</p>
<p><strong>React Compiler:</strong> the React team’s build-time
compiler, stable since v1.0 in October 2025 (with Next.js, Vite and Expo
integrations), automatically memoizes components and values, removing
most manual
<code>useMemo</code>/<code>useCallback</code>/<code>memo</code>. It
requires code to follow the Rules of React (pure render, no mutating
props/state). Worth mentioning: in codebases using it, manual
memoization becomes mostly unnecessary; in codebases without it, apply
the guidelines above.</p>
<p><strong>Measure, don’t guess:</strong> React DevTools Profiler (“why
did this render?” and flame chart), the “highlight updates” option, and
the browser Performance panel. Optimise what the profiler shows is
slow.</p>
<h3 id="how-id-answer-hour-1-8">How I’d answer — Hour 1</h3>
<p><strong>Q1. What triggers a re-render?</strong> “A state change in
the component, a consumed context changing, or its parent re-rendering.
The last one is the default behaviour even if props are identical. A
re-render is the render phase running; the DOM only changes if
reconciliation finds differences.”</p>
<p><strong>Q2. Why shouldn’t I use the index as a key?</strong> “Keys
tell React which item is which between renders. With indexes, inserting
or reordering items shifts keys, so React reuses component instances for
the wrong data: input values and local state end up on the wrong rows,
and performance suffers. Use a stable ID from the data; an index is only
fine for static lists with no state.”</p>
<p><strong>Q3. When do you use useMemo and useCallback?</strong> “For
expensive calculations, and to keep references stable when they’re
passed to memoized children or used as effect dependencies. Not by
default, since memoizing cheap work costs more than it saves. First I
try moving state down or passing children, and I measure with the
Profiler. With the React Compiler enabled, most manual memoization goes
away.”</p>
<p><strong>Q4. A context update re-renders half the app. How do you fix
it?</strong> “Memoize the provider value so it only changes when its
contents change, split the context so frequently changing values are
separate from stable ones, and put fast-changing global state into a
store with selectors, so components subscribe only to the slice they
use.”</p>
<h3 id="practice-24">Practice</h3>
<ul class="task-list">
<li><label><input type="checkbox" />Reproduce the index-as-key bug with
a prepend button and inputs; fix it with IDs</label></li>
<li><label><input type="checkbox" />Use the Profiler on a list of 2,000
rows; reduce re-renders by moving state down, then with
<code>memo</code> + <code>useCallback</code>; record
before/after</label></li>
<li><label><input type="checkbox" />Reset a form on user change with
<code>key</code> instead of an effect</label></li>
</ul>
<h2 id="hour-2-hooks-in-depth-react-18-and-19">Hour 2 — Hooks in depth,
React 18 and 19</h2>
<p>Hooks questions at senior level are mostly about effects: when you
shouldn’t use one, why a dependency array lies, why something runs
twice. Then the newer APIs: interviewers want to hear that you know what
transitions, Suspense, Actions and Server Components are for, even if
your last project didn’t use them.</p>
<h3 id="usestate-and-batching">2.1 useState and batching</h3>
<ul>
<li>State updates are <strong>batched</strong>: several
<code>setX</code> calls in one event produce one re-render. Since React
18 this applies everywhere (timeouts, promises, native handlers), not
just React event handlers.</li>
<li>State is a <strong>snapshot</strong> per render.
<code>setCount(count + 1)</code> three times in one handler gives +1,
because each call reads the same <code>count</code>. Use the functional
updater when the new value depends on the old:
<code>setCount(c =&gt; c + 1)</code>.</li>
<li><strong>Lazy initial state</strong> for expensive setup:
<code>useState(() =&gt; parseLargeJson(raw))</code> runs once, not on
every render.</li>
<li>Treat state as immutable:
<code>setItems([...items, newItem])</code>, never
<code>items.push()</code> then <code>setItems(items)</code> (same
reference, React bails out).</li>
</ul>
<h3 id="useeffect-the-hook-most-often-misused">2.2 useEffect: the hook
most often misused</h3>
<p><strong>What it’s for:</strong> synchronising a component with
something <strong>outside React</strong>: subscriptions, timers,
WebSockets, non-React widgets, <code>document.title</code>, analytics.
Not for transforming data or reacting to user events.</p>
<div class="sourceCode" id="cb139"><pre
class="sourceCode jsx"><code class="sourceCode javascriptreact"><span id="cb139-1"><a href="#cb139-1" aria-hidden="true" tabindex="-1"></a><span class="fu">useEffect</span>(() <span class="kw">=&gt;</span> {</span>
<span id="cb139-2"><a href="#cb139-2" aria-hidden="true" tabindex="-1"></a>  <span class="kw">const</span> socket <span class="op">=</span> <span class="fu">connect</span>(roomId)<span class="op">;</span></span>
<span id="cb139-3"><a href="#cb139-3" aria-hidden="true" tabindex="-1"></a>  socket<span class="op">.</span><span class="fu">on</span>(<span class="st">&#39;message&#39;</span><span class="op">,</span> onMessage)<span class="op">;</span></span>
<span id="cb139-4"><a href="#cb139-4" aria-hidden="true" tabindex="-1"></a>  <span class="cf">return</span> () <span class="kw">=&gt;</span> socket<span class="op">.</span><span class="fu">disconnect</span>()<span class="op">;</span>      <span class="co">// cleanup runs before the next effect and on unmount</span></span>
<span id="cb139-5"><a href="#cb139-5" aria-hidden="true" tabindex="-1"></a>}<span class="op">,</span> [roomId])<span class="op">;</span>                            <span class="co">// every reactive value used inside must be listed</span></span></code></pre></div>
<p><strong>“You might not need an effect”</strong> (cases to fix in code
review):</p>
<table>
<colgroup>
<col style="width: 50%" />
<col style="width: 50%" />
</colgroup>
<thead>
<tr>
<th>Effect misuse</th>
<th>Better</th>
</tr>
</thead>
<tbody>
<tr>
<td>Effect that computes <code>fullName</code> from <code>first</code> +
<code>last</code> into state</td>
<td>Compute it during render; <code>useMemo</code> if expensive</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>Effect that resets state when a prop changes</td>
<td>Change the component’s <code>key</code></td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>Effect that runs logic “when the user clicked submit” by watching a
flag</td>
<td>Put the logic in the event handler</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>Effect chains (effect sets state, which triggers another
effect)</td>
<td>One event handler, or derive values</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>Effect that fetches data with manual loading/error state</td>
<td>TanStack Query / framework data loading (Hour 3)</td>
</tr>
</tbody>
</table>
<p><strong>StrictMode runs effects twice in development</strong> (mount
→ unmount → mount) on purpose, to expose missing cleanups. If
double-running breaks something (two subscriptions, two analytics
events), the cleanup is missing. It doesn’t happen in production.</p>
<p><strong>Fetching in an effect correctly</strong> (when you must):</p>
<div class="sourceCode" id="cb140"><pre
class="sourceCode jsx"><code class="sourceCode javascriptreact"><span id="cb140-1"><a href="#cb140-1" aria-hidden="true" tabindex="-1"></a><span class="fu">useEffect</span>(() <span class="kw">=&gt;</span> {</span>
<span id="cb140-2"><a href="#cb140-2" aria-hidden="true" tabindex="-1"></a>  <span class="kw">const</span> controller <span class="op">=</span> <span class="kw">new</span> <span class="fu">AbortController</span>()<span class="op">;</span></span>
<span id="cb140-3"><a href="#cb140-3" aria-hidden="true" tabindex="-1"></a>  <span class="fu">setStatus</span>(<span class="st">&#39;loading&#39;</span>)<span class="op">;</span></span>
<span id="cb140-4"><a href="#cb140-4" aria-hidden="true" tabindex="-1"></a>  <span class="fu">fetch</span>(<span class="vs">`/api/products?q=</span><span class="sc">${</span><span class="pp">encodeURIComponent</span>(query)<span class="sc">}</span><span class="vs">`</span><span class="op">,</span> { <span class="dt">signal</span><span class="op">:</span> controller<span class="op">.</span><span class="at">signal</span> })</span>
<span id="cb140-5"><a href="#cb140-5" aria-hidden="true" tabindex="-1"></a>    <span class="op">.</span><span class="fu">then</span>((r) <span class="kw">=&gt;</span> r<span class="op">.</span><span class="fu">json</span>())</span>
<span id="cb140-6"><a href="#cb140-6" aria-hidden="true" tabindex="-1"></a>    <span class="op">.</span><span class="fu">then</span>((data) <span class="kw">=&gt;</span> { <span class="fu">setResults</span>(data)<span class="op">;</span> <span class="fu">setStatus</span>(<span class="st">&#39;success&#39;</span>)<span class="op">;</span> })</span>
<span id="cb140-7"><a href="#cb140-7" aria-hidden="true" tabindex="-1"></a>    <span class="op">.</span><span class="fu">catch</span>((e) <span class="kw">=&gt;</span> { <span class="cf">if</span> (e<span class="op">.</span><span class="at">name</span> <span class="op">!==</span> <span class="st">&#39;AbortError&#39;</span>) <span class="fu">setStatus</span>(<span class="st">&#39;error&#39;</span>)<span class="op">;</span> })<span class="op">;</span></span>
<span id="cb140-8"><a href="#cb140-8" aria-hidden="true" tabindex="-1"></a>  <span class="cf">return</span> () <span class="kw">=&gt;</span> controller<span class="op">.</span><span class="fu">abort</span>()<span class="op">;</span>       <span class="co">// prevents race conditions: stale responses are dropped</span></span>
<span id="cb140-9"><a href="#cb140-9" aria-hidden="true" tabindex="-1"></a>}<span class="op">,</span> [query])<span class="op">;</span></span></code></pre></div>
<p>The race condition interviewers look for: type “ab” then “abc”; if
the “ab” response arrives last, it overwrites the newer results.
Aborting (or an <code>ignore</code> flag) in cleanup fixes it.</p>
<p><strong>Lint rule:</strong> keep
<code>react-hooks/exhaustive-deps</code> on. If the rule demands a
dependency you don’t want, the fix is restructuring (move the function
inside the effect, use a functional updater, use a ref for values that
shouldn’t trigger), not suppressing the warning.</p>
<h3 id="other-hooks">2.3 Other hooks</h3>

</tr>

<p><strong>Custom hooks</strong> share <strong>logic</strong>, not
state: each component calling <code>useCart()</code> gets its own state
unless the hook reads from context or a store.</p>

<h3 id="concurrent-features-react-18">2.4 Concurrent features (React
18)</h3>
<ul>
<li><strong><code>useTransition</code>:</strong> mark an update as
non-urgent, so typing stays responsive while a heavy list re-renders.
<code>const [isPending, startTransition] = useTransition(); startTransition(() =&gt; setFilter(text));</code></li>
<li><strong><code>useDeferredValue</code>:</strong> render with a
lagging copy of a value:
<code>const deferredQuery = useDeferredValue(query);</code> pass
<code>deferredQuery</code> to the expensive child. Good when you don’t
control where the state is set.</li>
<li><strong>Suspense:</strong> declaratively show a fallback while a
child is waiting (lazy-loaded code with <code>React.lazy</code>, or data
in frameworks and libraries that support it). Nested Suspense boundaries
let parts of a page load independently.</li>
<li><strong>Automatic batching</strong> everywhere (2.1) and streaming
SSR with selective hydration.</li>
</ul>

</tr>

<p><strong>Server Components in one paragraph:</strong> RSCs render on
the server, can be <code>async</code> and read the database or call
internal APIs directly, and send no JavaScript for themselves to the
browser. Client Components (marked <code>'use client'</code>) handle
interactivity and state. You compose them: a server component fetches
products and renders a client <code>AddToCartButton</code>. Benefits:
smaller bundles, no client-side waterfalls for data, secrets stay on the
server. Costs: a new mental model, the server/client boundary (only
serialisable props cross it), and framework dependence. <strong>Server
Actions</strong> (<code>'use server'</code> functions) let client
components call server code like a function; they’re public HTTP
endpoints, so they need authentication and validation like any API.</p>
<h3 id="how-id-answer-hour-2-8">How I’d answer — Hour 2</h3>
<p><strong>Q1. When should you not use useEffect?</strong> “Whenever
there’s no external system to synchronise with. Derived data should be
computed during render, user-triggered logic belongs in the event
handler, resetting state on a prop change is better done with a key, and
data fetching is better handled by a library like TanStack Query or the
framework’s loaders. Effects are for subscriptions, timers, and
integrating non-React code.”</p>
<p><strong>Q2. Why does my effect run twice?</strong> “In development
under StrictMode, React mounts, unmounts and remounts components to
surface missing cleanups. If running twice causes a bug, the effect
needs a proper cleanup. It doesn’t happen in production.”</p>
<p><strong>Q3. How do you avoid race conditions when fetching on input
change?</strong> “Abort the previous request in the effect cleanup with
an AbortController, or ignore stale responses with a flag. Better still,
use TanStack Query, which keys requests by query and discards outdated
ones, combined with debouncing the input.”</p>
<p><strong>Q4. useTransition vs useDeferredValue vs debounce?</strong>
“Debounce delays the work by time. Transitions keep the work but mark it
as interruptible, so urgent updates like typing render first.
useDeferredValue does the same when I only have the value, not the
setter. For expensive client-side filtering I’d use a transition; for
network calls I still debounce.”</p>
<p><strong>Q5. What are Server Components and when would you use
them?</strong> “Components that render on the server, can fetch data
directly and ship no JavaScript, composed with client components for
interactivity. They suit content-heavy, data-driven pages like product
listings where bundle size and time-to-content matter. Highly
interactive app-like screens remain mostly client components.”</p>
<h3 id="practice-25">Practice</h3>
<ul class="task-list">

<code>useDebounce</code> + AbortController; prove the race condition
exists without the abort</label></li>
<li><label><input type="checkbox" />Make a 5,000-item client-side filter
responsive with <code>useTransition</code></label></li>
<li><label><input type="checkbox" />Build a “like” button with
<code>useOptimistic</code> that rolls back when the request
fails</label></li>
</ul>
<h2
id="hour-3-state-data-fetching-rendering-strategies-performance">Hour 3
— State, data fetching, rendering strategies, performance</h2>
<p>These are the architecture questions for a senior frontend or
full-stack role: how you’d structure state in a large app, why you’d
pick Next.js or a plain SPA, and how you’d fix a page with poor Core Web
Vitals. Answers should start from the kind of state or the kind of page,
not from a favourite library.</p>
<h3 id="kinds-of-state-and-where-each-belongs">3.1 Kinds of state, and
where each belongs</h3>
<table>
<colgroup>
<col style="width: 33%" />
<col style="width: 33%" />
<col style="width: 33%" />
</colgroup>
<thead>
<tr>
<th>Kind</th>
<th>Examples</th>
<th>Where</th>
</tr>
</thead>
<tbody>
<tr>
<td>Local UI state</td>
<td>Open/closed, input text, selected tab</td>
<td><code>useState</code> in the component</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>Shared UI state</td>
<td>Theme, sidebar open, current user</td>
<td>Context (low-frequency changes) or a small store</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td><strong>Server state</strong></td>
<td>Products, orders, profile from the API</td>
<td><strong>TanStack Query / RTK Query / SWR</strong>, not a global

</tr>
<tr>
<td>Form state</td>
<td>Values, touched, errors</td>
<td>React Hook Form + Zod schema</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>URL state</td>
<td>Filters, page, sort, selected item</td>
<td>Query string / route params (shareable, back button works)</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>Complex client state</td>
<td>Editor, multi-step wizard, offline cart</td>
<td>Zustand or Redux Toolkit; <code>useReducer</code> for one component

</tr>
</tbody>
</table>
<p>The biggest architectural mistake in older React codebases: putting
server data into Redux with hand-written loading flags, caching and
refetch logic. Server state has different problems (staleness, caching,
deduplication, background refresh, retries, pagination) that dedicated
libraries solve.</p>

<h3 id="rendering-strategies">3.2 Rendering strategies</h3>
<table>
<colgroup>
<col style="width: 25%" />
<col style="width: 25%" />
<col style="width: 25%" />
<col style="width: 25%" />
</colgroup>
<thead>
<tr>
<th>Strategy</th>
<th>How</th>
<th>Good for</th>
<th>Trade-off</th>
</tr>
</thead>
<tbody>
<tr>
<td>CSR (SPA)</td>
<td>Browser downloads JS, then fetches data and renders</td>
<td>Dashboards, admin tools, apps behind login</td>
<td>Slow first paint, weaker SEO</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>SSR</td>
<td>Server renders HTML per request, browser hydrates</td>
<td>Personalised pages needing SEO and fast first paint</td>
<td>Server cost per request; hydration cost</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>SSG</td>
<td>HTML built at build time</td>
<td>Docs, marketing, blogs</td>
<td>Stale until rebuilt</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>ISR / revalidation</td>
<td>Static pages regenerated in the background after N seconds or on
demand</td>
<td>Product pages, catalogue</td>
<td>Brief staleness</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>Streaming SSR + RSC</td>
<td>Server streams HTML in chunks as data resolves (Suspense
boundaries)</td>
<td>Large data-driven pages</td>
<td>Framework complexity</td>
</tr>
</tbody>
</table>
<p><strong>Next.js App Router</strong> in brief: file-based routes in
<code>app/</code>, Server Components by default,
<code>'use client'</code> for interactive parts, <code>fetch</code>
caching and revalidation, layouts, loading and error files per route
segment, Server Actions for mutations, middleware at the edge.
<strong>My framing:</strong> e-commerce storefront: Next.js (SEO, fast
product pages with ISR); internal admin dashboard: Vite SPA (or Angular,
as in the capstone), because SEO doesn’t matter and simpler deployment
wins.</p>
<h3 id="performance-and-core-web-vitals">3.3 Performance and Core Web
Vitals</h3>
<table>
<colgroup>
<col style="width: 25%" />
<col style="width: 25%" />
<col style="width: 25%" />
<col style="width: 25%" />
</colgroup>
<thead>
<tr>
<th>Metric</th>
<th>Measures</th>
<th>Good</th>
<th>Typical fixes</th>
</tr>
</thead>
<tbody>
<tr>
<td><strong>LCP</strong> (Largest Contentful Paint)</td>
<td>When the main content appears</td>
<td>≤ 2.5 s</td>
<td>SSR/SSG, optimised hero image (<code>fetchpriority="high"</code>,
proper size, modern format), CDN, less render-blocking JS/CSS</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td><strong>INP</strong> (Interaction to Next Paint)</td>
<td>Responsiveness to clicks and typing</td>
<td>≤ 200 ms</td>
<td>Less JS on the main thread, code splitting, transitions,
virtualization, avoid long tasks</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td><strong>CLS</strong> (Cumulative Layout Shift)</td>
<td>Visual stability</td>
<td>≤ 0.1</td>
<td>Width/height on images, reserved space for ads and embeds, font
loading strategy</td>
</tr>
</tbody>
</table>
<p>(INP replaced First Input Delay as a Core Web Vital in 2024.)</p>
<p><strong>Toolbox:</strong></p>
<ul>
<li><strong>Code splitting</strong> by route and for heavy components:
<code>const Chart = lazy(() =&gt; import('./Chart'))</code> inside
<code>&lt;Suspense&gt;</code>.</li>
<li><strong>Bundle analysis</strong>
(<code>vite-bundle-visualizer</code>,
<code>@next/bundle-analyzer</code>): find the date library or icon set
that ships 300 KB.</li>
<li><strong>Virtualization</strong> for long lists (TanStack Virtual,
react-window): render only visible rows.</li>
<li><strong>Images:</strong> responsive <code>srcset</code>, lazy
loading below the fold, <code>next/image</code> or a CDN image
service.</li>
<li><strong>Avoid waterfalls:</strong> fetch in parallel, prefetch on
hover, load data in route loaders or server components rather than in
nested effects.</li>
<li><strong>Measure real users:</strong> <code>web-vitals</code> library
sending field data to analytics; lab tools (Lighthouse) don’t show what
slow phones on Indian mobile networks experience.</li>
</ul>
<h3 id="testing-accessibility-security">3.4 Testing, accessibility,
security</h3>
<p><strong>Testing with React Testing Library:</strong> test what the
user sees and does, not implementation details.</p>
<div class="sourceCode" id="cb143"><pre
class="sourceCode jsx"><code class="sourceCode javascriptreact"><span id="cb143-1"><a href="#cb143-1" aria-hidden="true" tabindex="-1"></a><span class="fu">it</span>(<span class="st">&#39;adds a product to the cart&#39;</span><span class="op">,</span> <span class="kw">async</span> () <span class="kw">=&gt;</span> {</span>
<span id="cb143-2"><a href="#cb143-2" aria-hidden="true" tabindex="-1"></a>  <span class="kw">const</span> user <span class="op">=</span> userEvent<span class="op">.</span><span class="fu">setup</span>()<span class="op">;</span></span>
<span id="cb143-3"><a href="#cb143-3" aria-hidden="true" tabindex="-1"></a>  <span class="fu">render</span>(<span class="fu">&lt;ProductCard</span> <span class="ot">product</span><span class="op">=</span><span class="va">{</span>shoe<span class="va">}</span> <span class="fu">/&gt;</span><span class="op">,</span> { <span class="dt">wrapper</span><span class="op">:</span> TestProviders })<span class="op">;</span></span>
<span id="cb143-4"><a href="#cb143-4" aria-hidden="true" tabindex="-1"></a>  <span class="cf">await</span> user<span class="op">.</span><span class="fu">click</span>(<span class="bu">screen</span><span class="op">.</span><span class="fu">getByRole</span>(<span class="st">&#39;button&#39;</span><span class="op">,</span> { <span class="dt">name</span><span class="op">:</span> <span class="ss">/add to cart/i</span> }))<span class="op">;</span></span>
<span id="cb143-5"><a href="#cb143-5" aria-hidden="true" tabindex="-1"></a>  <span class="fu">expect</span>(<span class="cf">await</span> <span class="bu">screen</span><span class="op">.</span><span class="fu">findByText</span>(<span class="ss">/added to cart/i</span>))<span class="op">.</span><span class="fu">toBeInTheDocument</span>()<span class="op">;</span></span>
<span id="cb143-6"><a href="#cb143-6" aria-hidden="true" tabindex="-1"></a>})<span class="op">;</span></span></code></pre></div>
<p>Prefer <code>getByRole</code> and accessible names (which also checks
accessibility), mock the network with <strong>MSW</strong> rather than
mocking modules, and keep E2E (Playwright) for critical journeys.</p>
<p><strong>Accessibility basics a senior should enforce:</strong>
semantic HTML (<code>button</code>, not clickable <code>div</code>),
labels on inputs, keyboard navigation and visible focus, alt text,
colour contrast, ARIA only when native elements can’t do it,
<code>eslint-plugin-jsx-a11y</code> in CI.</p>
<p><strong>Security:</strong> React escapes values by default, so XSS
mostly enters through <code>dangerouslySetInnerHTML</code> (sanitise
with DOMPurify), <code>href={userInput}</code> (block
<code>javascript:</code> URLs), and third-party scripts. Don’t put
secrets in frontend env vars; anything in the bundle is public. Tokens:
Day 4.</p>
<h3 id="how-id-answer-hour-3-8">How I’d answer — Hour 3</h3>
<p><strong>Q1. How do you structure state in a large React app?</strong>
“By kind. Server data goes in TanStack Query with sensible stale times
and invalidation after mutations; that removes most global state.
Filters and pagination live in the URL so they’re shareable. Forms use
React Hook Form with Zod. What’s left, genuinely global client state,
goes into a small Zustand store with selectors, or Redux Toolkit for a
big team. Context is only for rarely changing values like theme or the
current user.”</p>
<p><strong>Q2. CSR, SSR, SSG or ISR for an e-commerce site?</strong>
“Product and category pages with SSG/ISR for speed and SEO, revalidated
when the catalogue changes. Personalised parts like the cart and
recommendations render on the client or stream in. Checkout and account
pages behind login can be SSR or client-rendered. The admin panel is a
plain SPA.”</p>
<p><strong>Q3. The product page has poor LCP on mobile. What do you
do?</strong> “Measure with field data first. Then check the LCP element,
usually the hero image: correct size, modern format, served from a CDN,
<code>fetchpriority=high</code>, not lazy-loaded. Render the page on the
server or statically so the image starts loading from the HTML, reduce
render-blocking JS and CSS, and move non-critical scripts after load.
Then re-measure.”</p>
<p><strong>Q4. Redux or TanStack Query?</strong> “They solve different
problems. TanStack Query manages server state: caching, refetching,
deduplication. Redux manages client state. Most apps that used Redux for
API data can drop most of it after adopting a server-state library.”</p>
