<h2 id="hour-4-react-machine-coding-frontend-system-design">Hour 4 —
React machine coding + frontend system design</h2>
<p>React machine-coding rounds give you 60–90 minutes to build a working
component. What gets scored: it works, state is modelled cleanly, edge
cases are handled (loading, empty, error, race conditions), it’s
accessible from the keyboard, and you explain trade-offs. Build each of
these three without AI, timed, then compare with the reference.</p>
<h3 id="autocomplete-typeahead">4.1 Autocomplete / typeahead</h3>
<p><strong>Requirements to confirm:</strong> debounce input; cancel
stale requests; cache results per query; keyboard navigation (up, down,
Enter, Escape); highlight the match; loading, empty and error states;
accessible combobox.</p>

<span id="cb146-33"><a href="#cb146-33" aria-hidden="true" tabindex="-1"></a>  <span class="cf">return </span><span class="kw">&lt;ul&gt;</span><span class="va">{</span>tree<span class="op">.</span><span class="fu">map</span>((c) <span class="kw">=&gt; </span><span class="fu">&lt;Comment</span> <span class="ot">key</span><span class="op">=</span><span class="va">{</span>c<span class="op">.</span><span class="at">id</span><span class="va">}</span> <span class="ot">comment</span><span class="op">=</span><span class="va">{</span>c<span class="va">}</span> <span class="ot">depth</span><span class="op">=</span><span class="va">{</span><span class="dv">0</span><span class="va">}</span> <span class="ot">onReply</span><span class="op">=</span><span class="va">{</span>onReply<span class="va">}</span> <span class="fu">/&gt;</span>)<span class="va">}</span><span class="kw">&lt;/ul&gt;</span><span class="op">;</span></span>
<span id="cb146-34"><a href="#cb146-34" aria-hidden="true" tabindex="-1"></a>}</span></code></pre></div>
<p>Talking points: flat list from the API converted to a tree once
(<code>useMemo</code>); recursive component; collapse state local to
each comment; cap visual indentation at a few levels (“continue thread”
link beyond that); optimistic replies with <code>useOptimistic</code> or
a TanStack mutation; lazy-load replies for very large threads.</p>
<h3 id="frontend-system-design-a-news-feed-30-minute-shape">4.4 Frontend
system design: a news feed (30-minute shape)</h3>
<ol type="1">
<li><strong>Requirements:</strong> infinite feed, posts with images,
like and comment, new-post notifications, works on slow mobile networks,
accessible.</li>
<li><strong>Architecture:</strong> component tree (<code>FeedPage</code>
→ <code>Feed</code> → <code>PostCard</code> → <code>LikeButton</code>,
<code>CommentPreview</code>); server state in TanStack Query; URL for
filters; minimal global client state.</li>
<li><strong>API contract:</strong>
<code>GET /feed?cursor=&amp;limit=20</code> returning posts and
<code>nextCursor</code>; <code>POST /posts/{id}/likes</code> idempotent;
media URLs from a CDN with size variants.</li>
<li><strong>Rendering:</strong> SSR the first page for fast LCP,
client-side after that; virtualization for long sessions; images
lazy-loaded with fixed aspect ratios (no CLS).</li>
<li><strong>Real-time:</strong> SSE or WebSocket pushes “N new posts”;
show a banner instead of inserting posts under the user’s thumb.</li>
<li><strong>Interactions:</strong> optimistic likes with rollback;
debounced like toggles to avoid spam.</li>
<li><strong>Resilience:</strong> retries with backoff, offline
indicator, cached last feed (service worker or persisted query cache),
error boundaries per section.</li>
<li><strong>Performance budget and monitoring:</strong> bundle size
budget, Core Web Vitals from real users, error tracking (Sentry).</li>
</ol>
<h3 id="how-id-answer-hour-4-8">How I’d answer — Hour 4</h3>
<p><strong>Q1. Walk me through your autocomplete’s edge cases.</strong>
“Debounced input so we don’t call the API on every keystroke; each
request aborted when a newer one starts so stale results can’t overwrite
new ones; a per-query cache; empty, loading, error and no-results
states; keyboard navigation with wrap-around; <code>onMouseDown</code>
so clicking an option isn’t cancelled by blur; and combobox ARIA roles
so screen readers announce options.”</p>
<p><strong>Q2. How would you render 10,000 comments?</strong> “Not all
at once. Paginate top-level comments, load replies on demand, collapse
deep threads, and virtualise the visible list. The flat-to-tree
conversion is O(n) and memoised, and each comment is memoised so
replying to one doesn’t re-render the rest.”</p>

<ul class="task-list">

nested comments each built in under 60 minutes without AI</label></li>
<li><label><input type="checkbox" />Storefront (Vite + React + TS) with

client</label></li>
<li><label><input type="checkbox" />Profiler before/after for one
optimisation; Core Web Vitals measured on the product page</label></li>
<li><label><input type="checkbox" />RTL + MSW tests and one Playwright
journey green in CI</label></li>
<li><label><input type="checkbox" />Day 9 answers rehearsed out loud,
including the news feed design in under 30 minutes</label></li>
</ul>
<h1 id="day-10-fri-angular-deep-dive">Day 10 (Fri) — Angular deep
dive</h1>
<h2 id="hour-1-modern-angular-architecture">Hour 1 — Modern Angular
architecture</h2>
<p>With six months of Angular, the risk in interviews is mixing older
patterns (NgModules everywhere, <code>*ngIf</code>, constructor
injection only, manual subscriptions) with newer ones without knowing
why things changed. Angular moved a lot between v14 and v22 (released
June 2026; Angular now ships one major per year, with v23 expected
around June 2027). Present yourself as someone who writes modern Angular
and can maintain the older style.</p>
<h3 id="standalone-components-and-bootstrapping">1.1 Standalone
components and bootstrapping</h3>
<p><strong>What changed:</strong> components, directives and pipes can
be <code>standalone</code> and import what they use directly, so
NgModules are optional. Since v19, standalone is the default.</p>
<div class="sourceCode" id="cb147"><pre
class="sourceCode ts"><code class="sourceCode typescript"><span id="cb147-1"><a href="#cb147-1" aria-hidden="true" tabindex="-1"></a><span class="co">// main.ts</span></span>
<span id="cb147-2"><a href="#cb147-2" aria-hidden="true" tabindex="-1"></a><span class="fu">bootstrapApplication</span>(AppComponent<span class="op">,</span> {</span>
<span id="cb147-3"><a href="#cb147-3" aria-hidden="true" tabindex="-1"></a>  providers<span class="op">:</span> [</span>
<span id="cb147-4"><a href="#cb147-4" aria-hidden="true" tabindex="-1"></a>    <span class="fu">provideRouter</span>(routes<span class="op">,</span> <span class="fu">withComponentInputBinding</span>())<span class="op">,</span></span>
<span id="cb147-5"><a href="#cb147-5" aria-hidden="true" tabindex="-1"></a>    <span class="fu">provideHttpClient</span>(<span class="fu">withInterceptors</span>([authInterceptor<span class="op">,</span> errorInterceptor]))<span class="op">,</span></span>
<span id="cb147-6"><a href="#cb147-6" aria-hidden="true" tabindex="-1"></a>    <span class="fu">provideZonelessChangeDetection</span>()<span class="op">,</span>        <span class="co">// zoneless is the default for new apps since v21; shown for clarity</span></span>
<span id="cb147-7"><a href="#cb147-7" aria-hidden="true" tabindex="-1"></a>  ]<span class="op">,</span></span>
<span id="cb147-8"><a href="#cb147-8" aria-hidden="true" tabindex="-1"></a>})<span class="op">;</span></span>
<span id="cb147-9"><a href="#cb147-9" aria-hidden="true" tabindex="-1"></a></span>
<span id="cb147-10"><a href="#cb147-10" aria-hidden="true" tabindex="-1"></a>@<span class="fu">Component</span>({</span>
<span id="cb147-11"><a href="#cb147-11" aria-hidden="true" tabindex="-1"></a>  selector<span class="op">:</span> <span class="st">&#39;app-order-list&#39;</span><span class="op">,</span></span>
<span id="cb147-12"><a href="#cb147-12" aria-hidden="true" tabindex="-1"></a>  imports<span class="op">:</span> [CurrencyPipe<span class="op">,</span> DatePipe<span class="op">,</span> OrderRowComponent<span class="op">,</span> RouterLink]<span class="op">,</span>   <span class="co">// what the template uses</span></span>
<span id="cb147-13"><a href="#cb147-13" aria-hidden="true" tabindex="-1"></a>  changeDetection<span class="op">:</span> ChangeDetectionStrategy<span class="op">.</span><span class="at">OnPush</span><span class="op">,</span></span>
<span id="cb147-14"><a href="#cb147-14" aria-hidden="true" tabindex="-1"></a>  templateUrl<span class="op">:</span> <span class="st">&#39;./order-list.component.html&#39;</span><span class="op">,</span></span>
<span id="cb147-15"><a href="#cb147-15" aria-hidden="true" tabindex="-1"></a>})</span>
<span id="cb147-16"><a href="#cb147-16" aria-hidden="true" tabindex="-1"></a><span class="im">export</span> <span class="kw">class</span> OrderListComponent { }</span></code></pre></div>
<p>Why it matters: smaller mental model, easier lazy loading per
component, better tree-shaking. NgModules still appear in existing
codebases; know how to read them (<code>declarations</code>,
<code>imports</code>, <code>exports</code>, <code>providers</code>) and
migrate them (<code>ng generate @angular/core:standalone</code>).</p>
<h3 id="dependency-injection-1">1.2 Dependency injection</h3>
<p>Angular’s DI is a hierarchical injector tree, and it’s the feature
most React developers underrate.</p>
<table>
<colgroup>
<col style="width: 50%" />
<col style="width: 50%" />
</colgroup>
<thead>
<tr>
<th>Where provided</th>
<th>Scope</th>
</tr>
</thead>
<tbody>
<tr>
<td><code>@Injectable({ providedIn: 'root' })</code></td>
<td>One app-wide singleton, tree-shakable</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td><code>providers</code> in <code>bootstrapApplication</code> / route
<code>providers</code></td>
<td>App-wide, or scoped to a lazy-loaded route and its children</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>Component <code>providers</code></td>
<td>New instance per component instance (and its children)</td>
</tr>
</tbody>
</table>
<div class="sourceCode" id="cb148"><pre
class="sourceCode ts"><code class="sourceCode typescript"><span id="cb148-1"><a href="#cb148-1" aria-hidden="true" tabindex="-1"></a>@<span class="fu">Injectable</span>({ providedIn<span class="op">:</span> <span class="st">&#39;root&#39;</span> })</span>
<span id="cb148-2"><a href="#cb148-2" aria-hidden="true" tabindex="-1"></a><span class="im">export</span> <span class="kw">class</span> OrderService {</span>
<span id="cb148-3"><a href="#cb148-3" aria-hidden="true" tabindex="-1"></a>  <span class="kw">private</span> http <span class="op">=</span> <span class="fu">inject</span>(HttpClient)<span class="op">;</span>           <span class="co">// inject() function, usable in field initialisers</span></span>
<span id="cb148-4"><a href="#cb148-4" aria-hidden="true" tabindex="-1"></a>  <span class="fu">list</span>(params<span class="op">:</span> OrderQuery) { <span class="cf">return</span> <span class="kw">this</span><span class="op">.</span><span class="at">http</span><span class="op">.</span><span class="fu">get</span><span class="op">&lt;</span>Page<span class="op">&lt;</span>Order<span class="op">&gt;&gt;</span>(<span class="st">&#39;/api/v1/orders&#39;</span><span class="op">,</span> { params })<span class="op">;</span> }</span>
<span id="cb148-5"><a href="#cb148-5" aria-hidden="true" tabindex="-1"></a>}</span>
<span id="cb148-6"><a href="#cb148-6" aria-hidden="true" tabindex="-1"></a></span>
<span id="cb148-7"><a href="#cb148-7" aria-hidden="true" tabindex="-1"></a><span class="co">// Tokens for config and non-class values</span></span>
<span id="cb148-8"><a href="#cb148-8" aria-hidden="true" tabindex="-1"></a><span class="im">export</span> <span class="kw">const</span> API_BASE_URL <span class="op">=</span> <span class="kw">new</span> <span class="fu">InjectionToken</span><span class="op">&lt;</span><span class="dt">string</span><span class="op">&gt;</span>(<span class="st">&#39;API_BASE_URL&#39;</span>)<span class="op">;</span></span>
<span id="cb148-9"><a href="#cb148-9" aria-hidden="true" tabindex="-1"></a>providers<span class="op">:</span> [{ provide<span class="op">:</span> API_BASE_URL<span class="op">,</span> useValue<span class="op">:</span> environment<span class="op">.</span><span class="at">apiUrl</span> }]</span>
<span id="cb148-10"><a href="#cb148-10" aria-hidden="true" tabindex="-1"></a></span>
<span id="cb148-11"><a href="#cb148-11" aria-hidden="true" tabindex="-1"></a><span class="co">// Swapping implementations (tests, feature flags)</span></span>
<span id="cb148-12"><a href="#cb148-12" aria-hidden="true" tabindex="-1"></a>providers<span class="op">:</span> [{ provide<span class="op">:</span> PaymentGateway<span class="op">,</span> useClass<span class="op">:</span> environment<span class="op">.</span><span class="at">mock</span> <span class="op">?</span> FakeGateway <span class="op">:</span> RazorpayGateway }]</span></code></pre></div>
<p>Provider types: <code>useClass</code>, <code>useValue</code>,
<code>useFactory</code> (with <code>deps</code>),
<code>useExisting</code> (alias), and <code>multi: true</code> (collect
many, like interceptors). Resolution modifiers:
<code>inject(X, { optional: true })</code>, <code>self</code>,
<code>skipSelf</code>, <code>host</code>.</p>
<p><strong>Senior point:</strong> component-level providers are how you
give each instance of a complex widget its own state service (a
“component store”) instead of putting everything in a global
singleton.</p>
<h3 id="inputs-outputs-signal-based-apis">1.3 Inputs, outputs,
signal-based APIs</h3>
<div class="sourceCode" id="cb149"><pre
class="sourceCode ts"><code class="sourceCode typescript"><span id="cb149-1"><a href="#cb149-1" aria-hidden="true" tabindex="-1"></a>@<span class="fu">Component</span>({ selector<span class="op">:</span> <span class="st">&#39;app-qty-picker&#39;</span><span class="op">,</span> template<span class="op">:</span> <span class="vs">`...`</span> })</span>
<span id="cb149-2"><a href="#cb149-2" aria-hidden="true" tabindex="-1"></a><span class="im">export</span> <span class="kw">class</span> QtyPickerComponent {</span>
<span id="cb149-3"><a href="#cb149-3" aria-hidden="true" tabindex="-1"></a>  max <span class="op">=</span> <span class="fu">input</span>(<span class="dv">10</span>)<span class="op">;</span>                              <span class="co">// signal input with default</span></span>
<span id="cb149-4"><a href="#cb149-4" aria-hidden="true" tabindex="-1"></a>  productId <span class="op">=</span> input<span class="op">.</span><span class="fu">required</span><span class="op">&lt;</span><span class="dt">string</span><span class="op">&gt;</span>()<span class="op">;</span>          <span class="co">// required</span></span>
<span id="cb149-5"><a href="#cb149-5" aria-hidden="true" tabindex="-1"></a>  unitPrice <span class="op">=</span> <span class="fu">input</span>(<span class="dv">0</span>)<span class="op">;</span></span>
<span id="cb149-6"><a href="#cb149-6" aria-hidden="true" tabindex="-1"></a>  quantity <span class="op">=</span> <span class="fu">model</span>(<span class="dv">1</span>)<span class="op">;</span>                           <span class="co">// two-way binding: [(quantity)]</span></span>
<span id="cb149-7"><a href="#cb149-7" aria-hidden="true" tabindex="-1"></a>  changed <span class="op">=</span> <span class="fu">output</span><span class="op">&lt;</span><span class="dt">number</span><span class="op">&gt;</span>()<span class="op">;</span>                    <span class="co">// replaces @Output() + EventEmitter</span></span>
<span id="cb149-8"><a href="#cb149-8" aria-hidden="true" tabindex="-1"></a>  total <span class="op">=</span> <span class="fu">computed</span>(() <span class="kw">=&gt;</span> <span class="kw">this</span><span class="op">.</span><span class="fu">quantity</span>() <span class="op">*</span> <span class="kw">this</span><span class="op">.</span><span class="fu">unitPrice</span>())<span class="op">;</span></span>
<span id="cb149-9"><a href="#cb149-9" aria-hidden="true" tabindex="-1"></a>}</span></code></pre></div>
<p>Older equivalents you’ll still see: <code>@Input()</code>,
<code>@Output() x = new EventEmitter()</code>, <code>ngOnChanges</code>
to react to input changes. With signal inputs, <code>computed()</code>
and <code>effect()</code> replace most <code>ngOnChanges</code>
logic.</p>
<h3 id="template-syntax-built-in-control-flow-and-defer">1.4 Template
syntax: built-in control flow and <code>@defer</code></h3>
<div class="sourceCode" id="cb150"><pre
class="sourceCode html"><code class="sourceCode html"><span id="cb150-1"><a href="#cb150-1" aria-hidden="true" tabindex="-1"></a>@if (orders().length) {</span>

<span id="cb150-3"><a href="#cb150-3" aria-hidden="true" tabindex="-1"></a>    @for (order of orders(); track order.id) {          <span class="co">&lt;!-- track is required --&gt;</span></span>

<span id="cb150-19"><a href="#cb150-19" aria-hidden="true" tabindex="-1"></a>  <span class="dt">&lt;</span><span class="kw">app-reviews</span><span class="ot"> [productId]</span><span class="op">=</span><span class="st">&quot;id()&quot;</span><span class="ot"> </span><span class="dt">/&gt;</span>                    <span class="co">&lt;!-- separate lazy chunk --&gt;</span></span>
<span id="cb150-20"><a href="#cb150-20" aria-hidden="true" tabindex="-1"></a>} @placeholder { <span class="dt">&lt;</span><span class="kw">div</span><span class="ot"> class</span><span class="op">=</span><span class="st">&quot;reviews-skeleton&quot;</span><span class="dt">&gt;&lt;/</span><span class="kw">div</span><span class="dt">&gt;</span> }</span>
<span id="cb150-21"><a href="#cb150-21" aria-hidden="true" tabindex="-1"></a>  @loading (minimum 300ms) { <span class="dt">&lt;</span><span class="kw">app-spinner</span><span class="ot"> </span><span class="dt">/&gt;</span> }</span></code></pre></div>
<ul>
<li>Built-in control flow (v17+) replaces <code>*ngIf</code>,
<code>*ngFor</code>, <code>ngSwitch</code>; it’s faster and needs no
imports. <code>track</code> is Angular’s version of React keys, and the
same rules apply (stable IDs, not index, for dynamic lists).</li>
<li><code>@defer</code> lazy-loads a part of a template and its
dependencies on a trigger (<code>on viewport</code>,
<code>on idle</code>, <code>on interaction</code>,
<code>on timer</code>, <code>when condition</code>). Great for
below-the-fold widgets.</li>
</ul>
<h3 id="lifecycle-projection-directives-pipes">1.5 Lifecycle,
projection, directives, pipes</h3>
<table>
<colgroup>
<col style="width: 33%" />
<col style="width: 33%" />
<col style="width: 33%" />
</colgroup>
<thead>
<tr>
<th>Hook</th>
<th>When</th>
<th>Typical use</th>
</tr>
</thead>
<tbody>
<tr>
<td><code>constructor</code> / field initialisers</td>
<td>Instance created</td>
<td><code>inject()</code> dependencies; no DOM, inputs not set yet</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td><code>ngOnChanges</code></td>
<td>Input values change</td>
<td>Legacy input reactions (signals reduce the need)</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td><code>ngOnInit</code></td>
<td>After first inputs are set</td>
<td>Initial data loading</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td><code>ngAfterViewInit</code></td>
<td>View and children rendered</td>
<td>DOM measurement, third-party widgets (<code>viewChild()</code>
signals now)</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td><code>ngOnDestroy</code> / <code>DestroyRef</code></td>
<td>Before destruction</td>
<td>Cleanup; <code>takeUntilDestroyed()</code> (Hour 3)</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td><code>afterNextRender</code> / <code>afterRender</code></td>
<td>After DOM updates (browser only)</td>
<td>SSR-safe DOM work</td>
</tr>
</tbody>
</table>
<ul>
<li><strong>Content projection:</strong>
<code>&lt;ng-content select="[card-title]"&gt;</code> for slots, like
React <code>children</code>.</li>
<li><strong>Directives:</strong> attribute directives add behaviour to
elements (<code>appAutofocus</code>, <code>appHasRole="admin"</code>);
host directives compose behaviour onto components.</li>
<li><strong>Pipes:</strong> <strong>pure</strong> pipes (default)
recompute only when inputs change by reference, which is why they’re
cheap; <strong>impure</strong> pipes run on every change detection, so
avoid them for expensive work. Prefer a pure pipe or
<code>computed()</code> over calling methods in templates
(<code>{{ getTotal() }}</code> runs on every check).</li>
</ul>
<h3 id="how-id-answer-hour-1-9">How I’d answer — Hour 1</h3>
<p><strong>Q1. What’s changed in modern Angular?</strong> “Standalone
components by default instead of NgModules, the <code>inject()</code>
function, signals for reactivity with signal inputs, outputs and
<code>model()</code>, built-in control flow with <code>@if</code>,
<code>@for</code> and <code>@defer</code>, functional guards and
interceptors, and zoneless change detection, now the default. v22 made
Signal Forms and resource/httpResource stable, made OnPush the default
for new components, and added the <span class="citation"
data-cites="Service">@Service</span>() decorator as shorthand for a
root-provided injectable. Together they make Angular lighter and closer
to fine-grained reactivity. I write new code that way and can migrate
older modules incrementally.”</p>
<p><strong>Q2. How does Angular DI work and how is it scoped?</strong>
“A hierarchy of injectors. <code>providedIn: 'root'</code> gives an
app-wide singleton; providers on a lazy route give a scope for that
feature; providers on a component give each instance its own copy.
Lookups go up the tree to the nearest provider. Tokens let me inject
config and swap implementations for tests or environments.”</p>
<p><strong>Q3. Why is calling a method in a template a problem?</strong>
“Template expressions are re-evaluated on every change detection pass
for that component, so an expensive method runs constantly. A pure pipe
or a <code>computed()</code> signal recalculates only when its inputs
change.”</p>
<p><strong>Q4. What does <code>@defer</code> do?</strong> “It splits a
block of the template and its dependencies into a separate lazy chunk,
loaded on a trigger like entering the viewport or idle time, with
placeholder and loading states. It’s a simple way to cut initial bundle
size for below-the-fold features.”</p>
<h3 id="practice-27">Practice</h3>
<ul class="task-list">
<li><label><input type="checkbox" />Scaffold the capstone admin app
(<code>apps/admin</code>) as standalone with <code>provideRouter</code>,
<code>provideHttpClient</code> and OnPush everywhere</label></li>
<li><label><input type="checkbox" />Build an order list with
<code>@for ... track</code>, <code>@empty</code> and a
<code>@defer</code>-loaded order analytics widget</label></li>
<li><label><input type="checkbox" />Create an <code>API_BASE_URL</code>
token and a component-scoped <code>OrderFilterStore</code>
service</label></li>
</ul>
<h2 id="hour-2-change-detection-and-signals">Hour 2 — Change detection
and signals</h2>
<p>Change detection is the Angular equivalent of “why does React
re-render?” and the most common deep-dive question in Angular
interviews. Signals changed the answer recently, so you need both the
classic zone.js model (most production apps) and the signals/zoneless
model (where Angular is going).</p>
<h3 id="classic-change-detection-with-zone.js">2.1 Classic change
detection with zone.js</h3>
<p><strong>What happens:</strong> zone.js patches browser async APIs
(events, timers, XHR/fetch, promises). When any of them completes,
Angular is notified and runs change detection: it walks the component
tree <strong>from the root down</strong>, re-evaluates template
bindings, and updates the DOM where values changed.</p>
<ul>
<li><strong>Default strategy:</strong> every component is checked on
every cycle. Simple, but cost grows with tree size and with expensive
template expressions.</li>
<li><strong>OnPush strategy:</strong> a component (and its subtree) is
checked only when:
<ol type="1">
<li>an <code>@Input</code> gets a <strong>new reference</strong> (not a
mutation),</li>
<li>an event fires inside the component or its children,</li>
<li>an <code>async</code> pipe in its template receives a value,</li>
<li>a signal read in its template changes,</li>
<li>it’s marked explicitly
(<code>ChangeDetectorRef.markForCheck()</code>).</li>
</ol></li>
</ul>
<div class="sourceCode" id="cb151"><pre
class="sourceCode ts"><code class="sourceCode typescript"><span id="cb151-1"><a href="#cb151-1" aria-hidden="true" tabindex="-1"></a><span class="co">// Bug under OnPush: mutation keeps the same reference, so the child isn&#39;t checked</span></span>
<span id="cb151-2"><a href="#cb151-2" aria-hidden="true" tabindex="-1"></a><span class="kw">this</span><span class="op">.</span><span class="at">order</span><span class="op">.</span><span class="at">items</span><span class="op">.</span><span class="fu">push</span>(newItem)<span class="op">;</span></span>
<span id="cb151-3"><a href="#cb151-3" aria-hidden="true" tabindex="-1"></a><span class="co">// Fix: immutable update creates a new reference</span></span>
<span id="cb151-4"><a href="#cb151-4" aria-hidden="true" tabindex="-1"></a><span class="kw">this</span><span class="op">.</span><span class="at">order</span> <span class="op">=</span> { <span class="op">...</span><span class="kw">this</span><span class="op">.</span><span class="at">order</span><span class="op">,</span> items<span class="op">:</span> [<span class="op">...</span><span class="kw">this</span><span class="op">.</span><span class="at">order</span><span class="op">.</span><span class="at">items</span><span class="op">,</span> newItem] }<span class="op">;</span></span></code></pre></div>

<p><strong>“ExpressionChangedAfterItHasBeenCheckedError”</strong>
(development only): a binding changed during the check itself, typically
setting a parent value from a child’s <code>ngAfterViewInit</code>. Fix
the data flow rather than wrapping in <code>setTimeout</code>.</p>
<p><strong>My rule:</strong> OnPush on every component, immutable data,
<code>async</code> pipe or signals in templates. This makes performance
predictable and also prepares the code for zoneless.</p>
<h3 id="signals">2.2 Signals</h3>
<p><strong>What they are:</strong> reactive values that know who reads
them. When a signal changes, Angular updates exactly the consumers that
depend on it, instead of checking everything.</p>

<p><strong>Common mistakes:</strong> using <code>effect()</code> to copy
one signal into another (use <code>computed</code> or
<code>linkedSignal</code>); mutating an array inside a signal instead of
<code>update</code> with a new array; reading signals in loops in
services without understanding that only reads inside a reactive context
(template, <code>computed</code>, <code>effect</code>) create
dependencies.</p>
<h3 id="signals-vs-rxjs">2.3 Signals vs RxJS</h3>
<table>
<colgroup>
<col style="width: 33%" />
<col style="width: 33%" />
<col style="width: 33%" />
</colgroup>
<thead>
<tr>
<th></th>
<th>Signals</th>
<th>RxJS Observables</th>
</tr>
</thead>
<tbody>
<tr>
<td>Models</td>
<td>A value that changes over time; always has a current value</td>
<td>A stream of events over time</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>Synchronous read</td>
<td>Yes: <code>count()</code></td>
<td>No (subscribe; or <code>BehaviorSubject.value</code>)</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>Strengths</td>
<td>UI state, derived state, fine-grained updates, simple mental
model</td>
<td>Async orchestration: debouncing, cancellation, retries, combining
streams, WebSockets</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>Cleanup</td>
<td>Automatic</td>
<td>Must unsubscribe (async pipe, <code>takeUntilDestroyed</code>)</td>
</tr>
</tbody>
</table>
<p><strong>My split:</strong> signals for component and UI state; RxJS
for event streams and async workflows (typeahead, polling, WebSocket
feeds), converted to signals at the edge with <code>toSignal()</code>
for the template.</p>
<h3 id="zoneless-angular">2.4 Zoneless Angular</h3>
<p><strong>What it is:</strong> running Angular without zone.js (stable
since v20.2, the default for new apps since v21; v22 also makes OnPush
the default for new components)
(<code>provideZonelessChangeDetection()</code>). Change detection is
scheduled only by signals changing, template events, <code>async</code>
pipe emissions and <code>markForCheck()</code>, not by every timer or
promise in the app.</p>
<p>Benefits: smaller bundle, no monkey-patching of browser APIs, clearer
stack traces, fewer unnecessary checks, better interop with other code.
Requirements: components must already notify Angular properly, which
OnPush + signals + <code>async</code> pipe guarantee. Code that relies
on “some setTimeout somewhere triggers a refresh” breaks.</p>
<p><strong>Migration path:</strong> OnPush everywhere → replace manual
state with signals → remove reliance on zone-triggered updates
(<code>markForCheck()</code> where needed) → switch to zoneless and run
the full test suite.</p>
<h3 id="how-id-answer-hour-2-9">How I’d answer — Hour 2</h3>
<p><strong>Q1. How does Angular change detection work?</strong>
“Traditionally zone.js patches async APIs and triggers a top-down check
of the component tree after every event, timer or request. With the
Default strategy every component is checked; with OnPush a component is
checked only when an input reference changes, an event happens inside
it, an async pipe emits, a signal it reads changes, or it’s marked for
check. Signals and zoneless mode move Angular to fine-grained updates
where only components whose signals changed are refreshed.”</p>
<p><strong>Q2. My OnPush component doesn’t update. Why?</strong>
“Usually the input object was mutated instead of replaced, so the
reference didn’t change; or the data arrives through a plain
subscription that sets a field without notifying Angular. Fix with
immutable updates, or expose the data as a signal or through the async
pipe; <code>markForCheck()</code> as a last resort.”</p>
<p><strong>Q3. Signals or RxJS?</strong> “Both, for different jobs.
Signals for state and derived values, because they’re synchronous,
memoised and clean up automatically. RxJS for streams and async
coordination, like debouncing search input, cancelling requests with
switchMap, or merging WebSocket events. I convert streams to signals
with <code>toSignal()</code> before they reach templates.”</p>
<p><strong>Q4. What do you gain from zoneless?</strong> “No zone.js in
the bundle, no patching of browser APIs, and change detection only when
state actually changes, so fewer wasted checks and clearer debugging.
The prerequisite is that components notify Angular explicitly, so OnPush
and signals first.”</p>

<h2 id="hour-3-rxjs-in-depth">Hour 3 — RxJS in depth</h2>
<p>RxJS is where Angular interviews get hard for developers coming from
React or Node. The question you will almost certainly get: “switchMap vs
mergeMap vs concatMap vs exhaustMap”. Know it by real use case, not just
definitions, plus subjects, hot vs cold, and how to avoid subscription
leaks.</p>
<h3 id="observable-basics">3.1 Observable basics</h3>
<p><strong>What it is:</strong> a lazy stream of values over time.
Nothing happens until someone subscribes; it can emit zero, one or many
values, then complete or error; it can be cancelled by
unsubscribing.</p>
<table>
<thead>
<tr>
<th></th>
<th>Promise</th>
<th>Observable</th>
</tr>
</thead>
<tbody>
<tr>
<td>Values</td>
<td>One</td>
<td>Zero to many</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>Execution</td>
<td>Eager (starts on creation)</td>
<td>Lazy (starts on subscribe)</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>Cancellable</td>
<td>No (only with AbortController)</td>
<td>Yes, unsubscribe</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>Operators</td>
<td><code>then</code> chain</td>
<td>Rich operator library</td>
</tr>
</tbody>
</table>
<p><strong>Cold vs hot:</strong> a <strong>cold</strong> observable
starts a new producer for each subscriber: two subscriptions to
<code>http.get()</code> make <strong>two HTTP requests</strong>. A
<strong>hot</strong> observable shares one producer: DOM events,
WebSocket messages, a Subject. Turn cold into shared with
<code>shareReplay</code>:</p>
<div class="sourceCode" id="cb154"><pre
class="sourceCode ts"><code class="sourceCode typescript"><span id="cb154-1"><a href="#cb154-1" aria-hidden="true" tabindex="-1"></a><span class="kw">readonly</span> config$ <span class="op">=</span> <span class="kw">this</span><span class="op">.</span><span class="at">http</span><span class="op">.</span><span class="fu">get</span><span class="op">&lt;</span>Config<span class="op">&gt;</span>(<span class="st">&#39;/api/config&#39;</span>)<span class="op">.</span><span class="fu">pipe</span>(</span>

<h3 id="subjects">3.2 Subjects</h3>
<table>
<colgroup>
<col style="width: 33%" />
<col style="width: 33%" />
<col style="width: 33%" />
</colgroup>
<thead>
<tr>
<th>Subject</th>
<th>Behaviour</th>
<th>Use</th>
</tr>
</thead>
<tbody>
<tr>
<td><code>Subject</code></td>
<td>Multicasts; late subscribers miss earlier values</td>
<td>Event bus, actions, “refresh” triggers</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td><code>BehaviorSubject</code></td>
<td>Needs an initial value; new subscribers get the current value;
<code>.value</code> reads it</td>
<td>State in services (the pre-signals way)</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td><code>ReplaySubject(n)</code></td>
<td>Replays the last n values to new subscribers</td>
<td>Caching recent events</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td><code>AsyncSubject</code></td>
<td>Emits only the last value, on completion</td>
<td>Rare</td>
</tr>
</tbody>
</table>
<p>Expose subjects read-only:
<code>private state = new BehaviorSubject(initial); readonly state$ = this.state.asObservable();</code>
so components can’t call <code>next()</code> directly. In new code, a
signal often replaces a <code>BehaviorSubject</code> for state.</p>
<h3 id="flattening-operators-the-big-one">3.3 Flattening operators (the
big one)</h3>
<p>All four map each outer value to an inner observable (usually an HTTP
call). They differ in what happens when a new outer value arrives while
an inner one is still running:</p>
<table>
<colgroup>
<col style="width: 33%" />
<col style="width: 33%" />
<col style="width: 33%" />
</colgroup>
<thead>
<tr>
<th>Operator</th>
<th>Behaviour</th>
<th>Real use case</th>
</tr>
</thead>
<tbody>
<tr>
<td><code>switchMap</code></td>
<td><strong>Cancels</strong> the previous inner, switches to the new
one</td>
<td>Typeahead search, route param changes, filter changes: only the
latest result matters</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td><code>mergeMap</code></td>
<td>Runs all inners <strong>in parallel</strong>, results in completion
order</td>
<td>Independent work: upload 5 files at once, mark many notifications
read (cap with <code>mergeMap(fn, 3)</code>)</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td><code>concatMap</code></td>
<td><strong>Queues</strong>: waits for each inner to finish, in
order</td>
<td>Order matters: saving edits sequentially, chat messages in
order</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td><code>exhaustMap</code></td>
<td><strong>Ignores</strong> new outer values while an inner is
running</td>
<td>Submit/login buttons: ignore double clicks until the request
finishes; refresh-token calls</td>
</tr>
</tbody>
</table>
<div class="sourceCode" id="cb155"><pre
class="sourceCode ts"><code class="sourceCode typescript"><span id="cb155-1"><a href="#cb155-1" aria-hidden="true" tabindex="-1"></a><span class="co">// Typeahead: the canonical RxJS example</span></span>
<span id="cb155-2"><a href="#cb155-2" aria-hidden="true" tabindex="-1"></a>results <span class="op">=</span> <span class="fu">toSignal</span>(</span>
<span id="cb155-3"><a href="#cb155-3" aria-hidden="true" tabindex="-1"></a>  <span class="kw">this</span><span class="op">.</span><span class="at">searchControl</span><span class="op">.</span><span class="at">valueChanges</span><span class="op">.</span><span class="fu">pipe</span>(</span>
<span id="cb155-4"><a href="#cb155-4" aria-hidden="true" tabindex="-1"></a>    <span class="fu">map</span>((q) <span class="kw">=&gt;</span> q<span class="op">.</span><span class="fu">trim</span>())<span class="op">,</span></span>

<p>The <code>catchError</code> placement is a classic follow-up: if the
error isn’t caught inside <code>switchMap</code>, it reaches the outer
stream, which then <strong>completes</strong>, and the search box stops
working for the rest of the session.</p>
<h3 id="combining-streams">3.4 Combining streams</h3>
<table>
<colgroup>
<col style="width: 33%" />
<col style="width: 33%" />
<col style="width: 33%" />
</colgroup>
<thead>
<tr>
<th>Operator</th>
<th>Emits</th>
<th>Use</th>
</tr>
</thead>
<tbody>
<tr>
<td><code>combineLatest([a$, b$])</code></td>
<td>Latest of each, whenever any emits (after all have emitted
once)</td>
<td>Filters + sort + page → query</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td><code>forkJoin([a$, b$])</code></td>
<td>Once, when all <strong>complete</strong>, with their last

<td>Parallel HTTP calls before rendering (like
<code>Promise.all</code>)</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td><code>withLatestFrom(b$)</code></td>
<td>When the source emits, paired with b’s latest</td>
<td>Button click + current form state</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td><code>merge(a$, b$)</code></td>
<td>Every value from any</td>
<td>Several event sources into one</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td><code>zip</code></td>
<td>Pairs values by index</td>
<td>Rare</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td><code>startWith</code>, <code>scan</code></td>
<td>Initial value; running accumulation</td>
<td>Building state from events (a mini reducer)</td>
</tr>
</tbody>
</table>
<p><code>forkJoin</code> trap: if any source never completes (like a
<code>BehaviorSubject</code> or <code>valueChanges</code>), it never
emits.</p>

<h3 id="unsubscribing-preventing-leaks">3.6 Unsubscribing: preventing
leaks</h3>
<p>HTTP observables complete on their own, but
<code>valueChanges</code>, <code>interval</code>, router events, store
selects and WebSocket streams don’t. A component that subscribes and
never unsubscribes keeps running after it’s destroyed.</p>
<p>In order of preference:</p>
<ol type="1">
<li><strong>Don’t subscribe manually:</strong> use the
<code>async</code> pipe or <code>toSignal()</code>; both clean up
automatically.</li>
<li><strong><code>takeUntilDestroyed()</code></strong> (inside an
injection context, or pass a <code>DestroyRef</code>) for subscriptions
you need in code.</li>
<li>Older code: a <code>destroy$</code> Subject with
<code>takeUntil(this.destroy$)</code>, completed in
<code>ngOnDestroy</code>. <code>takeUntil</code> must be the
<strong>last</strong> operator, or later operators can keep the
subscription alive.</li>
</ol>
<p>Also avoid nested subscribes (<code>subscribe</code> inside
<code>subscribe</code>); use a flattening operator instead.</p>
<h3 id="how-id-answer-hour-3-9">How I’d answer — Hour 3</h3>
<p><strong>Q1. switchMap vs mergeMap vs concatMap vs
exhaustMap?</strong> “They all map to an inner observable and differ
when a new value arrives mid-flight. switchMap cancels the old one, so
it’s for search and route changes where only the latest counts. mergeMap
runs them in parallel, for independent work like uploads, ideally with a
concurrency limit. concatMap queues them in order, for sequential saves.
exhaustMap ignores new ones until the current finishes, for submit
buttons and token refresh.”</p>
<p><strong>Q2. Subject vs BehaviorSubject?</strong> “A Subject only
delivers values emitted after you subscribe. A BehaviorSubject holds a
current value, gives it to new subscribers immediately, and can be read
synchronously, which is why it was used for service state before
signals.”</p>
<p><strong>Q3. Why did my search stop working after one failed
request?</strong> “The error propagated to the outer stream and
completed it. Catch errors inside the switchMap, on the inner HTTP
observable, and return a fallback, so the outer valueChanges stream
keeps going.”</p>
<p><strong>Q4. How do you avoid memory leaks with
subscriptions?</strong> “Prefer the async pipe or toSignal so I rarely
subscribe manually. When I must, <code>takeUntilDestroyed()</code>. And
no nested subscribes. HTTP calls complete on their own, but form
changes, intervals and sockets don’t.”</p>
<p><strong>Q5. Two components call the same HTTP observable and I see
two requests. Why?</strong> “HTTP observables are cold, so each
subscription runs the request. Share it with
<code>shareReplay({ bufferSize: 1, refCount: true })</code>, or cache it
in a service or a signal.”</p>

<p>Key points: <strong>lazy loading</strong> with
<code>loadComponent</code> / <code>loadChildren</code>;
<strong>functional guards</strong> (<code>CanActivateFn</code>,
<code>CanMatchFn</code>, <code>CanDeactivateFn</code> for unsaved
changes); <strong>resolvers</strong> to load data before navigation (use
sparingly; a loading state inside the page often feels faster);
<code>withComponentInputBinding()</code> so route params arrive as
component inputs (<code>id = input.required&lt;string&gt;()</code>);
preloading strategies to fetch lazy chunks in the background. Guards are
UX, not security: the API must still authorise every request.</p>
<h3 id="httpclient-and-functional-interceptors">4.2 HttpClient and
functional interceptors</h3>
<div class="sourceCode" id="cb158"><pre

<span id="cb158-2"><a href="#cb158-2" aria-hidden="true" tabindex="-1"></a>  <span class="kw">const</span> auth <span class="op">=</span> <span class="fu">inject</span>(AuthService)<span class="op">;</span></span>
<span id="cb158-3"><a href="#cb158-3" aria-hidden="true" tabindex="-1"></a>  <span class="kw">const</span> token <span class="op">=</span> auth<span class="op">.</span><span class="fu">accessToken</span>()<span class="op">;</span></span>
<span id="cb158-4"><a href="#cb158-4" aria-hidden="true" tabindex="-1"></a>  <span class="kw">const</span> authReq <span class="op">=</span> token <span class="op">?</span> req<span class="op">.</span><span class="fu">clone</span>({ setHeaders<span class="op">:</span> { Authorization<span class="op">:</span> <span class="vs">`Bearer </span><span class="sc">${</span>token<span class="sc">}</span><span class="vs">`</span> } }) <span class="op">:</span> req<span class="op">;</span></span>
<span id="cb158-5"><a href="#cb158-5" aria-hidden="true" tabindex="-1"></a></span>
<span id="cb158-6"><a href="#cb158-6" aria-hidden="true" tabindex="-1"></a>  <span class="cf">return</span> <span class="fu">next</span>(authReq)<span class="op">.</span><span class="fu">pipe</span>(</span>
<span id="cb158-7"><a href="#cb158-7" aria-hidden="true" tabindex="-1"></a>    <span class="fu">catchError</span>((err<span class="op">:</span> HttpErrorResponse) <span class="kw">=&gt;</span> {</span>
<span id="cb158-8"><a href="#cb158-8" aria-hidden="true" tabindex="-1"></a>      <span class="cf">if</span> (err<span class="op">.</span><span class="at">status</span> <span class="op">!==</span> <span class="dv">401</span> <span class="op">||</span> req<span class="op">.</span><span class="at">url</span><span class="op">.</span><span class="fu">includes</span>(<span class="st">&#39;/auth/refresh&#39;</span>)) <span class="cf">return</span> <span class="fu">throwError</span>(() <span class="kw">=&gt;</span> err)<span class="op">;</span></span>
<span id="cb158-9"><a href="#cb158-9" aria-hidden="true" tabindex="-1"></a>      <span class="cf">return</span> auth<span class="op">.</span><span class="fu">refresh</span>()<span class="op">.</span><span class="fu">pipe</span>(                              <span class="co">// shared: one refresh for many 401s</span></span>
<span id="cb158-10"><a href="#cb158-10" aria-hidden="true" tabindex="-1"></a>        <span class="fu">switchMap</span>((newToken) <span class="kw">=&gt;</span> <span class="fu">next</span>(req<span class="op">.</span><span class="fu">clone</span>({ setHeaders<span class="op">:</span> { Authorization<span class="op">:</span> <span class="vs">`Bearer </span><span class="sc">${</span>newToken<span class="sc">}</span><span class="vs">`</span> } })))<span class="op">,</span></span>
<span id="cb158-11"><a href="#cb158-11" aria-hidden="true" tabindex="-1"></a>        <span class="fu">catchError</span>((refreshErr) <span class="kw">=&gt;</span> { auth<span class="op">.</span><span class="fu">logout</span>()<span class="op">;</span> <span class="cf">return</span> <span class="fu">throwError</span>(() <span class="kw">=&gt;</span> refreshErr)<span class="op">;</span> })<span class="op">,</span></span>
<span id="cb158-12"><a href="#cb158-12" aria-hidden="true" tabindex="-1"></a>      )<span class="op">;</span></span>
<span id="cb158-13"><a href="#cb158-13" aria-hidden="true" tabindex="-1"></a>    })<span class="op">,</span></span>
<span id="cb158-14"><a href="#cb158-14" aria-hidden="true" tabindex="-1"></a>  )<span class="op">;</span></span>
<span id="cb158-15"><a href="#cb158-15" aria-hidden="true" tabindex="-1"></a>}<span class="op">;</span></span></code></pre></div>
<p>The detail to explain: when ten requests get 401 at once, you want
<strong>one</strong> refresh call, not ten.
<code>AuthService.refresh()</code> keeps the in-flight refresh
observable and shares it (<code>shareReplay(1)</code>, cleared when
done) so every waiting request reuses the same new token. Interceptors
run in the order provided; typical chain: base URL → auth → retry →
error toast → logging.</p>

<p>Reactive vs template-driven: reactive forms for anything non-trivial
(typed, testable, dynamic with <code>FormArray</code>, validators as
functions); template-driven (<code>ngModel</code>) for very simple
forms. Typed forms (v14+) catch mistakes like reading a non-existent
control at compile time. <strong>Signal Forms</strong> (experimental in
v21, stable in v22) are the new signal-based forms API with schema
validation; expect new projects to adopt them, while most existing
codebases still use reactive forms, so know both.</p>

<p><strong>My rule:</strong> services with signals by default;
SignalStore when a feature’s state grows complex; classic NgRx only
where the team already uses it or the app genuinely needs
event-sourced-style traceability. Don’t put server cache logic in a
global store without thinking; TanStack Query also has an Angular
adapter.</p>
<h3 id="testing-ssr-performance">4.5 Testing, SSR, performance</h3>
<ul>
<li><strong>Testing:</strong> <code>TestBed</code> for component tests
with <code>provideHttpClientTesting()</code> and
<code>HttpTestingController</code>; test services as plain classes where
possible; Angular Testing Library for user-centric tests; Playwright or
Cypress for E2E. Karma is deprecated; Vitest has been the default test
runner since v21.</li>
<li><strong>SSR:</strong> <code>@angular/ssr</code> with
<strong>hydration</strong> (reuses server-rendered DOM instead of
re-creating it), incremental hydration with <code>@defer</code> blocks,
and <code>afterNextRender</code> for browser-only code. Use for public,
SEO-relevant pages.</li>
<li><strong>Performance checklist:</strong> OnPush or zoneless,
<code>track</code> in <code>@for</code>, lazy routes and
<code>@defer</code>, pure pipes and <code>computed</code> instead of
template methods, <code>NgOptimizedImage</code> for images, bundle
budgets in <code>angular.json</code>, virtual scrolling
(<code>cdk-virtual-scroll-viewport</code>) for long lists.</li>
</ul>
<h3 id="react-vs-angular">4.6 React vs Angular</h3>
<table>

<th></th>

<th>Angular</th>
</tr>
</thead>
<tbody>
<tr>
<td>Type</td>
<td>UI library; you choose routing, forms, data, state</td>
<td>Full framework: router, forms, HTTP, DI, testing, CLI, i18n built
in</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>Language</td>
<td>JS or TS</td>
<td>TypeScript by design</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>Reactivity</td>
<td>Re-render components, reconcile</td>
<td>Signals (fine-grained) + change detection</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>Templates</td>
<td>JSX (JavaScript)</td>
<td>HTML templates with Angular syntax</td>
</tr>
<tr>

<td>None built in (Context, imports)</td>
<td>Hierarchical DI, a core strength</td>

<tr>

</tr>

<td>High: one way to do most things</td>
</tr>

<td>Large enterprise apps, internal portals, banks, many teams on one
codebase</td>
</tr>
</tbody>
</table>
<p><strong>How I’d frame it:</strong> neither is “better”. React gives
flexibility and a huge ecosystem; Angular gives a complete, opinionated
platform that keeps large teams consistent. I’d pick based on team
skills, app type and how much the organisation values uniformity.</p>
<h3 id="how-id-answer-hour-4-9">How I’d answer — Hour 4</h3>
<p><strong>Q1. How do you handle token refresh in Angular?</strong> “A
functional interceptor adds the access token. On a 401 it calls a
refresh method that shares one in-flight refresh across all failing
requests, then retries each original request with the new token. If
refresh fails, log out and redirect. Refresh tokens stay in an httpOnly
cookie, as in my backend design.”</p>
<p><strong>Q2. When would you use NgRx?</strong> “When many features
share complex state, multiple teams work on it, and the traceability of
actions and DevTools pays for the ceremony. For most features, a service
with signals or an NgRx SignalStore is simpler and enough. I avoid using
a global store as a hand-rolled HTTP cache.”</p>
<p><strong>Q3. Reactive vs template-driven forms?</strong> “Reactive
forms for anything beyond a trivial form: typed, testable, dynamic with
FormArray, with sync, async and cross-field validators defined in code.
Template-driven only for very simple cases.”</p>
<p><strong>Q4. React or Angular for a new enterprise admin
portal?</strong> “For a large internal portal built by several teams, I
lean Angular: routing, forms, HTTP, DI and testing come standard, so
every team builds the same way. If the team is React-heavy or the
product shares code with a React Native app, React with an agreed stack
is fine. The team’s strength usually decides it.”</p>

<h1 id="week-3-study-notes-microservices-messaging-devops">Week 3 Study
Notes — Microservices, messaging, DevOps</h1>
<p>This week moves from single services to systems: how services talk,
how data stays consistent across them, and how they’re built, shipped
and run. Most system design rounds lean heavily on this material.</p>
<h1 id="day-11-mon-node.js-microservices-and-distributed-patterns">Day
11 (Mon) — Node.js microservices and distributed patterns</h1>
<h2 id="hour-1-microservices-fundamentals">Hour 1 — Microservices
fundamentals</h2>
<p>The best signal you can give in a microservices interview is
restraint. Many teams split too early and end up with a
<strong>distributed monolith</strong>: all the network failures of
microservices plus all the coupling of a monolith. Interviewers want to
hear when microservices pay off, how you’d draw boundaries, and what
each split costs.</p>
<h3 id="monolith-modular-monolith-microservices">1.1 Monolith, modular
monolith, microservices</h3>
<table>
<colgroup>
<col style="width: 25%" />
<col style="width: 25%" />
<col style="width: 25%" />
<col style="width: 25%" />
</colgroup>
<thead>
<tr>
<th></th>
<th>Monolith</th>
<th>Modular monolith</th>
<th>Microservices</th>
</tr>
</thead>
<tbody>
<tr>
<td>Deploy</td>
<td>One unit</td>
<td>One unit</td>
<td>Each service independently</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>Code boundaries</td>
<td>Often blurry</td>
<td>Enforced modules with clear interfaces</td>
<td>Separate codebases or packages, network boundaries</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>Data</td>
<td>One database</td>
<td>One database, schema per module</td>
<td>Database per service</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>Calls between parts</td>
<td>In-process function calls</td>
<td>In-process, through module APIs</td>
<td>Network (HTTP, gRPC, messages)</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>Transactions</td>
<td>ACID across everything</td>
<td>ACID across modules</td>
<td>Sagas, eventual consistency</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>Strengths</td>
<td>Simple to build, test, debug, deploy</td>
<td>Simplicity plus boundaries; easy to split later</td>
<td>Independent deploys and scaling, team autonomy, fault isolation,
tech freedom</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>Costs</td>
<td>Coupling grows; one deploy for everything; scaling
all-or-nothing</td>
<td>Needs discipline to keep boundaries</td>
<td>Network failures, latency, data consistency, observability, ops
overhead, platform team needed</td>
</tr>
</tbody>
</table>
<p><strong>When microservices pay off:</strong> several teams (roughly
4+ teams, 25+ engineers) blocked by each other’s releases; parts with
very different scaling or reliability needs (checkout vs reporting); a
need for independent deploy cadence; strong DevOps maturity (CI/CD,
containers, monitoring) already in place.</p>
<p><strong>When they don’t:</strong> a small team, an early product
whose domain boundaries are still moving, or no platform support.
<strong>My default for a new product:</strong> a modular monolith with
strict module boundaries, extracting services only where there’s a
concrete reason (a module needing independent scaling, a separate team,
a different technology).</p>
<h3 id="drawing-boundaries-with-domain-driven-design">1.2 Drawing
boundaries with Domain-Driven Design</h3>
<ul>
<li><strong>Bounded context:</strong> a part of the domain with its own
model and language. “Product” in the catalogue (descriptions, images,
attributes) is a different model from “Product” in inventory (SKU,
stock, warehouse) and in orders (snapshot of name and price). Each
context owns its model.</li>
<li><strong>Ubiquitous language:</strong> the same words used by
business and code within one context.</li>
<li><strong>Aggregates:</strong> clusters of objects changed together
under one consistency boundary (an <code>Order</code> with its
<code>OrderItems</code>); transactions don’t span aggregates.</li>
<li><strong>Context map:</strong> how contexts relate:
upstream/downstream, shared kernel, anti-corruption layer (translating a
legacy or external model so it doesn’t leak in).</li>
</ul>
<p><strong>Good service boundaries:</strong> align with business
capabilities (catalogue, cart, ordering, payments, inventory, shipping,
notifications, identity), are owned by one team, and need few
synchronous calls to others for their core work.</p>
<p><strong>Warning signs of bad boundaries:</strong> services that must
deploy together; a request that synchronously chains through five
services; services sharing a database; constant cross-team coordination
for small features; “entity services” (a <code>UserService</code>,
<code>ProductService</code> that are just CRUD over tables) that every
other service calls.</p>
<h3 id="data-ownership-database-per-service">1.3 Data ownership:
database per service</h3>
<p>Each service owns its data; others access it only through its API or
events. No reaching into another service’s tables.</p>
<p>Why: a shared database couples deploys (a schema change breaks other
services), couples scaling, and hides dependencies. The costs you
accept: no cross-service joins (compose data via API calls, events, or
read models); no cross-service ACID transactions (sagas, Hour 3);
duplicated data that’s eventually consistent.</p>
<p>How services get data they don’t own:</p>
<ul>
<li><strong>Query the owner synchronously</strong> when they need fresh
data at request time (and can tolerate the dependency).</li>
<li><strong>Keep a local copy fed by events</strong> (the order service
keeps product names and prices it receives from
<code>product.updated</code> events) when they need it fast or
independently of the owner’s availability.</li>
<li><strong>API composition / BFF</strong> to merge data from several
services for a screen.</li>
</ul>
<h3 id="api-gateway-and-bff">1.4 API gateway and BFF</h3>
<p><strong>API gateway:</strong> the single entry point for clients.
Responsibilities: routing to services, authentication (validating JWTs),
rate limiting, TLS termination, request/response logging, CORS,
sometimes response caching and aggregation. Options: Kong, AWS API
Gateway, Apigee, Envoy-based gateways, NGINX, or a thin Node gateway for
small systems. Keep business logic out of it.</p>
<p><strong>Backend for Frontend (BFF):</strong> a backend per client
type (web, mobile, partner API), shaped for that client’s screens:
aggregates calls, trims payloads, adapts to the client’s release cycle.
Often owned by the frontend team. GraphQL is a common BFF technology
(Day 5).</p>
<p><strong>Service discovery:</strong> in Kubernetes, the platform
handles it with Services and DNS
(<code>http://order-service.orders.svc.cluster.local</code>). Outside
Kubernetes: Consul, Eureka, or cloud load balancers.</p>
<h3 id="node.js-in-a-microservices-estate">1.5 Node.js in a
microservices estate</h3>
<p>What a production-ready Node service needs (and what a service
template should give every team):</p>
<ul>
<li>Health endpoints: <code>/health/live</code> (process is up) and
<code>/health/ready</code> (dependencies reachable, ready for
traffic)</li>
<li>Structured logs with correlation IDs (Day 4), metrics endpoint,
OpenTelemetry tracing (Hour 4)</li>
<li>Config from environment, validated at startup (Day 2)</li>
<li>Graceful shutdown (Day 3)</li>
<li>Standard error format, validation, auth middleware, generated
OpenAPI docs</li>
<li>Dockerfile, Helm chart, CI pipeline (Days 13–15)</li>
</ul>
<p>A shared service template or internal package for these keeps 20
services consistent. Keep shared libraries small and
infrastructure-focused; sharing domain models between services recreates
coupling.</p>
<h3 id="how-id-answer-hour-1-10">How I’d answer — Hour 1</h3>
<p><strong>Q1. When would you NOT use microservices?</strong> “With a
small team, an early product whose domain is still changing, or without
the platform maturity for CI/CD, containers and observability. Then
microservices add network failures, distributed data problems and
operational overhead with little benefit. I’d build a modular monolith
with strict boundaries and extract services only when a module needs
independent scaling, deployment or ownership.”</p>
<p><strong>Q2. How do you decide service boundaries?</strong> “By
business capability and bounded context, not by database table. Each
service owns a coherent part of the domain and its data, can do its main
job without synchronous calls to many others, and is owned by one team.
If two services always change and deploy together, they’re probably one
service.”</p>
<p><strong>Q3. Why database per service? Isn’t that
duplication?</strong> “It’s what makes services independently deployable
and scalable; a shared schema couples everyone. Yes, some data is
duplicated, deliberately: services keep local, event-fed copies of what
they need, accepting eventual consistency. Cross-service joins become
API composition or read models.”</p>
<p><strong>Q4. What’s a distributed monolith?</strong> “Services that
are separate on the network but still tightly coupled: they share a
database, must deploy together, or call each other synchronously in long
chains. You pay the cost of distribution without getting independence.
The fix is better boundaries, async communication and real data
ownership, or merging services back.”</p>
<h3 id="practice-30">Practice</h3>
<ul class="task-list">
<li><label><input type="checkbox" />Draw the capstone’s bounded contexts
and a context map: identity, catalogue, cart, ordering, payments,
inventory, notifications</label></li>
<li><label><input type="checkbox" />For each service, list the data it
owns and the data it copies from events</label></li>
<li><label><input type="checkbox" />Write a one-page ADR: “Modular
monolith first, extract services when…” with explicit
criteria</label></li>
</ul>
<h2 id="hour-2-service-to-service-communication-and-resilience">Hour 2 —
Service-to-service communication and resilience</h2>
<p>In a monolith a function call either works or throws. Over the
network a call can succeed, fail, time out after succeeding, arrive
twice, or hang forever. Most microservice outages come from how services
call each other, so this hour is about choosing the communication style
and protecting each call.</p>
<h3 id="synchronous-vs-asynchronous">2.1 Synchronous vs
asynchronous</h3>
<table>
<colgroup>
<col style="width: 33%" />
<col style="width: 33%" />
<col style="width: 33%" />
</colgroup>
<thead>
<tr>
<th></th>
<th>Synchronous (REST, gRPC)</th>
<th>Asynchronous (events, commands via broker)</th>
</tr>
</thead>
<tbody>
<tr>
<td>Caller waits</td>
<td>Yes</td>
<td>No</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>Coupling</td>
<td>Temporal: callee must be up now</td>
<td>Loose: consumer can be down and catch up</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>Failure impact</td>
<td>Cascades up the call chain</td>
<td>Contained; messages queue up</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>Consistency</td>
<td>Immediate answer</td>
<td>Eventual</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>Good for</td>
<td>Queries needing an answer now (“is this coupon valid?”), user-facing
reads</td>
<td>Notifying others that something happened (“order placed”), long
workflows, fan-out</td>
</tr>
</tbody>
</table>
<p><strong>Availability maths worth quoting:</strong> if a request
synchronously depends on five services each at 99.9% availability, the
chain is at most about 99.5% (0.999⁵), roughly 3.6 hours of downtime a
month instead of 43 minutes. Long synchronous chains multiply
failure.</p>
<p><strong>My default:</strong> synchronous calls only where the caller
truly needs the answer to continue; everything else as events. Prefer
<strong>events</strong> (“OrderPlaced”, a fact) over
<strong>commands</strong> (“SendEmail”, an instruction) between
services, so the publisher doesn’t need to know who reacts.</p>
<h3 id="rest-vs-grpc-between-services">2.2 REST vs gRPC between
services</h3>
<p><strong>gRPC:</strong> contract-first RPC using Protocol Buffers over
HTTP/2: binary, compact, strongly typed generated clients, streaming in
both directions, deadlines built in.</p>

<p>REST for public and browser-facing APIs and for simple internal
calls; gRPC for high-volume internal calls, polyglot teams that want
generated clients, and streaming. Protobuf evolution rules: never reuse
field numbers, add fields as optional, don’t change types.</p>
<h3 id="resilience-patterns-for-every-outbound-call">2.3 Resilience
patterns for every outbound call</h3>
<table>
<colgroup>
<col style="width: 33%" />
<col style="width: 33%" />
<col style="width: 33%" />

<tr>

<tr>
