<span id="cb163-8"><a href="#cb163-8" aria-hidden="true" tabindex="-1"></a>  errorThresholdPercentage<span class="op">:</span> <span class="dv">50</span><span class="op">,</span>   <span class="co">// open when half of recent calls fail</span></span>
<span id="cb163-9"><a href="#cb163-9" aria-hidden="true" tabindex="-1"></a>  resetTimeout<span class="op">:</span> <span class="dv">10_000</span><span class="op">,</span>           <span class="co">// after 10 s, let one trial call through (half-open)</span></span>
<span id="cb163-10"><a href="#cb163-10" aria-hidden="true" tabindex="-1"></a>  volumeThreshold<span class="op">:</span> <span class="dv">20</span><span class="op">,</span>            <span class="co">// don&#39;t judge on tiny samples</span></span>
<span id="cb163-11"><a href="#cb163-11" aria-hidden="true" tabindex="-1"></a>})<span class="op">;</span></span>
<span id="cb163-12"><a href="#cb163-12" aria-hidden="true" tabindex="-1"></a>breaker<span class="op">.</span><span class="fu">fallback</span>(() <span class="kw">=&gt;</span> POPULAR_PRODUCTS)<span class="op">;</span>         <span class="co">// degrade, don&#39;t fail the page</span></span>
<span id="cb163-13"><a href="#cb163-13" aria-hidden="true" tabindex="-1"></a>breaker<span class="op">.</span><span class="fu">on</span>(<span class="st">&#39;open&#39;</span><span class="op">,</span> () <span class="kw">=&gt;</span> metrics<span class="op">.</span><span class="fu">increment</span>(<span class="st">&#39;reco.circuit_open&#39;</span>))<span class="op">;</span></span>
<span id="cb163-14"><a href="#cb163-14" aria-hidden="true" tabindex="-1"></a></span>
<span id="cb163-15"><a href="#cb163-15" aria-hidden="true" tabindex="-1"></a><span class="kw">const</span> items <span class="op">=</span> <span class="cf">await</span> breaker<span class="op">.</span><span class="fu">fire</span>(userId)<span class="op">;</span></span></code></pre></div>
<p><strong>Circuit breaker states:</strong> closed (calls flow, failures
counted) → open (calls fail fast immediately) → half-open (a trial call;
success closes it, failure re-opens).</p>
<p><strong>Retry rules that prevent outages:</strong> retry only
idempotent operations or ones carrying an idempotency key; cap attempts;
add jitter; respect <code>Retry-After</code>; and <strong>retry at one
layer only</strong>. If the gateway, the service and the client library
each retry 3 times, one failing call becomes 27 requests at the worst
moment (a retry storm).</p>
<p><strong>Timeout budgets:</strong> if the gateway gives a request 2
seconds, the service calling three dependencies can’t give each 2
seconds. Pass a deadline down (gRPC does this natively; for HTTP, an
<code>x-request-deadline</code> header) and give up early when it can’t
be met.</p>
<h3 id="service-mesh">2.4 Service mesh</h3>
<p><strong>What it is:</strong> a sidecar proxy (Envoy in Istio;
Linkerd’s own proxy) next to every service, or node-level proxies in
newer “ambient” designs, handling network concerns outside application
code: mutual TLS between services, retries, timeouts, circuit breaking,
traffic splitting for canaries, and uniform metrics and traces.</p>
<p>Trade-offs: consistent policies across languages and less code in
services, against extra latency per hop, resource overhead, and real
operational complexity. Worth it with many services and strict security
requirements (zero-trust mTLS); overkill for a handful of services. Even
with a mesh, application-level idempotency and fallbacks remain your
job.</p>
<h3 id="how-id-answer-hour-2-10">How I’d answer — Hour 2</h3>
<p><strong>Q1. Sync or async between services?</strong> “Synchronous
only when the caller needs an answer to continue, like checking a coupon
at checkout, with tight timeouts and a fallback. Everything that’s ‘tell
others what happened’, like order placed or payment succeeded, goes
through events, so services stay decoupled and a downstream outage
doesn’t fail the user’s request. Long synchronous chains multiply
failure probability.”</p>
<p><strong>Q2. REST or gRPC internally?</strong> “gRPC for high-volume
internal calls where performance, strict contracts and streaming matter,
especially across languages. REST when simplicity, debuggability and
HTTP tooling matter more, and always for public and browser APIs. Either
way, contracts are versioned and backward compatible.”</p>
<p><strong>Q3. Explain the circuit breaker pattern.</strong> “It wraps
calls to a dependency and tracks failures. Past a threshold it opens and
fails fast without calling the dependency, often returning a fallback,
which protects both sides. After a cool-down it lets a trial request
through; success closes it, failure keeps it open. I tune thresholds on
volume and error percentage and alert when circuits open.”</p>
<p><strong>Q4. What’s a retry storm and how do you prevent it?</strong>
“When retries at several layers multiply load on a struggling service,
turning a slowdown into an outage. Retry at one layer, with exponential
backoff and jitter, a small cap, only on idempotent or idempotency-keyed
calls, and combine with circuit breakers so we stop retrying a
dependency that’s clearly down.”</p>
<h3 id="practice-31">Practice</h3>
<ul class="task-list">
<li><label><input type="checkbox" />Expose <code>CheckStock</code> and
<code>ReserveStock</code> over gRPC from the inventory service; call
them from the order service with deadlines</label></li>
<li><label><input type="checkbox" />Wrap the recommendations call in an
opossum circuit breaker with a fallback; kill the dependency and watch
the circuit open and recover</label></li>
<li><label><input type="checkbox" />Add a per-dependency concurrency
limit (bulkhead) and a single retry layer with jitter</label></li>
</ul>
<h2 id="hour-3-distributed-data-sagas-outbox-idempotent-consumers">Hour
3 — Distributed data: sagas, outbox, idempotent consumers</h2>
<p>Once each service owns its database, “place an order” spans the
order, payment and inventory services, and there’s no single transaction
to wrap it in. This hour is the core of senior microservices interviews:
walking through a saga for a failed payment, and explaining why the
outbox pattern exists. Fintech work is exactly where these matter.</p>
<h3 id="why-not-distributed-transactions-2pc">3.1 Why not distributed
transactions (2PC)?</h3>
<p><strong>Two-phase commit:</strong> a coordinator asks every
participant to prepare, then tells all to commit. It gives atomicity
across databases, but participants hold locks while waiting, the
coordinator is a single point of failure (a crash mid-protocol leaves
participants blocked), latency adds up, and most modern stores and
brokers (MongoDB across services, Kafka with a database, third-party
APIs like payment gateways) can’t take part. So microservices use
<strong>sagas</strong> and accept eventual consistency.</p>
<h3 id="sagas">3.2 Sagas</h3>
<p><strong>What it is:</strong> a sequence of local transactions, one
per service. Each step publishes an event or triggers the next. If a
step fails, previously completed steps are undone by
<strong>compensating transactions</strong> (business-level reversals,
not database rollbacks).</p>
<p>Place-order saga:</p>
<table>
<colgroup>
<col style="width: 25%" />
<col style="width: 25%" />
<col style="width: 25%" />
<col style="width: 25%" />
</colgroup>
<thead>
<tr>
<th>Step</th>
<th>Service</th>
<th>Action</th>
<th>Compensation if a later step fails</th>
</tr>
</thead>
<tbody>
<tr>
<td>1</td>
<td>Order</td>
<td>Create order <code>PENDING</code></td>
<td>Mark order <code>CANCELLED</code></td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>2</td>
<td>Inventory</td>
<td>Reserve stock</td>
<td>Release reservation</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>3</td>
<td>Payment</td>
<td>Charge customer</td>
<td>Refund</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>4</td>
<td>Order</td>
<td>Mark <code>CONFIRMED</code></td>
<td>—</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>5</td>
<td>Shipping / Notifications</td>
<td>Create shipment, send email</td>
<td>— (after the point of no return)</td>
</tr>
</tbody>
</table>
<p>If payment fails at step 3: release stock (compensate step 2), cancel
order (compensate step 1), notify the customer. Compensations must
themselves be idempotent and retryable, because they can fail too.</p>
<p><strong>Choreography vs orchestration:</strong></p>
<table>
<colgroup>
<col style="width: 33%" />
<col style="width: 33%" />
<col style="width: 33%" />
</colgroup>
<thead>
<tr>
<th></th>
<th>Choreography</th>
<th>Orchestration</th>
</tr>
</thead>
<tbody>
<tr>
<td>How</td>
<td>Each service reacts to events and emits new ones; no central
controller</td>
<td>A saga orchestrator (often in the order service) sends commands and
tracks state</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>Flow</td>
<td><code>OrderCreated</code> → inventory reserves →
<code>StockReserved</code> → payment charges →
<code>PaymentSucceeded</code> → order confirms</td>
<td>Orchestrator: “reserve stock” → waits → “charge payment” → waits →
“confirm”</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>Good</td>
<td>Simple for 2–3 steps, very loosely coupled</td>
<td>Flow visible in one place, easy to add steps, timeouts and
compensations explicit</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>Bad</td>
<td>Hard to see the whole flow; cyclic dependencies creep in; debugging
across services</td>
<td>Orchestrator is more central (but not a shared database)</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>Tools</td>
<td>Events on Kafka/RabbitMQ</td>
<td>Custom state machine in a table, or workflow engines: Temporal, AWS
Step Functions, Camunda</td>
</tr>
</tbody>
</table>
<p><strong>My rule:</strong> choreography for short, simple reactions
(order placed → send email, update analytics); orchestration for
business-critical multi-step flows with compensations (checkout,
refunds, loan disbursement). For complex long-running workflows, a
durable workflow engine like Temporal removes a lot of hand-written
retry and state code.</p>
<p><strong>Saga pitfalls to mention:</strong> lack of isolation (another
request can see the order as <code>PENDING</code> with stock reserved;
design states and UIs for it), semantic locks (mark records as “in
progress” so other flows don’t act on them), and timeouts (what if
payment never responds? the orchestrator needs a deadline and a
decision).</p>
<h3 id="the-transactional-outbox">3.3 The transactional outbox</h3>
<p><strong>The problem (dual write):</strong> a service saves an order
to its database and publishes <code>OrderCreated</code> to Kafka. If the
publish fails after the commit, other services never hear about the
order. If you publish first and the DB commit fails, they hear about an
order that doesn’t exist.</p>
<p><strong>The fix:</strong> write the event into an <code>outbox</code>
table <strong>in the same local transaction</strong> as the business
change. A separate relay publishes outbox rows to the broker and marks
them sent.</p>
<div class="sourceCode" id="cb164"><pre
class="sourceCode ts"><code class="sourceCode typescript"><span id="cb164-1"><a href="#cb164-1" aria-hidden="true" tabindex="-1"></a><span class="cf">await</span> db<span class="op">.</span><span class="fu">transaction</span>(<span class="kw">async</span> (tx) <span class="kw">=&gt;</span> {</span>
<span id="cb164-2"><a href="#cb164-2" aria-hidden="true" tabindex="-1"></a>  <span class="kw">const</span> order <span class="op">=</span> <span class="cf">await</span> tx<span class="op">.</span><span class="at">orders</span><span class="op">.</span><span class="fu">insert</span>({ <span class="op">...</span>input<span class="op">,</span> status<span class="op">:</span> <span class="st">&#39;PENDING&#39;</span> })<span class="op">;</span></span>
<span id="cb164-3"><a href="#cb164-3" aria-hidden="true" tabindex="-1"></a>  <span class="cf">await</span> tx<span class="op">.</span><span class="at">outbox</span><span class="op">.</span><span class="fu">insert</span>({</span>
<span id="cb164-4"><a href="#cb164-4" aria-hidden="true" tabindex="-1"></a>    id<span class="op">:</span> crypto<span class="op">.</span><span class="fu">randomUUID</span>()<span class="op">,</span>               <span class="co">// becomes the event ID used for dedup downstream</span></span>
<span id="cb164-5"><a href="#cb164-5" aria-hidden="true" tabindex="-1"></a>    aggregateType<span class="op">:</span> <span class="st">&#39;order&#39;</span><span class="op">,</span></span>
<span id="cb164-6"><a href="#cb164-6" aria-hidden="true" tabindex="-1"></a>    aggregateId<span class="op">:</span> order<span class="op">.</span><span class="at">id</span><span class="op">,</span></span>
<span id="cb164-7"><a href="#cb164-7" aria-hidden="true" tabindex="-1"></a>    type<span class="op">:</span> <span class="st">&#39;OrderCreated&#39;</span><span class="op">,</span></span>
<span id="cb164-8"><a href="#cb164-8" aria-hidden="true" tabindex="-1"></a>    payload<span class="op">:</span> { orderId<span class="op">:</span> order<span class="op">.</span><span class="at">id</span><span class="op">,</span> customerId<span class="op">:</span> order<span class="op">.</span><span class="at">customerId</span><span class="op">,</span> lines<span class="op">:</span> order<span class="op">.</span><span class="at">lines</span><span class="op">,</span> total<span class="op">:</span> order<span class="op">.</span><span class="at">total</span> }<span class="op">,</span></span>
<span id="cb164-9"><a href="#cb164-9" aria-hidden="true" tabindex="-1"></a>    createdAt<span class="op">:</span> <span class="kw">new</span> <span class="bu">Date</span>()<span class="op">,</span></span>
<span id="cb164-10"><a href="#cb164-10" aria-hidden="true" tabindex="-1"></a>  })<span class="op">;</span></span>
<span id="cb164-11"><a href="#cb164-11" aria-hidden="true" tabindex="-1"></a>})<span class="op">;</span></span>
<span id="cb164-12"><a href="#cb164-12" aria-hidden="true" tabindex="-1"></a></span>
<span id="cb164-13"><a href="#cb164-13" aria-hidden="true" tabindex="-1"></a><span class="co">// Relay (separate worker): poll, publish, mark sent. Run this inside ONE transaction so the row locks hold</span></span>
<span id="cb164-14"><a href="#cb164-14" aria-hidden="true" tabindex="-1"></a><span class="kw">const</span> batch <span class="op">=</span> <span class="cf">await</span> db<span class="op">.</span><span class="fu">query</span>(</span>
<span id="cb164-15"><a href="#cb164-15" aria-hidden="true" tabindex="-1"></a>  <span class="vs">`SELECT * FROM outbox WHERE published_at IS NULL ORDER BY created_at LIMIT 100 FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED`</span>)<span class="op">;</span></span>
<span id="cb164-16"><a href="#cb164-16" aria-hidden="true" tabindex="-1"></a><span class="cf">for</span> (<span class="kw">const</span> e <span class="kw">of</span> batch) {</span>
<span id="cb164-17"><a href="#cb164-17" aria-hidden="true" tabindex="-1"></a>  <span class="cf">await</span> producer<span class="op">.</span><span class="fu">send</span>({ topic<span class="op">:</span> <span class="st">&#39;orders&#39;</span><span class="op">,</span> messages<span class="op">:</span> [{ key<span class="op">:</span> e<span class="op">.</span><span class="at">aggregate_id</span><span class="op">,</span> value<span class="op">:</span> <span class="bu">JSON</span><span class="op">.</span><span class="fu">stringify</span>(e)<span class="op">,</span> headers<span class="op">:</span> { eventId<span class="op">:</span> e<span class="op">.</span><span class="at">id</span> } }] })<span class="op">;</span></span>
<span id="cb164-18"><a href="#cb164-18" aria-hidden="true" tabindex="-1"></a>  <span class="cf">await</span> db<span class="op">.</span><span class="fu">query</span>(<span class="st">&#39;UPDATE outbox SET published_at = now() WHERE id = $1&#39;</span><span class="op">,</span> [e<span class="op">.</span><span class="at">id</span>])<span class="op">;</span></span>
<span id="cb164-19"><a href="#cb164-19" aria-hidden="true" tabindex="-1"></a>}</span></code></pre></div>
<p>Relay options: polling with <code>SKIP LOCKED</code> (simple, Day 7),
or <strong>CDC</strong> with Debezium reading the database log (lower
latency, no polling load). MongoDB: change streams (Day 6). The relay
can publish an event twice (crash between publish and mark), so delivery
is <strong>at least once</strong>, and consumers must be idempotent.</p>
<h3 id="idempotent-consumers-the-inbox">3.4 Idempotent consumers (the
inbox)</h3>
<p>Messages can arrive more than once (broker redelivery, relay retries,
consumer crash before acknowledging). Consumers must make duplicates
harmless:</p>
<div class="sourceCode" id="cb165"><pre
class="sourceCode ts"><code class="sourceCode typescript"><span id="cb165-1"><a href="#cb165-1" aria-hidden="true" tabindex="-1"></a><span class="kw">async</span> <span class="kw">function</span> <span class="fu">handlePaymentSucceeded</span>(event<span class="op">:</span> PaymentSucceeded) {</span>
<span id="cb165-2"><a href="#cb165-2" aria-hidden="true" tabindex="-1"></a>  <span class="cf">await</span> db<span class="op">.</span><span class="fu">transaction</span>(<span class="kw">async</span> (tx) <span class="kw">=&gt;</span> {</span>
<span id="cb165-3"><a href="#cb165-3" aria-hidden="true" tabindex="-1"></a>    <span class="kw">const</span> inserted <span class="op">=</span> <span class="cf">await</span> tx<span class="op">.</span><span class="fu">query</span>(</span>
<span id="cb165-4"><a href="#cb165-4" aria-hidden="true" tabindex="-1"></a>      <span class="st">&#39;INSERT INTO processed_events (event_id, consumer) VALUES ($1, $2) ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING RETURNING 1&#39;</span><span class="op">,</span></span>
<span id="cb165-5"><a href="#cb165-5" aria-hidden="true" tabindex="-1"></a>      [<span class="bu">event</span><span class="op">.</span><span class="at">eventId</span><span class="op">,</span> <span class="st">&#39;order-service&#39;</span>])<span class="op">;</span></span>
<span id="cb165-6"><a href="#cb165-6" aria-hidden="true" tabindex="-1"></a>    <span class="cf">if</span> (inserted<span class="op">.</span><span class="at">rowCount</span> <span class="op">===</span> <span class="dv">0</span>) <span class="cf">return</span><span class="op">;</span>                 <span class="co">// already handled: skip</span></span>
<span id="cb165-7"><a href="#cb165-7" aria-hidden="true" tabindex="-1"></a>    <span class="cf">await</span> tx<span class="op">.</span><span class="fu">query</span>(<span class="st">&quot;UPDATE orders SET status = &#39;CONFIRMED&#39; WHERE id = $1 AND status = &#39;PENDING&#39;&quot;</span><span class="op">,</span> [<span class="bu">event</span><span class="op">.</span><span class="at">orderId</span>])<span class="op">;</span></span>
<span id="cb165-8"><a href="#cb165-8" aria-hidden="true" tabindex="-1"></a>  })<span class="op">;</span>                                                      <span class="co">// dedup record and effect commit together</span></span>
<span id="cb165-9"><a href="#cb165-9" aria-hidden="true" tabindex="-1"></a>  <span class="co">// acknowledge the message only after the transaction commits</span></span>
<span id="cb165-10"><a href="#cb165-10" aria-hidden="true" tabindex="-1"></a>}</span></code></pre></div>
<p>Other ways to be idempotent: natural idempotency
(<code>SET status = 'CONFIRMED'</code> rather than
<code>INCREMENT</code>), conditional updates on state, unique
constraints on business keys (<code>provider_payment_id</code>).</p>
<p><strong>“Exactly once” in interviews:</strong> end-to-end
exactly-once delivery across systems isn’t achievable in general; what
you build is <strong>at-least-once delivery + idempotent processing =
effectively-once results</strong>. Kafka’s exactly-once semantics (Day
12) apply within Kafka (consume-transform-produce), not to your database
or an email provider.</p>
<h3 id="cqrs-and-event-sourcing">3.5 CQRS and event sourcing</h3>
<ul>
<li><strong>CQRS</strong> (Day 8): separate write model and read models,
kept in sync by events. Common and useful with microservices: a
<code>customer-orders-view</code> service builds a query-optimised view
from order, payment and shipping events, replacing cross-service
joins.</li>
<li><strong>Event sourcing:</strong> store the sequence of events
(<code>OrderCreated</code>, <code>ItemAdded</code>,
<code>OrderPaid</code>) as the source of truth instead of current state;
current state is computed by replaying (with snapshots for speed).
Benefits: complete audit trail, time travel, rebuild new read models
from history. Costs: harder querying, schema evolution of old events,
steeper learning curve. Good fit: ledgers, banking, audit-heavy domains.
<strong>Overkill for most CRUD services.</strong> A ledger table that’s
append-only (Day 7) captures much of the value with less machinery.</li>
</ul>
<h3 id="how-id-answer-hour-3-10">How I’d answer — Hour 3</h3>
<p><strong>Q1. Walk me through what happens when payment fails during
checkout.</strong> “Checkout is an orchestrated saga. The order service
creates the order as pending and writes a command to its outbox.
Inventory reserves stock and replies. Payment is attempted with an
idempotency key; it fails, and payment publishes PaymentFailed. The
orchestrator runs compensations in reverse: tells inventory to release
the reservation and marks the order cancelled, then notifies the
customer. Every step and compensation is idempotent, messages go through
outboxes, and the orchestrator has timeouts so a payment that never
answers doesn’t leave stock reserved forever.”</p>
<p><strong>Q2. Why do you need the outbox pattern?</strong> “Because
writing to the database and publishing to a broker are two separate
operations; either can fail after the other succeeds, leaving systems
inconsistent. Writing the event into an outbox table in the same
transaction makes the state change and the intent to publish atomic, and
a relay or CDC publishes it reliably. Delivery becomes at-least-once, so
consumers deduplicate.”</p>
<p><strong>Q3. Choreography or orchestration?</strong> “Choreography for
simple reactions with two or three steps, where loose coupling matters
most. Orchestration for critical multi-step processes with compensations
and timeouts, because the flow is explicit, observable and easier to
change. For long-running workflows I’d consider Temporal instead of
building a state machine by hand.”</p>
<p><strong>Q4. Can you guarantee exactly-once processing?</strong> “Not
delivery across systems. I design for at-least-once delivery and make
processing idempotent: record processed event IDs in the same
transaction as the side effect, use conditional updates and unique
business keys. The result is effectively once.”</p>
<h3 id="practice-32">Practice</h3>
<ul class="task-list">
<li><label><input type="checkbox" />Implement the outbox table and a
polling relay in the order service
(<code>FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED</code>)</label></li>
<li><label><input type="checkbox" />Implement an orchestrated checkout
saga as a state machine table: PENDING → STOCK_RESERVED → PAID →
CONFIRMED, with compensations and a timeout</label></li>
<li><label><input type="checkbox" />Add <code>processed_events</code>
dedup to the payment and inventory consumers; prove duplicates are
ignored by publishing the same event twice</label></li>
</ul>
<h2 id="hour-4-observability-migration-splitting-the-capstone">Hour 4 —
Observability, migration, splitting the capstone</h2>
<p>With one service, a stack trace and a log file usually explain a bug.
With fifteen, a slow checkout could be any of them, or the network
between them. Interviewers ask “a request is slow in production, how do
you find out why?” and “how would you move a monolith to microservices?”
This hour prepares both answers, then you split the capstone.</p>
<h3 id="the-three-signals">4.1 The three signals</h3>
<table>
<colgroup>
<col style="width: 33%" />
<col style="width: 33%" />
<col style="width: 33%" />
</colgroup>
<thead>
<tr>
<th>Signal</th>
<th>Answers</th>
<th>Tools</th>
</tr>
</thead>
<tbody>
<tr>
<td><strong>Metrics</strong></td>
<td>Is something wrong, and how much? (rates, latencies,
saturation)</td>
<td>Prometheus + Grafana, Datadog, CloudWatch</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td><strong>Logs</strong></td>
<td>What exactly happened in this service?</td>
<td>Structured JSON (pino) → Loki, ELK/OpenSearch, Datadog</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td><strong>Traces</strong></td>
<td>Where did this request spend its time across services?</td>
<td>OpenTelemetry → Jaeger, Tempo, Datadog, Honeycomb</td>
</tr>
</tbody>
</table>
<p><strong>Metrics that matter for each service:</strong></p>
<ul>
<li><strong>RED</strong> for request-driven services:
<strong>R</strong>ate (requests/s), <strong>E</strong>rrors (error
rate), <strong>D</strong>uration (p50/p95/p99 latency).</li>
<li><strong>USE</strong> for resources: <strong>U</strong>tilisation,
<strong>S</strong>aturation (queue length, event-loop delay, connection
pool waits), <strong>E</strong>rrors.</li>
<li>Plus business metrics: orders per minute, payment success rate.
These often catch problems before technical metrics do.</li>
</ul>
<p><strong>SLOs and alerting:</strong> define service level objectives
(“99.9% of checkout requests succeed in under 800 ms over 30 days”), and
alert on <strong>error budget burn rate</strong> rather than on every
CPU spike. Alerts should be actionable and rare; noisy alerts get
ignored.</p>
<h3 id="distributed-tracing-with-opentelemetry">4.2 Distributed tracing
with OpenTelemetry</h3>
<p><strong>How it works:</strong> each request gets a <strong>trace
ID</strong>; each unit of work (an HTTP handler, a DB query, an outbound
call) is a <strong>span</strong> with timing and attributes. The trace
context travels between services in the <code>traceparent</code> header
(W3C Trace Context) and in message headers for Kafka/RabbitMQ, so one
trace shows the whole journey.</p>
<div class="sourceCode" id="cb166"><pre
class="sourceCode ts"><code class="sourceCode typescript"><span id="cb166-1"><a href="#cb166-1" aria-hidden="true" tabindex="-1"></a><span class="co">// tracing.ts — loaded before anything else: node --import ./tracing.js server.js</span></span>
<span id="cb166-2"><a href="#cb166-2" aria-hidden="true" tabindex="-1"></a><span class="im">import</span> { NodeSDK } <span class="im">from</span> <span class="st">&#39;@opentelemetry/sdk-node&#39;</span><span class="op">;</span></span>

<span id="cb166-4"><a href="#cb166-4" aria-hidden="true" tabindex="-1"></a><span class="im">import</span> { OTLPTraceExporter } <span class="im">from</span> <span class="st">&#39;@opentelemetry/exporter-trace-otlp-http&#39;</span><span class="op">;</span></span>
<span id="cb166-5"><a href="#cb166-5" aria-hidden="true" tabindex="-1"></a></span>
<span id="cb166-6"><a href="#cb166-6" aria-hidden="true" tabindex="-1"></a><span class="kw">new</span> <span class="fu">NodeSDK</span>({</span>
<span id="cb166-7"><a href="#cb166-7" aria-hidden="true" tabindex="-1"></a>  serviceName<span class="op">:</span> <span class="st">&#39;order-service&#39;</span><span class="op">,</span></span>
<span id="cb166-8"><a href="#cb166-8" aria-hidden="true" tabindex="-1"></a>  traceExporter<span class="op">:</span> <span class="kw">new</span> <span class="fu">OTLPTraceExporter</span>({ url<span class="op">:</span> <span class="bu">process</span><span class="op">.</span><span class="at">env</span><span class="op">.</span><span class="at">OTEL_EXPORTER_OTLP_ENDPOINT</span> })<span class="op">,</span></span>

<span id="cb166-10"><a href="#cb166-10" aria-hidden="true" tabindex="-1"></a>})<span class="op">.</span><span class="fu">start</span>()<span class="op">;</span></span></code></pre></div>
<div class="sourceCode" id="cb167"><pre
class="sourceCode ts"><code class="sourceCode typescript"><span id="cb167-1"><a href="#cb167-1" aria-hidden="true" tabindex="-1"></a><span class="co">// A manual span around business logic</span></span>
<span id="cb167-2"><a href="#cb167-2" aria-hidden="true" tabindex="-1"></a><span class="kw">const</span> tracer <span class="op">=</span> trace<span class="op">.</span><span class="fu">getTracer</span>(<span class="st">&#39;order-service&#39;</span>)<span class="op">;</span></span>
<span id="cb167-3"><a href="#cb167-3" aria-hidden="true" tabindex="-1"></a><span class="cf">await</span> tracer<span class="op">.</span><span class="fu">startActiveSpan</span>(<span class="st">&#39;checkout.reserve-and-charge&#39;</span><span class="op">,</span> <span class="kw">async</span> (span) <span class="kw">=&gt;</span> {</span>
<span id="cb167-4"><a href="#cb167-4" aria-hidden="true" tabindex="-1"></a>  span<span class="op">.</span><span class="fu">setAttribute</span>(<span class="st">&#39;order.id&#39;</span><span class="op">,</span> orderId)<span class="op">;</span></span>
<span id="cb167-5"><a href="#cb167-5" aria-hidden="true" tabindex="-1"></a>  <span class="cf">try</span> { <span class="cf">await</span> saga<span class="op">.</span><span class="fu">run</span>(orderId)<span class="op">;</span> }</span>
<span id="cb167-6"><a href="#cb167-6" aria-hidden="true" tabindex="-1"></a>  <span class="cf">catch</span> (e) { span<span class="op">.</span><span class="fu">recordException</span>(e <span class="im">as</span> <span class="bu">Error</span>)<span class="op">;</span> span<span class="op">.</span><span class="fu">setStatus</span>({ code<span class="op">:</span> SpanStatusCode<span class="op">.</span><span class="at">ERROR</span> })<span class="op">;</span> <span class="cf">throw</span> e<span class="op">;</span> }</span>
<span id="cb167-7"><a href="#cb167-7" aria-hidden="true" tabindex="-1"></a>  <span class="cf">finally</span> { span<span class="op">.</span><span class="fu">end</span>()<span class="op">;</span> }</span>
<span id="cb167-8"><a href="#cb167-8" aria-hidden="true" tabindex="-1"></a>})<span class="op">;</span></span></code></pre></div>
<p>Put the trace ID in every log line so you can jump from a trace to
the logs of that exact request. Use <strong>sampling</strong> (e.g. keep
all errors and slow requests, a percentage of the rest) to control cost.
Run an <strong>OpenTelemetry Collector</strong> between services and
backends so you can change vendors without changing code.</p>
<h3 id="debugging-a-slow-request-across-services">4.3 Debugging a slow
request across services</h3>
<ol type="1">
<li>Dashboard: which service’s p99 rose, and when? Did it coincide with
a deploy or traffic change?</li>
<li>Find slow traces for that endpoint; look for the widest span: a slow
DB query, a dependency, retries, or time waiting in a queue.</li>
<li>Jump to logs for that trace ID for errors and details.</li>
<li>Check saturation metrics on the guilty service: event-loop delay,
connection pool waits, CPU throttling, consumer lag.</li>
<li>Fix, then add the missing metric or alert so it’s caught faster next
time.</li>
</ol>
<h3 id="migrating-a-monolith-the-strangler-fig">4.4 Migrating a
monolith: the strangler fig</h3>
<p><strong>What it is:</strong> put a routing layer (gateway or proxy)
in front of the monolith, build new functionality or extracted
capabilities as services, and route traffic to them piece by piece. The
monolith shrinks over time until it can be retired. No big-bang
rewrite.</p>
<p>Steps that work:</p>
<ol type="1">
<li>Map the domain and pick the first candidate: well-bounded, high
value or high change rate, few dependencies (notifications, search,
catalogue are common starts; avoid starting with the core transactional
heart).</li>
<li>Put a facade/gateway in front so clients don’t notice routing
changes.</li>
<li>Build the new service with its own data; sync data with CDC or
events from the monolith during transition (an <strong>anti-corruption
layer</strong> translates the old model).</li>
<li>Shift traffic gradually (feature flags, percentage rollout), compare
results (shadow traffic or parallel runs for risky paths).</li>
<li>Remove the old code path and the old tables once the new service
owns the data.</li>
</ol>
<p>What to say about risks: data migration is the hardest part; avoid a
period where both systems write the same data without a clear owner;
keep the team able to ship features during the migration.</p>
<h3 id="testing-and-running-many-services-locally">4.5 Testing and
running many services locally</h3>
<ul>
<li><strong>Contract tests</strong> (Pact) or OpenAPI/AsyncAPI
validation between services (Day 5); schema registry for event contracts
(Day 12).</li>
<li><strong>Component tests</strong> per service with its real database
and broker in Testcontainers, and fakes for other services.</li>
<li>A small set of end-to-end tests in a staging environment for
critical journeys.</li>
<li><strong>Local development:</strong> Docker Compose for dependencies
(Day 13), run only the services you’re changing; tools like Tilt or
Skaffold for running against a local Kubernetes.</li>
</ul>
<h3 id="how-id-answer-hour-4-10">How I’d answer — Hour 4</h3>
<p><strong>Q1. Checkout is slow in production. How do you find the cause
across 12 services?</strong> “Start from the checkout latency dashboard
to see when it started and whether it lines up with a deploy or traffic
change. Then open slow traces for that endpoint in our tracing tool; the
waterfall shows which span dominates, whether it’s a DB query, a
downstream call, retries or queue wait. From the trace ID I jump to that
service’s logs and check its saturation metrics like event-loop delay
and pool waits. After fixing, I add whatever alert would have caught it
sooner.”</p>
<p><strong>Q2. How would you migrate a monolith to
microservices?</strong> “Incrementally with the strangler fig pattern. A
gateway in front, then extract one well-bounded capability at a time,
starting with something valuable but not the most tangled core. Each new
service owns its data, synced from the monolith during transition
through CDC and an anti-corruption layer. Traffic shifts gradually
behind flags, and the old code is removed once the service is proven. No
big-bang rewrite, and feature delivery continues throughout.”</p>
<p><strong>Q3. What metrics do you put on every service?</strong> “RED
metrics per endpoint: request rate, error rate and latency percentiles.
Saturation: event-loop delay, connection pool usage, consumer lag,
memory. Plus one or two business metrics. Alerts are based on SLOs and
error budget burn, not raw thresholds.”</p>
<h3 id="end-of-day-11-checklist">End of Day 11 checklist</h3>
<ul class="task-list">
<li><label><input type="checkbox" />Capstone split into gateway, auth,
product, order, payment, inventory and notification services, each
owning its data</label></li>
<li><label><input type="checkbox" />gRPC between order and inventory;
circuit breaker + fallback on recommendations</label></li>
<li><label><input type="checkbox" />Outbox + relay in the order service;
orchestrated checkout saga with compensations; idempotent
consumers</label></li>
<li><label><input type="checkbox" />OpenTelemetry auto-instrumentation
in every service, traces visible in Jaeger locally, trace IDs in
logs</label></li>
<li><label><input type="checkbox" />ADR for the service boundaries and a
context map diagram committed</label></li>
<li><label><input type="checkbox" />Saga-for-failed-payment and
strangler-fig answers rehearsed out loud</label></li>
</ul>
<h1 id="day-12-tue-rabbitmq-and-kafka-1">Day 12 (Tue) — RabbitMQ and
Kafka</h1>
<h2 id="hour-1-messaging-fundamentals">Hour 1 — Messaging
fundamentals</h2>
<p>Before RabbitMQ or Kafka specifics, get the concepts straight;
interview questions on brokers are really questions about these: what
happens if a consumer crashes mid-message, can events arrive out of
order, and what happens when you change an event’s shape while old
consumers are still running.</p>
<h3 id="why-a-broker">1.1 Why a broker</h3>
<p>A message broker sits between producers and consumers so they don’t
need to be up at the same time or know about each other. It gives
you:</p>
<ul>
<li><strong>Decoupling:</strong> the order service publishes
<code>OrderPlaced</code>; it doesn’t know email, analytics and loyalty
services exist.</li>
<li><strong>Load levelling:</strong> a sale-day spike fills a queue;
workers drain it at their own pace instead of falling over.</li>
<li><strong>Reliability:</strong> messages survive consumer restarts and
are retried.</li>
<li><strong>Fan-out:</strong> one event, many independent
consumers.</li>
<li><strong>Async work:</strong> slow jobs (emails, PDFs, third-party
calls) leave the request path.</li>
</ul>
<h3 id="two-broker-models-queue-vs-log">1.2 Two broker models: queue vs
log</h3>
<table>
<colgroup>
<col style="width: 33%" />
<col style="width: 33%" />
<col style="width: 33%" />
</colgroup>
<thead>
<tr>
<th></th>
<th>Message queue (RabbitMQ, SQS, BullMQ)</th>
<th>Distributed log (Kafka, Kinesis, Redpanda, Pulsar)</th>
</tr>
</thead>
<tbody>
<tr>
<td>Storage</td>
<td>Messages removed once acknowledged</td>
<td>Messages appended and <strong>retained</strong> for a period (days,
forever with compaction)</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>Consumers</td>
<td>Compete for messages; each message goes to one consumer of a
queue</td>
<td>Each consumer group reads independently and tracks its own
<strong>offset</strong></td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>Replay</td>
<td>No (once consumed, gone)</td>
<td>Yes: reset offsets and reprocess history</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>Routing</td>
<td>Rich (exchanges, routing keys, headers)</td>
<td>Topics + partition keys; consumers filter</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>Ordering</td>
<td>Per queue, weakened by multiple consumers and redelivery</td>
<td>Per partition, strong</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>Throughput</td>
<td>High (tens of thousands/s per node)</td>
<td>Very high (hundreds of thousands to millions/s per cluster)</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>Think of it as</td>
<td>A to-do list for workers</td>
<td>A durable, ordered history of what happened</td>
</tr>
</tbody>
</table>
<h3 id="delivery-guarantees">1.3 Delivery guarantees</h3>
<table>
<colgroup>
<col style="width: 33%" />
<col style="width: 33%" />
<col style="width: 33%" />
</colgroup>
<thead>
<tr>
<th>Guarantee</th>
<th>How it happens</th>
<th>Risk</th>
</tr>
</thead>
<tbody>
<tr>
<td>At most once</td>
<td>Acknowledge before processing (or fire and forget)</td>
<td>Messages lost if the consumer crashes</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td><strong>At least once</strong></td>
<td>Acknowledge after processing succeeds</td>
<td>Duplicates after crashes, redeliveries, retries</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>Exactly once</td>
<td>Only within closed systems (e.g. Kafka consume-transform-produce
with transactions)</td>
<td>Not end-to-end across your DB, email provider, etc.</td>
</tr>
</tbody>
</table>
<p><strong>The standard production design:</strong> at-least-once
delivery + idempotent consumers (Day 11,
inbox/<code>processed_events</code>) = effectively-once outcomes. Say
this sentence in every messaging interview.</p>
<h3 id="ordering">1.4 Ordering</h3>
<p>Global ordering across a whole system is expensive and rarely needed.
What you usually need is <strong>ordering per entity</strong>: all
events for order 123 in order, while events for different orders can
interleave.</p>
<ul>
<li>Kafka: use the entity ID as the message <strong>key</strong>; same
key → same partition → ordered.</li>
<li>RabbitMQ: a single queue with a single consumer is ordered; multiple
consumers or redeliveries break strict order. Use consistent-hash
exchanges or single-active-consumer for per-key ordering.</li>
<li>In consumers, defend anyway: include a <strong>version or sequence
number</strong> per entity and ignore events older than what you’ve
already applied
(<code>UPDATE ... WHERE id = $1 AND version &lt; $2</code>).</li>
</ul>
<h3 id="designing-messages">1.5 Designing messages</h3>
<p><strong>Events vs commands:</strong></p>
<ul>
<li><strong>Event:</strong> a fact in the past, published by the owner,
any number of consumers: <code>OrderPlaced</code>,
<code>PaymentFailed</code>. Publisher doesn’t care who listens.</li>
<li><strong>Command:</strong> a request for something to happen, one
intended receiver: <code>SendEmail</code>, <code>ReserveStock</code>.
Used in orchestrated sagas.</li>
</ul>
<p><strong>A good event envelope:</strong></p>
<div class="sourceCode" id="cb168"><pre
class="sourceCode json"><code class="sourceCode json"><span id="cb168-1"><a href="#cb168-1" aria-hidden="true" tabindex="-1"></a><span class="fu">{</span></span>
<span id="cb168-2"><a href="#cb168-2" aria-hidden="true" tabindex="-1"></a>  <span class="dt">&quot;eventId&quot;</span><span class="fu">:</span> <span class="st">&quot;7f1c0b6e-2f5a-4b8e-9d3c-1a2b3c4d5e6f&quot;</span><span class="fu">,</span></span>
<span id="cb168-3"><a href="#cb168-3" aria-hidden="true" tabindex="-1"></a>  <span class="dt">&quot;type&quot;</span><span class="fu">:</span> <span class="st">&quot;order.placed&quot;</span><span class="fu">,</span></span>
<span id="cb168-4"><a href="#cb168-4" aria-hidden="true" tabindex="-1"></a>  <span class="dt">&quot;version&quot;</span><span class="fu">:</span> <span class="dv">2</span><span class="fu">,</span></span>
<span id="cb168-5"><a href="#cb168-5" aria-hidden="true" tabindex="-1"></a>  <span class="dt">&quot;occurredAt&quot;</span><span class="fu">:</span> <span class="st">&quot;2026-11-23T10:15:00Z&quot;</span><span class="fu">,</span></span>
<span id="cb168-6"><a href="#cb168-6" aria-hidden="true" tabindex="-1"></a>  <span class="dt">&quot;source&quot;</span><span class="fu">:</span> <span class="st">&quot;order-service&quot;</span><span class="fu">,</span></span>
<span id="cb168-7"><a href="#cb168-7" aria-hidden="true" tabindex="-1"></a>  <span class="dt">&quot;traceparent&quot;</span><span class="fu">:</span> <span class="st">&quot;00-4bf92f35...-01&quot;</span><span class="fu">,</span></span>
<span id="cb168-8"><a href="#cb168-8" aria-hidden="true" tabindex="-1"></a>  <span class="dt">&quot;subject&quot;</span><span class="fu">:</span> <span class="st">&quot;order/9c1d...&quot;</span><span class="fu">,</span></span>
<span id="cb168-9"><a href="#cb168-9" aria-hidden="true" tabindex="-1"></a>  <span class="dt">&quot;data&quot;</span><span class="fu">:</span> <span class="fu">{</span> <span class="dt">&quot;orderId&quot;</span><span class="fu">:</span> <span class="st">&quot;9c1d...&quot;</span><span class="fu">,</span> <span class="dt">&quot;customerId&quot;</span><span class="fu">:</span> <span class="st">&quot;...&quot;</span><span class="fu">,</span> <span class="dt">&quot;totalPaise&quot;</span><span class="fu">:</span> <span class="dv">499900</span><span class="fu">,</span> <span class="dt">&quot;currency&quot;</span><span class="fu">:</span> <span class="st">&quot;INR&quot;</span><span class="fu">,</span> <span class="dt">&quot;lines&quot;</span><span class="fu">:</span> <span class="ot">[]</span> <span class="fu">}</span></span>
<span id="cb168-10"><a href="#cb168-10" aria-hidden="true" tabindex="-1"></a><span class="fu">}</span></span></code></pre></div>
<p><code>eventId</code> for deduplication, <code>version</code> for
schema evolution, <code>occurredAt</code> for ordering and debugging,
<code>traceparent</code> for tracing across async hops. The CloudEvents
spec standardises a similar envelope.</p>
<p><strong>Thin vs fat events:</strong> thin events
(<code>{ orderId }</code>) force consumers to call back to the owner
(coupling, load); fat events (“event-carried state transfer”) include
the data consumers need, so they can act independently. Usually include
what typical consumers need, but not entire internal models.</p>
<p><strong>Schema evolution rules:</strong> add optional fields only;
never remove or rename fields or change types in place; for breaking
changes publish a new version (<code>order.placed.v3</code>) alongside
the old one until consumers migrate. Enforce with a schema registry
(Hour 3) or AsyncAPI specs and contract tests. Consumers ignore unknown
fields (tolerant reader).</p>
<h3 id="choosing-a-tool">1.6 Choosing a tool</h3>
<table>
<colgroup>
<col style="width: 50%" />
<col style="width: 50%" />
</colgroup>
<thead>
<tr>
<th>Need</th>
<th>Good fit</th>
</tr>
</thead>
<tbody>
<tr>
<td>Background jobs in a Node app (emails, PDFs), retries, delays,
schedules</td>
<td>BullMQ (Redis)</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>Task distribution, complex routing, per-message acks, RPC-style
request/reply, moderate volume</td>
<td>RabbitMQ</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>High-volume event streaming, replay, many independent consumers,
event sourcing, CDC, analytics pipelines</td>
<td>Kafka</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>Managed and simple on AWS</td>
<td>SQS (queue) + SNS / EventBridge (fan-out, routing)</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>Lightweight, low-latency messaging</td>
<td>NATS (JetStream for persistence)</td>
</tr>
</tbody>
</table>
<h3 id="how-id-answer-hour-1-11">How I’d answer — Hour 1</h3>
<p><strong>Q1. Queue or log, what’s the difference?</strong> “A queue
hands each message to one consumer and deletes it once acknowledged,
which is right for distributing work. A log keeps an ordered history
that many consumer groups read independently at their own offsets and
can replay, which is right for event streaming and building multiple
views of the same events.”</p>
<p><strong>Q2. How do you guarantee a message is processed exactly
once?</strong> “I don’t rely on exactly-once delivery. Consumers
acknowledge only after processing, giving at-least-once delivery, and
processing is idempotent: I store the event ID in the same transaction
as the effect and skip duplicates, or use conditional updates and unique
keys. The outcome is effectively once.”</p>
<p><strong>Q3. How do you keep events for one order in order?</strong>
“Partition by order ID in Kafka so they land in one partition, or use
per-key ordering in RabbitMQ. And consumers still carry a version per
entity and ignore stale updates, because retries and replays can reorder
things.”</p>
<p><strong>Q4. How do you change an event’s schema safely?</strong>
“Additive changes only within a version; consumers ignore unknown
fields. Breaking changes go out as a new event version published in
parallel until all consumers have moved. A schema registry with
compatibility rules blocks accidental breaking changes in CI.”</p>
<h3 id="practice-33">Practice</h3>
<ul class="task-list">
<li><label><input type="checkbox" />Define the capstone’s event
catalogue (AsyncAPI or a markdown table): name, owner, consumers,
payload, version</label></li>
<li><label><input type="checkbox" />Write a shared
<code>EventEnvelope&lt;T&gt;</code> type and a Zod schema per event in
<code>packages/types</code></label></li>
<li><label><input type="checkbox" />Decide, for each event, queue
(RabbitMQ) or log (Kafka), and write one line why</label></li>
</ul>
<h2 id="hour-2-rabbitmq">Hour 2 — RabbitMQ</h2>
<p>RabbitMQ interviews focus on the AMQP model (exchanges vs queues),
what makes a message survive a crash, and how you handle failures
without losing messages or looping forever on a bad one. If you can draw
the flow from producer to dead-letter queue and explain each setting,
you’re in good shape.</p>
<h3 id="the-model">2.1 The model</h3>
<p><strong>Flow:</strong> producer → <strong>exchange</strong> →
(bindings with routing keys) → <strong>queues</strong> → consumers.
Producers never publish to a queue directly (the default exchange hides
this for simple cases); exchanges decide routing.</p>
<table>
<colgroup>
<col style="width: 33%" />
<col style="width: 33%" />
<col style="width: 33%" />
</colgroup>
<thead>
<tr>
<th>Exchange type</th>
<th>Routes by</th>
<th>Example</th>
</tr>
</thead>
<tbody>
<tr>
<td>Direct</td>
<td>Exact routing key match</td>
<td><code>email.send</code> → email queue</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td><strong>Topic</strong></td>
<td>Pattern on dot-separated keys: <code>*</code> one word,
<code>#</code> zero or more</td>
<td><code>order.*</code> gets <code>order.placed</code>,
<code>order.cancelled</code>; <code>order.#.india</code></td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>Fanout</td>
<td>Ignores key; copies to every bound queue</td>
<td>Broadcast cache invalidation</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>Headers</td>
<td>Message header values</td>
<td>Rare; routing on several attributes</td>
</tr>
</tbody>
</table>
<p><strong>Pub/sub pattern:</strong> one topic exchange
<code>orders</code>; each consuming service declares <strong>its own
queue</strong> bound to the keys it cares about
(<code>notification.orders</code> bound to <code>order.placed</code>,
<code>loyalty.orders</code> bound to <code>order.paid</code>). Every
service gets its own copy; within one service, several instances share
that queue as <strong>competing consumers</strong>, which is how you
scale workers.</p>
<h3 id="not-losing-messages">2.2 Not losing messages</h3>
<p>Several settings together, each covering a different failure:</p>
<table>
<colgroup>
<col style="width: 50%" />
<col style="width: 50%" />
</colgroup>
<thead>
<tr>
<th>Setting</th>
<th>Protects against</th>
</tr>
</thead>
<tbody>
<tr>
<td><strong>Durable</strong> exchange and queue</td>
<td>Broker restart deleting the definitions</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td><strong>Persistent</strong> messages (<code>deliveryMode: 2</code> /
<code>persistent: true</code>)</td>
<td>Broker restart losing messages in a durable queue</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td><strong>Publisher confirms</strong></td>
<td>Producer believing a message was stored when the broker never got
it</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td><strong>Manual consumer acks</strong> after processing</td>
<td>Consumer crash losing a message it had received</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td><strong>Quorum queues</strong> (<code>x-queue-type: quorum</code>,
Raft-replicated)</td>
<td>Losing a node; the modern replacement for classic mirrored
queues</td>
</tr>
</tbody>
</table>
<h3 id="consumers-acks-and-prefetch">2.3 Consumers: acks and
prefetch</h3>
<ul>
<li><code>ack</code> after successful processing: message removed.</li>
<li><code>nack</code> / <code>reject</code> with
<code>requeue: true</code>: back to the queue (danger: a poison message
loops forever); <code>requeue: false</code>: dead-lettered if a DLX is
configured, else dropped.</li>
<li>If the consumer’s connection drops before acking, RabbitMQ
redelivers the message (with <code>redelivered: true</code>), which is
why consumers must be idempotent.</li>
<li><strong>Prefetch</strong> (<code>channel.prefetch(n)</code>): how
many unacknowledged messages one consumer may hold. Without it, RabbitMQ
pushes as many as it can to the first consumer, which may run out of
memory while other consumers sit idle. Start around 10–50 for fast
handlers, 1–5 for slow ones, and tune.</li>
</ul>

publisher with confirms, consumer with DLQ</h3>

<span id="cb169-25"><a href="#cb169-25" aria-hidden="true" tabindex="-1"></a>})<span class="op">;</span></span>

<span id="cb169-40"><a href="#cb169-40" aria-hidden="true" tabindex="-1"></a>}<span class="op">,</span> { noAck<span class="op">:</span> <span class="kw">false</span> })<span class="op">;</span></span></code></pre></div>
<p>Production notes: use a reconnecting wrapper
(<code>amqp-connection-manager</code>) because connections drop; handle
<code>connection.on('error' | 'close')</code>; close channels and
connections in graceful shutdown (Day 3) after finishing in-flight
messages.</p>
<h3 id="retries-with-delay">2.5 Retries with delay</h3>
<p>Immediate requeue hammers a failing dependency. The classic
delayed-retry pattern:</p>
<ol type="1">
<li>Consumer fails → publish the message to a <strong>retry
queue</strong> with a TTL (e.g. 30 s) and no consumers, then ack the
original.</li>
<li>The retry queue’s <code>x-dead-letter-exchange</code> points back to
the main exchange, so after the TTL the message returns to the main
queue.</li>
<li>Track attempts in a header (<code>x-retry-count</code>, or read
<code>x-death</code>). After N attempts, send it to a
<strong>parking-lot DLQ</strong> for manual inspection.</li>
<li>Use several retry queues for growing delays (10 s, 1 min, 10 min),
or the delayed-message plugin.</li>
</ol>
<p>Always alert on DLQ depth and build a small tool to inspect and
replay DLQ messages after a fix.</p>
<h3 id="other-features-worth-knowing">2.6 Other features worth
knowing</h3>
<ul>
<li><strong>Request/reply (RPC):</strong> <code>replyTo</code> queue +
<code>correlationId</code>. Works, but synchronous RPC over a broker
usually means you wanted HTTP or gRPC.</li>
<li><strong>Single active consumer:</strong> only one consumer receives
from a queue at a time, others on standby; gives ordering with
failover.</li>
<li><strong>Priority queues</strong> and per-message TTL.</li>
<li><strong>RabbitMQ Streams:</strong> an append-only, replayable log
type inside RabbitMQ for Kafka-like use cases at moderate scale.</li>
<li><strong>Management UI and metrics:</strong> queue depth, unacked
counts, publish/deliver rates, consumer utilisation. Growing queue depth
means consumers can’t keep up.</li>
</ul>
<h3 id="how-id-answer-hour-2-11">How I’d answer — Hour 2</h3>
<p><strong>Q1. Explain exchanges, queues and bindings.</strong>
“Producers publish to an exchange with a routing key; bindings connect
exchanges to queues with patterns; consumers read from queues. A topic
exchange per domain, like <code>orders</code>, with each consuming
service owning its own queue bound to the keys it needs, gives pub/sub
across services and competing consumers within a service.”</p>
<p><strong>Q2. How do you make sure messages aren’t lost?</strong>
“Durable exchanges and quorum queues, persistent messages, publisher
confirms so the producer knows the broker stored it, and manual acks
after processing so a crashed consumer’s message is redelivered.
Publishing goes through an outbox so a database commit and a publish
can’t disagree.”</p>
<p><strong>Q3. A message keeps failing. What happens?</strong> “Without
care it loops forever. I retry with delays through TTL retry queues,
count attempts, and after a limit dead-letter it to a parking-lot queue
that alerts the team. Validation errors skip retries and go straight to
the DLQ, since retrying won’t fix them. After a fix, we replay from the
DLQ.”</p>
<p><strong>Q4. What does prefetch do?</strong> “It caps how many
unacknowledged messages a consumer holds. Without it, one consumer can
be flooded while others idle, and a crash means a large batch is
redelivered. Small prefetch for slow work, larger for fast handlers,
tuned by watching throughput.”</p>

<ul class="task-list">

with notification and loyalty queues; competing consumers with two
notification instances</label></li>
<li><label><input type="checkbox" />Publisher confirms from the outbox
relay; manual acks and quorum queues</label></li>
<li><label><input type="checkbox" />Delayed retry (TTL queue, 3
attempts) and a parking-lot DLQ; simulate an email provider outage and
recover by replaying</label></li>
</ul>
<h2 id="hour-3-kafka">Hour 3 — Kafka</h2>
<p>Kafka questions test whether you understand partitions: they decide
ordering, parallelism and scaling, and most Kafka mistakes come from
misunderstanding them. Then durability settings (what
<code>acks=all</code> really means), consumer offsets, and what Kafka’s
“exactly once” does and doesn’t cover.</p>
<h3 id="core-concepts">3.1 Core concepts</h3>
<table>
<colgroup>
<col style="width: 50%" />
<col style="width: 50%" />

<th>Concept</th>
<th>Meaning</th>
</tr>

<tr>
<td><strong>Topic</strong></td>
<td>A named stream of records, like <code>orders</code></td>

<td>A topic is split into partitions; each is an ordered, append-only

<td>A Kafka server; partitions are spread across brokers</td>
</tr>
<tr>

<td>Each partition has a leader and follower replicas; ISR = in-sync
replicas caught up with the leader</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td><strong>Consumer group</strong></td>
<td>Consumers sharing work; each partition is read by exactly one

</tr>
<tr>

<td>How long records stay (time or size), regardless of consumption</td>
</tr>
<tr>

<td>Keep only the latest record per key (a changelog / current

</tr>
<tr>

<td>Kafka’s built-in consensus; ZooKeeper is gone in current Kafka
versions</td>
</tr>
</tbody>

<h3 id="partitions-and-consumer-groups-the-key-mental-model">3.2
Partitions and consumer groups: the key mental model</h3>
<ul>
<li>Within a consumer group, <strong>max parallelism = number of
partitions</strong>. 12 partitions and 20 consumers: 8 consumers sit
idle. 12 partitions and 3 consumers: each reads 4.</li>
<li>Different consumer groups are independent: the notification service
and the analytics service each read every record at their own pace.</li>
<li><strong>Ordering is per partition only.</strong> Use the entity ID
(<code>orderId</code>, <code>customerId</code>) as the key to keep each
entity’s events in order.</li>
<li><strong>Hot partitions:</strong> if one key is very hot (a giant
tenant, a celebrity), its partition becomes a bottleneck. Spread with a
compound key when per-entity ordering allows, or handle that key
separately.</li>
<li><strong>Choosing partition count:</strong> based on target
throughput divided by per-consumer throughput, with headroom; dozens per
topic is common, not thousands. Adding partitions later is possible but
changes which partition a key maps to, breaking per-key ordering during
the change, so size with headroom up front.</li>
<li><strong>Rebalancing:</strong> when consumers join or leave,
partitions are reassigned. Use cooperative-sticky assignment and static
membership to avoid stop-the-world rebalances on every deploy. Kafka 4.0
also made the new broker-driven consumer group protocol (KIP-848)
generally available, which makes rebalances incremental; check your
client library’s support.</li>
</ul>
<h3 id="durability-settings">3.3 Durability settings</h3>
<table>
<colgroup>
<col style="width: 33%" />
<col style="width: 33%" />
<col style="width: 33%" />
</colgroup>
<thead>
<tr>
<th>Setting</th>
<th>Recommended for important data</th>
<th>Why</th>
</tr>
</thead>
<tbody>
<tr>
<td>Replication factor</td>
<td>3</td>
<td>Survive a broker loss</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>Producer <code>acks</code></td>
<td><code>all</code></td>
<td>Leader waits for all in-sync replicas before acknowledging</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td><code>min.insync.replicas</code></td>
<td>2</td>
<td>With <code>acks=all</code>, a write needs at least 2 replicas; if
fewer are in sync, the producer gets an error instead of silently
writing to one copy</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>Producer idempotence</td>
<td>On (default in modern clients)</td>
<td>Retries don’t create duplicates within a partition</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td><code>unclean.leader.election.enable</code></td>
<td>false</td>
<td>Never elect an out-of-date replica as leader (which would lose
data)</td>
</tr>
</tbody>
</table>
<p><code>acks=1</code> is faster but can lose acknowledged writes if the
leader dies before replicating; <code>acks=0</code> is fire-and-forget
(metrics, logs where loss is acceptable).</p>
<h3 id="code-node">3.4 Code (Node)</h3>
<p>KafkaJS was the standard Node client for years but is now barely
maintained; Confluent’s <code>@confluentinc/kafka-javascript</code>
offers a KafkaJS-compatible API on top of librdkafka and is the safer
choice for new projects. It’s generally available and commercially
supported; in its KafkaJS-compatible mode, client settings move inside a
<code>kafkaJS: { ... }</code> object, so check its migration guide. The
concepts below are the same.</p>

<span id="cb170-23"><a href="#cb170-23" aria-hidden="true" tabindex="-1"></a>  }<span class="op">,</span></span>
<span id="cb170-24"><a href="#cb170-24" aria-hidden="true" tabindex="-1"></a>})<span class="op">;</span></span></code></pre></div>
<p>Committing the <strong>next</strong> offset (<code>offset + 1</code>)
marks this message done. Commit after processing = at-least-once; commit
before = at-most-once. For throughput, process in batches
(<code>eachBatch</code>) and commit per batch.</p>
<h3 id="exactly-once-semantics-eos-precisely">3.5 Exactly-once semantics
(EOS), precisely</h3>
<p>Kafka offers exactly-once <strong>within Kafka</strong>: an
idempotent producer plus <strong>transactions</strong> let a consumer
read from topic A, write results to topic B, and commit its input
offsets in one atomic transaction (consume-transform-produce, as Kafka
Streams does). Downstream consumers use
<code>isolation.level=read_committed</code> to see only committed
results.</p>
<p>It does <strong>not</strong> cover side effects outside Kafka:
writing to Postgres, calling a payment API, sending an email. For those,
it’s back to at-least-once + idempotency (Day 11).</p>
<h3 id="retention-compaction-replay">3.6 Retention, compaction,
replay</h3>
<ul>
<li><strong>Time/size retention</strong> (e.g. 7 days): consumers that
fall further behind lose data, so alert on lag well before that.</li>
<li><strong>Compacted topics</strong> keep the latest value per key
forever: perfect for “current state” streams
(<code>product-prices</code> keyed by SKU) that new services can
bootstrap from. A record with a null value (tombstone) deletes a
key.</li>
<li><strong>Replay:</strong> reset a consumer group’s offsets to an
earlier time to reprocess after fixing a bug, or start a new consumer
group from the beginning to build a new read model. Consumers must be
idempotent for this to be safe.</li>
</ul>
<h3 id="schema-registry">3.7 Schema registry</h3>
<p>A registry (Confluent Schema Registry, Apicurio, or managed
equivalents) stores versioned schemas (Avro, Protobuf, JSON Schema) for
each topic and enforces <strong>compatibility</strong> when producers
register new versions:</p>
<ul>
<li><strong>BACKWARD</strong> (common default): new consumers can read
old data (e.g. adding a field with a default).</li>
<li><strong>FORWARD:</strong> old consumers can read new data.</li>
<li><strong>FULL:</strong> both.</li>
</ul>
<p>Producers send a schema ID with each message instead of the whole
schema; incompatible changes fail at deploy time instead of breaking
consumers in production.</p>
<h3 id="ecosystem-in-one-breath">3.8 Ecosystem in one breath</h3>
<p>Kafka Connect (move data in and out with connectors, e.g. Debezium
CDC from Postgres, sinks to Elasticsearch or S3), Kafka Streams / ksqlDB
/ Flink (stream processing: joins, windows, aggregations), MirrorMaker
(cross-cluster replication). Managed options: Confluent Cloud, Amazon
MSK, Aiven; Redpanda is a Kafka-API-compatible alternative.</p>
<h3 id="how-id-answer-hour-3-11">How I’d answer — Hour 3</h3>
<p><strong>Q1. How does Kafka guarantee ordering?</strong> “Only within
a partition. Records with the same key go to the same partition, so I
key by the entity whose order matters, like the order ID. There’s no
ordering across partitions, and consumers still guard with per-entity
versions because retries and replays happen.”</p>
<p><strong>Q2. We have 6 partitions and added 10 consumers, but
throughput didn’t improve. Why?</strong> “Within a consumer group each
partition goes to only one consumer, so at most 6 do work and the other
4 idle. To scale further, increase partitions, keeping in mind it remaps
keys, or speed up each consumer with batching and concurrent processing
per partition where ordering allows.”</p>
<p><strong>Q3. What do <code>acks=all</code> and
<code>min.insync.replicas=2</code> give you?</strong> “With replication
factor 3, the leader only acknowledges once all in-sync replicas have
the write, and min ISR of 2 means a write fails rather than being
accepted with only one copy. So an acknowledged write survives a broker
failure. Combined with an idempotent producer, retries don’t duplicate
records.”</p>
<p><strong>Q4. Does Kafka’s exactly-once mean my consumer won’t
double-charge a customer?</strong> “No. Kafka’s transactions make
read-process-write atomic inside Kafka. A payment call or a database
write is outside that, so the consumer still needs idempotency: dedup on
event ID and idempotency keys with the payment provider.”</p>
<p><strong>Q5. How do you handle schema changes on a topic with many
consumers?</strong> “A schema registry with backward compatibility
enforced, so additive changes with defaults are allowed and breaking
ones are rejected when the producer deploys. Truly breaking changes get
a new topic or event version run in parallel until consumers
migrate.”</p>
<h3 id="practice-35">Practice</h3>
<ul class="task-list">
<li><label><input type="checkbox" />Run Kafka locally (KRaft, single
broker in Docker Compose); create <code>orders</code> with 6
partitions</label></li>
<li><label><input type="checkbox" />Producer keyed by
<code>orderId</code> with idempotence and <code>acks=all</code>;
consumer group <code>analytics</code> computing sales per minute with
manual commits</label></li>

and observe partition assignment; reset offsets to replay the last
hour</label></li>
</ul>
<h2 id="hour-4-kafka-vs-rabbitmq-in-practice">Hour 4 — Kafka vs RabbitMQ
in practice</h2>
<p>The comparison question is guaranteed, and the weak answer is “Kafka
is faster”. The strong answer picks per scenario and explains why. After
that, the operational problems that show up in incident reviews: poison
messages, consumer lag, and broker-induced outages.</p>
<h3 id="side-by-side">4.1 Side by side</h3>
<table>
<colgroup>
<col style="width: 33%" />
<col style="width: 33%" />
<col style="width: 33%" />
</colgroup>
<thead>
<tr>
<th></th>
<th>RabbitMQ</th>
<th>Kafka</th>
</tr>
</thead>
<tbody>
<tr>
<td>Model</td>
<td>Smart broker, simple consumers: routing, per-message acks,
redelivery</td>
<td>Simple broker, smart consumers: a partitioned log, consumers track
offsets</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>After consumption</td>
<td>Message deleted</td>
<td>Message retained; replayable</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>Routing</td>
<td>Exchanges, routing keys, headers</td>
<td>Topic + key; filtering in consumers</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>Ordering</td>
<td>Per queue (weakened by competing consumers)</td>
<td>Per partition (by key)</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>Scaling consumers</td>
<td>Add consumers to a queue freely</td>
<td>Bounded by partition count per group</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>Per-message retry / delay / priority / TTL</td>
<td>Built in</td>
<td>Not built in; build with retry topics</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>Throughput</td>
<td>High</td>
<td>Very high, sustained</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>Multiple independent readers of the same data</td>
<td>One queue per reader (copies)</td>
<td>Natural: consumer groups over one log</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>Ops complexity</td>
<td>Moderate</td>
<td>Higher (partitions, retention, rebalancing), though managed services
help</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>Best at</td>
<td>Work distribution, task queues, complex routing, RPC</td>
<td>Event streaming, event sourcing, CDC, analytics pipelines,
high-volume integration</td>
</tr>
</tbody>
</table>
<h3 id="scenario-answers">4.2 Scenario answers</h3>
<table>
<colgroup>
<col style="width: 33%" />
<col style="width: 33%" />
<col style="width: 33%" />
</colgroup>
<thead>
<tr>
<th>Scenario</th>
<th>Pick</th>
<th>Why</th>
</tr>
</thead>
<tbody>
<tr>
<td>Send order confirmation emails and SMS</td>
<td>RabbitMQ (or BullMQ / SQS)</td>
<td>Task per message, retries with delay, DLQ, no need for replay</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>Stream every order, payment and click event to analytics, fraud

<td>Kafka</td>

</tr>

<td>Ordered per product, new consumers bootstrap from current state</td>

<tr>

<td>RabbitMQ or BullMQ</td>
<td>Priorities, per-job acks and retries</td>

<tr>
<td>Event sourcing for a wallet ledger</td>
<td>Kafka (or the DB as the log + outbox)</td>
<td>Durable ordered history and replay</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>A few services, small team, modest volume</td>
<td>RabbitMQ / SQS+SNS / BullMQ</td>
<td>Simpler to operate; Kafka’s power unused</td>
</tr>
</tbody>
</table>
<p>Many systems use both: Kafka as the event backbone between domains,
RabbitMQ or BullMQ for work queues inside a service.</p>
<h3 id="poison-messages">4.3 Poison messages</h3>
<p>A <strong>poison message</strong> always fails (bad data, a bug for
one edge case). In RabbitMQ it loops on requeue (fixed with delivery
limits and DLQ, Hour 2). In Kafka it’s worse: the consumer can’t move
past it, so <strong>the whole partition is blocked</strong>.</p>
<p>Kafka retry pattern:</p>
<ol type="1">
<li>Consumer fails on a message → publish it to
<code>orders.retry.1m</code> (with an attempt header) and commit the
original offset, so the partition keeps moving.</li>
<li>A retry consumer reads <code>orders.retry.1m</code>, waits until the
message’s due time, processes it; on failure, forwards to
<code>orders.retry.10m</code>.</li>
<li>After the last retry, to <code>orders.dlt</code> (dead-letter
topic), with error details in headers; alert on it.</li>
<li>Non-retryable errors (validation, schema) go straight to the
DLT.</li>
</ol>
<p>Trade-off to mention: moving a message to a retry topic breaks strict
per-key ordering for that entity. If ordering matters (balance updates),
either block and alert (pause the partition until fixed) or park all
later events for that key too.</p>
<h3 id="consumer-lag-and-scaling">4.4 Consumer lag and scaling</h3>
<p><strong>Consumer lag</strong> = latest offset in a partition − the
group’s committed offset. It’s the main health metric for Kafka
consumers (and queue depth is the RabbitMQ equivalent). Growing lag
means consumers can’t keep up; if it exceeds retention, data is lost to
that consumer.</p>
<p>Fixes, in order: find slow processing (traces: a slow DB call per
message?); batch writes (<code>eachBatch</code> + bulk insert); process
partitions concurrently and keys concurrently within a partition where
ordering allows; add consumers up to the partition count; then add
partitions. On Kubernetes, <strong>KEDA</strong> autoscales consumers on
lag or queue depth instead of CPU.</p>
<p><strong>Backpressure from slow downstreams:</strong> if the database
or a partner API is the bottleneck, adding consumers makes it worse. Cap
concurrency (Day 4 limiter), pause consumption
(<code>consumer.pause()</code>), and let lag absorb the spike, which is
exactly what the broker is for.</p>
<h3 id="production-checklist-for-any-messaging-setup">4.5 Production
checklist for any messaging setup</h3>
<ul>
<li>Outbox for publishing (Day 11), idempotent consumers, event IDs on
every message</li>
<li>Schemas validated on consume (Zod) and governed by a registry or
AsyncAPI</li>
<li>Retries with backoff, DLQ/DLT with alerting and a replay tool</li>
<li>Metrics: publish rate, consume rate, lag/queue depth, processing
latency, DLQ count, rebalances</li>
<li>Trace context propagated in message headers</li>
<li>Graceful shutdown: stop fetching, finish in-flight messages, commit,
disconnect</li>
<li>Capacity: partitions/queues sized with headroom; retention longer
than your worst-case recovery time</li>
</ul>
<h3 id="how-id-answer-hour-4-11">How I’d answer — Hour 4</h3>
<p><strong>Q1. Kafka vs RabbitMQ: pick for three scenarios.</strong>
“Order confirmation emails: RabbitMQ, because each email is a task
needing per-message acks, delayed retries and a DLQ, with no need for
replay. Streaming every order and payment event to analytics, fraud and
recommendations: Kafka, because many independent consumers read the same
history at their own pace and we can replay to build new models. Keeping
the search index in sync with the catalogue: Kafka with CDC or a
compacted topic keyed by product, ordered per product and replayable for
a full rebuild.”</p>
<p><strong>Q2. One bad message is blocking a Kafka partition. What do
you do now, and what do you change?</strong> “Now: if it’s safe to skip,
move it to a dead-letter topic and advance the offset; if ordering for
that key matters, pause and fix. Afterwards: add retry topics with
backoff and a DLT, route validation errors straight to the DLT, alert on
DLT volume, and build a replay tool.”</p>
<p><strong>Q3. Consumer lag keeps growing. How do you handle
it?</strong> “Check whether it’s per-message slowness, usually a slow DB
call or downstream API, and fix that first with batching or caching.
Then increase concurrency within the ordering constraints and scale
consumers up to the partition count, using KEDA to autoscale on lag. If
the downstream is the bottleneck, cap concurrency and let the backlog
drain rather than overload it.”</p>
