<h1 id="day-13-wed-docker-1">Day 13 (Wed) — Docker</h1>
<h2 id="hour-1-container-fundamentals">Hour 1 — Container
fundamentals</h2>
<p>Most developers can write a Dockerfile; fewer can explain what a
container actually is. That explanation is what interviewers use to
separate “uses Docker” from “understands production”. It’s also what
lets you debug the strange cases: an OOM kill with no error, a container
that ignores Ctrl+C, an image that works on a laptop but not in the
cluster.</p>
<h3 id="what-a-container-is">1.1 What a container is</h3>
<p><strong>What it is:</strong> a normal Linux process (or group of
processes) isolated by kernel features so that it believes it has its
own machine. There’s no separate kernel; containers share the host
kernel.</p>
<table>
<colgroup>
<col style="width: 50%" />
<col style="width: 50%" />
</colgroup>
<thead>
<tr>
<th>Kernel feature</th>
<th>Gives the container</th>
</tr>
</thead>
<tbody>
<tr>
<td><strong>Namespaces</strong></td>
<td>Its own view of: process IDs (<code>pid</code>, so your app is PID
1), network interfaces and ports (<code>net</code>), filesystem mounts
(<code>mnt</code>), hostname (<code>uts</code>), users
(<code>user</code>), IPC</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td><strong>cgroups</strong></td>
<td>Resource limits and accounting: CPU, memory, I/O, number of
processes</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td><strong>Union / overlay filesystem</strong></td>
<td>A stack of read-only image layers plus a thin writable layer on
top</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>Capabilities, seccomp, AppArmor/SELinux</td>
<td>Restricted privileges, even for root inside the container</td>
</tr>
</tbody>
</table>
<p><strong>Container vs VM:</strong></p>
<table>
<colgroup>
<col style="width: 33%" />
<col style="width: 33%" />
<col style="width: 33%" />
</colgroup>
<thead>
<tr>
<th></th>
<th>Container</th>
<th>Virtual machine</th>
</tr>
</thead>
<tbody>
<tr>
<td>Isolation</td>
<td>Process-level, shared kernel</td>
<td>Hardware-level, own kernel</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>Startup</td>
<td>Milliseconds to seconds</td>
<td>Tens of seconds to minutes</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>Size</td>
<td>MBs</td>
<td>GBs</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>Density</td>
<td>Many per host</td>
<td>Fewer per host</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>Security boundary</td>
<td>Weaker (kernel shared)</td>
<td>Stronger</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>Use</td>
<td>Packaging and running apps</td>
<td>Running different OSes, stronger isolation, the hosts containers run
on</td>
</tr>
</tbody>
</table>
<p>In the cloud you usually have both: containers on VMs. For untrusted
multi-tenant workloads, sandboxed runtimes (gVisor, Kata Containers,
Firecracker micro-VMs) add a stronger boundary.</p>
<p><strong>Memory limits explain a classic incident:</strong> when a
container exceeds its cgroup memory limit, the kernel kills it (exit
code <strong>137</strong>, OOMKilled) with no application error. Day 3’s
heap sizing (<code>--max-old-space-size</code> below the container
limit) is why.</p>
<h3 id="images-and-layers">1.2 Images and layers</h3>
<p><strong>Image:</strong> a read-only template made of ordered
<strong>layers</strong> plus metadata (default command, env, exposed
ports, user). Each filesystem-changing Dockerfile instruction
(<code>RUN</code>, <code>COPY</code>, <code>ADD</code>) creates a
layer.</p>
<ul>
<li>Layers are content-addressed (by hash) and <strong>shared</strong>:
ten images on the same <code>node:22-slim</code> base store that base
once.</li>
<li><strong>Build cache:</strong> if an instruction and its inputs
haven’t changed, Docker reuses the cached layer; once one layer changes,
every layer after it rebuilds. Hence the rule: put rarely changing steps
(installing dependencies) before frequently changing ones (copying
source code). Hour 2 applies this.</li>
<li>Deleting a file in a later layer doesn’t shrink the image; the file
still exists in the earlier layer. That’s also why secrets copied in and
then deleted are still extractable.</li>
<li>A running container adds a writable layer; anything written there
disappears when the container is removed. Persistent data goes in
volumes (Hour 3).</li>
</ul>
<h3 id="tags-digests-registries">1.3 Tags, digests, registries</h3>
<ul>
<li><strong>Registry:</strong> stores and serves images: Docker Hub,
GitHub Container Registry, AWS ECR, Google Artifact Registry, Azure ACR,
Harbor.</li>
<li><strong>Tag:</strong> a movable human-readable label
(<code>order-service:1.4.2</code>, <code>:latest</code>). Tags can be
re-pointed, so <code>:latest</code> in production means you don’t know
what’s running.</li>
<li><strong>Digest:</strong> an immutable content hash
(<code>order-service@sha256:4f3c...</code>). Pin base images and
deployments by digest (or by unique tags like the git SHA) for
reproducibility.</li>
<li><strong>Tagging convention I’d use:</strong> git SHA for every build
(<code>order-service:9f2c1ab</code>), plus semantic version tags for
releases; never deploy <code>latest</code>.</li>
<li><strong>Multi-architecture images:</strong> one tag with a manifest
list for <code>linux/amd64</code> and <code>linux/arm64</code> (Apple
Silicon laptops, AWS Graviton). Built with <code>docker buildx</code>
(Hour 4).</li>
</ul>
<h3 id="the-ecosystem">1.4 The ecosystem</h3>
<ul>
<li><strong>OCI</strong> (Open Container Initiative): standard image and
runtime formats, so images built by Docker run under containerd, CRI-O,
Podman.</li>
<li><strong>Docker Engine</strong> = CLI + daemon (<code>dockerd</code>)
+ <strong>containerd</strong> (manages containers) +
<strong>runc</strong> (actually creates them using namespaces and
cgroups).</li>
<li><strong>Kubernetes</strong> talks to containerd or CRI-O directly
through the CRI; it hasn’t needed Docker Engine since the removal of
dockershim. Images you build with Docker still run unchanged.</li>
<li><strong>Podman:</strong> daemonless, rootless-friendly Docker
alternative with a compatible CLI.</li>
</ul>
<h3 id="how-id-answer-hour-1-12">How I’d answer — Hour 1</h3>
<p><strong>Q1. What is a container, really?</strong> “A Linux process
isolated with namespaces, so it has its own view of PIDs, network,
mounts and hostname, and limited with cgroups for CPU and memory,
running on a layered filesystem built from an image. It shares the
host’s kernel, which is why it starts in milliseconds and is lighter
than a VM, and also why its security boundary is weaker.”</p>
<p><strong>Q2. Container vs VM?</strong> “A VM virtualises hardware and
runs its own kernel; a container virtualises the OS view for a process
and shares the host kernel. Containers are smaller and faster, ideal for
packaging services; VMs give stronger isolation and run different
kernels. In practice containers run on VMs.”</p>
<p><strong>Q3. Why did my container exit with code 137 and no
error?</strong> “137 means it was killed with SIGKILL, usually by the
kernel’s OOM killer for exceeding the memory limit. Node didn’t get a
chance to log anything. I’d check memory metrics, set
<code>--max-old-space-size</code> below the limit, look for leaks or
Buffers outside the heap, and raise the limit only if the workload
really needs it.”</p>
<p><strong>Q4. Why not deploy <code>:latest</code>?</strong> “Tags are
mutable. <code>latest</code> can point to different images over time, so
two pods can run different code, rollbacks are ambiguous, and you can’t
tell what’s in production. I deploy immutable tags like the git SHA, or
pin by digest.”</p>
<h3 id="practice-36">Practice</h3>
<ul class="task-list">
<li><label><input type="checkbox" />Run
<code>docker run --rm -it --memory=128m node:22-slim node -e "const a=[];while(true)a.push(new Array(1e6))"</code>
and observe exit code 137</label></li>
<li><label><input type="checkbox" />Inspect an image’s layers with
<code>docker history</code> and <code>docker image inspect</code>; find
its digest</label></li>
<li><label><input type="checkbox" />Run
<code>docker run --rm alpine ps aux</code> and explain why PID 1 is the
command you ran</label></li>
</ul>
<h2 id="hour-2-production-dockerfiles-for-node">Hour 2 — Production
Dockerfiles for Node</h2>
<p>“Your image is 1.2 GB, shrink it” is a common practical question, and
a Dockerfile review is a quick way for an interviewer to see production
habits: multi-stage builds, cache-friendly ordering, non-root users, and
correct signal handling. Write the Dockerfile below from memory by the
end of the hour.</p>
<h3 id="a-production-dockerfile-annotated">2.1 A production Dockerfile,
annotated</h3>
<div class="sourceCode" id="cb171"><pre
class="sourceCode dockerfile"><code class="sourceCode dockerfile"><span id="cb171-1"><a href="#cb171-1" aria-hidden="true" tabindex="-1"></a><span class="co"># </span><span class="cv">syntax=docker/dockerfile:1</span></span>
<span id="cb171-2"><a href="#cb171-2" aria-hidden="true" tabindex="-1"></a></span>
<span id="cb171-3"><a href="#cb171-3" aria-hidden="true" tabindex="-1"></a><span class="co"># ---- 1. Dependencies: cached until package files change ----</span></span>
<span id="cb171-4"><a href="#cb171-4" aria-hidden="true" tabindex="-1"></a><span class="kw">FROM</span> node:24-slim <span class="kw">AS</span> deps</span>
<span id="cb171-5"><a href="#cb171-5" aria-hidden="true" tabindex="-1"></a><span class="kw">WORKDIR</span> /app</span>
<span id="cb171-6"><a href="#cb171-6" aria-hidden="true" tabindex="-1"></a><span class="kw">COPY</span> package.json package-lock.json ./</span>
<span id="cb171-7"><a href="#cb171-7" aria-hidden="true" tabindex="-1"></a><span class="kw">RUN</span> <span class="op">--mount=type=cache,target=/root/.npm</span> <span class="ex">npm</span> ci          <span class="co"># BuildKit cache mount: fast rebuilds</span></span>
<span id="cb171-8"><a href="#cb171-8" aria-hidden="true" tabindex="-1"></a></span>
<span id="cb171-9"><a href="#cb171-9" aria-hidden="true" tabindex="-1"></a><span class="co"># ---- 2. Build: compile TypeScript, then drop dev dependencies ----</span></span>
<span id="cb171-10"><a href="#cb171-10" aria-hidden="true" tabindex="-1"></a><span class="kw">FROM</span> deps <span class="kw">AS</span> build</span>
<span id="cb171-11"><a href="#cb171-11" aria-hidden="true" tabindex="-1"></a><span class="kw">COPY</span> tsconfig.json ./</span>
<span id="cb171-12"><a href="#cb171-12" aria-hidden="true" tabindex="-1"></a><span class="kw">COPY</span> src ./src</span>
<span id="cb171-13"><a href="#cb171-13" aria-hidden="true" tabindex="-1"></a><span class="kw">RUN</span> <span class="ex">npm</span> run build <span class="kw">&amp;&amp;</span> <span class="ex">npm</span> prune <span class="at">--omit</span><span class="op">=</span>dev</span>
<span id="cb171-14"><a href="#cb171-14" aria-hidden="true" tabindex="-1"></a></span>
<span id="cb171-15"><a href="#cb171-15" aria-hidden="true" tabindex="-1"></a><span class="co"># ---- 3. Runtime: only what&#39;s needed to run ----</span></span>
<span id="cb171-16"><a href="#cb171-16" aria-hidden="true" tabindex="-1"></a><span class="kw">FROM</span> node:24-slim <span class="kw">AS</span> runtime</span>
<span id="cb171-17"><a href="#cb171-17" aria-hidden="true" tabindex="-1"></a><span class="kw">ENV</span> NODE_ENV=production</span>
<span id="cb171-18"><a href="#cb171-18" aria-hidden="true" tabindex="-1"></a><span class="kw">WORKDIR</span> /app</span>
<span id="cb171-19"><a href="#cb171-19" aria-hidden="true" tabindex="-1"></a><span class="kw">COPY</span> <span class="op">--from=build</span> <span class="op">--chown=node:node</span> /app/node_modules ./node_modules</span>
<span id="cb171-20"><a href="#cb171-20" aria-hidden="true" tabindex="-1"></a><span class="kw">COPY</span> <span class="op">--from=build</span> <span class="op">--chown=node:node</span> /app/dist ./dist</span>
<span id="cb171-21"><a href="#cb171-21" aria-hidden="true" tabindex="-1"></a><span class="kw">COPY</span> <span class="op">--chown=node:node</span> package.json ./</span>
<span id="cb171-22"><a href="#cb171-22" aria-hidden="true" tabindex="-1"></a><span class="co"># never run as root</span></span>
<span id="cb171-23"><a href="#cb171-23" aria-hidden="true" tabindex="-1"></a><span class="kw">USER</span> node</span>
<span id="cb171-24"><a href="#cb171-24" aria-hidden="true" tabindex="-1"></a><span class="kw">EXPOSE</span> 3000</span>
<span id="cb171-25"><a href="#cb171-25" aria-hidden="true" tabindex="-1"></a><span class="co"># exec form (JSON array): node is PID 1 and receives signals directly.</span></span>
<span id="cb171-26"><a href="#cb171-26" aria-hidden="true" tabindex="-1"></a><span class="co"># Comments must sit on their own line: after CMD/USER they would break the instruction.</span></span>
<span id="cb171-27"><a href="#cb171-27" aria-hidden="true" tabindex="-1"></a><span class="kw">CMD</span> [<span class="st">&quot;node&quot;</span>, <span class="st">&quot;dist/server.js&quot;</span>]</span></code></pre></div>
<p>Why each decision:</p>
<ul>
<li><strong>Multi-stage:</strong> compilers, dev dependencies, source
TypeScript and caches stay in the build stages; the runtime image gets
only <code>dist</code> and production <code>node_modules</code>.</li>
<li><strong>Copy package files first, then <code>npm ci</code>, then
source:</strong> changing a <code>.ts</code> file doesn’t invalidate the
dependency layer, so rebuilds take seconds.</li>
<li><strong><code>npm ci</code></strong>, not <code>npm install</code>:
installs exactly what the lockfile says, fails if it’s out of sync.</li>
<li><strong><code>NODE_ENV=production</code>:</strong> frameworks enable
production behaviour; some libraries skip dev checks.</li>
<li><strong><code>USER node</code>:</strong> the official Node images
include a <code>node</code> user; running as root makes any container
escape or file-write bug far worse.</li>
<li><strong>Exec-form <code>CMD</code></strong> (JSON array), not
<code>CMD npm start</code> or shell form: covered in 2.3.</li>
</ul>
<p><strong>Monorepo variant (pnpm):</strong> build from the repo root,
use <code>pnpm fetch</code> for a cacheable dependency layer, then
<code>pnpm --filter order-service build</code> and
<code>pnpm --filter order-service deploy --prod /out</code> to produce a
self-contained folder with only that service’s production dependencies,
and copy <code>/out</code> into the runtime stage. pnpm 10 required
<code>inject-workspace-packages=true</code> (or the
<code>--legacy</code> flag) for <code>deploy</code>; since pnpm 12.2
that setting is no longer required.</p>
<h3 id="dockerignore">2.2 <code>.dockerignore</code></h3>
<pre class="text"><code>node_modules
dist
.git
.env*
*.log
coverage
.vscode
Dockerfile*
docker-compose*</code></pre>
<p>Without it, <code>COPY . .</code> sends <code>node_modules</code> and
<code>.git</code> to the build context (slow builds), may overwrite
Linux-built modules with macOS ones, and can copy <code>.env</code>
secrets into the image.</p>
<h3 id="pid-1-and-signals">2.3 PID 1 and signals</h3>
<p>In a container your process is PID 1, which behaves differently: the
kernel doesn’t apply default signal actions to PID 1, so SIGTERM only
works if the process installs a handler (our Day 3 graceful shutdown
does), and PID 1 is expected to reap zombie child processes.</p>
<ul>
<li><strong>Shell-form CMD</strong>
(<code>CMD node dist/server.js</code>) or
<code>CMD ["npm", "start"]</code> makes <code>sh</code> or
<code>npm</code> PID 1. They may not forward SIGTERM to Node, so
Kubernetes waits the full grace period and then SIGKILLs the app:
in-flight requests are cut on every deploy.</li>
<li>Use <strong>exec form</strong> with <code>node</code> directly, and
handle SIGTERM in the app.</li>
<li>If the app spawns child processes, add a tiny init:
<code>docker run --init</code>, or install <code>tini</code> and use
<code>ENTRYPOINT ["tini", "--"]</code>.</li>
</ul>
<h3 id="choosing-a-base-image">2.4 Choosing a base image</h3>
<table>
<colgroup>
<col style="width: 25%" />
<col style="width: 25%" />
<col style="width: 25%" />
<col style="width: 25%" />
</colgroup>
<thead>
<tr>
<th>Base</th>
<th>Approx. size</th>
<th>Good</th>
<th>Watch out</th>
</tr>
</thead>
<tbody>
<tr>
<td><code>node:22</code> (Debian full)</td>
<td>~1 GB</td>
<td>Every build tool available</td>
<td>Huge, large attack surface; use only as a build stage</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td><code>node:22-slim</code> (Debian)</td>
<td>~200 MB</td>
<td>glibc, compatible with native modules, small enough</td>
<td>Few tools for debugging</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td><code>node:22-alpine</code></td>
<td>~50–60 MB</td>
<td>Very small</td>
<td>musl libc: some native modules (bcrypt, sharp, Prisma engines) need
extra work; occasional DNS and performance differences</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>Distroless
(<code>gcr.io/distroless/nodejs22-debian12:nonroot</code>)</td>
<td>~100–150 MB</td>
<td>No shell or package manager: smaller attack surface, fewer CVEs</td>
<td>Can’t <code>exec</code> a shell to debug; use ephemeral debug
containers</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>Chainguard / Wolfi images</td>
<td>Small</td>
<td>Minimal, frequently rebuilt, low CVE counts</td>
<td>Newer ecosystem, versioning policies differ</td>
</tr>
</tbody>
</table>
<p><strong>My default:</strong> <code>node:24-slim</code> for build
stages (use the current LTS line: Node 24 or 26 as of Nov 2026; Node 22
reaches end of life in April 2027), slim or distroless for runtime, and
pin by digest in production pipelines. Alpine only if the team has
tested its native dependencies on musl.</p>
<h3 id="shrinking-a-1.2-gb-image-checklist">2.5 Shrinking a 1.2 GB image
(checklist)</h3>
<ol type="1">
<li>Multi-stage build; runtime stage from slim/distroless, not
<code>node:22</code>.</li>
<li>Production dependencies only (<code>npm prune --omit=dev</code>,
<code>pnpm deploy --prod</code>).</li>
<li><code>.dockerignore</code> so tests, docs, <code>.git</code> and
local <code>node_modules</code> don’t get in.</li>
<li>Look for heavy dependencies with <code>docker history</code> and
<code>dive</code> (a tool that shows each layer’s contents); common
culprits: a full browser for Puppeteer, <code>aws-sdk</code> v2,
duplicate copies of large packages.</li>
<li>Combine cleanup in the same <code>RUN</code> that creates files
(<code>apt-get install ... &amp;&amp; rm -rf /var/lib/apt/lists/*</code>),
because deleting in a later layer doesn’t shrink earlier ones.</li>
<li>Bundle the app (esbuild) if <code>node_modules</code> is still
large, keeping native modules external.</li>
</ol>
<p>Typical result: 1.2 GB → 150–250 MB, with faster pulls, faster pod
start-up and fewer vulnerabilities to patch.</p>
<h3 id="other-dockerfile-details">2.6 Other Dockerfile details</h3>
<ul>
<li><code>HEALTHCHECK</code> works in Docker and Compose, but Kubernetes
ignores it and uses its own probes (Day 14).</li>
<li><code>ARG</code> for build-time values (versions), <code>ENV</code>
for runtime defaults; never pass secrets through either (they end up in
image metadata). Use BuildKit secret mounts (Hour 4).</li>
<li>Label images with metadata
(<code>org.opencontainers.image.revision=$GIT_SHA</code>,
<code>source</code>) for traceability.</li>
<li>One process per container; run sidecars as separate containers.</li>
</ul>
<h3 id="how-id-answer-hour-2-12">How I’d answer — Hour 2</h3>
<p><strong>Q1. Your Node image is 1.2 GB. Shrink it.</strong>
“Multi-stage build: compile in a full image, then copy only
<code>dist</code> and production <code>node_modules</code> into a slim
or distroless runtime image. Install with <code>npm ci</code> and prune
dev dependencies, add a proper <code>.dockerignore</code>, and check
<code>dive</code> for heavy layers or dependencies. That usually takes
it to around 200 MB, and as a bonus the runtime image has fewer
CVEs.”</p>
<p><strong>Q2. How do you make Docker builds fast?</strong> “Order
layers from least to most frequently changing: copy package files and
install first, then copy source. Use BuildKit cache mounts for the npm
store, a tight build context through <code>.dockerignore</code>, and
registry-backed layer caching in CI.”</p>
<p><strong>Q3. Why is <code>CMD npm start</code> a problem?</strong>
“npm becomes PID 1 and doesn’t reliably forward SIGTERM to Node, so on
every deploy Kubernetes waits for the grace period and then kills the
app, dropping in-flight requests. I run node directly in exec form,
handle SIGTERM in the app, and add tini if the app spawns child
processes.”</p>
<p><strong>Q4. Alpine or slim?</strong> “Slim by default. Alpine is
smaller, but its musl libc causes problems with some native modules and
occasionally with DNS and performance. The size difference matters less
than compatibility, and distroless gives a smaller attack surface if
that’s the goal.”</p>

<ul class="task-list">
<li><label><input type="checkbox" />Write the Dockerfile above for the

<li><label><input type="checkbox" />Change one <code>.ts</code> file and
rebuild: confirm the dependency layer is cached</label></li>
<li><label><input type="checkbox" />Compare sizes for slim, alpine and
distroless runtime stages using <code>docker images</code> and
<code>dive</code></label></li>
<li><label><input type="checkbox" />Replace <code>CMD</code> with
<code>["npm", "start"]</code>, run <code>docker stop</code>, and time
the difference in shutdown</label></li>
</ul>
<h2 id="hour-3-docker-compose-networking-volumes">Hour 3 — Docker
Compose, networking, volumes</h2>
<p>Compose is how the whole team runs the capstone’s databases, brokers
and services locally with one command. Interview questions here are
practical: why a service can’t reach the database at
<code>localhost</code>, why data disappeared after
<code>docker compose down</code>, how to start services only when their
dependencies are actually ready.</p>
<h3 id="networking-in-one-page">3.1 Networking in one page</h3>
<ul>
<li>Compose creates a <strong>bridge network</strong> per project; every
service is reachable by its <strong>service name</strong> through
Docker’s built-in DNS: <code>postgres:5432</code>,
<code>kafka:9092</code>, <code>redis:6379</code>.</li>
<li>Inside a container, <strong><code>localhost</code> is the container
itself</strong>. The classic bug:
<code>DATABASE_URL=postgres://localhost:5432</code> works when running
Node on your laptop and fails inside Compose. Use the service name.</li>
<li><code>ports: "5433:5432"</code> publishes container port 5432 on
host port 5433 (host:container). Only needed for access from your
laptop; service-to-service traffic doesn’t need published ports.</li>
<li>From a container to something on the host:
<code>host.docker.internal</code> (built into Docker Desktop; on Linux
add
<code>extra_hosts: ["host.docker.internal:host-gateway"]</code>).</li>
<li>Network drivers: <code>bridge</code> (default), <code>host</code>
(share the host’s network stack, Linux only), <code>none</code>, and
<code>overlay</code> for multi-host setups.</li>
</ul>
<h3 id="storage">3.2 Storage</h3>
<table>
<colgroup>
<col style="width: 33%" />
<col style="width: 33%" />
<col style="width: 33%" />
</colgroup>
<thead>
<tr>
<th>Type</th>
<th>Lives</th>
<th>Use</th>
</tr>
</thead>
<tbody>
<tr>
<td>Container writable layer</td>
<td>Until the container is removed</td>
<td>Temporary files only</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td><strong>Named volume</strong>
(<code>pgdata:/var/lib/postgresql/data</code>)</td>
<td>Until explicitly deleted (<code>docker compose down -v</code>
deletes them)</td>
<td>Database data</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td><strong>Bind mount</strong> (<code>./src:/app/src</code>)</td>
<td>Your host folder</td>
<td>Source code for hot reload in development</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>tmpfs</td>
<td>Memory only</td>
<td>Sensitive scratch data, speed</td>
</tr>
</tbody>
</table>
<p><code>docker compose down</code> keeps named volumes;
<code>down -v</code> wipes them. Know which one you’re typing.</p>

<span id="cb173-49"><a href="#cb173-49" aria-hidden="true" tabindex="-1"></a><span class="at">  </span><span class="fu">jaeger</span><span class="kw">:</span></span>
<span id="cb173-50"><a href="#cb173-50" aria-hidden="true" tabindex="-1"></a><span class="at">    </span><span class="fu">image</span><span class="kw">:</span><span class="at"> jaegertracing/all-in-one:1.62</span></span>
<span id="cb173-51"><a href="#cb173-51" aria-hidden="true" tabindex="-1"></a><span class="at">    </span><span class="fu">ports</span><span class="kw">:</span><span class="at"> </span><span class="kw">[</span><span class="st">&quot;16686:16686&quot;</span><span class="kw">,</span><span class="at"> </span><span class="st">&quot;4318:4318&quot;</span><span class="kw">]</span><span class="co">                  # UI and OTLP/HTTP</span></span>
<span id="cb173-52"><a href="#cb173-52" aria-hidden="true" tabindex="-1"></a><span class="at">    </span><span class="fu">profiles</span><span class="kw">:</span><span class="at"> </span><span class="kw">[</span><span class="st">&quot;observability&quot;</span><span class="kw">]</span><span class="co">                          # started only with --profile observability</span></span>
<span id="cb173-53"><a href="#cb173-53" aria-hidden="true" tabindex="-1"></a></span>
<span id="cb173-54"><a href="#cb173-54" aria-hidden="true" tabindex="-1"></a><span class="at">  </span><span class="fu">order-service</span><span class="kw">:</span></span>
<span id="cb173-55"><a href="#cb173-55" aria-hidden="true" tabindex="-1"></a><span class="at">    </span><span class="fu">build</span><span class="kw">:</span><span class="at"> </span><span class="kw">{</span><span class="at"> </span><span class="fu">context</span><span class="kw">:</span><span class="at"> .</span><span class="kw">,</span><span class="at"> </span><span class="fu">dockerfile</span><span class="kw">:</span><span class="at"> services/order-service/Dockerfile </span><span class="kw">}</span></span>
<span id="cb173-56"><a href="#cb173-56" aria-hidden="true" tabindex="-1"></a><span class="at">    </span><span class="fu">env_file</span><span class="kw">:</span><span class="at"> services/order-service/.env.docker</span></span>
<span id="cb173-57"><a href="#cb173-57" aria-hidden="true" tabindex="-1"></a><span class="at">    </span><span class="fu">environment</span><span class="kw">:</span></span>
<span id="cb173-58"><a href="#cb173-58" aria-hidden="true" tabindex="-1"></a><span class="at">      </span><span class="fu">DATABASE_URL</span><span class="kw">:</span><span class="at"> postgres://app:app@postgres:5432/orders</span><span class="co">   # service name, not localhost</span></span>
<span id="cb173-59"><a href="#cb173-59" aria-hidden="true" tabindex="-1"></a><span class="at">      </span><span class="fu">KAFKA_BROKERS</span><span class="kw">:</span><span class="at"> kafka:9092</span></span>
<span id="cb173-60"><a href="#cb173-60" aria-hidden="true" tabindex="-1"></a><span class="at">      </span><span class="fu">OTEL_EXPORTER_OTLP_ENDPOINT</span><span class="kw">:</span><span class="at"> http://jaeger:4318</span></span>
<span id="cb173-61"><a href="#cb173-61" aria-hidden="true" tabindex="-1"></a><span class="at">    </span><span class="fu">ports</span><span class="kw">:</span><span class="at"> </span><span class="kw">[</span><span class="st">&quot;3002:3000&quot;</span><span class="kw">]</span></span>
<span id="cb173-62"><a href="#cb173-62" aria-hidden="true" tabindex="-1"></a><span class="at">    </span><span class="fu">depends_on</span><span class="kw">:</span></span>
<span id="cb173-63"><a href="#cb173-63" aria-hidden="true" tabindex="-1"></a><span class="at">      </span><span class="fu">postgres</span><span class="kw">:</span><span class="at"> </span><span class="kw">{</span><span class="at"> </span><span class="fu">condition</span><span class="kw">:</span><span class="at"> service_healthy </span><span class="kw">}</span><span class="co">           # wait for READY, not just started</span></span>
<span id="cb173-64"><a href="#cb173-64" aria-hidden="true" tabindex="-1"></a><span class="at">      </span><span class="fu">kafka</span><span class="kw">:</span><span class="at"> </span><span class="kw">{</span><span class="at"> </span><span class="fu">condition</span><span class="kw">:</span><span class="at"> service_started </span><span class="kw">}</span></span>
<span id="cb173-65"><a href="#cb173-65" aria-hidden="true" tabindex="-1"></a></span>
<span id="cb173-66"><a href="#cb173-66" aria-hidden="true" tabindex="-1"></a><span class="fu">volumes</span><span class="kw">:</span></span>
<span id="cb173-67"><a href="#cb173-67" aria-hidden="true" tabindex="-1"></a><span class="at">  </span><span class="fu">pgdata</span><span class="kw">:</span></span>
<span id="cb173-68"><a href="#cb173-68" aria-hidden="true" tabindex="-1"></a><span class="at">  </span><span class="fu">mongodata</span><span class="kw">:</span></span></code></pre></div>
<p>Points to explain: <code>depends_on</code> alone only waits for the
container to <strong>start</strong>, not for the database to accept
connections; <code>condition: service_healthy</code> with a healthcheck
fixes that. Even so, services should retry connections at start-up,
because in Kubernetes there’s no <code>depends_on</code> at all. The
Kafka listener setup gives one address for containers
(<code>kafka:9092</code>) and another for tools on your laptop
(<code>localhost:29092</code>), which is the most common Kafka-in-Docker
confusion.</p>
<h3 id="development-workflow">3.4 Development workflow</h3>
<ul>
<li><strong>Hot reload:</strong> run dependencies in Compose and the
service you’re editing directly on the host (<code>node --watch</code>,
<code>tsx watch</code>), or mount source into the container and run a
watcher there.</li>
<li><strong>Compose Watch</strong> (<code>develop.watch</code> in the
compose file, <code>docker compose watch</code>): syncs changed files
into the container or rebuilds on dependency changes, avoiding
bind-mount performance problems on macOS.</li>
<li>When bind-mounting a project into a container, keep the container’s
own <code>node_modules</code> (an anonymous volume at
<code>/app/node_modules</code>) so Linux-built native modules aren’t
overwritten by macOS ones.</li>
<li><strong>Profiles</strong> keep optional services (observability,
admin UIs) off by default.</li>
<li>Override files (<code>compose.override.yaml</code>) for
per-developer tweaks; seed scripts as one-off services
(<code>docker compose run --rm seed</code>).</li>
</ul>
<h3 id="useful-commands">3.5 Useful commands</h3>
<div class="sourceCode" id="cb174"><pre
class="sourceCode bash"><code class="sourceCode bash"><span id="cb174-1"><a href="#cb174-1" aria-hidden="true" tabindex="-1"></a><span class="ex">docker</span> compose up <span class="at">-d</span>                 <span class="co"># start in background</span></span>
<span id="cb174-2"><a href="#cb174-2" aria-hidden="true" tabindex="-1"></a><span class="ex">docker</span> compose up <span class="at">-d</span> <span class="at">--build</span> order-service</span>
<span id="cb174-3"><a href="#cb174-3" aria-hidden="true" tabindex="-1"></a><span class="ex">docker</span> compose ps                    <span class="co"># status and health</span></span>
<span id="cb174-4"><a href="#cb174-4" aria-hidden="true" tabindex="-1"></a><span class="ex">docker</span> compose logs <span class="at">-f</span> order-service</span>
<span id="cb174-5"><a href="#cb174-5" aria-hidden="true" tabindex="-1"></a><span class="ex">docker</span> compose exec postgres psql <span class="at">-U</span> app orders</span>
<span id="cb174-6"><a href="#cb174-6" aria-hidden="true" tabindex="-1"></a><span class="ex">docker</span> compose down                  <span class="co"># stop and remove containers (keep volumes)</span></span>
<span id="cb174-7"><a href="#cb174-7" aria-hidden="true" tabindex="-1"></a><span class="ex">docker</span> compose down <span class="at">-v</span>               <span class="co"># also delete volumes (data gone)</span></span>
<span id="cb174-8"><a href="#cb174-8" aria-hidden="true" tabindex="-1"></a><span class="ex">docker</span> compose <span class="at">--profile</span> observability up <span class="at">-d</span></span></code></pre></div>
<h3 id="how-id-answer-hour-3-12">How I’d answer — Hour 3</h3>
<p><strong>Q1. My service can’t connect to Postgres in Docker Compose,
but it works locally. Why?</strong> “Inside a container, localhost is
the container itself. The connection string must use the Compose service
name, like <code>postgres:5432</code>. Also check that the service waits
for Postgres to be healthy, not just started, and that it retries on
start-up.”</p>
<p><strong>Q2. Volumes vs bind mounts?</strong> “Named volumes are
managed by Docker and are for persistent data like databases; they
survive container removal until deleted. Bind mounts map a host folder
into the container, which suits source code during development. In
production on Kubernetes, persistence comes from persistent volumes
instead.”</p>
<p><strong>Q3. How do you make a service start only when the database is
ready?</strong> “In Compose, a healthcheck on the database and
<code>depends_on</code> with <code>condition: service_healthy</code>.
But the real fix is in the application: retry connections with backoff
on start-up and report not-ready until connected, because orchestrators
like Kubernetes don’t order start-up.”</p>
<h3 id="practice-38">Practice</h3>
<ul class="task-list">
<li><label><input type="checkbox" />Write the compose file above for the
capstone; <code>docker compose up</code> brings everything to
healthy</label></li>
<li><label><input type="checkbox" />Break <code>DATABASE_URL</code> by
using <code>localhost</code> and observe the error; fix it</label></li>
<li><label><input type="checkbox" />Add a <code>seed</code> one-off
service and an <code>observability</code> profile with Jaeger; see
traces from the order service</label></li>
</ul>
<h2 id="hour-4-image-security-ci-builds-debugging-containers">Hour 4 —
Image security, CI builds, debugging containers</h2>
<p>This hour covers the questions that come up once containers reach
production: how do you keep images secure, how do you build them
reliably in CI, and how do you debug one that keeps crashing.
Supply-chain security in particular has become a standard senior
topic.</p>
<h3 id="image-and-runtime-security">4.1 Image and runtime security</h3>
<p><strong>Build-time:</strong></p>
<ul>
<li>Minimal base images (slim/distroless) and only production
dependencies: fewer packages, fewer CVEs.</li>
<li><strong>Scan</strong> every image in CI with Trivy, Grype or Docker
Scout; fail the build on critical/high vulnerabilities that have a fix
available.</li>
<li><strong>Never put secrets in images:</strong> not in
<code>ENV</code>, not in <code>ARG</code>, not via
<code>COPY .env</code>. For build-time secrets (a private npm token),
use BuildKit secret mounts, which don’t end up in any layer:</li>
</ul>
<div class="sourceCode" id="cb175"><pre
class="sourceCode dockerfile"><code class="sourceCode dockerfile"><span id="cb175-1"><a href="#cb175-1" aria-hidden="true" tabindex="-1"></a><span class="kw">RUN</span> <span class="op">--mount=type=secret,id=npmrc,target=/root/.npmrc</span> <span class="ex">npm</span> ci</span></code></pre></div>
<div class="sourceCode" id="cb176"><pre
class="sourceCode bash"><code class="sourceCode bash"><span id="cb176-1"><a href="#cb176-1" aria-hidden="true" tabindex="-1"></a><span class="ex">docker</span> build <span class="at">--secret</span> id=npmrc,src=<span class="va">$HOME</span>/.npmrc <span class="at">-t</span> order-service:<span class="va">$GIT_SHA</span> .</span></code></pre></div>
<ul>
<li>Produce an <strong>SBOM</strong> (software bill of materials: every
package in the image) with <code>syft</code> or
<code>docker buildx build --sbom=true</code>, and <strong>sign</strong>
images with cosign so the cluster only runs images built by your
pipeline.</li>
<li>Pin base images by digest and let Renovate/Dependabot open PRs when
new patched versions appear; rebuild regularly even without code
changes.</li>
</ul>
<p><strong>Run-time:</strong></p>
<ul>
<li>Run as non-root (Hour 2), with a <strong>read-only root
filesystem</strong> and an explicit writable <code>tmpfs</code> for
<code>/tmp</code> if needed.</li>
<li>Drop Linux capabilities (<code>--cap-drop=ALL</code>), no
<code>--privileged</code>, <code>no-new-privileges</code>.</li>
<li>Never mount the Docker socket (<code>/var/run/docker.sock</code>)
into an app container; it’s root on the host.</li>
<li>Runtime secrets come from the orchestrator (Kubernetes Secrets
backed by a vault or cloud secret manager), injected as env vars or
files at start.</li>
<li>Resource limits on every container (CPU, memory) so one service
can’t starve the host.</li>
</ul>
<h3 id="building-images-in-ci">4.2 Building images in CI</h3>
<div class="sourceCode" id="cb177"><pre
class="sourceCode yaml"><code class="sourceCode yaml"><span id="cb177-1"><a href="#cb177-1" aria-hidden="true" tabindex="-1"></a><span class="co"># .github/workflows/image.yml (excerpt)</span></span>
<span id="cb177-2"><a href="#cb177-2" aria-hidden="true" tabindex="-1"></a><span class="kw">-</span><span class="at"> </span><span class="fu">uses</span><span class="kw">:</span><span class="at"> docker/setup-buildx-action@v3</span></span>
<span id="cb177-3"><a href="#cb177-3" aria-hidden="true" tabindex="-1"></a><span class="kw">-</span><span class="at"> </span><span class="fu">uses</span><span class="kw">:</span><span class="at"> docker/login-action@v3</span></span>
<span id="cb177-4"><a href="#cb177-4" aria-hidden="true" tabindex="-1"></a><span class="at">  </span><span class="fu">with</span><span class="kw">:</span><span class="at"> </span><span class="kw">{</span><span class="at"> </span><span class="fu">registry</span><span class="kw">:</span><span class="at"> ghcr.io</span><span class="kw">,</span><span class="at"> </span><span class="fu">username</span><span class="kw">:</span><span class="at"> ${{ github.actor </span><span class="kw">}</span><span class="at">}, password: ${{ secrets.GITHUB_TOKEN }} }</span></span>
<span id="cb177-5"><a href="#cb177-5" aria-hidden="true" tabindex="-1"></a><span class="kw">-</span><span class="at"> </span><span class="fu">uses</span><span class="kw">:</span><span class="at"> docker/build-push-action@v6</span></span>
<span id="cb177-6"><a href="#cb177-6" aria-hidden="true" tabindex="-1"></a><span class="at">  </span><span class="fu">with</span><span class="kw">:</span></span>
<span id="cb177-7"><a href="#cb177-7" aria-hidden="true" tabindex="-1"></a><span class="at">    </span><span class="fu">context</span><span class="kw">:</span><span class="at"> .</span></span>
<span id="cb177-8"><a href="#cb177-8" aria-hidden="true" tabindex="-1"></a><span class="at">    </span><span class="fu">file</span><span class="kw">:</span><span class="at"> services/order-service/Dockerfile</span></span>
<span id="cb177-9"><a href="#cb177-9" aria-hidden="true" tabindex="-1"></a><span class="at">    </span><span class="fu">platforms</span><span class="kw">:</span><span class="at"> linux/amd64,linux/arm64</span><span class="co">          # multi-arch</span></span>
<span id="cb177-10"><a href="#cb177-10" aria-hidden="true" tabindex="-1"></a><span class="at">    </span><span class="fu">push</span><span class="kw">:</span><span class="at"> </span><span class="ch">true</span></span>
<span id="cb177-11"><a href="#cb177-11" aria-hidden="true" tabindex="-1"></a><span class="at">    </span><span class="fu">tags</span><span class="kw">:</span><span class="at"> ghcr.io/acme/order-service:${{ github.sha }}</span></span>
<span id="cb177-12"><a href="#cb177-12" aria-hidden="true" tabindex="-1"></a><span class="at">    </span><span class="fu">cache-from</span><span class="kw">:</span><span class="at"> type=gha</span><span class="co">                          # reuse layers between CI runs</span></span>
<span id="cb177-13"><a href="#cb177-13" aria-hidden="true" tabindex="-1"></a><span class="at">    </span><span class="fu">cache-to</span><span class="kw">:</span><span class="at"> type=gha,mode=max</span></span>
<span id="cb177-14"><a href="#cb177-14" aria-hidden="true" tabindex="-1"></a><span class="at">    </span><span class="fu">sbom</span><span class="kw">:</span><span class="at"> </span><span class="ch">true</span></span>
<span id="cb177-15"><a href="#cb177-15" aria-hidden="true" tabindex="-1"></a><span class="at">    </span><span class="fu">provenance</span><span class="kw">:</span><span class="at"> </span><span class="ch">true</span></span>
<span id="cb177-16"><a href="#cb177-16" aria-hidden="true" tabindex="-1"></a><span class="kw">-</span><span class="at"> </span><span class="fu">run</span><span class="kw">:</span><span class="at"> trivy image --exit-code 1 --severity CRITICAL,HIGH --ignore-unfixed ghcr.io/acme/order-service:${{ github.sha }}</span></span></code></pre></div>
<p>Principles to state: <strong>build once, promote everywhere</strong>
(the exact image digest tested in staging is the one deployed to
production; never rebuild per environment); configuration comes from the
environment, not baked into the image; images are tagged with the git
SHA so any running container traces back to a commit.</p>
<h3 id="debugging-containers">4.3 Debugging containers</h3>
<table>
<colgroup>
<col style="width: 50%" />

<th>Command</th>
<th>Use</th>
</tr>
</thead>
<tbody>
<tr>
<td><code>docker logs -f --tail 200 &lt;c&gt;</code></td>
<td>Application output (stdout/stderr: always log there, not to

<td><code>docker ps -a</code></td>
<td>Includes exited containers and their exit codes</td>

<td>Explore an image that crashes immediately</td>

<p><strong>Exit codes worth knowing:</strong></p>
<table>
<colgroup>
<col style="width: 33%" />
<col style="width: 33%" />
<col style="width: 33%" />
</colgroup>
<thead>
<tr>
<th>Code</th>
<th>Meaning</th>
<th>Usual cause</th>
</tr>
</thead>
<tbody>
<tr>
<td>0</td>
<td>Clean exit</td>
<td>Process finished (a server shouldn’t)</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>1</td>
<td>Application error</td>
<td>Unhandled exception, failed config validation at start-up</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>137</td>
<td>SIGKILL (128 + 9)</td>
<td>OOM kill, or killed after the grace period because SIGTERM wasn’t
handled</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>139</td>
<td>SIGSEGV (128 + 11)</td>
<td>Native module crash, often an architecture or libc mismatch
(alpine/musl, arm64 vs amd64)</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>143</td>
<td>SIGTERM (128 + 15)</td>
<td>Normal stop when the app exits on SIGTERM</td>
</tr>
</tbody>
</table>
<p><strong>“Works on my machine, crashes in the cluster”
checklist:</strong> architecture mismatch (built on an M-series Mac for
arm64, running on amd64); missing env vars (config validation at
start-up catches this loudly, Day 2); file permissions after switching
to a non-root user; native modules compiled against a different libc;
read-only filesystem preventing writes to the app directory; memory
limit lower than local.</p>
<h3 id="how-id-answer-hour-4-12">How I’d answer — Hour 4</h3>
<p><strong>Q1. How do you secure container images?</strong> “Minimal
bases and production-only dependencies; scanning in CI that fails on
fixable critical issues; no secrets in layers, using BuildKit secret
mounts at build time and the orchestrator’s secret store at runtime;
SBOMs and signed images so the cluster only runs what our pipeline
built; and at runtime non-root, read-only filesystem, dropped
capabilities and resource limits. Base images are pinned and updated
automatically.”</p>
<p><strong>Q2. How do you pass an npm token to a Docker build
safely?</strong> “With a BuildKit secret mount: the token is available
only during that <code>RUN</code> step and never written into a layer.
ARG or ENV would leave it in the image history.”</p>
<p><strong>Q3. What does ‘build once, deploy many’ mean?</strong> “The
CI pipeline builds one image per commit, tagged with the git SHA. That
exact image moves through test, staging and production; only
configuration changes between environments. You never rebuild for
production, so what you tested is byte-for-byte what you ship.”</p>
<p><strong>Q4. A container keeps restarting. How do you debug
it?</strong> “Check the exit code and <code>OOMKilled</code> with
inspect, then the logs from the previous run. 137 with OOMKilled is
memory; 1 is usually a start-up error like missing config; 139 points to
a native module or architecture mismatch. If it dies too fast to exec
into, run the image with a shell entrypoint and start the app by
hand.”</p>
<h3 id="end-of-day-13-checklist">End of Day 13 checklist</h3>
<ul class="task-list">
<li><label><input type="checkbox" />Multi-stage, non-root, exec-form
Dockerfiles for every capstone service, each under ~250 MB</label></li>
<li><label><input type="checkbox" /><code>.dockerignore</code> per
service; dependency layer stays cached when only source
changes</label></li>
<li><label><input type="checkbox" />Compose stack with healthchecks,
named volumes, Kafka dual listeners, Mongo replica set and an
observability profile</label></li>
<li><label><input type="checkbox" />CI workflow building multi-arch
images tagged with the git SHA, cached, scanned with Trivy</label></li>
<li><label><input type="checkbox" />An OOM (137) and a SIGTERM-handling
(143 vs 137) experiment done and explained</label></li>
<li><label><input type="checkbox" />“Shrink a 1.2 GB image” and “what is
a container” answers rehearsed</label></li>
</ul>
<h1 id="day-14-thu-kubernetes-1">Day 14 (Thu) — Kubernetes</h1>
<h2 id="hour-1-kubernetes-architecture-and-core-objects">Hour 1 —
Kubernetes architecture and core objects</h2>
<p>As a backend lead you’re not expected to run clusters, but you are
expected to deploy services onto them correctly and debug them when they
misbehave. Interviewers start with “what happens when you run
<code>kubectl apply</code>?”, which tests whether you understand
Kubernetes’ central idea: declared desired state, continuously
reconciled by controllers.</p>
<h3 id="the-core-idea">1.1 The core idea</h3>
<p>You don’t tell Kubernetes to <em>do</em> things; you declare what you
<em>want</em> (“3 replicas of order-service v1.4 with 512 MB each”),
stored as objects in the API. <strong>Controllers</strong> run loops
that compare desired state with actual state and act to close the gap: a
pod dies, a controller creates a replacement; you change the image, a
controller rolls it out. Everything else follows from this.</p>
<h3 id="architecture-1">1.2 Architecture</h3>
<table>
<colgroup>
<col style="width: 33%" />
<col style="width: 33%" />
<col style="width: 33%" />
</colgroup>
<thead>
<tr>
<th>Component</th>
<th>Where</th>
<th>Role</th>
</tr>
</thead>
<tbody>
<tr>
<td><strong>kube-apiserver</strong></td>
<td>Control plane</td>
<td>The front door: validates and stores every object; everything talks
to it</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td><strong>etcd</strong></td>
<td>Control plane</td>
<td>Consistent key-value store holding all cluster state</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td><strong>kube-scheduler</strong></td>
<td>Control plane</td>
<td>Picks a node for each new pod (resources, affinity, taints)</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td><strong>kube-controller-manager</strong></td>
<td>Control plane</td>
<td>Runs controllers: Deployment, ReplicaSet, Node, Job, endpoints…</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>cloud-controller-manager</td>
<td>Control plane</td>
<td>Talks to the cloud: load balancers, volumes, nodes</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td><strong>kubelet</strong></td>
<td>Every node</td>
<td>Makes sure the pods assigned to its node are running and healthy;
runs probes</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td><strong>container runtime</strong></td>
<td>Every node</td>
<td>containerd / CRI-O actually runs containers</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td><strong>kube-proxy</strong> (or eBPF dataplane like Cilium)</td>
<td>Every node</td>
<td>Implements Service virtual IPs and load balancing</td>
</tr>
</tbody>
</table>
<p>On managed Kubernetes (EKS, GKE, AKS) the cloud provider runs the
control plane; you manage nodes (or not, with Fargate/Autopilot) and
workloads.</p>
<h3 id="what-happens-on-kubectl-apply--f-deployment.yaml">1.3 What
happens on <code>kubectl apply -f deployment.yaml</code></h3>
<ol type="1">
<li>kubectl sends the manifest to the <strong>API server</strong>, which
authenticates, authorises (RBAC), runs admission controllers (defaults,
policies), validates, and stores the Deployment in
<strong>etcd</strong>.</li>
<li>The <strong>Deployment controller</strong> sees a new or changed
Deployment and creates or updates a <strong>ReplicaSet</strong> for that
pod template.</li>
<li>The <strong>ReplicaSet controller</strong> sees it needs 3 pods and
creates 3 <strong>Pod</strong> objects (unscheduled).</li>
<li>The <strong>scheduler</strong> assigns each pod to a node based on
resource requests, affinity, taints and spread.</li>
<li>The <strong>kubelet</strong> on each chosen node sees the pod, pulls
the image, creates the containers through the runtime, mounts volumes
and config, and starts probes.</li>
<li>When readiness probes pass, the pod’s IP is added to the
<strong>Service’s endpoints</strong> (EndpointSlices), and traffic
starts flowing.</li>
<li>On an update, the Deployment creates a new ReplicaSet and shifts
pods over gradually (rolling update, Hour 2).</li>
</ol>
<h3 id="core-objects">1.4 Core objects</h3>
<table>
<colgroup>
<col style="width: 50%" />
<col style="width: 50%" />
</colgroup>
<thead>
<tr>
<th>Object</th>
<th>What it is</th>
</tr>
</thead>
<tbody>
<tr>
<td><strong>Pod</strong></td>
<td>Smallest unit: one or more containers sharing network (one IP) and
volumes. Ephemeral; never create bare pods for apps</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td><strong>ReplicaSet</strong></td>
<td>Keeps N identical pods running; managed by a Deployment</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td><strong>Deployment</strong></td>
<td>Declarative rollouts and rollbacks for stateless apps</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td><strong>Service</strong></td>
<td>Stable virtual IP and DNS name in front of a changing set of pods,
selected by labels</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td><strong>Ingress / Gateway API</strong></td>
<td>HTTP(S) routing from outside: hosts, paths, TLS</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td><strong>ConfigMap / Secret</strong></td>
<td>Configuration and sensitive values for pods</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td><strong>Namespace</strong></td>
<td>Logical grouping for names, quotas, RBAC and policies (per team or
per environment)</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>StatefulSet, DaemonSet, Job, CronJob</td>
<td>Hour 3</td>
</tr>
</tbody>
</table>
<p><strong>Labels and selectors</strong> connect everything: a Service
selects pods with <code>app: order-service</code>; a Deployment manages
pods matching its selector. A typo in a label is a classic “Service has
no endpoints” bug.</p>
<p><strong>Sidecar and init containers:</strong> init containers run to
completion before app containers start (run migrations, wait for a
dependency); sidecars run alongside (log shippers, proxies). Kubernetes
supports native sidecars (stable since v1.33) (init containers with
<code>restartPolicy: Always</code>) that start before and stop after the
main container.</p>
<h3 id="services-and-traffic">1.5 Services and traffic</h3>
<table>
<colgroup>
<col style="width: 33%" />
<col style="width: 33%" />
<col style="width: 33%" />
</colgroup>
<thead>
<tr>
<th>Service type</th>
<th>Reachable from</th>
<th>Use</th>
</tr>
</thead>
<tbody>
<tr>
<td><strong>ClusterIP</strong> (default)</td>
<td>Inside the cluster</td>
<td>Service-to-service:
<code>http://order-service.orders.svc.cluster.local</code> or just
<code>http://order-service</code> within the namespace</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>NodePort</td>
<td>Each node’s IP on a high port</td>
<td>Rare; building block</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td><strong>LoadBalancer</strong></td>
<td>A cloud load balancer with external IP</td>
<td>Exposing a gateway or ingress controller</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>Headless (<code>clusterIP: None</code>)</td>
<td>DNS returns pod IPs directly</td>
<td>StatefulSets, clients that load-balance themselves (gRPC)</td>
</tr>
</tbody>
</table>
<p><strong>Ingress</strong> (with an ingress controller such as Traefik,
HAProxy or a cloud provider’s controller; the community ingress-nginx
controller was retired in March 2026 and no longer receives security
fixes) routes external HTTP traffic by host and path to Services and
terminates TLS (often with cert-manager for certificates). The newer
<strong>Gateway API</strong> is the successor: more expressive (traffic
splitting, header matching, cross-namespace routes) and role-oriented;
it’s the recommended path for new setups and for migrating off
ingress-nginx.</p>
<p><strong>gRPC load-balancing gotcha:</strong> gRPC keeps long-lived
HTTP/2 connections, so a ClusterIP Service balances
<strong>connections</strong>, not requests: one client pod can stick to
one server pod. Fix with client-side balancing over a headless Service,
or a service mesh / L7 proxy.</p>
<h3 id="how-id-answer-hour-1-13">How I’d answer — Hour 1</h3>
<p><strong>Q1. What happens when you run <code>kubectl apply</code> on a
Deployment?</strong> “The API server authenticates, authorises, runs
admission and stores the Deployment in etcd. The Deployment controller
creates a ReplicaSet, which creates pods; the scheduler assigns them to
nodes based on requests and constraints; the kubelet on each node pulls
images and starts containers; once readiness probes pass, the pods are
added to the Service’s endpoints and receive traffic. Throughout,
controllers keep reconciling actual state toward what I declared.”</p>
<p><strong>Q2. Pod vs Deployment vs Service?</strong> “A pod runs
containers and is disposable. A Deployment declares how many pods of
which version should exist and handles rollouts and rollbacks. A Service
gives those changing pods one stable name and IP and load-balances
across the ready ones.”</p>
<p><strong>Q3. My Service returns 503 or has no endpoints. What do you
check?</strong> “That the Service selector matches the pods’ labels
exactly, that pods are Ready (failing readiness probes remove them from
endpoints), and that <code>targetPort</code> matches the port the
container actually listens on. <code>kubectl get endpointslices</code>
and <code>kubectl describe svc</code> show it quickly.”</p>
<p><strong>Q4. Ingress vs LoadBalancer Service?</strong> “A LoadBalancer
Service provisions a cloud load balancer per Service, at layer 4.
Ingress, or the newer Gateway API, puts one entry point in front of many
Services with HTTP routing by host and path plus TLS, which is cheaper
and easier to manage. Usually only the ingress controller or gateway
itself is exposed as a LoadBalancer.”</p>
<h3 id="practice-39">Practice</h3>
<ul class="task-list">
<li><label><input type="checkbox" />Create a local cluster with kind (or
minikube); deploy the order service with a Deployment and ClusterIP
Service</label></li>
<li><label><input type="checkbox" />Delete a pod and watch the
ReplicaSet replace it (<code>kubectl get pods -w</code>)</label></li>
<li><label><input type="checkbox" />Break the Service selector on
purpose, observe empty endpoints, fix it; expose the gateway through an
Ingress</label></li>
</ul>
<h2 id="hour-2-configuring-workloads-properly">Hour 2 — Configuring
workloads properly</h2>
<p>Most Kubernetes incidents in application teams come from the pod
spec: missing resource requests, liveness probes that restart healthy
pods, deploys that drop requests, or secrets handled carelessly. A
well-written Deployment is a strong signal of production experience, so
learn this one line by line.</p>

<h3 id="resources-requests-limits-qos">2.2 Resources: requests, limits,
QoS</h3>
<ul>
<li><strong>Requests:</strong> what the scheduler reserves for the pod
on a node; also the baseline for HPA percentages. No requests means the
scheduler can pack pods onto an overloaded node.</li>
<li><strong>Memory limit:</strong> exceeding it gets the container
OOMKilled (137). Set heap size below it.</li>
<li><strong>CPU limit:</strong> exceeding it doesn’t kill the container
but <strong>throttles</strong> it (CPU time is withheld in short
periods). For latency-sensitive Node services, throttling shows up as
p99 latency spikes and event-loop delay even when average CPU looks low.
Many teams set CPU requests but no CPU limit (or a generous one) for
this reason; others require limits for cost and fairness. Know the
trade-off and state your choice.</li>
<li><strong>QoS classes:</strong> Guaranteed (requests = limits for CPU
and memory), Burstable (requests below limits), BestEffort (nothing set,
first to be evicted under pressure).</li>
<li>Node is single-threaded for JS: a pod with <code>cpu: 2</code>
doesn’t make one Node process faster. Scale with more pods of about one
CPU each (Day 3).</li>
</ul>
<h3 id="probes-the-rules-that-prevent-outages">2.3 Probes: the rules
that prevent outages</h3>
<table>
<colgroup>
<col style="width: 25%" />
<col style="width: 25%" />
<col style="width: 25%" />
<col style="width: 25%" />
</colgroup>
<thead>
<tr>
<th>Probe</th>
<th>Question</th>
<th>Failure action</th>
<th>Should check</th>
</tr>
</thead>
<tbody>
<tr>
<td>Startup</td>
<td>Has it finished starting?</td>
<td>Keep waiting, then restart</td>
<td>Same as liveness, with a long budget</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>Liveness</td>
<td>Is the process hopelessly stuck?</td>
<td><strong>Restart</strong> the container</td>
<td>Only the process itself (event loop responsive)</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>Readiness</td>
<td>Can it serve traffic now?</td>
<td>Remove from Service endpoints</td>
<td>Process plus critical local readiness (DB pool connected, warm-up
done)</td>
</tr>
</tbody>
</table>
<p><strong>The classic outage:</strong> a liveness probe that checks the
database. The database has a brief hiccup, every pod fails liveness,
Kubernetes restarts all of them at once, and a 10-second blip becomes a
full outage with a thundering herd of reconnections. Liveness must not
depend on external systems. Be careful with readiness too: if all pods
go not-ready because a shared dependency is down, the Service has zero
endpoints; sometimes serving degraded responses is better.</p>
<h3 id="configmaps-and-secrets">2.4 ConfigMaps and Secrets</h3>
<ul>
<li><strong>ConfigMap:</strong> non-sensitive config as env vars or
mounted files.</li>
<li><strong>Secret:</strong> sensitive values. By default they’re only
<strong>base64-encoded</strong>, not encrypted. Protect them with RBAC
(few can read secrets), encryption at rest for etcd, and ideally keep
the source of truth in a secret manager (AWS Secrets Manager, Vault, GCP
Secret Manager) synced by the <strong>External Secrets Operator</strong>
or mounted by the Secrets Store CSI driver. Never commit plain Secret
manifests to git (use Sealed Secrets or SOPS if they must live in
git).</li>
<li>Changing a ConfigMap doesn’t restart pods that read it as env vars.
Helm charts commonly add a checksum annotation of the config to the pod
template so a config change triggers a rollout.</li>
</ul>
<h3 id="rolling-updates-and-graceful-shutdown">2.5 Rolling updates and
graceful shutdown</h3>
<p><strong>Rolling update:</strong> with <code>maxSurge: 25%</code> and
<code>maxUnavailable: 0</code>, Kubernetes starts new pods, waits until
they’re Ready, then removes old ones, so capacity never drops. Readiness
gates the rollout: if new pods never become ready, the rollout stalls
(and <code>progressDeadlineSeconds</code> marks it failed) while old
pods keep serving.</p>
<div class="sourceCode" id="cb179"><pre
class="sourceCode bash"><code class="sourceCode bash"><span id="cb179-1"><a href="#cb179-1" aria-hidden="true" tabindex="-1"></a><span class="ex">kubectl</span> rollout status deployment/order-service <span class="at">-n</span> orders</span>
<span id="cb179-2"><a href="#cb179-2" aria-hidden="true" tabindex="-1"></a><span class="ex">kubectl</span> rollout history deployment/order-service <span class="at">-n</span> orders</span>
<span id="cb179-3"><a href="#cb179-3" aria-hidden="true" tabindex="-1"></a><span class="ex">kubectl</span> rollout undo deployment/order-service <span class="at">-n</span> orders            <span class="co"># back to the previous ReplicaSet</span></span></code></pre></div>
<p><strong>Pod termination sequence</strong>, and why the
<code>preStop</code> sleep exists:</p>
<ol type="1">
<li>Pod is marked Terminating.</li>
<li><strong>At the same time</strong>: the endpoints controller removes
it from Services (this takes a moment to propagate to every node and
ingress), and the kubelet runs <code>preStop</code>, then sends
SIGTERM.</li>
<li>Without <code>preStop</code>, the app may receive SIGTERM and stop
accepting connections <strong>before</strong> load balancers stop
sending it traffic: some requests fail on every deploy.</li>
<li>With a short <code>preStop</code> sleep (5–10 s), routing updates
first; then the app’s SIGTERM handler (Day 3) drains in-flight requests
and closes connections.</li>
<li>If still running after <code>terminationGracePeriodSeconds</code>
(counted from the start of termination, including preStop),
SIGKILL.</li>
</ol>
<p><strong>PodDisruptionBudget:</strong> limits voluntary disruptions
(node drains, upgrades) so they can’t take down too many replicas at
once:</p>
<div class="sourceCode" id="cb180"><pre
class="sourceCode yaml"><code class="sourceCode yaml"><span id="cb180-1"><a href="#cb180-1" aria-hidden="true" tabindex="-1"></a><span class="fu">apiVersion</span><span class="kw">:</span><span class="at"> policy/v1</span></span>
<span id="cb180-2"><a href="#cb180-2" aria-hidden="true" tabindex="-1"></a><span class="fu">kind</span><span class="kw">:</span><span class="at"> PodDisruptionBudget</span></span>
<span id="cb180-3"><a href="#cb180-3" aria-hidden="true" tabindex="-1"></a><span class="fu">metadata</span><span class="kw">:</span><span class="at"> </span><span class="kw">{</span><span class="at"> </span><span class="fu">name</span><span class="kw">:</span><span class="at"> order-service</span><span class="kw">,</span><span class="at"> </span><span class="fu">namespace</span><span class="kw">:</span><span class="at"> orders </span><span class="kw">}</span></span>
<span id="cb180-4"><a href="#cb180-4" aria-hidden="true" tabindex="-1"></a><span class="fu">spec</span><span class="kw">:</span></span>
<span id="cb180-5"><a href="#cb180-5" aria-hidden="true" tabindex="-1"></a><span class="at">  </span><span class="fu">minAvailable</span><span class="kw">:</span><span class="at"> </span><span class="dv">2</span></span>
<span id="cb180-6"><a href="#cb180-6" aria-hidden="true" tabindex="-1"></a><span class="at">  </span><span class="fu">selector</span><span class="kw">:</span><span class="at"> </span><span class="kw">{</span><span class="at"> </span><span class="fu">matchLabels</span><span class="kw">:</span><span class="at"> </span><span class="kw">{</span><span class="at"> </span><span class="fu">app</span><span class="kw">:</span><span class="at"> order-service </span><span class="kw">}</span><span class="at"> </span><span class="kw">}</span></span></code></pre></div>
<h3 id="how-id-answer-hour-2-13">How I’d answer — Hour 2</h3>
<p><strong>Q1. Readiness vs liveness probes?</strong> “Liveness answers
‘is this process stuck beyond recovery?’ and failing it restarts the
container, so it should only check the process itself, never the
database. Readiness answers ‘should this pod get traffic now?’ and
failing it removes the pod from load balancing without restarting it. A
startup probe protects slow-starting apps from being killed by liveness
during boot.”</p>
<p><strong>Q2. Requests vs limits, and do you set CPU limits?</strong>
“Requests reserve capacity and drive scheduling; limits cap usage.
Exceeding a memory limit means an OOM kill, so I size the heap below it.
Exceeding a CPU limit means throttling, which hurts Node’s tail latency,
so for latency-sensitive services I set CPU requests with no CPU limit,
or a generous one, unless the platform requires limits. Memory limits
always.”</p>
<p><strong>Q3. How do you get zero-downtime deployments?</strong>
“Rolling updates with maxUnavailable 0 so capacity never drops,
readiness probes so new pods only get traffic when ready, a preStop
sleep so the pod leaves load balancing before shutdown starts, a SIGTERM
handler that drains in-flight requests, a PodDisruptionBudget for node
maintenance, and backward-compatible database migrations so old and new
versions can run side by side.”</p>
<p><strong>Q4. Are Kubernetes Secrets secure?</strong> “Not by
themselves; they’re base64, not encrypted. I’d enable encryption at
rest, restrict access with RBAC, keep the source of truth in a secret
manager synced by External Secrets, and never store plain secrets in
git.”</p>

</ul>
<h2 id="hour-3-scaling-stateful-workloads-jobs-scheduling">Hour 3 —
Scaling, stateful workloads, jobs, scheduling</h2>
<p>Interviewers ask how your service scales on a sale day, where its
database lives, how migrations run, and how you keep replicas from all
landing on one node. These are design decisions an application lead
makes, even when a platform team owns the cluster.</p>
<h3 id="autoscaling-layers">3.1 Autoscaling layers</h3>
<table>
<colgroup>
