<p><strong>Senior points:</strong> HPA percentages are relative to
<strong>requests</strong>, so wrong requests mean wrong scaling. CPU is
a weak signal for I/O-bound Node services; scale API services on request
rate or latency where possible, and consumers on lag (KEDA). Autoscaling
takes time (new nodes can take minutes), so for known peaks (a sale at 8
p.m.) scale up ahead of time with a scheduled minimum. And scaling pods
up is pointless if the database is the bottleneck: check connection pool
totals (Day 7).</p>
<h3 id="stateful-workloads-and-storage">3.2 Stateful workloads and
storage</h3>
<ul>
<li><strong>PersistentVolume (PV):</strong> a piece of storage (cloud
disk, NFS). <strong>PersistentVolumeClaim (PVC):</strong> a pod’s
request for storage. <strong>StorageClass:</strong> how volumes are
provisioned dynamically (disk type, replication, reclaim policy).</li>
<li><strong>StatefulSet:</strong> for workloads needing stable identity:
pods get fixed names (<code>kafka-0</code>, <code>kafka-1</code>),
stable DNS through a headless Service, their own PVC each, and ordered
start-up and shutdown. Used for databases, Kafka, Zookeeper-like
systems.</li>
<li><strong>My position for application teams:</strong> run stateless
services in Kubernetes and use <strong>managed databases and
brokers</strong> (RDS/Aurora, Atlas, ElastiCache, MSK/Confluent) unless
there’s a strong reason and a team skilled in running stateful systems
on Kubernetes (operators like CloudNativePG or Strimzi help). Backups,
upgrades, failover and storage performance are where in-cluster
databases hurt.</li>
</ul>
<h3 id="jobs-cronjobs-daemonsets">3.3 Jobs, CronJobs, DaemonSets</h3>
<ul>
<li><strong>Job:</strong> runs pods to completion, with retries
(<code>backoffLimit</code>). Good for one-off tasks and <strong>database
migrations</strong>.</li>
<li><strong>CronJob:</strong> scheduled Jobs. Set
<code>concurrencyPolicy: Forbid</code> so a slow run doesn’t overlap the
next, and make the job idempotent, since Kubernetes may occasionally
start it twice or miss a run.</li>
<li><strong>DaemonSet:</strong> one pod per node: log collectors, node
monitoring, CNI agents.</li>
</ul>
<p><strong>Running migrations safely:</strong> don’t run them in an init
container of a Deployment with many replicas (they’d race). Run them
once per release as a Job (a Helm pre-upgrade hook or a pipeline step)
before the new version rolls out, and keep migrations backward
compatible (expand and contract, Day 7) so old pods still work during
the rollout.</p>
<h3 id="scheduling-controls">3.4 Scheduling controls</h3>
<table>
<colgroup>
<col style="width: 50%" />
<col style="width: 50%" />
</colgroup>
<thead>
<tr>
<th>Tool</th>
<th>Use</th>
</tr>
</thead>
<tbody>
<tr>
<td>Requests</td>
<td>The scheduler only places pods where requested resources fit</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td><code>nodeSelector</code> / node affinity</td>
<td>Run on specific node types (GPU nodes, arm64, spot vs
on-demand)</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td><strong>Pod anti-affinity</strong></td>
<td>Keep replicas of the same app off the same node</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td><strong>Topology spread constraints</strong></td>
<td>Spread replicas evenly across zones and nodes</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>Taints and tolerations</td>
<td>Reserve nodes (e.g. only batch jobs on spot nodes)</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>PriorityClass</td>
<td>Important pods can preempt less important ones under pressure</td>
</tr>
</tbody>
</table>
<div class="sourceCode" id="cb183"><pre
class="sourceCode yaml"><code class="sourceCode yaml"><span id="cb183-1"><a href="#cb183-1" aria-hidden="true" tabindex="-1"></a><span class="co"># in the pod template: spread replicas across availability zones</span></span>
<span id="cb183-2"><a href="#cb183-2" aria-hidden="true" tabindex="-1"></a><span class="fu">topologySpreadConstraints</span><span class="kw">:</span></span>
<span id="cb183-3"><a href="#cb183-3" aria-hidden="true" tabindex="-1"></a><span class="at">  </span><span class="kw">-</span><span class="at"> </span><span class="fu">maxSkew</span><span class="kw">:</span><span class="at"> </span><span class="dv">1</span></span>
<span id="cb183-4"><a href="#cb183-4" aria-hidden="true" tabindex="-1"></a><span class="at">    </span><span class="fu">topologyKey</span><span class="kw">:</span><span class="at"> topology.kubernetes.io/zone</span></span>
<span id="cb183-5"><a href="#cb183-5" aria-hidden="true" tabindex="-1"></a><span class="at">    </span><span class="fu">whenUnsatisfiable</span><span class="kw">:</span><span class="at"> ScheduleAnyway</span></span>
<span id="cb183-6"><a href="#cb183-6" aria-hidden="true" tabindex="-1"></a><span class="at">    </span><span class="fu">labelSelector</span><span class="kw">:</span><span class="at"> </span><span class="kw">{</span><span class="at"> </span><span class="fu">matchLabels</span><span class="kw">:</span><span class="at"> </span><span class="kw">{</span><span class="at"> </span><span class="fu">app</span><span class="kw">:</span><span class="at"> order-service </span><span class="kw">}</span><span class="at"> </span><span class="kw">}</span></span></code></pre></div>
<p>Without spreading, three replicas can land on one node or one zone,
and a single failure takes the service down despite “3 replicas”.</p>
<h3 id="how-id-answer-hour-3-13">How I’d answer — Hour 3</h3>
<p><strong>Q1. How do you autoscale a Node API and a Kafka
consumer?</strong> “The API with an HPA, ideally on request rate or
latency via custom metrics, since CPU is a weak signal for I/O-bound
Node; with CPU, the target is relative to requests, so those must be
right. Consumers with KEDA on consumer lag, capped at the partition
count. The cluster autoscaler or Karpenter adds nodes when pods don’t
fit. For known peaks I raise the minimum ahead of time, and I check the
database can take the extra connections.”</p>
<p><strong>Q2. Would you run Postgres in Kubernetes?</strong> “Usually
not for an application team. A managed database handles backups,
failover, upgrades and storage performance, which are the hard parts. If
there’s a strong reason, I’d use a mature operator like CloudNativePG
with a StatefulSet and tested backup and restore.”</p>
<p><strong>Q3. How do you run database migrations in
Kubernetes?</strong> “Once per release, as a Job that runs before the
rollout, from a Helm hook or a pipeline step, never as an init container
racing across replicas. Migrations are backward compatible so old and
new pods can run together during the rolling update.”</p>
<p><strong>Q4. We have 3 replicas but still had an outage when one node
died. Why?</strong> “The replicas were probably on the same node or
zone. Topology spread constraints or pod anti-affinity spread them
across nodes and zones, and a PodDisruptionBudget keeps enough running
during maintenance.”</p>
<h3 id="practice-41">Practice</h3>
<ul class="task-list">
<li><label><input type="checkbox" />Add an HPA to the order service;
load-test with k6 and watch it scale up and slowly down</label></li>
<li><label><input type="checkbox" />Install KEDA on kind and scale the
analytics consumer on Kafka lag</label></li>
<li><label><input type="checkbox" />Run Prisma/Drizzle migrations as a
Kubernetes Job; add topology spread constraints to every
Deployment</label></li>
</ul>
<h2 id="hour-4-helm-gitops-security-debugging-pods">Hour 4 — Helm,
GitOps, security, debugging pods</h2>
<p>The last hour on Kubernetes covers how manifests are packaged and
delivered, how access and traffic are locked down, and the debugging
drill: given a pod in CrashLoopBackOff, what do you type? Expect the
debugging question in almost every Kubernetes interview.</p>
<h3 id="packaging-helm-and-kustomize">4.1 Packaging: Helm and
Kustomize</h3>
<p><strong>Helm:</strong> a package manager for Kubernetes. A
<strong>chart</strong> is templated manifests plus default values; a
<strong>release</strong> is an installed instance with its own
values.</p>
<pre class="text"><code>charts/node-service/
  Chart.yaml
  values.yaml                # defaults: replicas, image, resources, probes, HPA...
  templates/
    deployment.yaml          # {{ .Values.image.repository }}:{{ .Values.image.tag }}
    service.yaml
    hpa.yaml
    pdb.yaml
    configmap.yaml
    _helpers.tpl</code></pre>
<div class="sourceCode" id="cb185"><pre
class="sourceCode bash"><code class="sourceCode bash"><span id="cb185-1"><a href="#cb185-1" aria-hidden="true" tabindex="-1"></a><span class="ex">helm</span> upgrade <span class="at">--install</span> order-service charts/node-service <span class="dt">\</span></span>
<span id="cb185-2"><a href="#cb185-2" aria-hidden="true" tabindex="-1"></a>  <span class="at">-n</span> orders <span class="at">--create-namespace</span> <span class="dt">\</span></span>
<span id="cb185-3"><a href="#cb185-3" aria-hidden="true" tabindex="-1"></a>  <span class="at">-f</span> values/order-service.yaml <span class="at">-f</span> values/prod.yaml <span class="dt">\</span></span>
<span id="cb185-4"><a href="#cb185-4" aria-hidden="true" tabindex="-1"></a>  <span class="at">--set</span> image.tag=9f2c1ab <span class="at">--atomic</span> <span class="at">--timeout</span> 5m     <span class="co"># --atomic rolls back automatically if the rollout fails</span></span></code></pre></div>
<p>A strong pattern for many Node services: <strong>one shared
chart</strong> (<code>node-service</code>) encoding every best practice
from Hour 2, and a small values file per service. New services get
probes, PDBs, HPA, security context and spreading for free.</p>
<p><strong>Kustomize:</strong> no templating; a base set of plain YAML
plus per-environment <strong>overlays</strong> that patch it (built into
<code>kubectl apply -k</code>). Simpler for a few apps, less flexible
for many. Plenty of teams use Helm for third-party software and either
for their own services.</p>
<h3 id="gitops">4.2 GitOps</h3>
<p><strong>What it is:</strong> the desired state of each environment
lives in a git repository; an in-cluster agent (<strong>Argo CD</strong>
or <strong>Flux</strong>) continuously syncs the cluster to match git
and reports drift.</p>
<p>Flow: CI builds and pushes the image (Day 13) → CI (or an image
updater) commits the new tag to the environment repo → Argo CD notices
and applies it → the cluster converges.</p>
<p>Benefits: every change is a reviewed, audited commit; rollback is
<code>git revert</code>; no CI system needs cluster-admin credentials;
drift (someone ran <code>kubectl edit</code> by hand) is detected and
corrected. Day 15 builds on this for progressive delivery.</p>
<h3 id="access-and-network-security">4.3 Access and network
security</h3>
<ul>
<li><strong>RBAC:</strong> Roles (namespace-scoped) and ClusterRoles
define allowed verbs on resources; RoleBindings attach them to users,
groups or <strong>ServiceAccounts</strong>. Give each workload its own
ServiceAccount with no API permissions unless it needs them, and give
humans read access in production with write access through GitOps
only.</li>
<li><strong>Cloud identity for pods:</strong> IRSA / EKS Pod Identity on
AWS, Workload Identity on GCP and Azure, so pods get cloud permissions
(read one S3 bucket) without static access keys in Secrets.</li>
<li><strong>NetworkPolicies:</strong> by default every pod can talk to
every pod. Policies (enforced by the CNI, e.g. Calico or Cilium)
restrict that: default-deny per namespace, then allow only what’s
needed.</li>
</ul>
<div class="sourceCode" id="cb186"><pre
class="sourceCode yaml"><code class="sourceCode yaml"><span id="cb186-1"><a href="#cb186-1" aria-hidden="true" tabindex="-1"></a><span class="co"># Only the order service (and the ingress controller) may reach payment-service</span></span>
<span id="cb186-2"><a href="#cb186-2" aria-hidden="true" tabindex="-1"></a><span class="fu">apiVersion</span><span class="kw">:</span><span class="at"> networking.k8s.io/v1</span></span>
<span id="cb186-3"><a href="#cb186-3" aria-hidden="true" tabindex="-1"></a><span class="fu">kind</span><span class="kw">:</span><span class="at"> NetworkPolicy</span></span>
<span id="cb186-4"><a href="#cb186-4" aria-hidden="true" tabindex="-1"></a><span class="fu">metadata</span><span class="kw">:</span><span class="at"> </span><span class="kw">{</span><span class="at"> </span><span class="fu">name</span><span class="kw">:</span><span class="at"> payment-ingress</span><span class="kw">,</span><span class="at"> </span><span class="fu">namespace</span><span class="kw">:</span><span class="at"> payments </span><span class="kw">}</span></span>
<span id="cb186-5"><a href="#cb186-5" aria-hidden="true" tabindex="-1"></a><span class="fu">spec</span><span class="kw">:</span></span>
<span id="cb186-6"><a href="#cb186-6" aria-hidden="true" tabindex="-1"></a><span class="at">  </span><span class="fu">podSelector</span><span class="kw">:</span><span class="at"> </span><span class="kw">{</span><span class="at"> </span><span class="fu">matchLabels</span><span class="kw">:</span><span class="at"> </span><span class="kw">{</span><span class="at"> </span><span class="fu">app</span><span class="kw">:</span><span class="at"> payment-service </span><span class="kw">}</span><span class="at"> </span><span class="kw">}</span></span>
<span id="cb186-7"><a href="#cb186-7" aria-hidden="true" tabindex="-1"></a><span class="at">  </span><span class="fu">policyTypes</span><span class="kw">:</span><span class="at"> </span><span class="kw">[</span><span class="at">Ingress</span><span class="kw">]</span></span>
<span id="cb186-8"><a href="#cb186-8" aria-hidden="true" tabindex="-1"></a><span class="at">  </span><span class="fu">ingress</span><span class="kw">:</span></span>
<span id="cb186-9"><a href="#cb186-9" aria-hidden="true" tabindex="-1"></a><span class="at">    </span><span class="kw">-</span><span class="at"> </span><span class="fu">from</span><span class="kw">:</span></span>
<span id="cb186-10"><a href="#cb186-10" aria-hidden="true" tabindex="-1"></a><span class="at">        </span><span class="kw">-</span><span class="at"> </span><span class="fu">namespaceSelector</span><span class="kw">:</span><span class="at"> </span><span class="kw">{</span><span class="at"> </span><span class="fu">matchLabels</span><span class="kw">:</span><span class="at"> </span><span class="kw">{</span><span class="at"> </span><span class="fu">kubernetes.io/metadata.name</span><span class="kw">:</span><span class="at"> orders </span><span class="kw">}</span><span class="at"> </span><span class="kw">}</span></span>
<span id="cb186-11"><a href="#cb186-11" aria-hidden="true" tabindex="-1"></a><span class="at">          </span><span class="fu">podSelector</span><span class="kw">:</span><span class="at"> </span><span class="kw">{</span><span class="at"> </span><span class="fu">matchLabels</span><span class="kw">:</span><span class="at"> </span><span class="kw">{</span><span class="at"> </span><span class="fu">app</span><span class="kw">:</span><span class="at"> order-service </span><span class="kw">}</span><span class="at"> </span><span class="kw">}</span></span>
<span id="cb186-12"><a href="#cb186-12" aria-hidden="true" tabindex="-1"></a><span class="at">      </span><span class="fu">ports</span><span class="kw">:</span><span class="at"> </span><span class="kw">[{</span><span class="at"> </span><span class="fu">port</span><span class="kw">:</span><span class="at"> </span><span class="dv">3000</span><span class="at"> </span><span class="kw">}]</span></span></code></pre></div>
<ul>
<li><strong>Pod Security Standards</strong> (<code>restricted</code>
profile enforced per namespace) block privileged containers and root
users; policy engines (Kyverno, OPA Gatekeeper) enforce rules like
“images only from our registry, signed, with resource limits”.</li>
</ul>
<h3 id="debugging-pods">4.4 Debugging pods</h3>
<table>
<colgroup>
<col style="width: 33%" />
<col style="width: 33%" />
<col style="width: 33%" />
</colgroup>
<thead>
<tr>
<th>Status / symptom</th>
<th>Usual causes</th>
<th>First commands</th>
</tr>
</thead>
<tbody>
<tr>
<td><strong>Pending</strong></td>
<td>Not enough CPU/memory on any node for the requests; unsatisfiable
affinity or taints; PVC not bound</td>
<td><code>kubectl describe pod</code> → Events (“0/5 nodes available:
insufficient memory”)</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td><strong>ImagePullBackOff / ErrImagePull</strong></td>
<td>Wrong image name or tag; missing registry credentials
(<code>imagePullSecrets</code>); architecture mismatch</td>
<td><code>kubectl describe pod</code></td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td><strong>CrashLoopBackOff</strong></td>
<td>App exits at start: missing env/secret, failed config validation,
can’t reach DB and exits, wrong command, permission error with read-only
FS</td>
<td><code>kubectl logs &lt;pod&gt; --previous</code> (logs from the
crashed run)</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td><strong>OOMKilled</strong> (exit 137)</td>
<td>Memory limit too low or a leak</td>
<td><code>kubectl describe pod</code> (Last State: OOMKilled), memory
metrics</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>Running but not Ready</td>
<td>Readiness probe failing (wrong path/port, dependency down)</td>
<td><code>kubectl describe pod</code> (probe failures in Events), hit
the endpoint with port-forward</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>Restarting periodically</td>
<td>Liveness probe failing under load (event loop blocked longer than
the timeout)</td>
<td>Events, event-loop delay metric</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>Works but Service unreachable</td>
<td>Selector/label mismatch, wrong <code>targetPort</code>,
NetworkPolicy blocking</td>
<td><code>kubectl get endpointslices</code>, <code>kubectl exec</code> +
curl from another pod</td>
</tr>
</tbody>
</table>
<div class="sourceCode" id="cb187"><pre
class="sourceCode bash"><code class="sourceCode bash"><span id="cb187-1"><a href="#cb187-1" aria-hidden="true" tabindex="-1"></a><span class="ex">kubectl</span> get pods <span class="at">-n</span> orders <span class="at">-o</span> wide                     <span class="co"># status, restarts, node</span></span>
<span id="cb187-2"><a href="#cb187-2" aria-hidden="true" tabindex="-1"></a><span class="ex">kubectl</span> describe pod order-service-7d9f... <span class="at">-n</span> orders   <span class="co"># events, probe failures, last state, exit code</span></span>
<span id="cb187-3"><a href="#cb187-3" aria-hidden="true" tabindex="-1"></a><span class="ex">kubectl</span> logs order-service-7d9f... <span class="at">-n</span> orders <span class="at">--previous</span> <span class="co"># logs of the crashed container</span></span>
<span id="cb187-4"><a href="#cb187-4" aria-hidden="true" tabindex="-1"></a><span class="ex">kubectl</span> logs <span class="at">-l</span> app=order-service <span class="at">-n</span> orders <span class="at">--tail</span><span class="op">=</span>100 <span class="at">-f</span></span>
<span id="cb187-5"><a href="#cb187-5" aria-hidden="true" tabindex="-1"></a><span class="ex">kubectl</span> get events <span class="at">-n</span> orders <span class="at">--sort-by</span><span class="op">=</span>.lastTimestamp</span>
<span id="cb187-6"><a href="#cb187-6" aria-hidden="true" tabindex="-1"></a><span class="ex">kubectl</span> exec <span class="at">-it</span> order-service-7d9f... <span class="at">-n</span> orders <span class="at">--</span> sh  <span class="co"># if the image has a shell</span></span>
<span id="cb187-7"><a href="#cb187-7" aria-hidden="true" tabindex="-1"></a><span class="ex">kubectl</span> debug <span class="at">-it</span> order-service-7d9f... <span class="at">-n</span> orders <span class="at">--image</span><span class="op">=</span>busybox <span class="at">--target</span><span class="op">=</span>app   <span class="co"># ephemeral debug container</span></span>
<span id="cb187-8"><a href="#cb187-8" aria-hidden="true" tabindex="-1"></a><span class="ex">kubectl</span> port-forward svc/order-service 8080:80 <span class="at">-n</span> orders</span>
<span id="cb187-9"><a href="#cb187-9" aria-hidden="true" tabindex="-1"></a><span class="ex">kubectl</span> top pods <span class="at">-n</span> orders                              <span class="co"># CPU and memory now (metrics-server)</span></span>
<span id="cb187-10"><a href="#cb187-10" aria-hidden="true" tabindex="-1"></a><span class="ex">kubectl</span> rollout undo deployment/order-service <span class="at">-n</span> orders <span class="co"># fastest fix for a bad release</span></span></code></pre></div>
<p><strong>The drill to say out loud for CrashLoopBackOff:</strong>
describe the pod for the exit code and events → logs with
<code>--previous</code> → classify: config/secret missing (fix values),
dependency unreachable (check Service/DNS/NetworkPolicy and make
start-up retry instead of exiting), OOM (memory), permission (read-only
FS, non-root user) → if a release caused it, roll back first and
investigate after.</p>
<h3 id="how-id-answer-hour-4-13">How I’d answer — Hour 4</h3>
<p><strong>Q1. A pod is in CrashLoopBackOff. Walk me through
it.</strong> “<code>kubectl describe pod</code> for the exit code, last
state and events; then <code>kubectl logs --previous</code> to see why
the last run died. Exit 1 with a config error means a missing env var or
secret; 137 with OOMKilled means memory; connection errors mean the
dependency, DNS or a NetworkPolicy. If it started with a deploy, I roll
back first to restore service, then fix forward. Afterwards, I make sure
start-up validates config with a clear message and retries dependencies
instead of crashing.”</p>
<p><strong>Q2. Helm or Kustomize?</strong> “Helm when you need packaging
and reuse: one shared chart for all our Node services with per-service
values, plus installing third-party software. Kustomize for a few apps
where plain YAML with environment patches is enough. Both work well with
GitOps.”</p>
<p><strong>Q3. What is GitOps and why use it?</strong> “Git holds the
desired state of every environment, and an agent like Argo CD keeps the
cluster in sync with it. Every change is reviewed and auditable,
rollback is a revert, drift is corrected automatically, and CI doesn’t
need credentials to the cluster.”</p>
<p><strong>Q4. How would you restrict which services can call the
payment service?</strong> “A default-deny NetworkPolicy in the payments
namespace, then a policy allowing ingress only from the order service’s
pods on its port. On top of that, mTLS with identities from a service
mesh, and authorisation at the application level for defence in
depth.”</p>

<h1 id="day-15-fri-cicd-cloud-observability">Day 15 (Fri) — CI/CD,
cloud, observability</h1>
<h2 id="hour-1-cicd-pipeline-design-and-deployment-strategies">Hour 1 —
CI/CD pipeline design and deployment strategies</h2>
<p>A principal engineer is expected to own how code reaches production
safely and quickly. Interview questions here: design a pipeline for 20
microservices, blue-green vs canary, how to roll back in under a minute,
and how you’d measure whether delivery is getting better. Day 5 covered
the CI basics; this hour covers delivery.</p>
<h3 id="pipeline-stages">1.1 Pipeline stages</h3>
<table>
<colgroup>
<col style="width: 33%" />
<col style="width: 33%" />
<col style="width: 33%" />
</colgroup>
<thead>
<tr>
<th>Stage</th>
<th>What happens</th>
<th>Fails fast on</th>
</tr>
</thead>
<tbody>
<tr>
<td>1. Pull request checks</td>
<td>Lint, typecheck, unit tests, affected integration tests, OpenAPI
diff, dependency audit, secret scanning</td>
<td>Broken code before review</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>2. Merge to main</td>
<td>Same checks + build image once (git SHA tag), scan, SBOM, sign,
push</td>
<td>Vulnerabilities, build errors</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>3. Deploy to staging</td>
<td>GitOps commit of the new tag; migrations Job; smoke tests and
contract tests against staging</td>
<td>Integration problems</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>4. Production</td>
<td>Progressive rollout (canary), automated analysis of metrics, promote
or roll back</td>
<td>Regressions under real traffic</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>5. After deploy</td>
<td>Error rates, SLO burn, business metrics watched; deploy annotated on
dashboards</td>
<td>Slow-burning problems</td>
</tr>
</tbody>
</table>
<p><strong>Principles to state:</strong> trunk-based development with
small PRs (Day 5); <strong>build once, promote the same
artifact</strong> (Day 13); every environment configured, not rebuilt;
deployments automated and boring; fast feedback (PR checks under ~10
minutes); and decoupling <strong>deploy</strong> (code reaches
production) from <strong>release</strong> (users see the feature) with
feature flags.</p>
<h3 id="deployment-strategies">1.2 Deployment strategies</h3>
<table>
<colgroup>
<col style="width: 25%" />
<col style="width: 25%" />
<col style="width: 25%" />
<col style="width: 25%" />
</colgroup>
<thead>
<tr>
<th>Strategy</th>
<th>How</th>
<th>Good</th>
<th>Cost / risk</th>
</tr>
</thead>
<tbody>
<tr>
<td><strong>Rolling</strong></td>
<td>Replace pods gradually (Day 14)</td>
<td>Default, no extra infrastructure</td>
<td>Old and new run together; rollback is another rollout</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td><strong>Blue-green</strong></td>
<td>Run full new version (green) beside old (blue); switch traffic at
once; keep blue for instant rollback</td>
<td>Instant switch and rollback; test green before switching</td>
<td>Double capacity during deploy; database must work for both
versions</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td><strong>Canary</strong></td>
<td>Send a small share of traffic (1% → 10% → 50% → 100%) to the new
version, watching metrics at each step</td>
<td>Limits blast radius; real-traffic validation</td>
<td>Needs traffic splitting and good metrics; slower</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td><strong>Feature flags</strong></td>
<td>Ship code dark; enable per user/segment/percentage at runtime</td>
<td>Release without deploy; instant kill switch; A/B tests</td>
<td>Flag debt; code paths multiply; flags need cleanup</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>Shadow / dark launch</td>
<td>Copy production traffic to the new version without returning its
responses</td>
<td>Test performance and correctness with zero user impact</td>
<td>Side effects must be disabled; complex</td>
</tr>
</tbody>
</table>
<p><strong>Canary with automated analysis (Argo Rollouts):</strong></p>
<div class="sourceCode" id="cb188"><pre

<span id="cb188-13"><a href="#cb188-13" aria-hidden="true" tabindex="-1"></a><span class="at">        </span><span class="kw">-</span><span class="at"> </span><span class="fu">analysis</span><span class="kw">:</span><span class="at"> </span><span class="kw">{</span><span class="at"> </span><span class="fu">templates</span><span class="kw">:</span><span class="at"> </span><span class="kw">[{</span><span class="at"> </span><span class="fu">templateName</span><span class="kw">:</span><span class="at"> success-rate </span><span class="kw">}]</span><span class="at"> </span><span class="kw">}</span></span>

<span id="cb188-15"><a href="#cb188-15" aria-hidden="true" tabindex="-1"></a><span class="at">  </span><span class="fu">selector</span><span class="kw">:</span><span class="at"> </span><span class="kw">{</span><span class="at"> </span><span class="fu">matchLabels</span><span class="kw">:</span><span class="at"> </span><span class="kw">{</span><span class="at"> </span><span class="fu">app</span><span class="kw">:</span><span class="at"> order-service </span><span class="kw">}</span><span class="at"> </span><span class="kw">}</span></span>
<span id="cb188-16"><a href="#cb188-16" aria-hidden="true" tabindex="-1"></a><span class="at">  </span><span class="fu">template</span><span class="kw">:</span><span class="at"> </span><span class="kw">{</span><span class="at"> ... </span><span class="kw">}</span><span class="co">          # same pod template as the Deployment</span></span></code></pre></div>
<p>If the analysis fails (error rate above threshold), the rollout
aborts and traffic returns to the stable version automatically, without
anyone being paged first. Flagger does the same with Flux.</p>
<p><strong>The database constraint behind every strategy:</strong>
during any rollout, old and new code run against the same database at
the same time. Schema changes must be backward compatible (expand and
contract, Day 7), and message/event changes too (Day 12). This is what
makes rollback safe.</p>
<h3 id="rollback">1.3 Rollback</h3>
<ul>
<li>Fastest: revert traffic (blue-green switch back, canary abort, flag
off): seconds.</li>
<li>Next: redeploy the previous image tag (<code>git revert</code> in
the GitOps repo, <code>kubectl rollout undo</code>,
<code>helm rollback</code>): a minute or two.</li>
<li>Rollback is only safe if migrations are backward compatible;
<strong>never</strong> write “down” migrations that drop data as a
rollback plan. Roll forward with a fix when data has changed shape.</li>
<li>Practise rollbacks; a procedure that’s never been run doesn’t work
at 2 a.m.</li>
</ul>
<h3 id="measuring-delivery-dora-metrics">1.4 Measuring delivery: DORA
metrics</h3>
<table>
<colgroup>
<col style="width: 33%" />
<col style="width: 33%" />
<col style="width: 33%" />
</colgroup>
<thead>
<tr>
<th>Metric</th>
<th>Measures</th>
<th>Elite teams (roughly)</th>
</tr>
</thead>
<tbody>
<tr>
<td>Deployment frequency</td>
<td>How often you ship to production</td>
<td>On demand, many times a day</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>Lead time for changes</td>
<td>Commit to running in production</td>
<td>Under a day</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>Change failure rate</td>
<td>Share of deploys causing an incident or rollback</td>
<td>Low (around 0–15%)</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>Time to restore service</td>
<td>How fast you recover from a failure</td>
<td>Under an hour</td>
</tr>
</tbody>
</table>
<p>The insight to share: speed and stability go together. Small,
frequent, automated deploys fail less often and recover faster than big,
rare, manual ones.</p>
<h3 id="monorepo-pipelines">1.5 Monorepo pipelines</h3>
<p>For 20 services in one repo: build and test only what changed
(Turborepo/Nx <code>--affected</code>, path filters), one reusable
workflow template called per service, per-service image and version, and
parallel jobs. Shared packages that change trigger dependants. Keep a
single required status check so branch protection stays simple.</p>
<h3 id="how-id-answer-hour-1-14">How I’d answer — Hour 1</h3>
<p><strong>Q1. Design a CI/CD pipeline for 20 microservices.</strong>
“Trunk-based development with small PRs. PR checks run only for affected
services: lint, types, unit and integration tests, contract and API
diffs, security scans, under ten minutes. On merge, each affected
service builds one image tagged with the commit SHA, scanned, signed and
pushed. Deployment is GitOps: the new tag is committed to the staging
environment repo, Argo CD applies it, migrations run as a pre-sync Job,
smoke and contract tests run. Production uses canary rollouts with
automated metric analysis and automatic abort. Features are released
separately with flags. We track the DORA metrics to see if it’s
improving.”</p>
<p><strong>Q2. Blue-green or canary?</strong> “Blue-green when I want an
instant, all-at-once switch with instant rollback and can afford double
capacity briefly. Canary when I want to limit blast radius by exposing a
small share of real traffic first and promoting automatically based on
metrics; that’s my default for high-traffic services. Both require
backward-compatible database changes.”</p>
<p><strong>Q3. How do you roll back a bad release quickly?</strong>
“Abort the canary or flip the flag, which takes seconds. Otherwise
revert the image tag in the GitOps repo and let Argo CD sync, or
<code>helm rollback</code>. It’s only safe because migrations are
expand-and-contract, so the previous version still works with the
current schema.”</p>
<p><strong>Q4. Deploy vs release?</strong> “Deploying puts code in
production; releasing exposes it to users. Feature flags separate them,
so we deploy continuously with features hidden, then release gradually,
to internal users, then a percentage, and turn them off instantly if
needed.”</p>
<h3 id="practice-42">Practice</h3>
<ul class="task-list">
<li><label><input type="checkbox" />Write the pipeline diagram for the
capstone (PR → main → staging → canary → prod) as a Mermaid diagram in
the repo</label></li>
<li><label><input type="checkbox" />Convert the order service to an Argo
Rollouts canary with a Prometheus error-rate analysis; deploy a
deliberately broken version and watch it abort</label></li>
<li><label><input type="checkbox" />Add a feature flag (OpenFeature with
a simple provider, or Unleash) around a new checkout step</label></li>
</ul>
<h2 id="hour-2-cloud-essentials-for-a-node-backend-aws">Hour 2 — Cloud
essentials for a Node backend (AWS)</h2>
<p>Most job descriptions at this level say “cloud experience”, and
interviewers probe it inside system design answers: where would this
run, how do uploads work, how is the database reached securely, what
would it cost? AWS is used here because it’s the most common in Indian
product companies; the table at the end maps everything to GCP and
Azure.</p>
<h3 id="compute-choosing-where-code-runs">2.1 Compute: choosing where
code runs</h3>
<table>
<colgroup>
<col style="width: 25%" />
<col style="width: 25%" />
<col style="width: 25%" />
<col style="width: 25%" />
</colgroup>
<thead>
<tr>
<th>Option</th>
<th>What you manage</th>
<th>Good for</th>
<th>Watch out</th>
</tr>
</thead>
<tbody>
<tr>
<td>EC2</td>
<td>VMs, OS, scaling groups</td>
<td>Full control, legacy, special workloads</td>
<td>Patching, more ops work</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td><strong>ECS on Fargate</strong></td>
<td>Containers + task definitions; no servers</td>
<td>Simple container platform without Kubernetes</td>
<td>Less ecosystem than Kubernetes, AWS-specific</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td><strong>EKS</strong></td>
<td>Kubernetes workloads (control plane managed)</td>
<td>Many services, portability, platform teams, Days 13–14</td>
<td>Most complex; needs Kubernetes skills</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td><strong>Lambda</strong></td>
<td>Functions only</td>
<td>Event-driven glue (S3 upload → thumbnail, SQS consumer, cron), spiky
low-volume APIs</td>
<td>15-minute max run time, cold starts, per-invocation pricing at high
volume, DB connection storms (use RDS Proxy)</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>App Runner / Elastic Beanstalk</td>
<td>Very little</td>
<td>Small apps, prototypes</td>
<td>Limited control</td>
</tr>
</tbody>
</table>
<p><strong>My framing:</strong> a growing product with several services:
ECS Fargate (simplest) or EKS (if the organisation has a platform team
or needs portability). Lambda for event handlers and scheduled jobs
around them. Monthly cost and team skills decide more than
technology.</p>
<p><strong>Serverless trade-offs worth saying:</strong> Lambda scales to
zero and from zero to thousands quickly, and you pay per use, which is
great for spiky or low traffic. For steady high traffic, containers are
usually cheaper. Each concurrent Lambda instance opens its own DB
connections, so a traffic spike can exhaust Postgres; RDS Proxy pools
them.</p>

bandwidth pressure), uploads scale with S3, and the server only issues
short-lived, scoped permissions.</p>
<h3 id="messaging">2.3 Messaging</h3>
<table>
<colgroup>
<col style="width: 33%" />

<p>The common pattern: <strong>SNS topic → one SQS queue per consuming
service</strong>, which is the managed equivalent of the RabbitMQ
pub/sub layout. SQS <strong>visibility timeout</strong> must be longer
than processing time, or the message reappears and is processed
twice.</p>
<h3 id="networking-and-security-basics">2.4 Networking and security
basics</h3>
<ul>
<li><strong>VPC</strong> with subnets across at least two or three
availability zones: <strong>public subnets</strong> for load balancers
(and NAT gateways), <strong>private subnets</strong> for services, and
isolated subnets for databases. Nothing but the load balancer needs a
public IP.</li>
<li><strong>Security groups:</strong> stateful firewalls on resources
(“DB accepts 5432 only from the app’s security group”). NACLs: stateless
subnet-level rules, rarely needed.</li>
<li><strong>ALB</strong> (layer 7: HTTP routing, host/path rules, TLS)
for APIs; <strong>NLB</strong> (layer 4: TCP, very high throughput,
static IPs) for gRPC/TCP or extreme scale.</li>
<li><strong>Route 53</strong> for DNS and health-checked failover;
<strong>ACM</strong> for free TLS certificates; <strong>WAF</strong> for
common attacks and rate limiting at the edge.</li>
<li><strong>IAM:</strong> roles for services (task roles, pod identity),
no long-lived access keys, least privilege per service, MFA and SSO for
humans. <strong>Secrets Manager / Parameter Store</strong> for secrets,
with rotation for DB passwords.</li>
<li><strong>VPC endpoints</strong> let private services reach S3 or
DynamoDB without going through a NAT gateway (cheaper and more
private).</li>
</ul>
<h3 id="cost-awareness-a-senior-signal">2.5 Cost awareness (a senior
signal)</h3>
<p>The usual surprises: NAT gateway data processing charges, cross-AZ
data transfer between chatty services, idle over-provisioned instances
and databases, unbounded CloudWatch logs retention, forgotten dev
environments, large Lambda memory settings. Habits: tag every resource
by team and service, set budgets and alerts, right-size with real
metrics, use Savings Plans or reserved capacity for steady load and Spot
for interruptible workloads.</p>

<h3 id="how-id-answer-hour-2-14">How I’d answer — Hour 2</h3>
<p><strong>Q1. How would you handle large file uploads?</strong> “The
API issues a short-lived presigned URL scoped to one key, and the
browser uploads directly to S3, so files never pass through our servers.
An S3 event triggers processing through SQS or Lambda: scanning,
thumbnails, metadata, and then the record is marked ready. For very
large files, multipart upload with presigned part URLs.”</p>
<p><strong>Q2. ECS, EKS or Lambda?</strong> “Lambda for event-driven
glue and spiky, low-volume work. For a set of long-running services, ECS
on Fargate if we want the simplest managed container platform, EKS if we
have Kubernetes skills, many services, or need portability and the
ecosystem. Steady high traffic is usually cheaper on containers than on
Lambda.”</p>
<p><strong>Q3. How do you secure database access in AWS?</strong> “The
database lives in private subnets with no public IP; its security group
only allows the application’s security group on the DB port. The app
authenticates with credentials from Secrets Manager, rotated
automatically, or IAM database authentication, and gets them through its
task or pod role rather than static keys. Encryption at rest and TLS in
transit are on, and backups use point-in-time recovery.”</p>
<p><strong>Q4. SQS Standard vs FIFO?</strong> “Standard gives nearly
unlimited throughput with at-least-once delivery and best-effort
ordering. FIFO guarantees order within a message group and deduplicates
within five minutes, at lower throughput. I use Standard with idempotent
consumers by default, and FIFO only where per-entity ordering matters
and volume allows.”</p>
<h3 id="practice-43">Practice</h3>
<ul class="task-list">
<li><label><input type="checkbox" />Implement presigned uploads for
product images (LocalStack or a real S3 bucket) with a processing
step</label></li>
<li><label><input type="checkbox" />Sketch the capstone’s AWS
architecture: VPC, subnets, ALB, EKS or ECS, RDS, Atlas, ElastiCache,
MSK or SQS/SNS, S3 + CloudFront</label></li>
<li><label><input type="checkbox" />Estimate its monthly cost roughly
with the AWS pricing calculator and list three ways to reduce
it</label></li>
</ul>
<h2 id="hour-3-observability-in-practice">Hour 3 — Observability in
practice</h2>
<p>Day 11 covered tracing and the three signals. Today is the practical
side a lead owns: what metrics to emit from Node, how logs flow, what to
alert on so on-call isn’t miserable, and how incidents are run and
learned from. “Tell me about a production incident you handled” is one
of the most common senior behavioural questions; this hour gives you the
vocabulary to tell it well.</p>
<h3 id="logs-from-pino-to-a-searchable-store">3.1 Logs: from
<code>pino</code> to a searchable store</h3>
<ul>
<li>Services log <strong>structured JSON to stdout</strong> (never to
files inside containers). Every line has: timestamp, level, service,
environment, version, request ID, trace ID, and an event name or
message.</li>
<li>A node-level agent (<strong>Fluent Bit</strong>, Vector, or the
OpenTelemetry Collector) collects container stdout and ships it to
<strong>Loki</strong>, <strong>Elasticsearch/OpenSearch</strong>,
CloudWatch, or Datadog.</li>
<li>Log levels mean something: <code>error</code> (someone may need to
act), <code>warn</code> (unexpected but handled), <code>info</code>
(business events and lifecycle), <code>debug</code> (off in production,
switchable at runtime).</li>
<li>Never log secrets, tokens, passwords, card numbers or full PII (pino
<code>redact</code>, Day 4). Logs are often retained and widely
readable.</li>
<li>Control volume and cost: no per-request debug logs in production,
sample noisy logs, set retention (e.g. 14–30 days hot, archive longer to
S3).</li>
</ul>
<h3 id="metrics-from-node-with-prometheus">3.2 Metrics from Node with
Prometheus</h3>

<span id="cb190-21"><a href="#cb190-21" aria-hidden="true" tabindex="-1"></a>  res<span class="op">.</span><span class="fu">type</span>(client<span class="op">.</span><span class="at">register</span><span class="op">.</span><span class="at">contentType</span>)<span class="op">.</span><span class="fu">send</span>(<span class="cf">await</span> client<span class="op">.</span><span class="at">register</span><span class="op">.</span><span class="fu">metrics</span>())<span class="op">;</span></span>
<span id="cb190-22"><a href="#cb190-22" aria-hidden="true" tabindex="-1"></a>})<span class="op">;</span></span></code></pre></div>
<p><strong>Cardinality is the trap:</strong> every unique combination of
label values is a separate time series. Labels like <code>userId</code>,
<code>orderId</code> or the raw URL (<code>/orders/8f3c...</code>)
create millions of series and can take down your metrics system. Use
bounded labels (route template, status code, method); put
high-cardinality detail in logs and traces.</p>
<p><strong>PromQL you should be able to write:</strong></p>
<pre class="text"><code># Request rate per route
sum by (route) (rate(http_request_duration_seconds_count[5m]))

# Error ratio (5xx share)
sum(rate(http_request_duration_seconds_count{status=~&quot;5..&quot;}[5m]))
  / sum(rate(http_request_duration_seconds_count[5m]))

# p99 latency per route
histogram_quantile(0.99, sum by (le, route) (rate(http_request_duration_seconds_bucket[5m])))</code></pre>
<p><strong>Histograms vs summaries:</strong> histograms can be
aggregated across pods (needed for p99 over a whole service); summaries
compute quantiles per process and can’t be meaningfully combined. Use
histograms.</p>
<h3 id="alerting-with-slos">3.3 Alerting with SLOs</h3>
<ul>
<li><strong>SLI</strong> (indicator): what you measure, e.g. the share
of checkout requests that succeed within 800 ms.</li>
<li><strong>SLO</strong> (objective): the target, e.g. 99.9% over 30
days.</li>
<li><strong>Error budget:</strong> what’s left to fail: 0.1% of
requests, about 43 minutes of full outage per 30 days. Spending it fast
means slow down releases; plenty left means ship faster.</li>
<li><strong>Burn-rate alerts:</strong> page when the budget is being
consumed fast enough to matter. Common multi-window setup: page if the
burn rate is above ~14× over both the last hour and the last 5 minutes
(a serious, current problem); open a ticket if it’s above ~6× over 6
hours (a slow leak).</li>
<li><strong>Page only on symptoms users feel</strong> (error rate,
latency, failed payments), not on causes like CPU at 80%. Cause metrics
go on dashboards for diagnosis.</li>
<li>Every alert links to a <strong>runbook</strong>: what it means, how
to check, how to mitigate.</li>
</ul>
<h3 id="error-tracking-and-dashboards">3.4 Error tracking and
dashboards</h3>
<ul>
<li><strong>Sentry</strong> (or similar) for exceptions in Node and the
browser: grouped errors, stack traces with source maps, release tracking
(which deploy introduced it), user impact counts. Complements logs;
doesn’t replace them.</li>
<li><strong>Dashboards per service</strong> with the same layout: RED
metrics at the top, saturation (event-loop delay, pool waits, memory,
consumer lag) below, dependencies, then business metrics. Annotate
deploys. A standard layout means anyone on call can read any service’s
dashboard.</li>
</ul>
<h3 id="incident-management-and-postmortems">3.5 Incident management and
postmortems</h3>
<p><strong>During an incident:</strong></p>
<ol type="1">
<li>Declare it and assign roles: <strong>incident commander</strong>
(coordinates, decides), operations lead (hands on keyboard),
communications (status page, stakeholders).</li>
<li>Severity by user impact (SEV1: checkout down for everyone; SEV3: a
minor feature degraded).</li>
<li><strong>Mitigate first, diagnose later:</strong> roll back the last
deploy, flip a feature flag, scale up, fail over, shed load. Restoring
service beats finding the root cause.</li>
<li>Keep a timeline in the incident channel as you go.</li>
</ol>
<p><strong>After:</strong> a <strong>blameless postmortem</strong>:
timeline, impact, root cause and contributing factors (often several: a
bug, a missing alert, a risky deploy process), what went well, and
<strong>action items with owners and dates</strong> that address the
system, not the person. Track them to completion; a postmortem without
done action items is a story, not an improvement.</p>
<h3 id="how-id-answer-hour-3-14">How I’d answer — Hour 3</h3>
<p><strong>Q1. What do you alert on?</strong> “Symptoms users feel,
defined as SLOs: error rate and latency for key journeys like checkout,
and business signals like payment success rate. I use burn-rate alerts
on the error budget, fast-burn to page and slow-burn to ticket, with
runbooks attached. Causes like CPU or memory go on dashboards, not
pagers, unless they reliably predict an outage, like disk filling or
consumer lag nearing retention.”</p>
<p><strong>Q2. What metrics does every Node service expose?</strong>
“RED metrics per route from a histogram, using route templates as labels
to keep cardinality bounded; default Node metrics for heap, GC and
event-loop lag; saturation like DB pool waits and consumer lag; and a
few business counters. Scraped by Prometheus, viewed on a standard
dashboard layout.”</p>
<p><strong>Q3. Tell me about an incident you handled.</strong>
(Structure, fill with your own story) “Situation and impact in one
sentence with numbers. How it was detected (alert or customer). What I
did first to mitigate, and how long until service was restored. How we
found the root cause. What we changed afterwards: the fix, the missing
alert or test, the process change. What I learned.” Prepare one story
from your fintech work in this shape before Day 19.</p>
<p><strong>Q4. Why are high-cardinality labels a problem?</strong> “Each
unique label combination is a separate time series, so labels like user
ID or raw URLs explode the number of series, slowing queries and
potentially crashing the metrics backend, plus the cost. Bounded labels
in metrics; per-request detail belongs in logs and traces.”</p>

<h2
id="hour-4-infrastructure-as-code-disaster-recovery-end-to-end-pipeline">Hour
4 — Infrastructure as code, disaster recovery, end-to-end pipeline</h2>
<p>The final hour of Week 3 ties everything together: infrastructure
defined in code and reviewed like application code, a disaster recovery
plan with real numbers, and the full path from a commit to a canary in
production for the capstone. Then the Week 3 self-check.</p>
<h3 id="infrastructure-as-code">4.1 Infrastructure as code</h3>
<p><strong>What it is:</strong> cloud resources (VPCs, clusters,
databases, queues, IAM) declared in code, versioned in git, reviewed in
PRs and applied by a pipeline, instead of being clicked together in a
console.</p>
<table>
<colgroup>
<col style="width: 33%" />

<col style="width: 33%" />
</colgroup>

<tr>
<th>Tool</th>

</tr>

<tbody>
<tr>
<td><strong>Terraform / OpenTofu</strong></td>
<td>Declarative HCL, multi-cloud</td>
<td>Most common; huge provider ecosystem; OpenTofu is the open-source
fork</td>

<td>AWS CDK / Pulumi</td>

<pre class="hcl"><code># Terraform: a private Postgres for the order service, using a shared module
module &quot;orders_db&quot; {
  source                  = &quot;../modules/postgres&quot;
  name                    = &quot;orders-${var.env}&quot;
  instance_class          = var.env == &quot;prod&quot; ? &quot;db.r6g.large&quot; : &quot;db.t4g.medium&quot;
  multi_az                = var.env == &quot;prod&quot;
  backup_retention_days   = var.env == &quot;prod&quot; ? 14 : 3
  subnet_ids              = module.vpc.database_subnet_ids
  allowed_security_groups = [module.eks.node_security_group_id]
  tags                    = { team = &quot;orders&quot;, service = &quot;order-service&quot;, env = var.env }
}</code></pre>
<p>Practices to mention: <strong>remote state</strong> with locking (an
S3 bucket with state locking, or Terraform Cloud), never local state for
shared infrastructure; <code>terraform plan</code> output posted on the
PR and reviewed; <code>apply</code> only from the pipeline; separate
state per environment and per component (network, data, apps) so one
mistake can’t destroy everything; reusable modules with sane defaults;
drift detection on a schedule; secrets never in <code>.tf</code> files
or state outputs in plain text.</p>
<h3 id="disaster-recovery">4.2 Disaster recovery</h3>
<ul>
<li><strong>RPO</strong> (recovery point objective): how much data you
can afford to lose, e.g. 5 minutes.</li>
<li><strong>RTO</strong> (recovery time objective): how long until
service is back, e.g. 1 hour.</li>
</ul>
<table>
<colgroup>
<col style="width: 25%" />
<col style="width: 25%" />
<col style="width: 25%" />
<col style="width: 25%" />
</colgroup>
<thead>
<tr>
<th>Strategy</th>
<th>RPO / RTO</th>
<th>Cost</th>
<th>How</th>
</tr>
</thead>
<tbody>
<tr>
<td>Backup and restore</td>
<td>Hours / hours</td>
<td>Lowest</td>
<td>Regular backups copied to another region; rebuild with IaC</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>Pilot light</td>
<td>Minutes / tens of minutes</td>
<td>Low</td>
<td>Data replicated to a second region; minimal core running; scale up
on disaster</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>Warm standby</td>
<td>Seconds-minutes / minutes</td>
<td>Medium</td>
<td>Scaled-down full copy running in a second region</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>Active-active (multi-region)</td>
<td>Near zero / near zero</td>
<td>Highest</td>
<td>Both regions serve traffic; hard data consistency problems (Day 8
CAP)</td>
</tr>
</tbody>
</table>
<p>What a senior says beyond the table: most outages are
<strong>within</strong> a region (a bad deploy, a dependency, a zone),
so multi-AZ, good rollbacks and backups cover far more real incidents
than multi-region; choose the strategy per system based on business
impact (payments vs reporting); and <strong>test restores and
failovers</strong> regularly, since untested backups and runbooks fail
when needed. Point-in-time recovery for databases, versioning plus
cross-region replication for critical S3 buckets, and IaC so
environments can be recreated.</p>
<h3 id="the-capstone-end-to-end">4.3 The capstone, end to end</h3>
<p>The full path from commit to production, combining Weeks 1–3:</p>
<ol type="1">
<li>Developer opens a small PR; CI runs affected lint, typecheck, unit,
Testcontainers integration tests, OpenAPI diff, audit (Day 5).</li>
<li>Merge to main: one multi-arch image per affected service, tagged
with the git SHA, cached, scanned with Trivy, SBOM attached, signed,
pushed to GHCR (Day 13).</li>
<li>Pipeline commits the new tag to the GitOps repo for staging; Argo CD
syncs the shared Helm chart (Day 14); a pre-sync Job runs
backward-compatible migrations.</li>
<li>Smoke and contract tests run against staging; dashboards annotate
the deploy.</li>
<li>Promotion PR to production; Argo Rollouts canary at 10% → 50% → 100%
with Prometheus analysis on error rate and p99; automatic abort on
regression (Hour 1).</li>
<li>New features stay behind flags until released gradually.</li>
<li>Observability throughout: traces (Day 11), RED metrics and SLO burn
alerts (Hour 3), logs with trace IDs, Sentry releases.</li>
<li>Infrastructure for all of it (VPC, cluster, databases, brokers,
buckets) defined in Terraform and changed only through reviewed
PRs.</li>
</ol>
<p>Be able to draw this on a whiteboard in 5 minutes; it’s a strong
answer to “how do you ship software?” for a lead role.</p>
<h3 id="how-id-answer-hour-4-14">How I’d answer — Hour 4</h3>
<p><strong>Q1. How do you manage infrastructure?</strong> “As code in
Terraform, in git, with reusable modules. Every change is a PR with the
plan output attached and reviewed, and only the pipeline applies it,
using remote state with locking. State is split per environment and per
layer, and scheduled drift detection catches manual changes.”</p>
<p><strong>Q2. What’s your disaster recovery approach?</strong> “Start
from RPO and RTO per system, agreed with the business. For most
services: multi-AZ databases with point-in-time recovery, backups copied
to another region, infrastructure reproducible from code, and tested
restore drills. For the most critical flows, a warm standby in a second
region. Active-active only when the business case justifies the
consistency complexity.”</p>
<p><strong>Q3. Walk me through how code gets to production in your ideal
setup.</strong> Use 4.3 as the outline, about two minutes, ending with
“and we track DORA metrics to see whether it’s getting faster and
safer.”</p>

<h1 id="day-16-mon-system-design-framework-and-classic-problems">Day 16
(Mon) — System design framework and classic problems</h1>
<h2 id="hour-1-the-system-design-framework">Hour 1 — The system design
framework</h2>
<p>System design rounds are judged less on the final diagram than on how
you get there: clarifying before drawing, quantifying, making explicit
trade-offs, and going deep where it matters. You already have the parts
from Weeks 1–3. This hour gives you the structure and the numbers so
every design round follows the same reliable path.</p>
<h3 id="the-35-minute-structure">1.1 The 35-minute structure</h3>
<table>
<colgroup>
<col style="width: 33%" />
<col style="width: 33%" />
<col style="width: 33%" />
</colgroup>
<thead>
<tr>
<th>Time</th>
<th>Step</th>
<th>What you produce</th>
</tr>
</thead>
<tbody>
<tr>
<td>0–5 min</td>
<td><strong>Requirements</strong></td>
<td>Functional (3–5 core features, explicitly out-of-scope items),
non-functional (scale, latency, availability, consistency, durability,
security)</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>5–10 min</td>
<td><strong>Estimates</strong></td>
<td>Users, requests per second (average and peak), read/write ratio,
storage per year, bandwidth</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>10–15 min</td>
<td><strong>API and data model</strong></td>
<td>Key endpoints or events; core entities and storage choice</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>15–25 min</td>
<td><strong>High-level design</strong></td>
<td>Boxes and arrows: clients, CDN, load balancer, services, caches,
databases, queues</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>25–32 min</td>
<td><strong>Deep dives</strong></td>
<td>2–3 hardest parts, usually the ones the interviewer steers toward:
scaling the hot path, consistency, failure handling</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>32–35 min</td>
<td><strong>Wrap-up</strong></td>
<td>Bottlenecks, trade-offs made, what you’d do at 10×, monitoring</td>
</tr>
</tbody>
</table>
<p>Habits that score well: ask questions before drawing; write
requirements and numbers where the interviewer can see them; state
assumptions out loud (“I’ll assume 10 million daily users”); name the
trade-off whenever you make a choice; check in (“I’d like to go deeper
on the feed generation. Is that the most interesting part for you?”);
and keep the design as simple as the requirements allow.</p>
<h3 id="back-of-envelope-numbers">1.2 Back-of-envelope numbers</h3>
<p><strong>Time conversions:</strong></p>
<ul>
<li>1 day ≈ 86,400 s ≈ <strong>10⁵ s</strong> (use this for quick
maths)</li>
<li>1 million requests/day ≈ <strong>12 per second</strong>; 100
million/day ≈ 1,200/s</li>
<li>Peak is typically <strong>2–5× average</strong> (sale days can be
far higher)</li>
</ul>
<p><strong>Sizes:</strong></p>
<ul>
<li>A tweet-like text record with metadata: ~1 KB; a typical JSON API
response: 1–10 KB; a compressed image: 200 KB–2 MB; a minute of
compressed video: ~5–10 MB</li>
<li>1 million × 1 KB = 1 GB; 1 billion × 1 KB = 1 TB</li>
</ul>
<p><strong>Latency, roughly (orders of magnitude matter, not exact
values):</strong></p>
<table>
<thead>
<tr>
<th>Operation</th>
<th>Approximate time</th>
</tr>
</thead>
<tbody>
<tr>
<td>Main memory reference</td>
<td>~100 ns</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>Read 1 MB sequentially from memory</td>
<td>~10–100 µs</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>SSD random read</td>
<td>~100 µs</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>Round trip within a data centre</td>
<td>~0.5 ms</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>Redis GET over the network</td>
<td>~0.5–1 ms</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>Indexed DB query in the same region</td>
<td>~1–10 ms</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>Round trip Mumbai ↔︎ Singapore</td>
<td>~50–70 ms</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>Round trip India ↔︎ US East</td>
<td>~200–250 ms</td>
</tr>
</tbody>
</table>
<p>Conclusions to draw out loud: memory is far faster than network,
which is far faster than cross-region; avoid sequential cross-region
calls in a request; caching and data locality are the biggest
levers.</p>
<p><strong>Worked example:</strong> 50 million daily active users, each
makes 20 reads and 2 writes a day. Reads: 10⁹/day ≈ 11,500/s average,
~35,000/s peak. Writes: 10⁸/day ≈ 1,150/s average, ~3,500/s peak. Each
write stores 2 KB: 200 GB/day ≈ 73 TB/year before replication.
Conclusion: read-heavy, so cache aggressively; storage grows fast enough
to plan partitioning and archiving from day one.</p>
<p><strong>Rough capacity of single components</strong> (order of
magnitude, varies hugely with workload; always say “I’d load-test”):</p>
<table>
<colgroup>
<col style="width: 50%" />
<col style="width: 50%" />
</colgroup>
<thead>
<tr>
<th>Component</th>
<th>Ballpark</th>
</tr>
</thead>
<tbody>
<tr>
<td>One Node.js instance, simple I/O-bound API</td>
<td>1,000–5,000 req/s</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>One Postgres primary on good hardware</td>
<td>Thousands to tens of thousands of simple queries/s</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>One Redis node</td>
<td>~100,000+ simple ops/s</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>One Kafka broker</td>
<td>Hundreds of MB/s</td>
</tr>
</tbody>
</table>

<h3 id="non-functional-requirements-as-questions">1.4 Non-functional
requirements as questions</h3>
<ul>
<li><strong>Scale:</strong> how many users, requests, data? Growth
rate?</li>
<li><strong>Latency:</strong> p99 target for the main flow?</li>
<li><strong>Availability:</strong> 99.9% (43 min/month down) or 99.99%
(4.3 min/month)? Each nine costs a lot more.</li>
<li><strong>Consistency:</strong> can users see stale data? Where must
it be strong (money, inventory)?</li>
<li><strong>Durability:</strong> can we ever lose a write?</li>
<li><strong>Security and compliance:</strong> PII, payments (PCI), data
residency (India’s DPDP Act)?</li>
<li><strong>Cost and team:</strong> budget, team size, existing stack.
Real designs are constrained by these.</li>
</ul>
<h3 id="how-id-answer-hour-1-15">How I’d answer — Hour 1</h3>
<p><strong>Q1. How do you approach a system design question?</strong>
“Clarify functional and non-functional requirements first, then estimate
the load so the design has numbers behind it. Then the API and data
model, a simple high-level design, and deep dives into the two or three
hardest parts, usually scaling the hot path, consistency and failure
handling. I state assumptions and trade-offs as I go and finish with
bottlenecks and what changes at 10×.”</p>
<p><strong>Q2. Estimate the QPS for 50 million daily users.</strong>
Work through the example in 1.2 out loud, ending with the conclusion it
leads to (read-heavy → caching; storage growth → partitioning).</p>
<h3 id="practice-45">Practice</h3>
<ul class="task-list">
<li><label><input type="checkbox" />Memorise the time and size
conversions; do three estimates in under 3 minutes each (a social app, a
food delivery app, a payment gateway)</label></li>
<li><label><input type="checkbox" />Write the 35-minute structure on one
index card and use it for every design this week</label></li>
<li><label><input type="checkbox" />Record yourself doing only the
requirements and estimates for “design YouTube” in 8 minutes;
review</label></li>
</ul>
<h2 id="hour-2-design-a-url-shortener">Hour 2 — Design a URL
shortener</h2>
<p>The URL shortener is the most common warm-up design question, and
because it’s familiar, interviewers judge it on depth: how you generate
unique short keys at scale, 301 vs 302, how you handle a link that goes
viral, and how analytics stays off the hot path. Work through it once on
paper with the framework, then compare.</p>
<h3 id="requirements">2.1 Requirements</h3>
<p><strong>Functional:</strong> create a short link for a long URL
(optional custom alias, optional expiry); redirect a short link to the
original; basic click analytics per link. Out of scope: user accounts
management, editing links.</p>
<p><strong>Non-functional:</strong> redirects must be very fast (p99
under ~50 ms server-side) and highly available (99.99%: a broken
redirect breaks every page that used the link); short keys unpredictable
enough not to be enumerated; creation can be slightly slower; analytics
can be minutes behind.</p>
<h3 id="estimates">2.2 Estimates</h3>
<ul>
<li>100 million new links/month → ~40 writes/s average, peak
~200/s.</li>
<li>Read:write ≈ 100:1 → ~4,000 redirects/s average, peak ~20,000/s
(viral links much higher, but on few keys).</li>
<li>Each record ~500 bytes → 50 GB/month → ~600 GB/year, ~3 TB over 5
years before replication.</li>
<li><strong>Key space:</strong> base62 (<code>a–z</code>,
<code>A–Z</code>, <code>0–9</code>) with 7 characters = 62⁷ ≈ 3.5
trillion keys, far more than the ~6 billion needed for 5 years.</li>
</ul>
<p>Conclusion: tiny write load, heavy and very skewed read load, modest
storage. The design is about fast reads and key generation.</p>
<h3 id="api">2.3 API</h3>
<pre class="text"><code>POST /v1/links           { &quot;url&quot;: &quot;https://...&quot;, &quot;alias&quot;?: &quot;diwali-sale&quot;, &quot;expiresAt&quot;?: &quot;...&quot; }
                         -&gt; 201 { &quot;code&quot;: &quot;aZ3x9Qk&quot;, &quot;shortUrl&quot;: &quot;https://sho.rt/aZ3x9Qk&quot; }
GET  /{code}             -&gt; 302 Location: https://original...   (or 404 / 410 if expired)
GET  /v1/links/{code}/stats -&gt; clicks by day, country, referrer</code></pre>
<h3 id="generating-short-keys">2.4 Generating short keys</h3>
<table>
<colgroup>
<col style="width: 25%" />
<col style="width: 25%" />
<col style="width: 25%" />
<col style="width: 25%" />
</colgroup>
<thead>
<tr>
<th>Approach</th>
<th>How</th>
<th>Good</th>
<th>Problems</th>
</tr>
</thead>
<tbody>
<tr>
<td>Hash the URL</td>
<td><code>base62(md5(url))[0..7]</code></td>
<td>Same URL gives same code (dedup)</td>
<td>Collisions: must check and retry with salt; dedup often not wanted
(different users, different stats)</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>Counter + base62</td>
<td>Global incrementing ID encoded in base62</td>
<td>No collisions, short</td>
<td>Single counter is a bottleneck/SPOF; codes are <strong>sequential
and guessable</strong></td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td><strong>Range allocation (key generation service)</strong></td>
<td>A coordinator hands each app server a block of IDs (e.g. 1,000,000
at a time); servers encode locally; optionally shuffle/permute the ID
before encoding</td>
<td>No coordination per request, no collisions, scales horizontally</td>
<td>Lost unused ranges on restart (fine, key space is huge)</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>Snowflake-style IDs</td>
<td>Timestamp + machine ID + sequence</td>
<td>Distributed, sortable</td>
<td>Longer codes (64-bit → ~11 base62 chars)</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>Random + check</td>
<td>Random 7 chars, insert with unique constraint, retry on
conflict</td>
<td>Simple, unpredictable</td>
<td>Retries grow as space fills (negligible at this scale)</td>
</tr>
</tbody>
</table>
<p><strong>My choice:</strong> range allocation with a bijective
scramble (e.g. a keyed permutation) of the ID before base62 encoding, so
codes are unique without collision checks and not guessable in sequence.
“Random + unique constraint” is also a perfectly defensible simple
answer at this scale. Custom aliases go through the same unique
constraint.</p>
<h3 id="data-model-and-storage">2.5 Data model and storage</h3>
<pre class="text"><code>links(code PK, long_url, owner_id, created_at, expires_at, is_active)</code></pre>
<p>Access is pure key-value by <code>code</code>, so a key-value or
wide-column store (DynamoDB, Cassandra) fits naturally and scales
horizontally; Postgres also works fine at 3 TB with the code as primary
key and partitioning or sharding by hash of code later. Expired links:
TTL in DynamoDB, or a periodic cleanup job.</p>
<h3 id="high-level-design">2.6 High-level design</h3>
<pre class="text"><code>Client -&gt; CDN/edge (caches hot redirects) -&gt; Load balancer -&gt; Redirect service -&gt; Redis cache -&gt; Links DB
                                                       \-&gt; publish click event -&gt; Kafka -&gt; analytics consumers -&gt; ClickHouse
Client -&gt; API gateway (auth, rate limit) -&gt; Link service (key ranges from KGS) -&gt; Links DB</code></pre>
<p><strong>Redirect path (the hot path):</strong> look up
<code>code</code> in Redis (cache-aside, LRU eviction; the distribution
is very skewed, so a small cache serves most traffic); on miss read the
DB and populate; return the redirect; publish a click event
asynchronously (non-blocking, fire into a buffer or Kafka producer). The
redirect never waits on analytics.</p>
<p><strong>301 vs 302:</strong> 301 (permanent) lets browsers and
proxies cache the redirect, reducing load but hiding subsequent clicks
from analytics and making later changes impossible. 302/307 (temporary)
sends every click through you. With analytics as a requirement: 302,
plus short CDN caching for viral links if load demands it.</p>
<h3 id="deep-dives">2.7 Deep dives</h3>
<ul>
<li><strong>Viral link (hot key):</strong> CDN or edge caching for a few
seconds, in-process LRU cache in each redirect instance in front of
Redis, and Redis replicas for reads. Thousands of requests per second
for one key never reach the database.</li>
<li><strong>Analytics at scale:</strong> click events to Kafka keyed by
code; consumers aggregate per minute and write to a columnar store
(ClickHouse, BigQuery); dashboards read aggregates. Don’t increment a
counter row per click in the main database (hot-row contention).</li>
<li><strong>Abuse:</strong> rate-limit link creation per user/IP; check
target URLs against malware/phishing lists (Google Safe Browsing)
asynchronously and disable bad links; never allow
<code>javascript:</code> URLs; consider interstitial warnings.</li>
<li><strong>Availability:</strong> redirect service is stateless and
multi-AZ; Redis with replicas; DB multi-AZ; if the DB is down, cached
links still work. Multi-region read replicas for a global audience.</li>
</ul>
<h3 id="how-id-answer-hour-2-15">How I’d answer — Hour 2</h3>
<p><strong>Q1. How do you generate unique short codes?</strong> “Each
link-service instance gets a block of numeric IDs from a small
key-generation service, scrambles each ID with a keyed permutation so
codes aren’t sequential, and base62-encodes it to 7 characters, giving
3.5 trillion possible codes. No per-request coordination and no
collisions. Custom aliases use the same unique key and fail with 409 if
taken.”</p>
<p><strong>Q2. 301 or 302?</strong> “302, because we need every click
for analytics and may want to disable or change links; 301 would be
cached by browsers. If load is a problem, I cache at the CDN for a short
time instead.”</p>
<p><strong>Q3. One link gets 200,000 clicks a minute. What
happens?</strong> “It’s one hot key. It’s served from the CDN for a few
seconds and from an in-process cache in each redirect instance, so
almost nothing reaches Redis, and nothing reaches the database. Click
events are aggregated asynchronously through Kafka, so analytics doesn’t
create hot-row contention.”</p>
<h3 id="practice-46">Practice</h3>
<ul class="task-list">
<li><label><input type="checkbox" />Do this design on paper in 35
minutes without notes, then compare</label></li>
<li><label><input type="checkbox" />Implement base62 encoding and a
keyed permutation of IDs in TypeScript</label></li>
<li><label><input type="checkbox" />Write the redirect handler with a
two-level cache (in-process LRU + Redis) and async click
publishing</label></li>
</ul>
<h2 id="hour-3-distributed-rate-limiter-real-time-transport">Hour 3 —
Distributed rate limiter + real-time transport</h2>
<p>Two shorter designs that appear constantly, both on their own and as
components of bigger ones. Day 4 covered the algorithms in a single
process; here the questions are where the limiter lives, how it stays
accurate across 50 instances, and what happens when Redis is down. The
second half covers how servers push data to clients, which you need for
the chat design in Hour 4.</p>
<h3 id="rate-limiter-requirements">3.1 Rate limiter: requirements</h3>
<ul>
<li>Limit requests per client (API key, user, or IP) per rule:
e.g. 100/min for free tier, 1,000/min for paid, 5 login attempts/15 min
per account.</li>
<li>Accurate enough across all instances (not per instance).</li>
<li>Adds very little latency (a few ms at most).</li>
<li>Clear responses: <code>429</code> with <code>Retry-After</code> and
remaining-quota headers.</li>
<li>Highly available: the limiter failing must not take the API
down.</li>
</ul>
<h3 id="where-it-runs">3.2 Where it runs</h3>
<table>
<colgroup>
<col style="width: 33%" />
<col style="width: 33%" />
<col style="width: 33%" />
</colgroup>
<thead>
<tr>
<th>Placement</th>
<th>Good</th>
<th>Trade-off</th>
</tr>
</thead>
<tbody>
<tr>
<td>Edge / WAF / CDN</td>
<td>Stops abuse before it reaches you; IP-based floods</td>
<td>Coarse; doesn’t know users or plans</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td><strong>API gateway</strong></td>
<td>One place for all services; knows API keys</td>
<td>Gateway must call a shared store</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>Service middleware</td>
<td>Rules that need business context (per tenant, per endpoint
cost)</td>
<td>Every service implements it (use a shared library)</td>
</tr>
</tbody>
</table>
<p>Usually layered: coarse IP limits at the edge, per-key/plan limits at
the gateway, a few business limits in services.</p>
<h3 id="shared-state-in-redis-atomically">3.3 Shared state in Redis,
atomically</h3>
<p>Per-instance counters multiply the real limit by the number of
instances (Day 4). Use one Redis (cluster) as the shared store, and do
read-modify-write <strong>atomically</strong> in a Lua script so
concurrent requests can’t both pass:</p>

<span id="cb196-10"><a href="#cb196-10" aria-hidden="true" tabindex="-1"></a><span class="va">tokens</span> <span class="op">=</span> <span class="fu">math.min</span><span class="op">(</span><span class="va">capacity</span><span class="op">,</span> <span class="va">tokens</span> <span class="op">+</span> <span class="op">(</span><span class="va">now</span> <span class="op">-</span> <span class="va">ts</span><span class="op">)</span> <span class="op">*</span> <span class="va">rate</span><span class="op">)</span></span>
<span id="cb196-11"><a href="#cb196-11" aria-hidden="true" tabindex="-1"></a><span class="kw">local</span> <span class="va">allowed</span> <span class="op">=</span> <span class="dv">0</span></span>
<span id="cb196-12"><a href="#cb196-12" aria-hidden="true" tabindex="-1"></a><span class="cf">if</span> <span class="va">tokens</span> <span class="op">&gt;=</span> <span class="va">cost</span> <span class="cf">then</span> <span class="va">tokens</span> <span class="op">=</span> <span class="va">tokens</span> <span class="op">-</span> <span class="va">cost</span><span class="op">;</span> <span class="va">allowed</span> <span class="op">=</span> <span class="dv">1</span> <span class="cf">end</span></span>
<span id="cb196-13"><a href="#cb196-13" aria-hidden="true" tabindex="-1"></a><span class="va">redis</span><span class="op">.</span>call<span class="op">(</span><span class="st">&#39;HSET&#39;</span><span class="op">,</span> <span class="cn">KEYS</span><span class="op">[</span><span class="dv">1</span><span class="op">],</span> <span class="st">&#39;tokens&#39;</span><span class="op">,</span> <span class="va">tokens</span><span class="op">,</span> <span class="st">&#39;ts&#39;</span><span class="op">,</span> <span class="va">now</span><span class="op">)</span></span>
<span id="cb196-14"><a href="#cb196-14" aria-hidden="true" tabindex="-1"></a><span class="va">redis</span><span class="op">.</span>call<span class="op">(</span><span class="st">&#39;EXPIRE&#39;</span><span class="op">,</span> <span class="cn">KEYS</span><span class="op">[</span><span class="dv">1</span><span class="op">],</span> <span class="fu">math.ceil</span><span class="op">(</span><span class="va">capacity</span> <span class="op">/</span> <span class="va">rate</span><span class="op">)</span> <span class="op">*</span> <span class="dv">2</span><span class="op">)</span> <span class="co">-- idle buckets disappear</span></span>
<span id="cb196-15"><a href="#cb196-15" aria-hidden="true" tabindex="-1"></a><span class="cf">return</span> <span class="op">{</span> <span class="va">allowed</span><span class="op">,</span> <span class="fu">math.floor</span><span class="op">(</span><span class="va">tokens</span><span class="op">)</span> <span class="op">}</span></span></code></pre></div>
<p>The gateway calls it with <code>EVALSHA</code> (script cached on the
server), keyed like <code>rl:{apiKey}:orders-write</code>. The braces
are a Redis Cluster hash tag (Day 8) so related keys stay on one slot.
Sliding-window counters (two fixed windows weighted) are an equally good
choice and slightly cheaper.</p>
<h3 id="deep-dives-1">3.4 Deep dives</h3>
<ul>
<li><strong>Rules configuration:</strong> stored centrally (DB or config
service), cached in each gateway instance, hot-reloadable:
<code>{ match: { plan: 'free', route: 'POST /orders' }, limit: 100, window: '1m' }</code>.</li>
<li><strong>Redis is down: fail open or closed?</strong> Usually
<strong>fail open</strong> (allow traffic, log, alert) because the
limiter shouldn’t cause an outage, combined with a local in-memory
fallback limit per instance as a rough safety net. Fail closed only for
security-critical limits like login attempts.</li>
<li><strong>Latency:</strong> one Redis round trip (~1 ms in-region).
For very high volume, keep a small local token allowance per instance
and sync with Redis in batches, trading a little accuracy for
latency.</li>
<li><strong>Multi-region:</strong> a global exact limit needs
cross-region coordination (slow). Usually limits are enforced per
region, with the global limit split across regions, accepting
approximate fairness.</li>
<li><strong>Hot keys:</strong> one huge customer hammering one bucket:
shard that key’s bucket, or give big tenants dedicated limits.</li>
</ul>
<h3 id="real-time-how-servers-push-to-clients">3.5 Real-time: how
servers push to clients</h3>
<table>
<colgroup>
<col style="width: 25%" />
<col style="width: 25%" />
<col style="width: 25%" />
<col style="width: 25%" />
</colgroup>
<thead>
<tr>
<th>Technique</th>
<th>How</th>
<th>Good</th>
<th>Weak</th>
</tr>
</thead>
<tbody>
<tr>
<td>Short polling</td>
<td>Client asks every N seconds</td>
<td>Trivial, works everywhere</td>
<td>Wasteful, delayed</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>Long polling</td>
<td>Request held open until data or timeout, then re-sent</td>
<td>Works through any proxy</td>
<td>Overhead per message, awkward at scale</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td><strong>Server-Sent Events (SSE)</strong></td>
<td>One long HTTP response streaming events, server → client only</td>
<td>Simple, plain HTTP, auto-reconnect with <code>Last-Event-ID</code>,
works with HTTP/2</td>
<td>One direction only; text only</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td><strong>WebSockets</strong></td>
<td>Upgraded persistent TCP connection, both directions</td>
<td>Low latency, bidirectional, binary</td>
<td>Stateful connections to manage; proxies and LBs need
configuration</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>WebTransport (HTTP/3)</td>
<td>Newer, multiplexed, unreliable datagrams possible</td>
<td>Games, media</td>
<td>Browser and infrastructure support still maturing</td>
</tr>
</tbody>
</table>
<p><strong>Rule of thumb:</strong> notifications, live scores, order
status, dashboards, streaming LLM responses: <strong>SSE</strong>. Chat,
collaborative editing, multiplayer: <strong>WebSockets</strong>. Polling
only when updates are rare and simplicity wins.</p>
<h3 id="scaling-websocket-servers">3.6 Scaling WebSocket servers</h3>
<ul>
<li>Connections are <strong>stateful</strong>: a user is connected to
one specific server. To send a message to user B, you must find B’s
server. Common approach: each server subscribes to a pub/sub channel
(Redis pub/sub, NATS, or Kafka) and keeps a local map of its
connections; or a <strong>connection registry</strong> (user → server)
in Redis and direct routing. Socket.IO’s Redis adapter implements the
first.</li>
<li><strong>Capacity:</strong> a well-tuned Node process can hold tens
of thousands of mostly idle connections (with <code>ws</code> or
uWebSockets.js); memory per connection and message rate are the real
limits. Raise file descriptor limits.</li>
<li><strong>Load balancers:</strong> must support WebSocket upgrade and
long idle timeouts (or send heartbeats/pings every ~30 s to keep
connections alive and detect dead ones).</li>
<li><strong>Deploys and failures</strong> drop connections: clients
reconnect with exponential backoff and jitter (avoid a thundering herd
after a deploy), then resync missed data using a cursor or last-seen
message ID.</li>
<li><strong>Authentication:</strong> validate the token during the
upgrade handshake, re-check on expiry; don’t trust user IDs sent in
messages.</li>
</ul>
<h3 id="how-id-answer-hour-3-15">How I’d answer — Hour 3</h3>
<p><strong>Q1. Design a rate limiter for an API with 50 gateway
instances.</strong> “Limits at the gateway, keyed by API key and rule,
with shared state in a Redis cluster. Each check is one atomic Lua
script implementing a token bucket using Redis server time, returning
allowed and remaining tokens, so it’s accurate across instances at about
1 ms of added latency. Rules are config, cached and hot-reloaded.
Responses include 429 with Retry-After. If Redis fails we fail open with
a local fallback limit and alert, except for login limits, which fail
closed. Coarse IP limits sit at the edge in front of all this.”</p>
<p><strong>Q2. WebSockets or SSE?</strong> “SSE when the server pushes
and the client only listens, like order status, notifications or
streaming AI responses: plain HTTP, automatic reconnect, simple to
scale. WebSockets when both sides send frequently, like chat or
collaborative editing.”</p>
<p><strong>Q3. How do you send a message to a user connected to a
different WebSocket server?</strong> “Either every server subscribes to
a pub/sub channel and delivers to its local connections, or a registry
in Redis maps each user to their server and we route directly. At large
scale the registry with direct routing is more efficient than
broadcasting every message to every server.”</p>

<li><label><input type="checkbox" />Stream order status to the
