<p>They complement each other: completions for flow while typing, an
agent for multi-step tasks, chat for design.</p>
<h3 id="claude-code-features-worth-knowing">4.2 Claude Code features
worth knowing</h3>
<ul>
<li><strong><code>CLAUDE.md</code></strong> files: project memory loaded
every session (commands, architecture, conventions, “never do X”). Keep
it short and specific; it’s the highest-leverage setup step (Day
1).</li>
<li><strong>Plan first:</strong> ask for (or use plan mode for) a plan
before edits on anything non-trivial; review and adjust the plan, then
let it implement.</li>
<li><strong>Custom slash commands:</strong> repeatable prompts checked
into the repo (e.g. <code>/new-endpoint</code>,
<code>/write-tests</code>).</li>
<li><strong>Subagents:</strong> specialised helpers with their own
context and instructions (a reviewer, a test writer) that keep the main
context clean.</li>
<li><strong>Hooks:</strong> commands that run automatically at points in
the workflow (e.g. run the formatter or linter after every edit, block
edits to certain paths).</li>
<li><strong>Skills:</strong> folders of instructions and scripts for
specific kinds of work, loaded when relevant (e.g. your team’s API
conventions or a release checklist).</li>
<li><strong>MCP servers:</strong> give it access to tools like your
issue tracker, docs, or a read-only staging database (Hour 2).</li>
<li><strong>Permissions:</strong> control which commands and edits it
may run without asking; keep approval on for anything destructive.</li>
<li><strong>Headless / CI use:</strong> run non-interactively in
pipelines or GitHub Actions for tasks like triaging issues or proposing
fixes, with review gates.</li>
</ul>
<h3 id="a-workflow-that-keeps-quality-high">4.3 A workflow that keeps
quality high</h3>
<ol type="1">
<li><strong>Write the spec yourself:</strong> the problem, acceptance
criteria, constraints, the API contract, edge cases. The quality of the
spec sets the ceiling on the output.</li>
<li><strong>Ask for a plan,</strong> review it like a design review:
files touched, approach, risks. Correct the approach before any code is
written.</li>
<li><strong>Implement in small steps,</strong> each ending with tests
passing and a commit. Small diffs are reviewable; a 2,000-line AI diff
isn’t.</li>
<li><strong>Tests as the contract:</strong> write or review the tests
first for critical logic; let the agent iterate until they pass, then
check the tests actually test behaviour (Day 5).</li>
<li><strong>Review every line like a PR from a new hire:</strong>
correctness, edge cases, security, performance, consistency with the
codebase, and whether it’s needed at all (AI tends to over-build).</li>
<li><strong>Run the full gate:</strong> lint, types, tests, security
scan, as for any code.</li>
<li><strong>Feed lessons back</strong> into <code>CLAUDE.md</code>,
commands and skills, so the same mistake isn’t corrected twice.</li>
</ol>
<p><strong>Where AI shines:</strong> boilerplate and scaffolding, tests,
migrations between libraries, explaining unfamiliar code, writing
scripts, first drafts of docs, debugging with logs and stack traces.
<strong>Where I keep tight control:</strong> core domain logic,
security-sensitive code (auth, payments), concurrency, data migrations
on production data, architecture decisions.</p>
<h3 id="risks-of-ai-generated-code">4.4 Risks of AI-generated code</h3>
<ul>
<li><strong>Plausible but wrong:</strong> compiles and reads well but
mishandles edge cases, time zones, money, concurrency.</li>
<li><strong>Security issues:</strong> injection, missing authorisation
checks, secrets in code, insecure defaults, overly permissive CORS.</li>
<li><strong>Hallucinated or typo-squatted dependencies:</strong> a
suggested package that doesn’t exist can be registered by an attacker
(“slopsquatting”). Verify every new dependency.</li>
<li><strong>Inconsistency:</strong> new patterns that don’t match the
codebase; mitigated by <code>CLAUDE.md</code>, examples and review.</li>
<li><strong>Licence and data concerns:</strong> follow company policy on
which tools may see which code; use enterprise plans with appropriate
data handling.</li>
<li><strong>Skill atrophy and over-trust:</strong> juniors accepting
code they don’t understand. Reviews must ask “explain why this
works”.</li>
</ul>
<h3 id="measuring-impact-and-leading-adoption">4.5 Measuring impact and
leading adoption</h3>
<p><strong>Measure outcomes, not output:</strong> lines of code and “%
of code written by AI” are vanity metrics. Look at lead time and cycle
time, PR review time, deployment frequency and change failure rate
(DORA, Day 15), escaped defects, and developer experience surveys.
Compare teams or periods honestly; perceived speed-ups and measured ones
can differ.</p>
<p><strong>Rolling it out to a team:</strong></p>
<ul>
<li>Clear guidelines: what’s allowed, which data the tools may see,
review requirements (AI-written code gets the same review bar, author
owns it).</li>
<li>Shared setup: a repo <code>CLAUDE.md</code>, custom commands, skills
for team conventions, MCP servers for internal tools.</li>
<li>Enablement: demos of real workflows, pairing sessions, a channel for
tips, champions per team.</li>
<li>Guardrails in CI rather than trust: tests, lint, type checks,
security scans, dependency review.</li>
<li>Iterate: retrospectives on what works; update shared
instructions.</li>
</ul>
<h3 id="your-story-prepare-this">4.6 Your story (prepare this)</h3>
<p>Interviewers will ask “how do you use AI in your development work?”
Prepare a 2–3 minute answer with one concrete example from this month’s
capstone, for instance: “I built the order service’s outbox and saga
with Claude Code. I wrote the spec and acceptance tests, reviewed its
plan and changed the retry approach, then let it implement in four
steps. It saved roughly X hours on boilerplate and tests. Two things I
corrected: it initially published events outside the transaction, which
would have broken consistency, and it added a dependency we didn’t need.
I added both lessons to CLAUDE.md.” Real numbers and real corrections
make it credible.</p>
<h3 id="how-id-answer-hour-4-17">How I’d answer — Hour 4</h3>
<p><strong>Q1. How do you use AI tools without lowering
quality?</strong> “I own the spec and the design: I write acceptance
criteria, review the agent’s plan before it codes, and have it work in
small, tested steps. Every diff gets the same review as a colleague’s
PR, with extra attention to edge cases, security and unnecessary
complexity, and CI gates don’t change. Lessons go back into our
CLAUDE.md and shared commands so the tools improve with the team.”</p>
<p><strong>Q2. How would you introduce Claude Code or Copilot to a team
of 15?</strong> “Start with guidelines on data, review and ownership;
set up shared project instructions, commands and skills so everyone gets
consistent results; run hands-on sessions with real tasks; keep quality
enforced by CI; and measure cycle time, review time and defect rates
before and after rather than counting AI-written lines. Then adjust
based on retrospectives.”</p>
<p><strong>Q3. What are the risks of AI-generated code?</strong> “Code
that looks right but fails on edge cases, missing security checks,
hallucinated or malicious dependencies, patterns inconsistent with the
codebase, and developers accepting code they don’t understand.
Mitigation is process: specs, small diffs, tests, thorough review,
dependency checks and CI security scans.”</p>

<h1 id="day-19-thu-agile-leadership-behavioural-design-practice">Day 19
(Thu) — Agile, leadership, behavioural, design practice</h1>
<h2 id="hour-1-agile-delivery">Hour 1 — Agile delivery</h2>
<p>At principal level, Agile questions aren’t about naming ceremonies.
They test whether you can help a team deliver predictably: how you
estimate when things are uncertain, how you keep tech debt from
swallowing the roadmap, and which metrics you’d watch. Answer with
practices you’ve seen work, not textbook definitions.</p>
<h3 id="scrum-vs-kanban">1.1 Scrum vs Kanban</h3>
<table>
<colgroup>
<col style="width: 33%" />
<col style="width: 33%" />
<col style="width: 33%" />
</colgroup>
<thead>
<tr>
<th></th>
<th>Scrum</th>
<th>Kanban</th>
</tr>
</thead>
<tbody>
<tr>
<td>Cadence</td>
<td>Fixed sprints (usually 2 weeks)</td>
<td>Continuous flow</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>Planning</td>
<td>Sprint planning commits to a sprint goal</td>
<td>Pull the next highest-priority item when capacity frees up</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>Roles</td>
<td>Product owner, Scrum master, developers</td>
<td>No prescribed roles</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>Key control</td>
<td>Sprint scope</td>
<td><strong>WIP limits</strong> per column</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>Metrics</td>
<td>Velocity, sprint goal success</td>
<td>Cycle time, throughput, flow efficiency</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>Fits</td>
<td>Product feature teams with a roadmap, stakeholders who like regular
demos</td>
<td>Support, platform, ops teams with unpredictable incoming work</td>
</tr>
</tbody>
</table>
<p>Many teams run a hybrid: sprints for planning and demos, Kanban-style
WIP limits within the sprint, and a separate lane for unplanned
work.</p>
<p><strong>Ceremonies, and what makes them useful:</strong> planning (a
clear goal, not a list of tickets), daily stand-up (blockers and
coordination, 15 minutes, not status reporting to a manager), refinement
(stories small and understood before planning), review/demo (real
working software to real stakeholders), retrospective (one or two
concrete improvements with owners, followed up next time).</p>
<h3 id="stories-definition-of-ready-definition-of-done">1.2 Stories,
Definition of Ready, Definition of Done</h3>
<ul>
<li><strong>Good story:</strong> user-centred, with acceptance criteria,
small enough to finish in a few days (split by workflow step, data
variation or business rule, not by layer like “backend” and
“frontend”).</li>
<li><strong>Definition of Ready:</strong> acceptance criteria clear,
dependencies known, designs available, estimated. Prevents
half-understood work entering a sprint.</li>
<li><strong>Definition of Done:</strong> code reviewed, tests written
and passing, deployed to staging (or production behind a flag),
monitoring and alerts in place, docs updated, product owner accepted.
“Done” means shippable, not “code written”.</li>
</ul>
<h3 id="estimation">1.3 Estimation</h3>
<table>
<colgroup>
<col style="width: 33%" />
<col style="width: 33%" />
<col style="width: 33%" />
</colgroup>
<thead>
<tr>
<th>Method</th>
<th>How</th>
<th>Use</th>
</tr>
</thead>
<tbody>
<tr>
<td>Story points</td>
<td>Relative size (Fibonacci 1, 2, 3, 5, 8, 13) via planning poker</td>
<td>Sprint planning; teams with stable composition</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>T-shirt sizes</td>
<td>S/M/L/XL</td>
<td>Roadmap-level sizing of epics</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>Time ranges</td>
<td>“3–6 days, 70% confident”</td>
<td>Communicating with stakeholders</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>Throughput forecasting</td>
<td>Count of items completed per week, Monte Carlo simulation</td>
<td>Predicting delivery dates from history, often better than
points</td>
</tr>
</tbody>
</table>
<p>Senior points: estimates are ranges with confidence, not promises;
split big unknowns into a <strong>spike</strong> (time-boxed
investigation) before estimating; points are for the team’s planning,
not for comparing teams or measuring individuals; when deadlines are
fixed, negotiate <strong>scope</strong> (MVP and phased delivery), not
quality.</p>
<h3 id="tech-debt">1.4 Tech debt</h3>
<ul>
<li><strong>Make it visible:</strong> a debt register with impact
(“slows every payment change by ~2 days”, “caused 3 incidents this
quarter”), not vague complaints.</li>
<li><strong>Pay continuously:</strong> reserve a share of each sprint
(often 15–20%), follow the boy-scout rule (leave touched code better),
and attach refactoring to features in the same area.</li>
<li><strong>Prioritise by business impact:</strong> debt that causes
incidents, slows high-change areas, or blocks upcoming roadmap items
first. Debt in stable code nobody touches can wait.</li>
<li><strong>Communicate in business terms</strong> to product managers:
lead time, incident risk, cost, not “the code is ugly”.</li>
<li>Big rewrites are rarely the answer; incremental replacement
(strangler fig, Day 11) usually is.</li>
</ul>
<h3 id="delivery-metrics">1.5 Delivery metrics</h3>
<p>Useful: cycle time (start to done), lead time (request to
production), throughput, DORA metrics (Day 15), escaped defects, sprint
goal success, unplanned work percentage.</p>
<p>Harmful when misused: velocity as a productivity target (teams
inflate points), lines of code, number of commits, individual
comparisons. Metrics should help the team see bottlenecks, not judge
people.</p>
<h3 id="how-id-answer-hour-1-18">How I’d answer — Hour 1</h3>
<p><strong>Q1. Scrum or Kanban?</strong> “Scrum for feature teams with a
roadmap and stakeholders who benefit from a regular rhythm of planning
and demos. Kanban for teams with unpredictable incoming work, like
platform or support, where WIP limits and cycle time matter more than
sprint commitments. Often a hybrid works best.”</p>
<p><strong>Q2. How do you handle tech debt with a product manager who
only wants features?</strong> “Make the cost visible in their terms: how
much it slows delivery, the incidents it causes, the risk to upcoming
roadmap items. Then agree a steady allocation, around 15–20% of
capacity, and tie refactors to features in the same area so they deliver
value together. I prioritise debt by business impact, not by how much it
bothers engineers.”</p>
<p><strong>Q3. A stakeholder needs a firm date for a large, uncertain
feature. What do you do?</strong> “Run a short spike to reduce the
biggest unknowns, give a range with a confidence level based on similar
past work, and identify an MVP that can land by their date. Then show
progress against it every sprint so any slip is visible early, and
negotiate scope rather than quality if needed.”</p>
<h3 id="practice-54">Practice</h3>
<ul class="task-list">
<li><label><input type="checkbox" />Write the capstone backlog for Week
4 as stories with acceptance criteria; split two that are too
big</label></li>
<li><label><input type="checkbox" />Draft a Definition of Done you’d
propose to a new team</label></li>
<li><label><input type="checkbox" />Write a one-page tech-debt register
for a past project (anonymised) with business impact per
item</label></li>
</ul>
<h2 id="hour-2-technical-leadership">Hour 2 — Technical leadership</h2>
<p>For a Principal or Lead title, interviewers want evidence that you
multiply a team’s output, not just your own: you make and record good
decisions, raise code quality through reviews and standards, grow other
engineers, and handle disagreement without drama. Have concrete examples
ready for each.</p>
<h3 id="what-changes-at-principal-level">2.1 What changes at principal
level</h3>
<table>
<colgroup>
<col style="width: 50%" />
<col style="width: 50%" />
</colgroup>
<thead>
<tr>
<th>Senior engineer</th>
<th>Lead / principal engineer</th>
</tr>
</thead>
<tbody>
<tr>
<td>Delivers complex features well</td>
<td>Shapes what the team builds and how; unblocks several streams</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>Owns a component</td>
<td>Owns cross-cutting quality: architecture, reliability, security,
developer experience</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>Solves problems</td>
<td>Finds the right problems; says no to the wrong ones</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>Writes good code</td>
<td>Sets standards others follow; reviews and mentors at scale</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>Influences the team</td>
<td>Influences across teams and with product and leadership, usually
without formal authority</td>
</tr>
</tbody>
</table>
<h3 id="decisions-adrs-and-design-docs">2.2 Decisions: ADRs and design
docs</h3>
<p><strong>Architecture Decision Record (ADR):</strong> a short document
per significant decision, kept in the repo. It captures <em>why</em>,
which is what gets lost.</p>
<div class="sourceCode" id="cb211"><pre
class="sourceCode markdown"><code class="sourceCode markdown"><span id="cb211-1"><a href="#cb211-1" aria-hidden="true" tabindex="-1"></a><span class="fu"># ADR-007: Use the transactional outbox for order events</span></span>
<span id="cb211-2"><a href="#cb211-2" aria-hidden="true" tabindex="-1"></a></span>
<span id="cb211-3"><a href="#cb211-3" aria-hidden="true" tabindex="-1"></a>Status: Accepted (2026-11-25)</span>
<span id="cb211-4"><a href="#cb211-4" aria-hidden="true" tabindex="-1"></a></span>
<span id="cb211-5"><a href="#cb211-5" aria-hidden="true" tabindex="-1"></a><span class="fu">## Context</span></span>
<span id="cb211-6"><a href="#cb211-6" aria-hidden="true" tabindex="-1"></a>Order service writes to Postgres and must publish OrderPlaced to Kafka. Direct publishing after commit</span>
<span id="cb211-7"><a href="#cb211-7" aria-hidden="true" tabindex="-1"></a>lost events twice in staging when the broker was unavailable.</span>
<span id="cb211-8"><a href="#cb211-8" aria-hidden="true" tabindex="-1"></a></span>
<span id="cb211-9"><a href="#cb211-9" aria-hidden="true" tabindex="-1"></a><span class="fu">## Decision</span></span>
<span id="cb211-10"><a href="#cb211-10" aria-hidden="true" tabindex="-1"></a>Write events to an outbox table in the same transaction; a relay publishes with SKIP LOCKED polling.</span>
<span id="cb211-11"><a href="#cb211-11" aria-hidden="true" tabindex="-1"></a></span>
<span id="cb211-12"><a href="#cb211-12" aria-hidden="true" tabindex="-1"></a><span class="fu">## Consequences</span></span>
<span id="cb211-13"><a href="#cb211-13" aria-hidden="true" tabindex="-1"></a><span class="ss">+ </span>No lost or phantom events; replayable.</span>
<span id="cb211-14"><a href="#cb211-14" aria-hidden="true" tabindex="-1"></a><span class="ss">- </span>At-least-once delivery: consumers must be idempotent (processed_events table).</span>
<span id="cb211-15"><a href="#cb211-15" aria-hidden="true" tabindex="-1"></a><span class="ss">- </span>~1 s extra publish latency; relay must be monitored.</span>
<span id="cb211-16"><a href="#cb211-16" aria-hidden="true" tabindex="-1"></a></span>
<span id="cb211-17"><a href="#cb211-17" aria-hidden="true" tabindex="-1"></a><span class="fu">## Alternatives considered</span></span>
<span id="cb211-18"><a href="#cb211-18" aria-hidden="true" tabindex="-1"></a>Debezium CDC (lower latency, more infrastructure); dual write with retries (rejected: not atomic).</span></code></pre></div>
<p><strong>Design docs / RFCs</strong> for larger changes: problem and
goals, non-goals, proposed design, alternatives with trade-offs, risks,
rollout and rollback plan, open questions. Shared early for comment; a
review meeting for contentious points. The aim is better decisions and
shared understanding, not bureaucracy; skip them for small or easily
reversible changes (“two-way doors”).</p>
<h3 id="code-review-culture">2.3 Code review culture</h3>
<ul>
<li><strong>Purpose:</strong> catch defects, share knowledge, keep the
codebase consistent, and mentor.</li>
<li><strong>Speed matters:</strong> aim to review within a working day;
slow reviews kill flow more than anything else.</li>
<li><strong>Small PRs:</strong> ask for them, and set the example.</li>
<li><strong>What to focus on:</strong> correctness, design, tests,
security, readability. Automate style and formatting so humans never
argue about it.</li>
<li><strong>Tone:</strong> comment on the code, not the person; ask
questions (“what happens if this list is empty?”); label severity
(“nit:”, “blocking:”); explain the why; praise good work.</li>
<li><strong>Approve with minor comments</strong> when trust exists;
don’t hold PRs hostage for preferences.</li>
</ul>
<h3 id="mentoring-and-growing-engineers">2.4 Mentoring and growing
engineers</h3>
<ul>
<li>Pair on hard problems rather than taking them over; let others drive
while you navigate.</li>
<li>Delegate meaningful work with context and clear expectations, then
support; resist rescuing too early.</li>
<li>Give specific, timely feedback (situation → behaviour → impact),
privately for corrections.</li>
<li>Create stretch opportunities: let a mid-level engineer write the
design doc, present in architecture review, lead an incident
review.</li>
<li>Share knowledge at scale: internal talks, written guides, onboarding
docs, good PR descriptions.</li>
</ul>
<h3 id="disagreement-and-influence">2.5 Disagreement and influence</h3>
<ul>
<li><strong>Disagree with data and options:</strong> prototype,
benchmark, cite incidents or costs; present two or three options with
trade-offs rather than a single demand.</li>
<li><strong>Separate reversible from irreversible decisions:</strong>
move fast on reversible ones; slow down and document irreversible
ones.</li>
<li><strong>Disagree and commit:</strong> once a decision is made with a
fair hearing, support it fully, and set a checkpoint to revisit with
evidence.</li>
<li><strong>With product managers:</strong> share their goals, translate
technical concerns into user and business impact, offer alternatives
(“we can ship X by Friday if we defer Y”).</li>
<li><strong>With leadership:</strong> short written updates with status,
risks and asks; bad news early.</li>
</ul>
<h3 id="operating-responsibilities">2.6 Operating responsibilities</h3>
<p>On-call health (sustainable rotations, actionable alerts, runbooks),
incident leadership and blameless postmortems (Day 15), security and
dependency hygiene, onboarding quality, and interviewing and hiring are
all part of the role. Be ready to give one example of improving
something in this list.</p>
<h3 id="how-id-answer-hour-2-18">How I’d answer — Hour 2</h3>
<p><strong>Q1. How do you make architectural decisions in a
team?</strong> “For significant or hard-to-reverse decisions, a short
design doc or RFC with options and trade-offs, reviewed by the people
affected, and the final decision recorded as an ADR in the repo with
context and consequences. Small, reversible decisions get made quickly
by whoever owns the work. The goal is good decisions and a record of
why, not ceremony.”</p>
<p><strong>Q2. Tell me about a time you disagreed with a technical
decision.</strong> (Use STAR from Hour 3) Structure: the decision and
why you disagreed; how you raised it (data, prototype, options); the
outcome; and if it went the other way, how you committed and what you
learned.</p>
<p><strong>Q3. How do you mentor engineers?</strong> “By giving them
real ownership with support: pairing on hard problems, letting them lead
design docs or incident reviews with me reviewing, giving specific
feedback quickly, and making sure their work is visible. I measure
success by what they can do without me after a few months.”</p>
<p><strong>Q4. What does good code review look like?</strong> “Fast,
small, focused on correctness, design, tests and security, with style
automated away. Comments explain why, ask questions, and mark what’s
blocking versus a nit. It’s also a teaching channel, so I explain
reasoning rather than just requesting changes.”</p>
<h3 id="practice-55">Practice</h3>
<ul class="task-list">
<li><label><input type="checkbox" />Write 2 ADRs for the capstone
(outbox, and modular monolith vs microservices or Postgres vs Mongo
split)</label></li>
<li><label><input type="checkbox" />Write a 2-page design doc for the
order-support agent from Day 18 using the structure above</label></li>
<li><label><input type="checkbox" />List three concrete mentoring or
leadership examples from your work at Virtusa and Persistent with
outcomes</label></li>
</ul>
<h2 id="hour-3-behavioural-interviews">Hour 3 — Behavioural
interviews</h2>
<p>At 8+ years, behavioural rounds carry as much weight as technical
ones, and they’re where well-prepared candidates pull ahead.
Interviewers want specific stories showing ownership, judgement,
collaboration and growth, told concisely with your own role clear. This
hour builds a story bank you’ll reuse across every company. The stories
must be <strong>yours</strong>: the outlines below are prompts to fill
with real details, not scripts to recite.</p>
<h3 id="the-starl-structure">3.1 The STAR(L) structure</h3>
<table>
<colgroup>
<col style="width: 33%" />
<col style="width: 33%" />
<col style="width: 33%" />
</colgroup>
<thead>
<tr>
<th>Part</th>
<th>Content</th>
<th>Time</th>
</tr>
</thead>
<tbody>
<tr>
<td><strong>S</strong>ituation</td>
<td>Context in one or two sentences: company, product, scale, why it
mattered</td>
<td>~15 s</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td><strong>T</strong>ask</td>
<td>Your specific responsibility or the problem you owned</td>
<td>~10 s</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td><strong>A</strong>ction</td>
<td>What <strong>you</strong> did, step by step: decisions, trade-offs,
how you worked with others</td>
<td>~60–90 s</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td><strong>R</strong>esult</td>
<td>Measurable outcome: numbers, time saved, incidents reduced,
adoption</td>
<td>~15 s</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td><strong>L</strong>earning</td>
<td>What you’d keep or change; how it shaped how you work now</td>
<td>~10 s</td>
</tr>
</tbody>
</table>
<p>Rules: about two minutes per story; say “I” for your actions and “we”
for the team’s; numbers wherever honest; include the hard part (a
constraint, a disagreement, a mistake); be ready for follow-ups (“what
would you do differently?”, “what did your manager think?”).</p>
<h3 id="six-stories-to-prepare">3.2 Six stories to prepare</h3>
<p>Prepare each in writing, then say it out loud until it fits in two
minutes.</p>
<ol type="1">
<li><strong>Biggest technical impact.</strong> Your fintech loyalty
platform work that cut processing time by 30% is the natural candidate.
Prompts: what was slow and why it mattered to the business; how you
diagnosed it (profiling, query analysis, architecture?); what you
changed and which alternatives you rejected; how you measured the 30%;
what it enabled afterwards.</li>
<li><strong>Disagreement or conflict.</strong> A technical decision, a
deadline, or a design debate with a peer, lead or product manager. Show
how you used data and options, listened, and either persuaded or
committed.</li>
<li><strong>Failure or mistake.</strong> A production bug, a missed
estimate, a wrong design choice. Own it plainly, show how you fixed it,
and what process or habit changed. Avoid fake failures (“I work too
hard”).</li>
<li><strong>Leadership without authority / ownership.</strong> Driving a
cross-team change, rescuing a struggling delivery, or the work behind
your team awards (Bravo, Star Team). What did <strong>you</strong>
specifically do to earn them?</li>
<li><strong>Mentoring or growing someone.</strong> A junior you helped
level up: starting point, what you did, where they ended up.</li>
<li><strong>Delivery under pressure or an incident.</strong> A tight
deadline or production outage: how you prioritised, communicated, and
what you changed afterwards.</li>
</ol>
<p>Plus two you’ll certainly need:</p>
<ol start="7" type="1">
<li><strong>“How do you use AI in your work?”</strong> (Day 18, 4.6),
using the capstone as a concrete example.</li>
<li><strong>“Why are you looking for a change?”</strong> Keep it
forward-looking and positive: you’re moving toward AI-driven full-stack
and architecture work, and you’ve used your current availability to
deepen system design and GenAI skills, with a capstone to show for it.
Never criticise past employers.</li>
</ol>

<h3 id="tell-me-about-yourself-90-seconds">3.4 “Tell me about yourself”
(90 seconds)</h3>
<p>Structure: present → past highlights → what you’re looking for.</p>
<p>“I’m a full-stack engineer with about eight years in Node.js, most
recently as Principal Software Engineer at Zemoso, and before that at
Virtusa and Persistent. My core is the MERN stack and cloud-native
systems: Node.js microservices, React and now Angular, MongoDB and
Postgres, Docker and Kubernetes. A highlight was [the fintech loyalty
platform, where we cut processing time by 30% by …]. Over the last
couple of years I’ve focused on bringing generative AI into products
with Claude: I’m a Claude Certified Architect, and I recently built
[capstone in one line: an AI-powered commerce platform with RAG, an
order-support agent and an MCP server]. I’m looking for a lead or
principal role where I can own architecture and bring AI-driven
development to a product team.”</p>
<p>Fill the brackets with your real specifics and keep it under 90
seconds.</p>
<h3 id="questions-to-ask-interviewers">3.5 Questions to ask
interviewers</h3>
<p>Ask two or three; they show judgement and help you decide:</p>
<ul>
<li>“What does success look like for this role in the first 6
months?”</li>
<li>“What’s the biggest technical challenge the team is facing right
now?”</li>
<li>“How are architecture decisions made and recorded here?”</li>
<li>“How does the team deploy, and how often? What does on-call look
like?”</li>
<li>“How is the team using AI tools today, and where do you want to take
it?”</li>
<li>“How do engineers grow toward principal/architect roles here?”</li>
</ul>
<h3 id="how-id-answer-hour-3-18">How I’d answer — Hour 3</h3>
<p>The answers here are your stories, so the practice is the answer:</p>
<ul class="task-list">

<h2
id="hour-4-two-designs-ai-support-platform-food-delivery-backend">Hour 4
— Two designs: AI support platform, food delivery backend</h2>
<p>Two designs that combine this week’s themes. The AI support platform
is the one most likely to come up given your profile; food delivery is a
classic for Indian product companies (think Swiggy or Zomato) and tests
geo, real-time and peak-load thinking. Spend about 30 minutes on each,
out loud, then compare with these notes.</p>
<h3 id="design-ai-customer-support-platform">4.1 Design: AI
customer-support platform</h3>
<p><strong>Requirements:</strong> customers contact support via web
chat, email and WhatsApp; AI answers common questions from the help
centre and order data, takes simple actions (track order, start a
return, cancel if eligible) with confirmation, and hands off to human
agents with full context; human agents get AI-suggested replies and
summaries; managers see quality and resolution metrics. Non-functional:
first response in seconds, PII protected, auditable actions,
Hindi/English/Hinglish support, cost under control.</p>
<p><strong>Estimates:</strong> 100,000 conversations/day, ~8 turns each
→ ~10 LLM calls/s average, ~40/s peak. At a few thousand tokens per
call, that’s hundreds of millions of tokens a day, so model routing and
caching matter for cost; do the arithmetic with current prices in the
interview.</p>
<p><strong>Architecture:</strong></p>
<pre class="text"><code>Channels (web chat SSE/WebSocket, email webhook, WhatsApp Business API webhook)
  -&gt; channel adapters -&gt; conversation service (state in Postgres; messages; channel-agnostic)
  -&gt; AI orchestrator
       1. classify intent, language, urgency, sentiment (small model)
       2. route: FAQ -&gt; RAG answer | order intents -&gt; tool-using agent | complaint/legal/high-value -&gt; human
       3. RAG over help centre + policies (hybrid search, Day 17)
       4. agent tools: order/shipment/returns APIs scoped to the verified customer (Day 18)
       5. consequential actions -&gt; pending action -&gt; customer confirms
       6. output checks: PII, policy, tone; then send via channel adapter
  -&gt; handoff: ticket in the agent desk with summary, intent, actions taken, suggested reply
  -&gt; events (Kafka) -&gt; analytics, evals sampling, QA review, training data for evals
Observability: traces per conversation, cost per conversation, resolution and escalation rates</code></pre>
<p><strong>Deep dives:</strong></p>
<ul>
<li><strong>Identity:</strong> verify the customer before order tools
work (logged-in session, or OTP on email/WhatsApp); tools use the
verified identity only.</li>
<li><strong>Handoff quality:</strong> a human sees a summary, the
customer’s intent, everything the AI already tried, and the order
context, so the customer never repeats themselves. Easy handoff on
request (“talk to a human”) and on low confidence or negative
sentiment.</li>
<li><strong>Quality loop:</strong> evals per intent before release;
production sampling reviewed by QA; customer satisfaction and re-contact
rate per intent; bad answers become eval cases and help-centre
fixes.</li>
<li><strong>Cost:</strong> small model for classification and routing,
mid-tier for answers, prompt caching for system prompts and policies,
deterministic workflows for the most common intents (order status
doesn’t need an agent).</li>
<li><strong>Compliance:</strong> PII redaction in logs, data retention
policies, audit log of every AI action, disclosure that the customer is
talking to AI.</li>
</ul>
<h3 id="design-food-delivery-backend">4.2 Design: food delivery
backend</h3>
<p><strong>Requirements:</strong> users browse nearby restaurants and
menus, order and pay; restaurants accept and prepare; the system assigns
a delivery partner; users track the order live; ETAs shown throughout.
Non-functional: huge lunch and dinner peaks, real-time tracking,
payments correct, high availability during peaks.</p>
<p><strong>Estimates:</strong> 3 million orders/day, with ~60% in two
2-hour peaks → peak ~250 orders/s. 300,000 active delivery partners
sending location every 5 s → <strong>~60,000 location
updates/s</strong>, which is the write-heavy hot path, far more than
orders.</p>
<p><strong>Services and data:</strong></p>
<table>
<colgroup>
<col style="width: 33%" />
<col style="width: 33%" />
<col style="width: 33%" />
</colgroup>
<thead>
<tr>
<th>Service</th>
<th>Data / store</th>
<th>Notes</th>
</tr>
</thead>
<tbody>
<tr>
<td>Restaurant &amp; menu</td>
<td>Postgres or MongoDB; search index (Elasticsearch) with geo</td>
<td>Menus cached heavily; availability toggles pushed to cache</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>Discovery / search</td>
<td>Elasticsearch geo queries, ranking</td>
<td>“Restaurants delivering to me now” with delivery-radius
polygons</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>Cart &amp; order</td>
<td>Postgres (orders, items, state machine)</td>
<td>Idempotency keys; saga for payment (Day 11)</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>Payment</td>
<td>Postgres + gateway (Razorpay, PayU, UPI)</td>
<td>Webhooks, reconciliation jobs</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>Partner location</td>
<td><strong>Redis GEO</strong> or an in-memory geo index keyed by
H3/geohash cells; stream to Kafka</td>
<td>Latest location only in Redis; history in a time-series store for
analytics</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>Dispatch / assignment</td>
<td>Reads nearby available partners, scores and offers</td>
<td>Core algorithm</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>Tracking</td>
<td>WebSocket/SSE gateway (Day 16)</td>
<td>Pushes partner location and status to the customer</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>ETA</td>
<td>ML model service</td>
<td>Prep time + travel time + traffic</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>Notifications</td>
<td>Queue + push/SMS</td>
<td>—</td>
</tr>
</tbody>
</table>
<p><strong>Order flow:</strong> place order (idempotent) → payment saga
(authorise) → restaurant notified (accept within N seconds, or
auto-cancel and refund) → dispatch starts when estimated prep time minus
travel time is reached → partner accepts offer → pickup → live tracking
→ delivered → payment captured, partner payout recorded.</p>
<p><strong>Deep dives:</strong></p>
<ul>
<li><strong>Location ingestion:</strong> partners send updates over a
persistent connection or batched HTTP; gateways write the latest
position to Redis GEO (<code>GEOADD</code>) partitioned by city, and
publish to Kafka for tracking and analytics. Don’t write every ping to
Postgres.</li>
<li><strong>Assignment:</strong> query available partners within a
radius (<code>GEOSEARCH</code>), score by distance, partner direction,
current load and fairness, then <strong>offer</strong> to one (or a few)
with a timeout. Prevent double assignment with an atomic conditional
update or a short Redis lock per partner plus a DB unique constraint on
active assignment. Batch nearby orders to one partner when routes
align.</li>
<li><strong>Peaks:</strong> pre-scale before lunch and dinner (scheduled
minimums, Day 14); cache menus and restaurant lists; queue non-critical
work; degrade gracefully (disable heavy recommendations at peak);
per-city partitioning so one city’s spike doesn’t affect another.</li>
<li><strong>Consistency:</strong> orders and payments CP (Postgres,
sagas, idempotency); partner locations and ETAs AP (eventually
consistent, a few seconds stale is fine).</li>
<li><strong>Failure handling:</strong> restaurant doesn’t accept →
timeout, cancel, refund automatically; partner goes offline mid-delivery
→ reassign; payment webhook delayed → reconciliation job against the
gateway.</li>
</ul>
<h3 id="how-id-answer-hour-4-18">How I’d answer — Hour 4</h3>
<p><strong>Q1. What’s the hardest part of a food delivery system, and
how do you handle it?</strong> “Partner location and assignment. With
hundreds of thousands of partners updating every few seconds, it’s tens
of thousands of writes a second, so latest locations live in an
in-memory geo index like Redis GEO partitioned by city, with a stream to
Kafka for tracking and analytics. Assignment searches nearby available
partners, scores them, and offers orders with timeouts, using an atomic
update to prevent double assignment. Orders and payments stay in
Postgres with sagas and idempotency, because they need strong
consistency while locations don’t.”</p>
<p><strong>Q2. How would you keep an AI support platform’s cost and
quality under control?</strong> “Route by intent: deterministic
workflows for common intents like order status, a small model for
classification, a mid-tier model for answers, RAG with caching, and
escalation to humans on low confidence. Quality comes from per-intent
evals before release, QA sampling and customer-satisfaction metrics in
production, with every bad answer becoming a new test case. Cost and
resolution rate are tracked per intent on a dashboard.”</p>

compressed version of a real interview loop, score yourself honestly,
and turn the results into a short gap list for Hour 2. Use a peer if you
can for at least one round; Claude works well as an interviewer for the
rest.</p>

<h3 id="prompts-for-using-claude-as-an-interviewer">1.2 Prompts for
using Claude as an interviewer</h3>
<p><strong>Technical deep dive:</strong></p>
<pre class="text"><code>You are a principal engineer interviewing me for a Lead Node.js / full-stack role at an Indian product
company. Ask me one question at a time on Node.js internals, databases, messaging and system scaling.
After each answer, ask one or two probing follow-ups the way a strict interviewer would, especially
where my answer was vague. Don&#39;t give me the answers during the interview. After 10 questions, give
me a scorecard: each question rated 1-5 for correctness, depth and clarity, the three weakest areas,
and what a strong answer would have included.</code></pre>
<p><strong>System design:</strong></p>
<pre class="text"><code>Act as a senior system design interviewer. Give me this problem: [problem]. Stay in character: answer
my clarifying questions with realistic numbers, push back on weak choices, and steer me to one deep
dive I haven&#39;t covered. Interrupt if I spend too long on trivial parts. At the end (I&#39;ll say &quot;done&quot;),
evaluate me on requirements, estimation, high-level design, deep dives, trade-offs and communication,
1-5 each, with specific improvements.</code></pre>
<p><strong>Behavioural:</strong></p>
<pre class="text"><code>You are a hiring manager for an engineering lead role. Ask me behavioural questions one at a time.
For each answer, ask follow-ups that test what I personally did, how I handled disagreement, and what
I&#39;d do differently. Score each story on structure (STAR), ownership, impact with numbers, and
self-awareness. Point out any vague claims.</code></pre>
<h3 id="unseen-design-problems-for-mocks">1.3 Unseen design problems for
mocks</h3>
<p>Pick one you haven’t practised: notification system (push, SMS, email
with preferences and rate limits); payment gateway integration with
reconciliation; ride-hailing dispatch; Google Docs-style collaborative
editor; video upload and streaming; ticketing system for a flash sale
with 1 million users at 8 p.m.; multi-tenant SaaS analytics dashboard;
job scheduler for millions of scheduled tasks; e-commerce search with
filters and autocomplete; an AI coding-assistant backend.</p>
<h3 id="scoring-rubric">1.4 Scoring rubric</h3>
<p>Score each round 1–5 on these; anything at 3 or below goes on the gap
list.</p>
<table>
<colgroup>
<col style="width: 50%" />
<col style="width: 50%" />
</colgroup>
<thead>
<tr>
<th>Dimension</th>
<th>5 looks like</th>
</tr>
</thead>
<tbody>
<tr>
<td>Correctness</td>
<td>Accurate, no hand-waving on facts</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>Depth</td>
<td>Explains why, mechanisms and failure modes, not just what</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>Trade-offs</td>
<td>Names alternatives and when they’d be better</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>Structure</td>
<td>Clear flow (framework for design, STAR for stories), no
rambling</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>Communication</td>
<td>Thinks aloud, checks in, concise, recovers well from not

</tr>
<tr>
<td>Production sense</td>
<td>Mentions monitoring, failure handling, rollout, security
unprompted</td>
</tr>
</tbody>
</table>
<p><strong>When you don’t know something</strong> in a real interview:
say what you do know, reason from first principles out loud, say how
you’d find out. “I haven’t used X, but it’s likely similar to Y, so I’d
expect…” scores far better than guessing confidently or freezing.</p>
<h3 id="practice-56">Practice</h3>
<ul class="task-list">
<li><label><input type="checkbox" />Run all five rounds today; record
system design and behavioural</label></li>
<li><label><input type="checkbox" />Fill the rubric for each round
honestly</label></li>
<li><label><input type="checkbox" />Write the gap list: every dimension
scored 3 or below, plus every question where you hesitated</label></li>
</ul>
<h2 id="hour-2-closing-gaps-rapid-fire-revision">Hour 2 — Closing gaps:
rapid-fire revision</h2>
<p>First 15 minutes: merge today’s gap list with the unticked items from
the Week 1–3 wrap-ups and Day 16–19 checklists, and pick the five that
matter most for the roles you’re targeting. Spend 30 minutes re-reading
only those sections. Then do the rapid-fire round below: cover the
answer column, answer each question aloud in one or two sentences, then
check. Anything you miss goes back on the list for next week.</p>

<h2 id="hour-3-portfolio-capstone-resume-linkedin">Hour 3 — Portfolio:
capstone, resume, LinkedIn</h2>
<p>The capstone is your strongest proof: most candidates claim
microservices, Kafka, Kubernetes and GenAI; very few can show a working,
documented system with tests, a pipeline and an AI agent. This hour
packages it so a recruiter understands it in 30 seconds and an engineer
can verify it in 5 minutes, then updates your resume and LinkedIn to
match.</p>
<h3 id="capstone-readme-structure">3.1 Capstone README structure</h3>

<p>Keep the README honest about what’s production-grade and what’s

<h3 id="demo-video-3-minutes">3.2 Demo video (3 minutes)</h3>
<ol type="1">
<li>0:00–0:20: what it is and the architecture diagram.</li>
<li>0:20–1:00: place an order; show the saga progressing in logs/Jaeger
trace across services.</li>
<li>1:00–1:40: product assistant answering with citations; a question it
correctly can’t answer.</li>
<li>1:40–2:20: support agent cancelling an order with the confirmation
step; a prompt-injection attempt failing.</li>
<li>2:20–2:50: a canary rollout aborting on a bad version; Grafana
dashboard.</li>
<li>2:50–3:00: link to the repo and ADRs.</li>
</ol>
<h3 id="resume-bullets">3.3 Resume bullets</h3>
<p>Pattern: <strong>action verb + what + how + measurable
result.</strong> Fill the brackets with your real details; don’t claim
numbers you can’t explain.</p>
<ul>
<li>“Reduced transaction processing time by 30% in a fintech loyalty
platform by [e.g. redesigning the batch pipeline / optimising MongoDB
queries and indexes / moving to event-driven processing], serving [N
users / transactions per day].”</li>
<li>“Designed and delivered [N] Node.js microservices for [domain] using
[Kafka/RabbitMQ, Postgres/MongoDB], improving [latency / reliability /
release frequency] by [X].”</li>
<li>“Led [N] engineers on [project]; introduced [code review standards /
CI/CD / test strategy], cutting [lead time / defects] by [X].”</li>
<li>“Integrated Anthropic Claude into [product feature], building [RAG /
agent / classification] with evals, prompt versioning and cost controls;
[outcome].”</li>
<li>“Introduced AI-assisted development with Claude Code across the team
([shared CLAUDE.md, commands, review guidelines]), [measured outcome,
e.g. reduced PR cycle time by X%].”</li>
<li>Capstone line under a Projects section: “ecommerce-ai: event-driven
commerce platform with RAG assistant, safe order-support agent and MCP
server (Node.js, React, Angular, Kafka, Kubernetes, Claude). [repo
link]”</li>
</ul>
<p>Keep the resume to two pages, most recent role first, skills grouped
(Backend, Frontend, Data, Cloud/DevOps, AI), certifications listed
(Claude Certified Architect – Foundations, MCP courses).</p>
<h3 id="linkedin">3.4 LinkedIn</h3>
<ul>
<li><strong>Headline:</strong> you already have a strong one. Keep it
focused: “Principal Software Engineer | Node.js · React · Angular ·
Microservices | Building AI-powered products with Claude &amp; agentic
workflows | Claude Certified Architect”.</li>
<li><strong>About:</strong> your current summary is good; add one
sentence on system design and architecture ownership, the capstone with
a link, and the kinds of roles you’re open to.</li>
<li><strong>Featured:</strong> pin the capstone repo, the demo video,
and an article or post explaining one design decision (e.g. “Making an
AI agent safe to cancel orders”). A thoughtful technical post is a
strong signal for principal roles.</li>
<li><strong>Experience:</strong> add 2–3 outcome bullets per recent role
(same pattern as the resume); your Virtusa and Persistent entries
currently have none.</li>
<li><strong>Open to Work:</strong> set to recruiters only if you prefer
discretion, with target titles (Lead Engineer, Principal Engineer, Staff
Engineer, Solutions Architect) and locations (Pune, remote).</li>
</ul>

<h2 id="hour-4-interview-strategy-and-staying-sharp">Hour 4 — Interview
strategy and staying sharp</h2>
<p>The preparation is done; the last hour is about using it well:
targeting the right roles, preparing per company, performing on the day,
and keeping skills fresh while you interview, which can take several
weeks.</p>
<h3 id="targeting-and-applying">4.1 Targeting and applying</h3>
<ul>
<li><strong>Pick 15–25 target companies</strong> in tiers: a few
stretch, most realistic, a few safe. Product companies and well-funded
startups building with AI value your profile most.</li>
<li><strong>Titles to search:</strong> Lead / Staff / Principal Engineer
(Node.js, full-stack), Engineering Lead, Solutions Architect, AI
Engineer (applied, full-stack).</li>
<li><strong>Referrals beat cold applications</strong> by a wide margin:
message former colleagues from Persistent, Virtusa and Zemoso, and
people you know at target companies, with a two-line ask and your
resume.</li>
<li><strong>Sequence interviews:</strong> a couple of lower-priority
companies first as warm-ups, then your top choices once you’re sharp;
try to bunch final rounds so offers arrive close together.</li>
<li>Track everything in one sheet: company, role, contact, stage, next
step, date, notes.</li>
</ul>
<h3 id="per-company-preparation-45-minutes-each">4.2 Per-company
preparation (45 minutes each)</h3>
<ol type="1">
<li>Product and business model; read their engineering blog and recent
news.</li>
<li>Their stack (job post, blog, GitHub, LinkedIn profiles of their
engineers): adapt examples to it.</li>
<li>Likely system design topics for their domain (a fintech: payments,
ledgers, reconciliation; e-commerce: catalogue, checkout, search; SaaS:
multi-tenancy).</li>
<li>Pick which of your stories best fit their values.</li>
<li>Prepare two questions specific to them.</li>
</ol>
<h3 id="on-the-day">4.3 On the day</h3>
<ul>
<li><strong>Before:</strong> sleep beats last-minute cramming; review
only your one-page notes (the rapid-fire table, framework card and story
list). Test camera, mic, internet and the coding/whiteboard tool for
remote rounds.</li>
<li><strong>During coding:</strong> clarify, state the approach and
complexity, code cleanly, test with an example, then optimise. Talk
throughout.</li>
<li><strong>During design:</strong> follow the framework, write
requirements and numbers visibly, check in, name trade-offs.</li>
<li><strong>During behavioural:</strong> STAR, two minutes, “I” for your
actions, numbers, honest learning.</li>
<li><strong>If stuck:</strong> say what you know, reason aloud, ask a
clarifying question; recovering well is itself a positive signal.</li>
<li><strong>After each round:</strong> write down every question asked
and where you were weak, within the hour. That list drives the next
study session.</li>
</ul>
<h3 id="keeping-sharp-during-the-interview-period">4.4 Keeping sharp
during the interview period</h3>
<p>A lighter routine, about 90 minutes a day:</p>
<table>
<colgroup>
<col style="width: 50%" />
<col style="width: 50%" />
</colgroup>
<thead>
<tr>
<th>Day</th>
<th>Focus</th>
</tr>
</thead>
<tbody>
<tr>
<td>Mon</td>
<td>One system design problem, out loud (30 min) + review a weak
topic</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>Tue</td>
<td>One coding/machine-coding problem without AI + rapid-fire table</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>Wed</td>
<td>One behavioural story refined + one Claude mock round</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>Thu</td>
<td>Capstone improvement (one feature or fix) + one ADR</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>Fri</td>
<td>Review the week’s interview notes; update the gap list</td>
</tr>
</tbody>
</table>
<p>And once the notes are complete, the <strong>verification
pass</strong> we agreed on: a web search through the version-sensitive
items (React, Angular, Kafka client, pnpm, Redis/Valkey, Kubernetes
features, Claude API features), corrections in place, and a Sources
section added to this document.</p>
<h3 id="final-checklist-the-whole-month">4.5 Final checklist: the whole
month</h3>
<ul class="task-list">
<li><label><input type="checkbox" />Weeks 1–3 wrap-up checklists
